hist.racine.0.dit: The whole Terminaworld has a starting point: {racine}, the foot of the great tree where every path begins. Let's go! The path of the Root is written with a single slash: /.
hist.racine.0.bravo: Here we are at {racine}! The whole computer starts from here.
hist.racine.0.adulte: `cd /` goes to the root of the single directory tree: every file on the system is somewhere under /, even disks and USB sticks (mounted in /media/<name> on Ubuntu, /run/media/<name> on Fedora, /Volumes on macOS). On Windows, the root is C:\.
hist.racine.1.dit: Look around you: these are the great places of the Terminaworld.
hist.racine.1.bravo: home is {village}; etc, the hall of rules; bin, the command armoury; tmp, the wasteland… Here we look, we don't touch!
hist.racine.1.adulte: `ls` at the root shows the standard directories (FHS): /home (users), /etc (configuration), /bin and /usr (programs), /tmp (temporary files), /var (changing data, including /var/log, the logs), /dev and /proc (special files provided by the kernel).
hist.racine.2.bravo: The sign just says "/": that's {racine}, the start of every path.
hist.racine.2.adulte: `pwd` always prints an absolute path, starting with /; here it is just /. Each following / separates one level of the tree.
hist.racine.3.dit: Go back to {camp} in one go: its nickname is ~.
hist.racine.3.bravo: Back at camp! Its full path is {chemin}: the Root → the village → your base camp.
hist.racine.3.adulte: The shell replaces `~` with your home directory ($HOME, here {chemin}); `cd` on its own does the same. On Linux, home directories live in /home (on macOS, in /Users).
hist.racine.4.dit: A path that starts with / works from anywhere: it's {chemin_absolu}. Go to the hall with the full path, in a single command (Tab completes names!).
hist.racine.4.bravo: Well done, you know both kinds of paths: `cd vestibule` is {chemin_relatif}; `cd /…/vestibule` is {chemin_absolu}.
hist.racine.4.adulte: An absolute path starts with / and leaves from the root; a relative path leaves from the current directory (. here, .. the parent). `~/terrain_terminagotchi/vestibule` is absolute too once `~` is replaced. Same in a real Linux or macOS terminal.
hist.gardien.0.dit: Welcome to {systeme}! The world's keeper keeps the rules in a hall: the hall of rules. Read the world's name, written on its door. (We look, we don't touch!)
hist.gardien.0.bravo: That's the name of this world! The keeper wrote it in the hall of rules.
hist.gardien.0.adulte: /etc holds the system configuration; /etc/hostname gives the machine's name (like the `hostname` command, which also works on macOS where this file doesn't exist). Most of these files can be read freely (not /etc/shadow, the encrypted passwords); only root (the administrator) can change them.
hist.gardien.1.dit: Visit the armoury: that's where every command you type sleeps.
hist.gardien.1.bravo: All these weapons are commands! ls, cat, mkdir… each one sleeps here until you call it.
hist.gardien.1.adulte: /bin and /usr/bin hold the executables; when you type `ls`, the shell looks for an ls file in the directories of the PATH variable (`echo $PATH`, `which ls`).
hist.gardien.2.dit: Walk past the archives: the keeper writes down everything that happens in the world.
hist.gardien.2.bravo: Registers everywhere! Some are secret: only the keeper can read them.
hist.gardien.2.adulte: /var/log holds the system logs (logins, boot, errors). Many are readable only by root; on recent systems, `journalctl` shows them.
hist.gardien.3.dit: Who has the key to the hall of rules? Look at the padlocks on the door.
hist.gardien.3.bravo: The owner is root: the world's keeper. You are only allowed to read (r). If you tried to write here, the keeper would say no: "Permission denied".
hist.gardien.3.adulte: `ls -l` shows the owner (root) and the permissions rw-r--r--: root can write, everyone else can only read. Changing this file would need `sudo`, the keeper's key, which the game never uses.
hista.gardien.3.bravo: On the phone, the Terminaworld's hall of rules is read-only (r--r--r--): nobody writes in it. If you tried, the keeper would say no: "Permission denied".
hista.gardien.3.adulte: On Android, the app's terminal simulates this tree: /etc is a read-only copy (r--r--r--) owned by the app. On a real Linux, `ls -l /etc/hostname` would show root as the owner.
lieu.racine.i: the foot of the great tree, where every path in the world begins
lieu.racine.t: /: the root of the single directory tree; every absolute path starts with /.
lieu.village.i: the houses of everyone who lives in the world
lieu.village.t: /home: the users' home directories (/Users on macOS).
lieu.camp.i: your very own house; its nickname is ~
lieu.camp.t: ~ = $HOME, your home directory (/home/<name>); the shell replaces ~ with that path.
lieu.zone.i: the playground: the only place where we build and break things
lieu.zone.t: ~/terrain_terminagotchi: the game's sandbox, the only folder where it creates, moves or deletes files.
lieu.regles.i: the world's rules, which only the keeper can change
lieu.regles.t: /etc: the system configuration (hostname, os-release, hosts, passwd), writable only by root.
lieu.armurerie.i: where all the commands sleep, ready to help
lieu.armurerie.t: /bin, /usr/bin: the executables; the PATH variable tells the shell where to look for them.
lieu.vague.i: you leave things there and they blow away by themselves
lieu.archives.i: the register where the keeper writes down everything that happens
lieu.archives.t: /var/log: the system logs (often readable only by root; see also journalctl).
lieu.portails.i: a magic place: doors to the screen, the disk… and a black hole
lieu.portails.t: /dev: the device files; /dev/null throws away everything written to it.
lieu.miroir.i: a magic place: a mirror that shows what every program is doing, live
lieu.miroir.t: /proc: a pseudo-filesystem from the kernel (/proc/cpuinfo, /proc/<pid>); nothing in it is stored on disk.
lieu.systeme.i: a corner of the world tidied by the keeper
lieu.systeme.t: a system directory, outside your home directory: read-only for a normal user.
terme.camp: your base camp (~, your home folder)
racine.refus.adulte: the app's terminal simulates the tree of a real Linux: / and the system places are read-only, ~ is the app's private folder. On a computer, writing to /etc would fail too ("Permission denied") without `sudo`.
racine.refus.adulte.tmp: the app's terminal simulates a real Linux, but keeps /tmp read-only to protect the phone. On a computer, /tmp is open to everyone: you can write temporary files there (many programs do).
racine.motd: Welcome to the Terminaworld! This is the hall of rules: we look, we don't touch.
racine.osrelease: This file is scenery: on a real Linux, /etc/os-release gives the name and version of the system.
lec.indice.lieu: Right command, wrong place! It must be typed from {lieu}. Go there first: `{cmd}`, then type `{etape}`.
lec.indice.nom: Almost! There is no “{tape}” here. Did you mean “{proche}”? Check the letters.
lec.indice.casse: Watch the capital letters! For the computer, “{tape}” and “{proche}” are two different names. Write “{proche}”.
lec.indice.manque: “{nom}”: not found here. To see what is here: `ls` · to know where you are: `pwd`
lec.indice.absent: The tool “{cmd}” is not installed on this computer: it's not your fault!
lec.indice.minuscules: Careful: commands are written in small letters. Type `{cmd}`, not “{tape}”.
lec.indice.rate: The command answered with an error, so the step is not done yet. Read the message, fix it and try again: `{cmd}`
lec.indice.grep_rien: No line contains “{mot}”: grep finds nothing. To see what is in the file: `{cmd}`
lec.indice.variante: ✔ Your command works too, well done! But this step wants you to discover `{cmd}`: try it and see the difference.
lec.indice.cd_moins: `cd -` took you back to the previous place (where you came from). Here, the step wants: `{cmd}`
lec.indice.cd_pas_ici: There is no place “{nom}” where you are. This path works from anywhere: `{cmd}`
core.inconnue.casse: “{cmd}” with capital letters doesn't exist: commands are written in small letters. Type `{proche}`.
vrai.pareil: 💻 In a real terminal (Linux, macOS): `{cmd}` works the same.
vrai.mac: 💻 In a real terminal: the same on Linux; on macOS, type `{mac}` instead.
vrai.absent: 💻 In a real terminal: `{cmd}` is not installed everywhere; an adult can add it (their password will be needed).
vrai.autre: 💻 In a real terminal (Linux, macOS), type `{cmd}` instead.
garde.repare: 🛡️ Your command went poking around backstage in the app (where I keep my save and the Root): I put everything back as it was. Here, we play in the camp: `cd ~`
garde.repare.adulte: the phone's shell has the same rights as the app and can reach its private folder. Before each command, the game takes a snapshot of that folder (outside the camp); afterwards, it puts back what was changed or deleted and removes what was added ({n} item(s) here).
garde.lien: 🔗 I removed {liens}: this symbolic link led out of the camp. A link that stays inside the camp (or shows a place of the Root) still works.
garde.lien.adulte: a symbolic link to the app's private folder or to the real system would let you write there from the camp: the game deletes them after each command (only the link, never its target).
garde.processus: 🧹 {n} program(s) started by your command were still running in the background: I stopped them, they would have drained the battery.
garde.processus.adulte: each line runs in its own session (setsid); when it ends, everything it started (jobs with &, nohup, setsid) is killed (kill -9). Each process also gets at most {s} s of CPU time.
garde.sceau: 🩹 My save was changed outside the game: I'm going back to my last good copy.
garde.sceau.sans: 🩹 My save was changed outside the game and I have no good backup copy: I'm keeping it anyway, so I don't lose you.
garde.illisible: 🩹 My save was damaged: I went back to my backup copy, nothing is lost.
garde.perdue: 🩹 My save was damaged with no backup copy: I kept it aside (sauvegarde.json.refusee) and a new egg is coming.

bulle.permission.texte:
For {nom} to walk around on top of your other apps, the phone must allow it to “display over other apps”.

It can't see what's on the screen and doesn't read anything you type: it just walks around.

If you're not sure, ask a grown-up. On the next page, choose Terminagotchi and turn the switch on.

prog.pwd.limite: A real signpost is planted in the ground; `pwd` only writes the path from the Root.
prog.pwd.idee: `pwd` doesn't say who you are: that's `whoami`.
prog.ls.limite: `ls` only gives the names of the objects, in alphabetical order.
prog.ls.idee: An empty place shows nothing: that is not an error.
prog.ls_a.limite: A secret passage has no lock: the dot hides the name, it protects nothing.
prog.ls_a.idee: A hidden file is neither protected nor dangerous.
prog.ls_l.limite: The r, w, x padlocks are not real locks: root, the guardian, gets through anyway.
prog.ls_l.idee: The first sign (d or -) is not a permission: it says whether it is a folder or a file.
prog.ls_r.limite: The map only shows what is under the place where you are, not the whole computer.
prog.ls_r.idee: `tree` is not installed everywhere; `ls -R` almost always works.
prog.cd.limite: You don't really walk: only the place “where you are” changes, nothing moves on the disk.
prog.cd.idee: `cd` on its own doesn't stay put: it takes you back to base camp.
prog.camp.limite: Base camp is not the whole computer: it's only your own folder.
prog.camp.idee: `~` is not a folder called ~: the shell replaces it with the path of your folder.
prog.parent.limite: Going up is not “going back”: `..` goes to the place that contains this one.
prog.parent.idee: From base camp, `cd ..` doesn't lead to the playground: it goes up to /home.
prog.racine.limite: The Root is not a disk: disks and USB sticks are stored somewhere under /.
prog.racine.idee: A path that starts with / doesn't start from where you are, but always from the Root.
prog.mkdir.limite: A new place is empty: it contains nothing until you put something in it.
prog.mkdir.idee: `mkdir` doesn't create a file: for an empty file, use `touch`.
prog.touch.limite: `touch` fills nothing: the object it creates is empty (0 bytes).
prog.touch.idee: On a file that already exists, `touch` erases nothing: it only changes its date.
prog.rmdir.limite: `rmdir` only removes empty places: if an object is left inside, it refuses.
prog.rmdir.idee: A removed place doesn't go into a recycle bin.
prog.rm.limite: The shredder has no way back: there is no recycle bin in the terminal.
prog.rm.idee: `rm` without -r doesn't delete a place: it answers “Is a directory”.
prog.rm_r.limite: `rm -r` asks nothing: all the contents go at once, with no way back.
prog.rm_r.idee: Adding -f doesn't make `rm` more careful: on the contrary, it no longer warns you of anything.
prog.cp.limite: A copy is a separate object: changing the copy doesn't change the original.
prog.cp.idee: Copying onto a name that already exists overwrites it without warning.
prog.mv.limite: `mv` doesn't copy: the object changes place or name, there aren't two left.
prog.mv.idee: Renaming and moving are the same command: `mv`.
prog.echo.limite: Without `>`, the sentence is only shown: it is stored nowhere.
prog.echo.idee: The quotes are not shown: they keep the sentence in one piece.
prog.redir.limite: The funnel only takes the normal output: error messages go past it (you need 2>).
prog.redir.idee: `>` doesn't add: it first erases what was there.
prog.ajout.limite: `>>` always sticks at the bottom, never in the middle.
prog.ajout.idee: If the file doesn't exist, `>>` creates it: that is not an error.
prog.cat.limite: `cat` shows everything at once: for a long book, `less` turns the pages.
prog.cat.idee: `cat` doesn't change the file: it only reads it.
prog.less.limite: The phone doesn't have `less`: there, `cat` shows everything at once.
prog.less.idee: `less` changes nothing; you leave it with the q key.
prog.head.limite: `head` doesn't cut the file: it only shows its beginning.
prog.head.idee: Without -n, `head` shows 10 lines, not just one.
prog.wc.limite: `wc -l` counts line breaks: a last line without a line break is not counted.
prog.wc.idee: `wc -c` counts bytes, not letters: “é” takes two.
prog.grep.limite: The magnifying glass shows whole lines, not just the word found.
prog.grep.idee: `grep` tells capital and small letters apart (except with -i).
prog.find.limite: `find` searches by name, not in what is written inside: that's `grep`.
prog.find.idee: Without quotes, the star can be replaced too early by the shell.
prog.sort.limite: `sort` sorts lines, not the words of one line.
prog.sort.idee: Without -n, 10 comes before 9: `sort` compares characters, not numbers.
prog.tuyau.limite: Nothing really flows: the system passes the text from one program to the other, which run at the same time.
prog.tuyau.idee: The pipe doesn't carry files, only the text the first command shows.
prog.rev.limite: `rev` turns each line around, not the order of the lines (that's `tac`).
prog.rev.idee: `rev` doesn't change the file: it shows the reversed text.
prog.chmod.limite: Padlocks protect against mistakes, not thieves: root and the owner can remove them.
prog.chmod.idee: `chmod 444` doesn't stop the file being deleted: that depends on the permissions of the place that contains it.
prog.whoami.limite: The game calls you explorer, but the system only knows your user name.
prog.whoami.idee: `whoami` doesn't give the computer's name: that's `hostname`.
prog.id.limite: The clubs (the groups) are not friends: they are lists of shared permissions.
prog.id.idee: UID 0 is not “nobody”: it's root, the guardian.
prog.sudo.limite: The guardian's key is not a game power: with it, one mistake can damage the whole computer.
prog.sudo.idee: `sudo` doesn't make a command more correct, only more powerful.
prog.systeme.limite: The system places are not scenery: they are the real files that make the computer work.
prog.systeme.idee: Being able to read a system file doesn't mean being able to change it.
prog.hostname.limite: The world's name is not its address: on the network, you find it by its IP address.
prog.hostname.idee: You don't change the machine's name without the guardian's key (root).
prog.ps.limite: A process is not a window: many run without showing anything.
prog.ps.idee: `ps` on its own only shows the processes of this terminal; `ps aux` shows them all.
prog.fond.limite: The faraway nap doesn't travel: the process stays on the same machine, it just no longer blocks the terminal.
prog.fond.idee: A background task is not stopped: it is still working.
prog.kill.limite: `kill` erases nothing: it sends a message (a signal) asking the process to stop.
prog.kill.idee: `kill` doesn't only stop: it can send other signals (`kill -l` lists them).
prog.free.limite: The work table (the RAM) is wiped when you switch off; the disk keeps everything.
prog.free.idee: Memory taken by the cache is not lost: the system gives it back when it needs it.
prog.du.limite: `du` weighs what is stored on the disk, in whole blocks: a tiny file often weighs 4.0K.
prog.df.limite: `df` talks about whole disks, not a single folder.
prog.df.idee: kB and KiB are not the same: `df -h` counts by 1024, `df -H` by 1000.
prog.uptime.limite: `uptime` counts since the last start-up, not since the computer was bought.
prog.uptime.idee: The “load average” is not a percentage.
prog.uname.limite: `uname` gives the name of the kernel (Linux), not of the distribution (Fedora, Ubuntu).
prog.uname.idee: Android has a Linux kernel too.
prog.getprop.limite: The phone's properties are written by the maker: they are not measurements.
prog.getprop.idee: `getprop` doesn't exist on a computer: it belongs to Android.
prog.date.limite: The clock comes from the computer: if it is wrong, `date` is wrong too.
prog.date.idee: Computers count time in seconds since 1 January 1970.
prog.script.limite: A recipe doesn't think: the shell reads the lines one by one, in order.
prog.script.idee: A script doesn't need the x permission for `sh file`, only for `./file`.
prog.alias.limite: A nickname is forgotten when you close the terminal, unless it is written in ~/.bashrc.
prog.alias.idee: An alias doesn't create a program: the shell only replaces the word with its text.
prog.fonction.limite: A function is also forgotten when you close, unless it is written in ~/.bashrc (or ~/.tgrc).
prog.fonction.idee: The empty brackets receive nothing: the words you give arrive in $1, $2…
prog.config_shell.limite: ~/.bashrc is read again when a new terminal opens; `source` reads it again straight away.
prog.config_shell.idee: Writing in ~/.bashrc doesn't change terminals that are already open.
prog.boucle.limite: The loop guesses nothing: it repeats for each word of the list, no more, no less.
prog.boucle.idee: The loop variable doesn't disappear afterwards: it keeps its last value.
prog.condition.limite: `if` doesn't understand sentences: it only checks whether a command succeeds.
prog.condition.idee: The spaces around [ and ] are required: [ is a command.
prog.git_depot.limite: The album doesn't take photos on its own: nothing is kept without `git add` and `git commit`.
prog.git_depot.idee: Git is not GitHub: Git works without the Internet, on your computer.
prog.git_photo.limite: A photo (a commit) only keeps what was added with `git add`.
prog.git_photo.idee: A commit sends nothing to the Internet: `git push` is what sends.
prog.git_histoire.limite: `git diff` compares with the last photo, not with yesterday.
prog.git_histoire.idee: `git log` doesn't show the contents of files, only the photos and their messages.
prog.ping.limite: The echo is not a sound: it's a small packet of data making the round trip.
prog.ping.idee: A ping with no answer doesn't mean the site is down: some never answer.
prog.ip.limite: An IP address looks like a house number, but it changes when you change network.
prog.ip.idee: 127.0.0.1 is not a faraway machine: it's the computer itself.
prog.curl.limite: The postman brings back the page as text (HTML): he doesn't display it like a browser.
prog.curl.idee: `curl -I` doesn't download the page: only its headers.
prog.dns.limite: A real phone book doesn't change every hour; DNS does (time to live, TTL).
prog.dns.idee: The Internet and the Web are not the same thing.
prog.ssh.limite: The encrypted tunnel hides what goes through it, not the fact that you are connecting.
prog.ssh.idee: `ssh -V` opens no connection: it only shows the version.
prog.traceroute.limite: The relays shown are the ones that answer: some stay silent (* * *).
prog.traceroute.idee: The route is not always the same from one time to the next.
prog.termux.limite: These commands talk to the phone (torch, vibrator): they don't exist on a computer.
prog.termux.idee: Termux is not all of Android: it's an app that gives a Linux terminal.
prog.am.limite: `am` asks Android to open an app: Android decides.
prog.am.idee: A package name (com.android.settings) is not the app's displayed name.
prog.appli.limite: These commands are game shortcuts: a real Android terminal uses `am` or `termux-…`.
prog.appli.idee: A game command doesn't work in another terminal.
prog.createur.limite: The level is a simple text file: each character is a square of the maze.
prog.createur.idee: Changing the file doesn't restart the game: run `doom` again to see the difference.
maths.comptage.question: Can you count objects one by one?
maths.comptage.enfant: Counting means touching each object only once while saying the next number: 1, 2, 3…
maths.comptage.grands: Counting a finite set: each element is matched with a whole number from 1 to n; n is its cardinality. In computing, numbering often starts at 0.
maths.comptage.limite: Computers often number from 0: the first box has the number 0.
maths.comptage.idee: Counting the same object twice doesn't make one more object.
maths.comptage.ex2: `seq 5` counts up to 5 in the terminal: one number per line.
maths.comptage.ex3: `ls | wc -l` counts the objects in a place: each name is on one line.
maths.comptage.erreur: Touch each star with your finger while saying the next number, only once each.
maths.comptage.kw: count counting number numbers how many digit digits one two three
maths.addition.question: Can you do an addition?
maths.addition.enfant: Adding means putting together: 3 apples and 2 apples make 5 apples.
maths.addition.grands: The sum a + b. Addition is commutative (a + b = b + a) and associative.
maths.addition.limite: In a computer, numbers have a maximum size: an addition that is too big can “overflow”.
maths.addition.erreur: Start from the bigger number, then move forward as many steps as the smaller one.
maths.addition.kw: addition add adding plus sum total together
maths.soustraction.question: Can you do a subtraction?
maths.soustraction.enfant: Subtracting means taking away: I have 8 marbles, I give 3 away, I have 5 left.
maths.soustraction.grands: The difference a − b. Unlike addition, the order matters: a − b is not b − a.
maths.soustraction.limite: Below zero, you find negative numbers: 3 − 5 = −2.
maths.soustraction.ex1: 8 − 3 = 5: eight marbles, we give three away.
maths.soustraction.erreur: Start from the first number and go back as many steps as the second.
maths.soustraction.kw: subtraction subtract minus take away remove difference
maths.multiplication.question: Can you do a multiplication?
maths.multiplication.enfant: Multiplying means adding the same number several times: 3 bags of 4 sweets make 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
maths.multiplication.grands: a × b is the repeated addition of a, b times. It is commutative and distributive over addition.
maths.multiplication.limite: Multiplying doesn't always make bigger: × 1 changes nothing, × 0 gives 0.
maths.multiplication.erreur: Add {a} as many times as needed: {b} times.
maths.multiplication.kw: multiplication multiply times product table tables
maths.division.question: Can you share sweets between friends?
maths.division.enfant: Dividing means sharing into equal parts: 17 sweets for 5 friends, each gets 3, and 2 are left.
maths.division.grands: Euclidean division: a = b × q + r with 0 ≤ r < b; q is the quotient, r the remainder. In the shell, $((a / b)) gives q.
maths.division.limite: In the terminal, $((17 / 5)) gives 3: whole numbers throw away the pieces (no decimal point).
maths.division.idee: You can't divide by 0: the terminal answers “division by 0”.
maths.division.ex1: 12 ÷ 3 = 4: 12 sweets for 3 friends, 4 each, nothing left.
maths.division.ex3: `echo $((17 / 5))` shows 3: the terminal keeps the quotient.
maths.division.exo: {a} sweets shared between {b} friends: how many does each one get?
maths.division.erreur: Find how many times {b} goes into {a} without going over: {b} × ? must stay smaller than {a}, or equal.
maths.division.kw: division divide dividing share sharing parts part quotient equal
maths.modulo.question: Do you know the remainder of a division?
maths.modulo.enfant: The modulo is what is left after sharing: 17 sweets for 5 friends, 2 are left. It's like a clock: after the last box, you start again from 0.
maths.modulo.grands: a mod b is the remainder r of Euclidean division (0 ≤ r < b). In the shell: $((a % b)). It is used for clocks, days of the week, Caesar's cipher.
maths.modulo.limite: With negative numbers, each language has its own rule: $((-7 % 3)) gives -1 in bash.
maths.modulo.idee: The remainder is always smaller than the number of parts.
maths.modulo.ex2: 14 h + 12 h = 26 h, and 26 % 24 = 2: it will be 2 in the morning.
maths.modulo.ex3: `echo $((10 % 2))` shows 0: 10 is even (the remainder by 2 is 0).
maths.modulo.exo: {a} sweets shared between {b} friends: how many are left?
maths.modulo.erreur: Share first ({b} × quotient), then take that number away from {a}: what is left is the modulo.
maths.modulo.kw: modulo remainder left over division clock mod even odd caesar
maths.puissances.question: Do you know powers (2 × 2 × 2…)?
maths.puissances.enfant: A power means multiplying a number by itself several times: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. We write it 2³ (“2 to the power 3”).
maths.puissances.grands: aⁿ = a × a × … × a (n factors) and a⁰ = 1. In bash: $((2**10)) = 1024. Powers of 2 measure memory (1 KiB = 2¹⁰ bytes).
maths.puissances.limite: It grows very fast: 2⁶³ is already too big for the shell, which shows a negative number.
maths.puissances.ex2: 10² = 10 × 10 = 100: the small number at the top counts the zeros.
maths.puissances.exo: How much is {a} to the power {b} ({calcul})?
maths.puissances.erreur: Write the number {a}, {b} times, with × between them, then work it out step by step.
maths.puissances.kw: power powers exponent square cube itself exponential
maths.binaire.question: Do you know binary (the 0s and 1s)?
maths.binaire.enfant: In binary, there are only two digits, 0 and 1, like switches off or on. From right to left, each switch is worth double the one before: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16.
maths.binaire.grands: Base-2 numbering: each position is worth a power of 2. 1011 in binary = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11. In bash: $((2#1011)).
maths.binaire.limite: The switches are a picture: inside the machine, they are electric voltages, magnets or charges.
maths.binaire.idee: 10 in binary doesn't mean ten: it's two.
maths.binaire.exo: The switches {bits}: what number do they make?
maths.binaire.erreur: Under each 1, write its value (1, 2, 4, 8… starting from the right), then add them up.
maths.binaire.kw: binary base two bit bits zero one switch switches byte

app.pan.envies.dit: And here are my wishes: look at my gauges to see how I'm doing.

app.pan.deploie.dit: Look, your command unfolds above the terminal: each piece lights up in turn!
app.pan.assiette.dit: My plate of the day is here: the more varied your commands, the better I eat!

hist.biblio1.4.dit: A pipe, now! `cat` reads the whole book, and `|` sends its lines to `grep`, which keeps only the ones where Abyssor sleeps.
hist.biblio1.4.bravo: Your first pipe! The lines flowed from `cat` to `grep`. Watch them go by in the unfolded view.
hist.biblio1.4.adulte: `|` (pipe) connects one command's output to the next one's input: `cat file | grep word` is the same here as `grep word file`.
hist.port.debut: ⚓ Welcome to the Harbour! Here, every biome of the Terminaworld is a machine with its own address, and little messengers carry packets from one to another. We'll find our address, read the directory, send the postman and light our own lighthouse.
hist.port.fin: All the lighthouses are shining! You know where each machine lives, how messengers travel and how to recognise a real seal. You are Harbour Captain.
port.ouvert.log: 🌍 A world opens at the Crossroads: the Harbour
port.ouvert.dit: You can read, search and connect pipes: the Harbour opens its docks to you! Whenever you like: `cd ~/terrain_terminagotchi/port`.
hist.port1.titre: Who am I on the network?
hist.port0.1.dit: Look at what's on the docks: `ls`.
hist.port0.1.bravo: A sign, the harbour directory, the logbook, your dock and the teleporter. Let's visit it all!
hist.port0.1.adulte: `ls` lists the port folder the game prepared in your play area; the game writes nothing elsewhere.
hist.port0.2.bravo: The captain was waiting for you! Every biome is a machine, and every machine has an address.
hist.port0.2.adulte: The Harbour simulates a small network of 11 machines at 127.x.x.x addresses: these are loopback addresses, nothing leaves your computer.
hist.port1.0.dit: Every machine has a name. What is yours called? `hostname`.
hist.port1.0.bravo: That's your computer's name on the network. Other machines can call it that.
hist.port1.0.adulte: `hostname` prints the system's host name (/etc/hostname on Linux). A name is not an address: you need a directory to go from one to the other.
hist.port1.1.dit: And your address? The network cards are in `ip a`. Look for lo and 127.0.0.1.
hist.port1.1.bravo: lo is the loop: a card that only leads back to yourself. 127.0.0.1 is your base camp: localhost.
hist.port1.1.adulte: `ip a` (ip address) lists the interfaces with their IPv4 (inet) and IPv6 (inet6) addresses. lo is the loopback interface: 127.0.0.1/8, the whole 127.0.0.0 to 127.255.255.255 block.
hist.port1.2.dit: Shout "Ahoy!" towards your own camp: `ping -c 3 localhost`.
hist.port1.2.bravo: 3 echoes sent, 3 came back: 0% loss. The time in ms is the round trip.
hist.port1.2.adulte: ping sends ICMP Echo requests and measures the reply time; -c 3 stops after 3. Towards localhost, packets never leave the machine.
hist.port2.0.dit: Your computer has its own tiny directory: `cat /etc/hosts`.
hist.port2.0.bravo: You see localhost next to 127.0.0.1: the directory says which address goes with that name.
hist.port2.0.adulte: /etc/hosts maps names to addresses; it is checked before DNS (order set in /etc/nsswitch.conf). We only read it: it belongs to the guardian (root).
hist.port2.1.dit: Ask your computer for the address of the name localhost: `getent hosts localhost`.
hist.port2.1.bravo: It looked in the directory and answered with the address. Your browser does the same before every visit.
hist.port2.1.adulte: `getent hosts` queries the system's name databases (hosts file, then DNS) the way programs do. DNS does the same at Internet scale.
hist.port2.2.dit: The harbour directory knows every machine in the Terminaworld. Look for the Fire biome: `grep feu annuaire.txt`.
hist.port2.2.bravo: feu.terminaworld lives at 127.42.0.2. Address on the left, name on the right, just like /etc/hosts.
hist.port2.2.adulte: annuaire.txt uses the /etc/hosts format. The 127.42.0.x addresses are in the loopback range: on Linux, `ping -c 1 127.42.0.2` answers, and nothing leaves the machine.
hist.port3.0.dit: The harbour lighthouse is a real little web server. Send the postman to ask for the envelope only: `curl -I http://localhost:8042/`.
hist.port3.0.bravo: HTTP/1.1 200 OK: "all good". Below, the headers: who answers, what kind of letter, its size.
hist.port3.0.adulte: `curl -I` sends a HEAD request: only the status line and the response headers. The lighthouse only listens on 127.0.0.1 (loopback).
hist.port3.1.dit: Now the letter itself, but only the beginning: `curl -s http://localhost:8042/eau | head -n 3`.
hist.port3.1.bravo: The postman brought back the Water biome's page, and the pipe kept only 3 lines.
hist.port3.1.adulte: Without -I, curl does a GET and writes the response body to its output; -s hides the progress bar; head -n 3 keeps 3 lines.
hist.port3.2.dit: Put a letter in your bag: `curl -o colis.html http://localhost:8042/feu`.
hist.port3.2.bravo: colis.html arrived on the dock. You can open it with cat.
hist.port3.2.adulte: -o writes the response body to a file instead of the screen: the postman drops off the parcel.
hist.port3.3.dit: And if we ask for a page that doesn't exist? `curl -I http://localhost:8042/volcan_perdu`.
hist.port3.3.bravo: 404 Not Found: the lighthouse did answer, but that page doesn't exist. The postman still comes back!
hist.port3.3.adulte: HTTP codes: 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error (404: resource not found), 5xx server error.
hist.port4.0.dit: The ssh teleporter links two machines through a secret tunnel. What version is it? `ssh -V`.
hist.port4.0.bravo: OpenSSH is here. We won't teleport anywhere: we'll make the key.
hist.port4.0.adulte: ssh opens an encrypted session on another machine. `ssh -V` opens nothing: it only prints the version.
hist.port4.1.dit: Make your key pair, here in the harbour: `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N "" -C explorateur -f cle_du_port`.
hist.port4.1.bravo: Two files: cle_du_port, the secret key you must NEVER give away, and cle_du_port.pub, the padlock you can show.
hist.port4.1.adulte: ssh-keygen creates an Ed25519 pair: the private key (mode 600) and the public key (.pub). -N "": no passphrase, only for playing here; -C: a comment with no personal data.
hist.port4.2.dit: Look at the padlock, the public key: `cat cle_du_port.pub`.
hist.port4.2.bravo: ssh-ed25519, a long string of letters, then explorateur. That's what you put on a machine so it recognises you.
hist.port4.2.adulte: The public key is copied into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the target machine; the private key proves your identity without ever travelling.
hist.port5.0.dit: Write your dock's page: `echo "Bienvenue sur mon quai" > quai/index.html`.
hist.port5.0.bravo: Your page is ready. Now someone has to serve it.
hist.port5.0.adulte: index.html is the page a web server returns when a folder is requested.
hist.port5.1.dit: Light your lantern at dock 8000, just for you: `python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory quai &`.
hist.port5.1.bravo: Your lantern shines at dock 8000! Thanks to --bind 127.0.0.1, nobody else on the Wi-Fi can see it.
hist.port5.1.adulte: http.server serves the files of a folder. Without --bind it listens on every interface (0.0.0.0): any machine on the local network could read the folder. & runs it in the background.
hist.port5.2.bravo: "Bienvenue sur mon quai": your server answered. Your browser would do exactly the same.
hist.port5.2.adulte: curl plays the client and http.server the server: both are on your machine, linked by the loopback.
hist.port5.3.bravo: Lantern out. A server you no longer use should be stopped: one less open door.
hist.port5.3.adulte: %1 refers to job number 1 of this shell (the one started with &); kill sends it the SIGTERM signal.
hist.port6.0.dit: Watch the postman work in detail: `curl -v http://localhost:8042/`.
hist.port6.0.bravo: The "*" lines talk about the address and transport, the ">" lines are your letter, the "<" lines the reply. Several envelopes!
hist.port6.0.adulte: -v (verbose) shows the TCP connection (address and port), the HTTP request sent (>) and the headers received (<).
hist.port6.1.dit: Open the envelopes one by one: `port couches`.
hist.port6.1.bravo: The letter (application) inside the envelope (transport), inside the parcel (network), inside the truck (link).
hist.port6.1.adulte: The Internet model has 4 layers (RFC 1122); the OSI model has 7. Each layer adds its header around the data of the layer above.
hist.port6.2.dit: Write the 4 layers in order, from the letter to the truck: `echo "application transport reseau liaison" > couches.txt`.
hist.port6.2.bravo: In the right order! On arrival, you unpack the other way round: the truck first, the letter last.
hist.port6.2.adulte: Encapsulation when sending (application → link), decapsulation when receiving (link → application).
hist.port7.0.dit: Who is listening inside your computer? The open doors: `ss -tln`.
hist.port7.0.bravo: Each LISTEN line is an open door waiting for visitors: an address, a colon, a door number.
hist.port7.0.adulte: `ss -tln` lists TCP sockets (-t) that are listening (-l) without translating numbers (-n). 127.0.0.1:8042 only accepts local connections; 0.0.0.0 accepts the whole network.
hist.port7.1.dit: Find the lighthouse's door with a pipe: `ss -tln | grep 8042`.
hist.port7.1.bravo: 127.0.0.1:8042: dock 127.0.0.1, door 8042. An IP address plus a port is the full address of a service.
hist.port7.1.adulte: The IP address names the machine, the port (0 to 65535) the program listening. Ports below 1024 are reserved for system services.
hist.port7.2.dit: A machine can have several addresses. Note down all the Terminaworld's: `port carte`.
hist.port7.2.bravo: 11 machines, 11 addresses, and the lighthouses linking them. Your map is written in the logbook.
hist.port7.2.adulte: All these addresses are in 127.0.0.0/8: on Linux, your machine answers on each of them. A real machine can also have several cards and several addresses (IPv4 and IPv6).
hist.port8.0.bravo: TCP opens a connection, numbers the packets and waits for an acknowledgement for each one.
hist.port8.0.adulte: `ss -t` lists established TCP connections. TCP guarantees order and delivery (lost segments are resent): it carries the Web, ssh and e-mail.
hist.port8.1.bravo: UDP sends without a connection and without acknowledgements: fast, but nothing is guaranteed.
hist.port8.1.adulte: `ss -u` lists UDP sockets. UDP is used when speed matters more than a loss: DNS, online games, live voice and video.
hist.port8.2.dit: Start the race between the TCP messenger and the UDP messenger: `port course`.
hist.port8.2.bravo: TCP delivered everything in order by resending packets 2 and 5. UDP was faster, but lost 2 packets and mixed up 2.
hist.port8.2.adulte: Same network, same losses: TCP fixes them (retransmission, reordering), UDP leaves them to the application.
hist.port9.0.dit: Your computer has a map of routes: `ip route`.
hist.port9.0.bravo: The default via… line shows the gateway: the door through which every far-travelling messenger leaves.
hist.port9.0.adulte: `ip route` shows the routing table: for each destination, the interface and gateway to use. The default route covers everything else.
hist.port9.1.dit: Follow a messenger lighthouse by lighthouse to your own camp: `tracepath -n 127.0.0.1`.
hist.port9.1.bravo: Just one hop: your camp is right here! Towards a far-away site you'd see a dozen lighthouses.
hist.port9.1.adulte: tracepath sends packets with an increasing TTL; each router that brings the TTL down to 0 replies, which reveals the path. Towards a public site, only with an adult.
hist.port9.2.dit: Send a messenger from the camp to the Fire biome: `port messager feu`.
hist.port9.2.bravo: Camp → Root → Rock → Fire: 3 hops. At each lighthouse its time to live (TTL) drops by 1.
hist.port9.2.adulte: Each router picks the next hop from its routing table and decrements the TTL; at 0 the packet is dropped (no endless loop).
hist.port9.3.dit: Oh no, a storm! Turn off the Rock lighthouse: `port eteins roche`.
hist.port9.3.bravo: The Rock is in the dark. The usual path to Fire is cut: a detour is needed.
hist.port9.3.adulte: A router failure makes a route invalid; routing protocols (OSPF, BGP…) compute another path if one exists.
hist.port9.4.dit: Guide a messenger to Fire yourself without going through the Rock. Look at the map, then give the lighthouses in order: `port guide racine … feu`.
hist.port9.4.bravo: Arrived without loss! You found the detour lighthouse by lighthouse. A packet's path can change every time.
hist.port9.4.adulte: This is source routing: the sender sets the path. On the Internet, routers choose, hop by hop.
hist.port10.0.dit: Who is the caretaker of your home? Find the default route: `ip route | grep default`.
hist.port10.0.bravo: That address is your home router (or the school's): the building caretaker.
hist.port10.0.adulte: The default gateway is usually the home router, which is also the DHCP server and NAT for the local network.
hist.port10.1.dit: The neighbours your machine knows: `ip neigh`.
hist.port10.1.bravo: Each line links an IP address on the local network to a hardware (MAC) address. The caretaker is often there.
hist.port10.1.adulte: `ip neigh` shows the ARP/NDP table: the IP ↔ MAC address mapping of direct neighbours. A MAC address never leaves the local network.
hist.port10.2.dit: Watch the caretaker welcome new devices: `port gardien`.
hist.port10.2.bravo: The caretaker gives each one a flat number (DHCP) and posts all the mail with the building's address (NAT).
hist.port10.2.adulte: DHCP hands out private addresses (192.168.x.x, RFC 1918); NAT translates them into a single public address. 203.0.113.7 is an address reserved for documentation.
hist.port11.0.dit: The lighthouse also has a sealed door, over https. Knock: `curl https://localhost:8443`.
hist.port11.0.bravo: curl refuses: "self-signed certificate". The seal was signed by the lighthouse itself: nobody vouches for it.
hist.port11.0.adulte: With HTTPS the server presents a certificate; curl checks it is signed by a trusted authority and carries the right name. A self-signed certificate fails (error 60).
hist.port11.1.dit: The harbour notary gave you the lighthouse's seal. Tell curl to trust it: `curl --cacert sceau_du_phare.pem https://localhost:8443`.
hist.port11.1.bravo: This time the door opens: the seal matches the one you know. The letter travelled encrypted.
hist.port11.1.adulte: --cacert replaces the known authorities with this certificate. Only trust a certificate you received through a safe channel.
hist.port11.2.dit: The notary shows you 4 seals. Read them carefully: `port sceau`.
hist.port11.2.bravo: Look at who signed, for which name, and the date.
hist.port11.2.adulte: A valid certificate: signed by a recognised authority, for the exact site name, within its validity period.
hist.port11.3.dit: Which one is the real seal? Give its number: `port sceau ?`.
hist.port11.3.bravo: Well spotted! The padlock proves WHO you're talking to, not that what it says is true.
hist.port11.3.adulte: TLS guarantees the server's authenticity and the confidentiality of the trip; it says nothing about the site's honesty.
port.f.localhost.enfant: localhost is your base camp: an address that always leads back home.
port.f.localhost.grands: localhost (127.0.0.1, and ::1 in IPv6) means the machine itself; the whole 127.0.0.0/8 block stays inside the machine.
port.f.localhost.limite: The base camp is not a place on the network: a message sent to localhost goes through no cable.
port.f.localhost.idee: "127.0.0.1 is my computer's address on the Internet": no, every machine has its own loopback, which never leaves it.
port.f.hosts.enfant: The harbour directory: you give a name, it gives you the dock number.
port.f.hosts.grands: Name resolution turns a name into an IP address: the /etc/hosts file first, then DNS.
port.f.hosts.limite: A real phone book doesn't change every hour; DNS answers do: they have a time to live (TTL).
port.f.hosts.idee: "The name is enough to connect": no, the computer always needs the IP address.
port.f.http.enfant: curl is the postman: it carries your request and brings back the letter with its envelope.
port.f.http.grands: HTTP: a request (method, path, headers) and a response (status code, headers, body).
port.f.http.limite: The letter isn't paper: it's bytes, and the envelope (the headers) is text too.
port.f.http.idee: "404 means the site is down": no, the server answered; it's the page that doesn't exist.
port.f.ssh_cles.enfant: A secret key you always keep, and a padlock you can show everyone.
port.f.ssh_cles.grands: Public-key cryptography: what the public key can verify, only the private key can produce.
port.f.ssh_cles.limite: The padlock can be copied as much as you like, safely; the secret key never: whoever has it can pretend to be you.
port.f.ssh_cles.idee: "The public key must stay secret": no, it's the private key you protect.
port.f.serveur.enfant: A lantern on your dock: it answers whoever comes knocking.
port.f.serveur.grands: A server is a program that listens on an address and port and answers requests; bound to 127.0.0.1 it is invisible to the network.
port.f.serveur.limite: A server isn't necessarily a big machine: it's a role, and your computer can play it.
port.f.serveur.idee: "Only I can see my server": only if it listens on 127.0.0.1; on 0.0.0.0 the whole local network sees it.
port.f.couches.enfant: A letter in an envelope, in a parcel, in a truck.
port.f.couches.grands: The layered model: application, transport, network, link (the Internet's 4 layers; 7 in the OSI model).
port.f.couches.limite: Layers aren't objects: they're headers added around the data.
port.f.couches.idee: "The Internet and the Web are the same": no, the Web (HTTP) is only one application travelling over the Internet.
port.f.ports.enfant: The dock is the IP address; the warehouse door is the port number.
port.f.ports.grands: A socket = an IP address + a port (0 to 65535); a service listens on a port, and ss shows it.
port.f.ports.limite: A machine can have several addresses (several docks), and thousands of doors.
port.f.ports.idee: "An open port is a security hole": no, it's a listening service; the danger comes from a useless or badly protected service.
port.f.tcp_udp.enfant: TCP is the registered letter with proof of delivery; UDP is the postcard.
port.f.tcp_udp.grands: TCP: connection, acknowledgements, ordering, retransmission. UDP: independent datagrams, no guarantee.
port.f.tcp_udp.limite: "Lost" doesn't mean "stolen": a lost packet was dropped, for example by an overloaded router.
port.f.tcp_udp.idee: "UDP is worse": no, it's chosen on purpose when speed matters more (games, video, DNS).
port.f.routage.enfant: The lighthouses pass the light along, one to the next, up to the right machine.
port.f.routage.grands: Routing: each router picks the next hop from its table; the TTL limits the number of hops.
port.f.routage.limite: The path can change for each packet, and the way there and back can take different paths.
port.f.routage.idee: "A message goes straight from one computer to the other": no, it hops from router to router.
port.f.box_nat.enfant: The home router is the building caretaker: it gives each device a number and sorts the mail.
port.f.box_nat.grands: The home router acts as gateway, DHCP server (private addresses) and NAT (a single public address for the whole home).
port.f.box_nat.limite: Wi-Fi isn't "the Internet": it's only the last metre between your device and the router.
port.f.box_nat.idee: "My 192.168… address is my address on the Internet": no, the Internet sees the router's public address.
port.f.tls.enfant: The envelope sealed with wax, with a seal checked by the notary.
port.f.tls.grands: HTTPS = HTTP inside TLS: the trip is encrypted and the certificate is signed by an authority, in the site's name.
port.f.tls.limite: The padlock proves WHO you're talking to, not that the site is honest.
port.f.tls.idee: "A site with a padlock is always safe": no, a deceptive site can have a real certificate too.
port.meuble.panneau:
⚓ THE MESSENGER HARBOUR
Welcome, {nom}!
Here, every biome of the Terminaworld is a machine with an address.
The base camp is you: localhost, 127.0.0.1.
The Root is the great router: messengers go through it.
Read the directory (annuaire.txt), keep your logbook (carnet_de_bord.txt)
and light your lantern on your dock (quai/).
— The harbour captain
port.meuble.carnet: # Harbour logbook: the `port …` commands write here what you discover.
port.meuble.quai: Your dock. Write here the page your lantern will serve (index.html).
port.meuble.teleporteur:
THE TELEPORTER (ssh)
To go into another machine you need a key pair:
- the secret key stays with you, always;
- the padlock (the public key) goes on the machine you visit.
On arrival, the machine sets a challenge only your secret key can solve.
No password travels.

hista.port1.1.dit: And your address? The phone's network cards: `ifconfig`. Look for lo and 127.0.0.1.
hista.port1.1.bravo: lo is the loop: a card that only leads back to the phone itself. 127.0.0.1 is your base camp: localhost.
hista.port1.1.adulte: `ifconfig` (the old command, replaced by `ip a` on Linux computers) lists the interfaces; lo is the loopback, 127.0.0.1/8.
hista.port2.1.dit: Ask for the address of the name localhost: `nslookup localhost`.
hista.port2.1.bravo: Answer: 127.0.0.1. The directory found the name's address.
hista.port2.1.adulte: Here `nslookup` is a Terminagotchi command: it resolves localhost and the Terminaworld names, without ever querying the Internet.
hista.port4.0.dit: The ssh teleporter doesn't exist on the phone. Listen to its story: `port teleporteur`.
hista.port4.0.bravo: A secret key that never travels, a padlock you can show everyone.
hista.port4.0.adulte: On a computer, `ssh-keygen` makes the pair; the public key goes into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the target machine.
hista.port4.1.dit: The story is also written on the dock: `cat teleporteur.txt`.
hista.port4.1.bravo: Keep it in mind: you'll make your real key pair on a computer.
hista.port4.1.adulte: An asymmetric key pair: what the public key can verify, only the private key can produce.
hista.port5.1.bravo: Your lantern shines at dock 8000, only inside the phone (127.0.0.1).
hista.port5.1.adulte: `serveur` is a small Terminagotchi HTTP server: it serves the quai folder and only listens on 127.0.0.1; no other machine can reach it.
hista.port5.3.bravo: Lantern out. A server you no longer use should be stopped: one less open door.
hista.port5.3.adulte: Stopping a useless service closes a door: fewer open doors, fewer risks.
hista.port7.0.bravo: Each LISTEN line is an open door: an address, a colon, a door number.
hista.port7.0.adulte: Here `ss` is a Terminagotchi command: it shows the doors the app opens (lighthouse 8042, lantern 8000), all on 127.0.0.1. On a computer, `ss -tln` shows them all.
hista.port9.0.bravo: For every Terminaworld machine: which lighthouse to go through, and in how many hops.
hista.port9.0.adulte: On a computer, `ip route` shows the real routing table; here, the one of the simulated Terminaworld network.
hista.port9.1.dit: Read the messengers' lifetime: `ping -c 3 127.0.0.1`, then look at ttl=.
hista.port9.1.bravo: ttl=64: the messenger could still pass 64 lighthouses before vanishing.
hista.port9.1.adulte: The TTL (time to live) drops by 1 at each router; at 0 the packet is dropped. Linux starts at 64.

hist.citadelle.debut: 🛡 Welcome to the Citadel! Here, we DEFEND. Every attack is fake: glitches made up by the game, harmless, only inside the Terminaworld. We will set locks, read the guard's register, chase glitches and repair boxes.
hist.citadelle.fin: The towers shine, the glitches are gone, the boxes are repaired. You can read a log, set the right locks, check a fingerprint and never give away a secret. You are Guardian of the Citadel.
cit.ouvert.log: 🌍 A world opens at the Crossroads: the Citadel
cit.ouvert.dit: You can set locks and read logs: the Citadel opens its gates to you! Whenever you like: `cd ~/terrain_terminagotchi/citadelle`.
recomp.citadelle.vague: Push back the Citadel's great wave
hist.cit0.titre: The gate and the golden rule
cit.meuble.regle:
🛡 THE GUARDIANS' CITADEL
Welcome, {nom}!
GOLDEN RULE: here, we DEFEND.
• Every attack is FAKE: glitches made up by the game, harmless.
• We only ever attack what belongs to us: the game's boxes.
• Never a real password here: only examples.
• Never sudo: the guardian's key (root) is something you ask an adult for.
— The Citadel's guardian
cit.meuble.carnet: 🛡 Guard log: what you check gets written here.

💰 The Citadel's chest: 3 gold coins and the map of the tunnels.
Lock it so only you can open it.

cit.meuble.cadeau1: A present for you! Run me quickly!
cit.meuble.cadeau3: ← the trap (it only acts in the sandbox)
