cit.meuble.repere: 📍 Marker set at the start of the patrol: anything newer than me has changed since.
cit.meuble.glitch: 👾 FAKE VIRUS: a pretend game virus, harmless. Find me and delete me!
cit.decor: 🏰 {lieu}: a quiet corner of the Citadel.
cit.tresor: {icone} The Citadel's treasure: {nom}. Do not touch!
cit.tresor.altere: 👾 Hee hee, a glitch was here!
cit.boite.enumeration.lisez: 📦 Box “The forgotten cellar” (easy). Someone hid things here, thinking nobody would find them. List everything, even what is hidden.
cit.boite.note:
🚩 Entry flag: {drapeau}
Hidden is not protected!
cit.boite.droits.lisez: 📦 Box “The badly set permissions” (easy). Here the locks are set wrong. Find what everyone can read or change.
cit.boite.journal:
📓 The guardian's secret diary (readable by everyone, oops!)
🚩 Entry flag: {drapeau}
cit.boite.secrets.lisez: 📦 Box “The forgotten secrets” (easy). A secret written in plain text always ends up being read. Look for forgotten passwords (examples!).
hist.cit0.1.dit: Look at what is behind the gate.
hist.cit0.1.bravo: The golden rule, the guard log, a chest, logs… Everything is fake and harmless: it's our training ground.
hist.cit0.1.adulte: ls lists the citadelle folder the game prepared in your playground; the game writes nothing anywhere else.
hist.cit0.2.bravo: Here we defend, we only attack the game's boxes, and never a real password. Promise?
hist.cit0.2.adulte: Defensive security only acts on what belongs to us; entering a system without permission is a crime (in France: Penal Code, art. 323-1).
hist.cit1.0.dit: Who may open the chest? Look at its locks.
hist.cit1.0.bravo: rw- r-- r--: you read and write, but your club AND the others can read. The chest is wide open!
hist.cit1.0.adulte: The 1st column of ls -l: the type, then 3 rwx groups (owner, group, others). r = read, w = write, x = execute.
hist.cit1.1.dit: Lock the chest: only you, to read and write (6 for you, 0 for your club, 0 for the others).
hist.cit1.1.bravo: rw- --- ---: the chest only obeys you now. 🔒
hist.cit1.1.adulte: In octal, r = 4, w = 2, x = 1: 6 = rw-, 0 = ---. chmod 600 = rw-------, the setting for secret files (ssh keys…).
hist.cit1.2.dit: The patrol is a script: give it the right to run, for you only (u = you, + = add, x = execute).
hist.cit1.2.bravo: rwx r-- r--: the patrol can run, and only you hold the x key.
hist.cit1.2.adulte: chmod with letters: u, g, o, a (who), + - = (how), r w x (what). u+x adds execute for the owner without touching the rest.
hist.cit2.0.dit: Who are you to the computer? Ask for your identity.
hist.cit2.0.bravo: Your number (uid), your main group (gid) and your clubs (groups). The computer knows you by these numbers.
hist.cit2.0.adulte: id shows the uid, gid and groups of the current account; the names come from /etc/passwd and /etc/group.
hist.cit2.1.dit: The Citadel has its residents and clubs. Who is in the watchers' club (veilleurs)?
hist.cit2.1.bravo: veilleurs:x:2001:gardien,sentinelle: the guardian and the sentinel. A club is a group.
hist.cit2.1.adulte: /etc/group format: name:password (x):gid:members. Here it is a Citadel example file, not your computer's one.
hist.cit2.2.dit: Hand the watchtower to the sentinel and the watchers' club. (For real you must be root: here the Citadel simulates it.)
hist.cit2.2.bravo: The tower now belongs to sentinelle, club veilleurs. Only the guardian (root) can really do that.
hist.cit2.2.adulte: chown user:group file changes the owner; it needs root rights (sudo), which is why the game simulates it and never uses sudo.
hist.cit3.0.dit: The blacksmith has a mask: it decides the locks of NEW files. Look at yours.
hist.cit3.0.bravo: Four digits (often 0022): what gets REMOVED from new files. 022 removes w from the club and the others.
hist.cit3.0.adulte: umask is taken away from the default rights: 666 for a file, 777 for a folder. 666 − 022 = 644 (rw-r--r--).
hist.cit3.1.dit: Make a secret notebook with mask 077, inside a little bubble (the parentheses) so your everyday mask does not change.
hist.cit3.1.bravo: Born already locked: rw- --- ---. No need for chmod afterwards!
hist.cit3.1.adulte: ( … ) starts a subshell: umask 077 only lasts for that command. 666 − 077 = 600.
hist.cit3.2.dit: Ask the blacksmith to explain the 077 mask sum.
hist.cit3.2.bravo: 666 minus 077 = 600: the locks are set as soon as the file is born.
hist.cit3.2.adulte: The exact sum is an AND with the inverted mask (666 & ~077), not a subtraction; it matches when there is no borrowing.
hist.cit4.0.dit: The guard writes every visit in his register. Read the last 5 lines.
hist.cit4.0.bravo: Date, time, OK or ECHEC (failure), the visitor's address, the gate, the name. The end looks calm… but let's search.
hist.cit4.0.adulte: tail -n 5 shows the last 5 lines: that's where you look first, because logs grow at the end.
hist.cit4.1.dit: How many times did someone get the password wrong? Count the ECHEC lines.
hist.cit4.1.bravo: 52 failures! That's far too many for simple mistakes.
hist.cit4.1.adulte: grep -c counts the lines containing the pattern (instead of printing them).
hist.cit4.2.dit: Who failed? Keep the address (4th word) of each ECHEC, sort, and count the identical ones.
hist.cit4.2.bravo: 50 failures for 203.0.113.66: someone is trying every password at the postern! (The rest: 2 slips.)
hist.cit4.2.adulte: cut -d ' ' -f 4 keeps the 4th field; uniq -c counts identical consecutive lines, hence the sort before; sort -n orders by number. 203.0.113.0/24 is reserved for documentation (RFC 5737).
hist.cit4.3.dit: Write the intruder's address in intrus.txt (replace ? with the address).
hist.cit4.3.bravo: Intruder spotted: the guard will close the postern. Defenders do exactly this every day.
hist.cit4.3.adulte: A brute-force attack shows up like this: many failures, one address, in a short time. Then: block it, and change the targeted password.
hist.cit5.0.dit: A glitch worm is crawling around the Citadel! Search everywhere for files ending in .glitch.
hist.cit5.0.bravo: Four glitches, one of them hidden (its name starts with a dot). find catches them all.
hist.cit5.0.adulte: find . -name '*.glitch' goes down into every subfolder; the quotes stop the shell from expanding * too early.
hist.cit5.1.dit: The worm is copying itself! What has changed since the marker set at the start of the patrol?
hist.cit5.1.bravo: Everything newer than repere.txt: the glitches, and the new one that just copied itself. 🌉 This trick will help in the Library of Time.
hist.cit5.1.adulte: find -newer f keeps files modified after f. It's the basis of digital forensics: what changed since the attack?
hist.cit5.2.dit: Delete all the glitches at once (only the .glitch files, inside the Citadel).
hist.cit5.2.bravo: Not a single glitch left! The worm is gone.
hist.cit5.2.adulte: -delete removes what find found: always run find WITHOUT -delete first to check the list.
hist.cit6.0.dit: A present arrived: cadeau.sh. Before running a program, we READ it.
hist.cit6.0.bravo: It says “Run me quickly!”… but further down there is an rm. It's a Trojan horse!
hist.cit6.0.adulte: A Trojan looks useful but hides a harmful action; the user runs it themselves. Reading a script before running it is often enough to unmask it.
hist.cit6.1.dit: Show only the dangerous line: search for rm in the present.
hist.cit6.1.bravo: rm -f bac_a_sable/tresor_*.txt: it wanted to delete the sandbox treasures. Unmasked!
hist.cit6.1.adulte: grep rm spots delete commands; a real audit also looks for curl, wget, base64, eval… anything that downloads or hides code.
hist.cit6.2.dit: Disarm it: take away its right to run, for everyone (- = remove, x = execute).
hist.cit6.2.bravo: No more x: the horse can't gallop off any more. And the sandbox treasures are safe.
hist.cit6.2.adulte: chmod -x removes execute from u, g and o; ./cadeau.sh will answer “Permission denied”. sh cadeau.sh would still run it: never run a doubtful script.
hist.cit7.0.dit: 🌉 A short detour via the Control Room: ghost processes are tiring your creature. Who is working in secret?
hist.cit7.0.bravo: miner_fictif and flood_fictif! The 2nd number on each line is their number (PID).
hist.cit7.0.adulte: They are plain “sleep” processes renamed by the game (exec -a): they only sleep and stop on their own. ps aux lists processes; grep keeps the ones we care about.
hist.cit7.1.dit: Stop them with kill and their numbers (replace ? with the PIDs, separated by a space).
hist.cit7.1.bravo: The ghosts are gone: your creature can breathe. kill printed nothing: that means it worked.
hist.cit7.1.adulte: kill sends the TERM signal (polite: “please stop”); kill -9 (KILL) forces it, as a last resort. Without root you can only stop YOUR own processes.
hist.cit7.2.dit: Look at the Citadel's guard board.
hist.cit7.2.bravo: All green: no more glitches, no more ghosts. Defenders watch boards like this all day long.
hist.cit7.2.adulte: A monitoring dashboard (SOC) gathers indicators; here three: suspicious files, suspicious processes, world-readable secrets.
hist.cit8.0.dit: Every file has a fingerprint, like a finger. Take the treasure map's.
hist.cit8.0.bravo: 64 characters: the SHA-256 fingerprint. Change a single letter of the file and it changes completely.
hist.cit8.0.adulte: A cryptographic hash function: same input, same fingerprint; in practice impossible to recover the file or forge another with the same fingerprint.
hist.cit8.1.dit: The guard wrote down the treasure's fingerprints. Check them all at once.
hist.cit8.1.bravo: couronne.txt: FAILED! A glitch touched it. The other two are OK.
hist.cit8.1.adulte: sha256sum -c reads the fingerprint file and recomputes each one; a single mismatch makes the exit code non-zero. That's how you check a download.
hist.cit8.2.dit: Write the name of the touched object in altere.txt (replace ?).
hist.cit8.2.bravo: The crown! Thanks to the fingerprints, the guard knows exactly what to repair.
hist.cit8.2.adulte: A fingerprint proves a file changed, not who changed it; for the author you need a signature (the Crypt of Codes).
hist.cit9.0.dit: 🌉 The Locker is prowling! Before it strikes, pack the scrolls into a backup chest (an archive).
hist.cit9.0.bravo: Backup done. Just in time… 😱 The Locker has just struck!
hist.cit9.0.adulte: tar c = create an archive, f = its name (z = compress with gzip). 🌉 A Control Room notion. Against ransomware, a backup made BEFORE is the best defence (3-2-1 rule).
hist.cit9.1.dit: The scrolls became unreadable .verrou files. Take them back out of the backup chest.
hist.cit9.1.bravo: The scrolls are back, just like before! No need to pay the Locker.
hist.cit9.1.adulte: tar x = extract. Real ransomware encrypts files; here the game only base64-encoded them and set mode 000, inside the playground.
hist.cit9.2.bravo: Not a single red lock left among the scrolls.
hist.cit9.2.adulte: rm -f doesn't need read permission on the file: it's the folder (w) that decides whether its contents can be removed.
hist.cit9.3.dit: Check with the fingerprints that the scrolls are exactly the ones from before.
hist.cit9.3.bravo: Everything is OK: restored and checked. The Locker lost. 🛡
hist.cit9.3.adulte: Restore, then check integrity: a backup you've never read back is not a backup.
hist.cit10.0.dit: Here is the letter for your creature. Read it: right now anyone can read it.
hist.cit10.0.bravo: In plain text: a glitch could read it as easily as you.
hist.cit10.0.adulte: “Plain text”: readable as is. Encryption transforms the text so only those with the key can read it back.
hist.cit10.1.dit: Lock it in a one-key chest. The key here is an EXAMPLE (never your real password!).
hist.cit10.1.bravo: lettre.enc starts with “Salted__” then gibberish: without the key it is unreadable.
hist.cit10.1.adulte: AES-256 in CBC mode; -pbkdf2 derives the real key from the password (slowly, with a random salt). Typing -pass pass:… in a real command leaves it in the history: elsewhere, let openssl ask for it.
hist.cit10.2.dit: A glitch tries to open the chest with a wrong key. Do the same to see.
hist.cit10.2.bravo: “bad decrypt”: refused! Without the right key it's not “hard”, it's impossible in practice.
hist.cit10.2.adulte: With a wrong key, decryption produces invalid padding: openssl stops with an error (non-zero code).
hist.cit10.3.dit: Now open the chest with the right example key.
hist.cit10.3.bravo: The letter comes back in plain text, word for word. One key locks AND opens: that's symmetric encryption.
hist.cit10.3.adulte: The remaining problem: how to give the key to a friend without it being stolen on the way? Answer in the Crypt of Codes (public key, key exchange).
hist.cit11.0.dit: Two letters “from the Harbour captain”. Compare them line by line.
hist.cit11.0.bravo: < the real one, > the fake: URGENT, a weird link, and it asks for your password…
hist.cit11.0.adulte: diff shows the changed lines (< file 1, > file 2) and returns 1 when there are differences. port-du-terminaworld.example is a reserved name (RFC 2606): it doesn't exist.
hist.cit11.1.dit: 🌉 A Harbour reflex: check through another channel. Ask the lighthouse directly for the captain's real mail.
hist.cit11.1.bravo: The lighthouse confirms it: the captain sent nothing urgent, and never asks for a password.
hist.cit11.1.adulte: curl asks the game's lighthouse on 127.0.0.1 (nothing leaves the computer). Checking through another channel (calling, going to the site yourself) defeats phishing.
hist.cit11.2.dit: The guard wrote 6 remarks about the fake letter. Read them.
hist.cit11.2.bravo: Three are real signs of a trap, three prove nothing. Which ones?
hist.cit11.2.adulte: Classic phishing signs: urgency or threat, a request for a secret, an address or link that doesn't match. Layout or time are not signs.
hist.cit11.3.dit: Give the numbers of the 3 real signs (replace the ? with the numbers).
hist.cit11.3.bravo: Well done, the fake mail carrier is unmasked: he turns back into a shadow. Never a password by letter!
hist.cit11.3.adulte: No serious service asks for a password by message. If in doubt: don't click, check through another channel, tell an adult.
hist.cit12.0.dit: Here is a list of words (creature names). How many are there?
hist.cit12.0.bravo: 128 words. Remember that number: we'll use it to measure a passphrase's strength.
hist.cit12.0.adulte: wc -l counts lines. 128 = 2⁷: each randomly drawn word adds 7 bits of uncertainty.
hist.cit12.1.dit: Draw 4 random words: that's an EXAMPLE passphrase. (Never use it for real!)
hist.cit12.1.bravo: 4 random words: easy for you to remember, very hard for a glitch to guess.
hist.cit12.1.adulte: shuf shuffles lines; -n 4 keeps 4. The randomness must be real (people choose badly). These are examples: a real passphrase is never typed into a game.
hist.cit12.2.dit: How long would a glitch take to guess? Ask the Citadel to compare.
hist.cit12.2.bravo: Short and complicated: an instant. 6 random words: centuries. Length beats weird symbols!
hist.cit12.2.adulte: Assumption: a billion guesses per second against a stolen hash. A known password falls in a split second (leak lists); 6 words out of 7776 ≈ 77 bits. Add a password manager and two-factor authentication.
hist.cit13.0.dit: Boxes are little trap-worlds made by the game. Round 1: the investigation (find 2 flags). Round 2: the rampart (repair). Look at the list.
hist.cit13.0.bravo: Three easy boxes to start. We attack ONLY the game's boxes: they belong to you.
hist.cit13.0.adulte: Like on Root-Me or Hack The Box: a “user” flag then a “root” flag (here entry and dungeon), then the fix, checked by the inspector who replays the attack.
hist.cit13.1.dit: Box “The forgotten cellar”: list EVERYTHING, even what's hidden.
hist.cit13.1.bravo: A .cave_oubliee! Its dot hid it from plain ls, not from ls -a.
hist.cit13.1.adulte: Enumerating = methodically listing everything. Hiding with a dot isn't protection (“security through obscurity”).
hist.cit13.2.dit: Search the whole box for TG{…} flags, even in the corners.
hist.cit13.2.bravo: Two flags: entry and dungeon, even inside .plus_profond!
hist.cit13.2.adulte: grep -r searches every file in subfolders, hidden ones included. The flags change each game (a hash of your seed).
hist.cit13.3.dit: Hand in the flags, one by one (replace ? with a whole flag, TG{…} included).
hist.cit13.3.bravo: Investigation round won! Now the Rampart round: fix the weakness.
hist.cit13.3.adulte: A flag is only proof you reached a place. A defender's real goal is the second round: fixing.
hist.cit13.4.dit: Rampart: the cellar is open to everyone (r-x for others). Close it to the others (o = others, - = remove, rwx = everything).
hist.cit13.4.bravo: Hidden AND locked: now the cellar is really protected.
hist.cit13.4.adulte: On a folder, r = list, x = go through. Without r or x for “o”, the others can neither see inside nor enter.
hist.cit13.5.dit: Call the inspector: he replays the attack to check your repair.
hist.cit13.5.bravo: Box mastered, both rounds! A “glitch” guardian creature may come to visit…
hist.cit13.5.adulte: The inspector reads the box's real permissions (stat): the fix is checked, not just claimed.
hist.cit14.0.dit: Box “The badly set permissions”: read every file's locks.
hist.cit14.0.bravo: journal_secret.txt readable by all, and ronde.sh with a w for others (rwxr-xrwx). Ouch!
hist.cit14.0.adulte: A script anyone can edit but the guardian runs: anyone could slip their own orders into it. It's a real, common weakness.
hist.cit14.1.dit: Automatically find everything “the others” can change.
hist.cit14.1.bravo: ronde.sh: the only file anyone can change. Defenders run this search across whole servers.
hist.cit14.1.adulte: find -perm -o+w: files with at least the “others” w bit set. Variant: -perm -o+r for world-readable files.
hist.cit14.2.bravo: Entry in the diary, dungeon in the patrol script. Anything badly locked can be read.
hist.cit14.2.adulte: In a real audit, a readable file holding a secret is already a leak, even if nobody has read it yet.
hist.cit14.3.dit: Hand in both flags (replace ? with a flag, once each).
hist.cit14.3.bravo: Investigation done. Now least privilege: everyone gets only the keys they need.
hist.cit14.3.adulte: Principle of least privilege: give the minimum necessary rights to every account and every file.
hist.cit14.4.dit: Rampart: remove all of “others'” rights on the box's files.
hist.cit14.4.bravo: Nothing left for others: they can't read the diary or touch the patrol.
hist.cit14.4.adulte: The * wildcard means every visible file in the folder; chmod handles them one by one.
hist.cit14.5.dit: Call the inspector for the permissions box.
hist.cit14.5.bravo: Second box mastered! You think like a defender.
hist.cit14.5.adulte: The inspector checks that no r bit (diary) or w bit (patrol) remains for “o”.
hist.cit15.0.dit: Box “The forgotten secrets”: list everything, hidden files included.
hist.cit15.0.bravo: A .historique_fictif and a config.ini… Secrets love places like these.
hist.cit15.0.adulte: The shell history (~/.bash_history) keeps everything typed, including a password written in a command. Here it is a fake history.
hist.cit15.1.dit: Search the whole box for the word mot_de_passe (password).
hist.cit15.1.bravo: Two plain-text secrets (game examples): one in the history, one in the config. They are the flags!
hist.cit15.1.adulte: Forgotten plain-text secrets (config files, histories, backups) are among the most frequent leaks; tools scan for them automatically before each release.
hist.cit15.2.dit: Hand in both flags (replace ? with a flag, once each).
hist.cit15.2.bravo: Investigation done. Rampart: erase what's lying around, then CHANGE the secret.
hist.cit15.2.adulte: A leaked secret is lost, even if you erase it afterwards: it must be changed (rotation).
hist.cit15.3.dit: Erase the fake history that keeps the secret.
hist.cit15.3.adulte: To avoid writing a secret into the history: let the program ask for it (without showing it), or use a secrets manager.
hist.cit15.4.dit: Change the drawbridge secret (the Citadel makes a new example).
hist.cit15.4.bravo: New secret, stored as 600. The old flag no longer works: try it and see!
hist.cit15.4.adulte: Rotation: generate a new secret, store it protected (600), invalidate the old one. The game only invents examples.
hist.cit15.5.dit: Call the inspector for the secrets box.
hist.cit15.5.bravo: Three boxes mastered! Only the great wave remains.
hist.cit15.5.adulte: The inspector checks: history erased, config.ini closed to others, secret changed.
hist.cit16.0.dit: Before the wave: which doors of your computer are open? (Read-only.)
hist.cit16.0.bravo: Each LISTEN line is a door that listens. A firewall is the list of doors we leave open, and to whom.
hist.cit16.0.adulte: ss -tln lists listening TCP ports; 127.0.0.1 = this machine only, 0.0.0.0 = the whole network. We only read: setting the real firewall (nftables) needs root.
hist.cit16.1.dit: Start the great training wave (everything is fake, everything stays in the Citadel).
hist.cit16.1.bravo: 🌊 Glitches everywhere, a ghost, a secret left open! Use everything you know, then check the board.
hist.cit16.1.adulte: The wave combines C2 (find -delete), C4 (ps/kill) and a leak (chmod 600). It's a “blue team” exercise: defending your own ground.
hist.cit16.2.dit: When you've fixed everything, check the guard board: everything must be green.
hist.cit16.2.bravo: Wave pushed back! The Citadel's towers light up one by one.
hist.cit16.2.adulte: Defending is a loop: detect (logs, board), respond (stop, erase, close), restore, then verify.
cit.f.utilisateurs.enfant: Every resident of the computer has a number and belongs to clubs: groups.
cit.f.utilisateurs.grands: An account = a uid; a group = a gid; /etc/passwd and /etc/group describe them. chown changes the owner (root only).
cit.f.utilisateurs.limite: A “club” can contain programs, not only people (www-data, systemd…).
cit.f.utilisateurs.idee: “Being admin is better for everything”: false, you work as a normal account and only ask for root rights when needed.
cit.f.umask.enfant: The mask decides the locks of newborn files.
cit.f.umask.grands: umask removes bits from the default rights (666 files, 777 folders): mode = default AND NOT mask.
cit.f.umask.limite: The mask doesn't touch existing files; it never adds a right.
cit.f.umask.idee: “umask 777 gives all rights”: false, it removes them all.
cit.f.journaux.enfant: The guard's register notes who came, when, and whether it worked.
cit.f.journaux.grands: Logs (/var/log, journalctl) are read with tail, grep, cut, sort | uniq -c: counting failures per address reveals brute force.
cit.f.journaux.limite: The game's register is invented; real logs come in a thousand formats and can be erased by an intruder.
cit.f.journaux.idee: “If the logs are empty, nothing happened”: false, nothing may have been recorded, or everything erased.
cit.f.find_newer.enfant: We set a marker, then ask: what has changed since?
cit.f.find_newer.grands: find -newer f compares modification time with f's; -name filters by pattern; -delete erases what is found.
cit.f.find_newer.limite: A date is easy to change (touch): it helps an investigation but proves nothing on its own.
cit.f.find_newer.idee: “-newer means created after”: false, it's the last modification time.
cit.f.cheval.enfant: A Trojan horse looks like a present but hides a trap: read before you run.
cit.f.cheval.grands: A script only runs if it is executable (x) or given to an interpreter; reading (cat, grep) then removing x (chmod -x) neutralises the trap.
cit.f.cheval.limite: A real trap may be hidden (encoded, downloaded later): when in doubt, don't run it at all.
cit.f.cheval.idee: “An antivirus is enough, no need to read”: false, many traps are not recognised by any antivirus.
cit.f.processus_suspects.enfant: Programs working in secret tire the computer; find them with ps and stop them with kill.
cit.f.processus_suspects.grands: ps aux lists all processes (user, PID, %CPU, command); kill PID sends SIGTERM. A process name can lie (exec -a).
cit.f.processus_suspects.limite: The game's ghosts only sleep; a real malicious process may restart itself or hide better.
cit.f.processus_suspects.idee: “kill destroys the program”: false, it stops one run; the program file stays.
cit.f.empreinte.enfant: Every file has a fingerprint: if the file changes, the fingerprint changes.
cit.f.empreinte.grands: SHA-256 gives 256 bits (64 hex digits); sha256sum -c checks a list of fingerprints. Used to verify a download or detect a change.
cit.f.empreinte.limite: Unlike a finger, the fingerprint doesn't say WHO changed the file; and if the intruder also changes the fingerprint list, it proves nothing.
cit.f.empreinte.idee: “A fingerprint is encryption: you can get the file back”: false, there's no going back.
cit.f.sauvegarde.enfant: A backup is a spare chest: you put a copy away BEFORE trouble comes.
cit.f.sauvegarde.grands: tar c (create), x (extract), t (list), z (gzip), f (file). 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 media, 1 offline; and test restoring.
cit.f.sauvegarde.limite: A backup in the same folder can get locked with the rest: a real spare copy lives elsewhere.
cit.f.sauvegarde.idee: “Paying the ransom gets the files back”: false, nothing guarantees it; only a backup does.
cit.f.chiffrement.enfant: Encrypting is locking a text in a chest: without the key, impossible to read.
cit.f.chiffrement.grands: openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2: symmetric AES encryption, key derived from the password by PBKDF2 with a salt; gpg --symmetric does the same.
cit.f.chiffrement.limite: The chest protects the contents, not the fact that it exists nor its size; and a weak key opens by guessing.
cit.f.chiffrement.idee: “Base64 encoding is encryption”: false, base64 decodes without a key.
cit.f.hameconnage.enfant: A fake message imitates someone you trust to steal a secret: compare, check elsewhere, give nothing.
cit.f.hameconnage.grands: Phishing: urgency, request for a secret, mismatched link or sender. diff and grep http help spot the differences.
cit.f.hameconnage.limite: A fake letter can be perfect (no typo, no weird link): it's the REQUEST for a secret that gives it away.
cit.f.hameconnage.idee: “The browser padlock proves the site is honest”: false, it only proves who you are talking to.
cit.f.phrase_de_passe.enfant: Several randomly drawn words make a secret that's easy to remember and very hard to guess. Never your real secret in a game!
cit.f.phrase_de_passe.grands: Entropy = words × log2(list size): 6 words from 7776 (Diceware) ≈ 77 bits. Length matters more than complexity (NIST SP 800-63B).
cit.f.phrase_de_passe.limite: The calculation only holds if the words are TRULY random; a known phrase (a song) falls immediately.
cit.f.phrase_de_passe.idee: “A short password with symbols is safer”: false, length wins.
cit.f.boites.enfant: A box is a little trap-world made by the game: you find the weakness, then you fix it.
cit.f.boites.grands: Inspired by Root-Me and Hack The Box, but fully simulated in your playground: enumerate (ls -la, find -perm, grep -r), then fix (chmod, erase, rotate).
cit.f.boites.limite: The game's boxes are easy and tidy; a real system is much bigger, and you never touch it without permission.
cit.f.boites.idee: “If I can find a flaw, I'm allowed to try anywhere”: false, the law forbids it outside what belongs to you.
cit.f.pare_feu.enfant: A firewall is the list of doors you leave open, and for whom.
cit.f.pare_feu.grands: ss -tln shows what is listening; the firewall (nftables, firewalld) filters who can reach it. Fewer open services = smaller attack surface.
cit.f.pare_feu.limite: A firewall doesn't protect against a trap you run yourself, nor a password given to a fake mail carrier.
cit.f.pare_feu.idee: “With a firewall I'm protected from everything”: false, it's one layer among many.
