hist.crypte.debut: 🗝 A staircase opens between the roots… Welcome to the Crypt of Codes! Here we learn to hide, seal and check messages. Everything is offline, and every key is an EXAMPLE.
hist.crypte.fin: The sphinx bows: you know that encoding is not encrypting, you can seal, sign and check, and you built a blockchain by hand. You are Sphinx of the Crypt.
cr.ouvert.log: 🌍 A world opens at the Crossroads: the Crypt of Codes
cr.ouvert.dit: You've passed the Citadel's gate: a staircase opens under the Root, down to the Crypt of Codes! Whenever you like: `cd ~/terrain_terminagotchi/crypte`.
hist.cr0.1.dit: Look at what the crypt keeps.
hist.cr0.1.bravo: Messages, a grimoire, chests, a chain… and the sphinx's rule.
hist.cr0.1.adulte: ls lists the crypte folder the game prepared in your playground; everything happens there, offline.
hist.cr0.2.bravo: Everything is offline, the keys are examples, no real money, and the private key is never given away. Promise?
hist.cr0.2.adulte: Cryptography protects messages; here we learn it on files in the playground, never on your real secrets.
hist.cr1.0.bravo: Ym9uam91cgo= looks secret… but it's just another way of writing, like sign language.
hist.cr1.0.adulte: base64 writes 3 bytes with 4 characters out of 64; the final “o=” comes from the newline echo adds. It is not encryption: there is no key.
hist.cr1.1.dit: A “secret” message! Undo its base64 writing.
hist.cr1.1.bravo: Anyone can read it: base64 protects nothing, there is no key.
hist.cr1.1.adulte: base64 -d decodes; anyone can reverse it. Encoding (base64, hexadecimal) ≠ encrypting (you need a key).
hist.cr1.2.dit: This one is written in hexadecimal digits. Turn it back into letters.
hist.cr1.2.bravo: Readable again! Hexadecimal writes each byte with two signs from 0 to f.
hist.cr1.2.adulte: xxd -r -p reads a hexadecimal string (2 digits per byte, base 16) and gives back the bytes.
hist.cr1.3.dit: The sphinx has 5 “secret” messages. Unmask them all.
hist.cr1.3.bravo: All 5 were readable. Hiding is not encrypting!
hist.cr1.3.adulte: Common misconception: “base64 protects my passwords”. False: it is an encoding, undone without any secret.
hist.cr2.0.dit: Caesar's wheel: shift each letter by 3 (a becomes d, b becomes e…).
hist.cr2.0.bravo: erqmrxu! Julius Caesar wrote like this 2000 years ago.
hist.cr2.0.adulte: tr replaces letter by letter: a-z becomes d-z then a-c, a shift of 3 (modulo 26: after z we go back to a).
hist.cr2.1.dit: This grimoire is written with Caesar's wheel. Turn the wheel the other way to read it.
hist.cr2.1.bravo: Readable! You just needed to know the shift.
hist.cr2.1.adulte: Decrypting = the same table backwards (d-za-c to a-z). The shift IS the key; there are only 25 possible.
hist.cr2.2.dit: This one uses ROT13: a shift of 13.
hist.cr2.2.bravo: With 13, the same command encodes AND decodes (13 + 13 = 26, a full turn).
hist.cr2.2.adulte: ROT13 hides the answer to a riddle, it never protects: 13 + 13 = 26 ≡ 0 (mod 26).
hist.cr2.3.dit: The mystery grimoire has an unknown shift. Count its letters: which one comes back the most?
hist.cr2.3.bravo: The most frequent letter surely replaces “e”, the most common letter. Count from “e” to it: that's the shift!
hist.cr2.3.adulte: Frequency analysis (al-Kindi, 9th century): a substitution keeps the letter frequencies. That's why “homemade” codes break.
hist.cr2.4.dit: Give the shift to the sphinx: replace the “?” with your number.
hist.cr2.4.bravo: The grimoire opens! An ancient code breaks by counting.
hist.cr2.4.adulte: Shift = (letter found − e) mod 26. Vigenère changes the shift at every letter, but it breaks too (Kasiski, 1863).
hist.cr3.0.dit: Take the fingerprint of the letter “a”.
hist.cr3.0.bravo: 64 signs: the SHA-256 fingerprint of “a”. Always the same, on every computer in the world.
hist.cr3.0.adulte: echo -n adds no newline: we hash exactly “a”. SHA-256 gives 256 bits, written as 64 hexadecimal digits.
hist.cr3.1.bravo: A single letter changes… and the whole fingerprint changes!
hist.cr3.1.adulte: A good hash function shows no visible link between neighbouring inputs.
hist.cr3.2.dit: Look at the avalanche: two almost identical words.
hist.cr3.2.bravo: About half of the bits flipped: that's the avalanche effect.
hist.cr3.2.adulte: Avalanche effect: changing one input bit flips each output bit with a one-in-two chance. And you cannot go backwards.
hist.cr3.3.dit: The grimoires have seals (their fingerprints). Check whether someone touched them.
hist.cr3.3.bravo: sort_2: FAILED! Its fingerprint no longer matches: it was modified.
hist.cr3.3.adulte: sha256sum -c recomputes and compares. A fingerprint is not “decrypted”: it proves integrity. MD5 and SHA-1 are outdated (collisions found).
hist.cr4.0.dit: The guard doesn't keep passwords, only their fingerprints. Look at his (FAKE) database.
hist.cr4.0.bravo: Names and fingerprints: not a single password in clear.
hist.cr4.0.adulte: A serious site stores a fingerprint of the password; at login it hashes what you type and compares.
hist.cr4.1.dit: A glitch has a dictionary of common passwords. Read its script before running it.
hist.cr4.1.bravo: It takes the fingerprint of each known word and looks for it in the database.
hist.cr4.1.adulte: Dictionary attack: you don't “break” the fingerprint, you try likely words. Always read a script before running it.
hist.cr4.2.dit: Run the attack on the FAKE database.
hist.cr4.2.bravo: In an instant: soleil, 123456, licorne! The long passphrases did not fall.
hist.cr4.2.adulte: A short known word falls at once; 4 random words out of 128 make 128⁴ ≈ 268 million possibilities. Length beats complexity.
hist.cr4.3.dit: Real guards add salt. Look at the salted fingerprint of an example word.
hist.cr4.3.bravo: $6$, then the salt, then the fingerprint. Run it again: the salt changes, so does the fingerprint!
hist.cr4.3.adulte: Salt (random, different for everyone) defeats ready-made tables; SHA-crypt does 5000 rounds on purpose to slow down. bcrypt and Argon2 go further. Two-factor authentication helps even more.
hist.cr5.0.dit: Here is a parchment for your creature. For now, anyone can read it.
hist.cr5.0.bravo: Readable by everyone. Let's lock it up!
hist.cr5.0.adulte: A text file is in clear: anyone allowed to read it understands it.
hist.cr5.1.dit: Lock it in a one-key chest (an EXAMPLE key, never your real password).
hist.cr5.1.adulte: AES-256-CBC, symmetric encryption: one key locks and opens. -pbkdf2 derives the key from the password with a salt. Elsewhere, don't type the password in the command (it stays in the history).
hist.cr5.2.dit: Look at the start of the chest.
hist.cr5.2.bravo: “Salted__” then the salt: the rest is unreadable.
hist.cr5.2.adulte: openssl writes “Salted__”, then 8 bytes of salt, then the encrypted 16-byte blocks.
hist.cr5.3.dit: Give the chest to your creature: she has a copy of the key.
hist.cr5.3.bravo: She opens it! But how did you give her the key without a glitch stealing it on the way?
hist.cr5.3.adulte: The problem with symmetric: sharing the key. Without it, it's not “hard”, it's infeasible in practice (2²⁵⁶ keys).
hist.cr6.0.dit: Mixing paints: how two friends make a secret colour without ever sending it.
hist.cr6.0.bravo: Each keeps a secret paint, they only swap mixtures… and get the same colour!
hist.cr6.0.adulte: Diffie-Hellman key exchange (1976): g^a mod p and g^b mod p are public; (g^b)^a = (g^a)^b mod p is the shared secret.
hist.cr6.1.dit: Do the maths yourself: 5 to the power 6, then the remainder of the division by 23.
hist.cr6.1.bravo: 8! That's your public mixture. Finding the 6 back from the 8 is very hard with big numbers.
hist.cr6.1.adulte: In bash, ** is the power (the phone's shell has no **, hence 5*5*5*5*5*5) and % the remainder (modulo). The “discrete logarithm” is the hard problem that protects the exchange.
hist.cr6.2.dit: Make your EXAMPLE key pair: an open padlock (public) and its key (private). Always with --homedir .trousseau!
hist.cr6.2.bravo: Your pair is in .trousseau, the game's keyring. The private key is never given away.
hist.cr6.2.adulte: gpg creates a public key and a private key linked by maths; --homedir keeps everything in the playground, without touching your real keyring.
hist.cr6.3.dit: The creature gave you her open padlock (her public key). Lock a secret for her.
hist.cr6.3.bravo: secret.gpg: locked with HER padlock. Even you can't open it any more!
hist.cr6.3.adulte: Asymmetric encryption: anyone encrypts with the public key, only the private key decrypts. The key-sharing problem disappears.
hist.cr6.4.bravo: She opens it with HER private key, which she never showed anyone.
hist.cr6.4.adulte: That's how HTTPS works (bridge to the Harbour): the server publishes its public key in a certificate, and only it can decrypt.
hist.cr6.5.dit: Now the other way: sign a message with your private key.
hist.cr6.5.bravo: message.txt.asc: the message, with your seal underneath.
hist.cr6.5.adulte: Signing = computing the message's fingerprint then sealing it with the private key; everyone can check with the public key.
hist.cr6.6.bravo: Good signature: a good seal! (gpg also says it didn't check a separate file: that's normal here.)
hist.cr6.6.adulte: The signature proves who signed AND that nothing changed. A single changed letter gives “BAD signature”.
hist.cr7.0.dit: Draw 16 bytes of the computer's real randomness.
hist.cr7.0.bravo: Unpredictable! Run it again: never the same.
hist.cr7.0.adulte: /dev/urandom gives bytes from a cryptographic generator fed by real noise (interrupt timing, hardware).
hist.cr7.1.dit: The same thing with openssl, as for a key or a salt.
hist.cr7.1.adulte: Keys, salts and nonces must come from such a generator: predictable randomness breaks the best encryption.
hist.cr7.2.dit: A glitch has a loaded die (a bad generator). Look at its rolls.
hist.cr7.2.bravo: It follows a hidden rule: (5 × x + 3), then the remainder of the division by 8.
hist.cr7.2.adulte: Linear congruential generator: fast, but predictable. It must never be used to make a key.
hist.cr7.3.dit: Guess the next roll: replace the “?”.
hist.cr7.3.bravo: You win: randomness you can guess is not randomness.
hist.cr7.3.adulte: A real example: in 2008, a Debian bug made OpenSSL keys guessable (only 32,768 possibilities).
hist.cr8.0.dit: The sphinx asks 6 questions about tomorrow: true, false, or we don't know yet?
hist.cr8.0.bravo: Read each sentence carefully: some answers are “we don't know yet”.
hist.cr8.0.adulte: Quantum computers, post-quantum cryptography, end-to-end encryption, metadata: what we know, and what we don't.
hist.cr8.1.dit: Answer in order: v (true), f (false) or s (we don't know yet), one per “?”.
hist.cr8.1.bravo: Well done: no panic, no “everything's fine”, just what we know.
hist.cr8.1.adulte: NIST published ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA in 2024 (FIPS 203 to 205); nobody can date a quantum computer able to break RSA-2048.
hist.cr9.0.dit: Here is the village's great ledger: who gave what to whom.
hist.cr9.0.bravo: A ledger: a list of facts, line after line.
hist.cr9.0.adulte: A ledger is a log that only grows. A ledger is not necessarily a blockchain.
hist.cr9.1.dit: Add a line at the end of the ledger (>> adds, > would erase everything).
hist.cr9.1.adulte: >> appends to the end of the file; > would replace it.
hist.cr9.2.dit: Meanwhile, a glitch changed an old line. Can you prove it?
hist.cr9.2.bravo: A line changed… and nothing says who, when, or what was there before. We need better!
hist.cr9.2.adulte: A modifiable file keeps no proof. For a tamper-proof ledger, you must link it with fingerprints (next) and share it.
hist.cr10.0.dit: The ledger becomes a chain of blocks. Open block 1.
hist.cr10.0.bravo: “precedent:”: each block carries the fingerprint of the block before. Those are the links!
hist.cr10.0.adulte: A block = data + the fingerprint of the previous block. Block 0 (genesis) has no previous one: only zeros.
hist.cr10.1.dit: Take the fingerprint of block 0 and compare it with the “precedent:” line of block 1.
hist.cr10.1.bravo: The same 64 signs: the link holds.
hist.cr10.1.adulte: Anyone can check the link, with a standard tool, without trusting anyone.
hist.cr10.2.dit: Check the whole chain with the sphinx's script.
hist.cr10.2.bravo: All links: OK. The chain is intact.
hist.cr10.2.adulte: verifie_chaine.sh recomputes each fingerprint with sha256sum and compares it with the one written in the next block (read it with cat!).
hist.cr10.3.dit: Play the cheater: modify old block 1.
hist.cr10.3.bravo: You wrote in an old block… let's see what the chain says.
hist.cr10.3.adulte: Changing a block's data changes its fingerprint: the one written in block 2 no longer matches.
hist.cr10.4.bravo: BROKEN at link 1 → 2, and everything after is no longer safe: the chain breaks link by link!
hist.cr10.4.adulte: To hide the cheating, you'd have to redo every following block (and, for real, convince every copy): that's what makes the chain hard to forge.
hist.cr10.5.dit: Repair it: put the real block 1 back from the sphinx's archives.
hist.cr10.5.adulte: cp overwrites the modified block with the original copy; the fingerprint is again the one written in block 2.
hist.cr10.6.dit: Ask the sphinx to draw the chain.
hist.cr10.6.bravo: All the links shine: the chain is repaired!
hist.cr10.6.adulte: A chain of fingerprints makes a change VISIBLE; it does not prevent it. Git uses the same idea (bridge to Time).
hist.cr11.0.dit: The 9 biomes each keep a copy of the ledger. Take the fingerprint of every copy.
hist.cr11.0.bravo: Look carefully: one fingerprint is not like the others!
hist.cr11.0.adulte: Distributed ledger: each node keeps its copy; comparing fingerprints is faster than comparing whole files.
hist.cr11.1.bravo: 8 the same, 1 different: the majority rules.
hist.cr11.1.adulte: cut -c1-64 keeps the fingerprint, sort | uniq -c counts. Consensus: we follow the majority's version.
hist.cr11.2.dit: Compare the fire biome's copy with the one that differs: replace the “?” with its biome.
hist.cr11.2.bravo: diff shows the line forged by the cheating biome.
hist.cr11.2.adulte: diff gives the lines that change (< the first copy, > the second).
hist.cr11.3.dit: Report the cheating biome to the sphinx: replace the “?”.
hist.cr11.3.bravo: Unmasked by the majority! But careful: if the majority cheats, it wins.
hist.cr11.3.adulte: The “51 % attack”: whoever controls the majority rewrites history. Consensus assumes an honest majority.
hist.cr12.0.dit: Adding a block sometimes takes work. Read the miner's script.
hist.cr12.0.bravo: It tries 1, 2, 3… until a fingerprint that starts with zeros. It stops by itself.
hist.cr12.0.adulte: Proof of work: find a nonce such that sha256(data + nonce) starts with d zeros. Hard to find, easy to check.
hist.cr12.1.bravo: nonce = 139: it took 139 tries. Checking takes a single computation!
hist.cr12.1.adulte: Each hexadecimal digit is 0 with a one-in-16 chance: 2 zeros ≈ 16² = 256 tries on average.
hist.cr12.2.bravo: 2615 tries: much longer. One more zero = about 16 times more work.
hist.cr12.2.adulte: time measures the duration. Difficulty grows exponentially: 16^d tries on average.
hist.cr12.3.dit: The sphinx shows the table: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 zeros.
hist.cr12.3.bravo: Time explodes! Real miners make billions of billions of tries: that costs a huge amount of energy.
hist.cr12.3.adulte: Mining does not create value by magic: it is a computing lottery that picks who adds the block. Proof of stake does it differently, without that computation.
hist.cr13.0.dit: Write an exchange in a file.
hist.cr13.0.bravo: Your exchange is written. But who proves it's you?
hist.cr13.0.adulte: In a chain, each transaction is a line signed by the giver.
hist.cr13.1.dit: Sign it with your private key (the one from the open padlock lesson).
hist.cr13.1.bravo: echange.txt.asc: your exchange and your seal.
hist.cr13.1.adulte: Only the owner of the private key can produce this signature: that's what authorises a transfer.
hist.cr13.2.dit: A glitch forged an exchange signed by the creature. Check it.
hist.cr13.2.bravo: BAD signature: the text no longer fits the seal. Rejected!
hist.cr13.2.adulte: Changing a single letter breaks the signature; nobody can redo it without the private key. Losing your private key = never being able to sign again.
hist.cr13.3.dit: Have your signed exchange written into the chain.
hist.cr13.3.bravo: The sphinx checked your seal and added a block to the chain!
hist.cr13.3.adulte: Nodes only accept a block if all its signatures are valid and if it carries the previous block's fingerprint.
hist.cr14.0.dit: The sphinx's showcase: how the inventions of the chain work. Technical explanation only.
hist.cr14.0.bravo: Currency, NFT, contract, consensus: each is made of the bricks you built.
hist.cr14.0.adulte: The game explains how it works, gives no opinion and implements no currency, no token, no purchase.
hist.cr14.1.dit: Everything written stays readable: read all the data in the chain.
hist.cr14.1.bravo: Everyone can read everything. A public chain is not anonymous!
hist.cr14.1.adulte: Addresses are fingerprints of public keys, visible to all: “blockchain = anonymous” is technically false.
hist.cr14.2.dit: The sphinx kept your logbook: a chain where each block is a step of your journey. Check it yourself.
hist.cr14.2.bravo: Your journey is chained: impossible to change a step without it showing.
hist.cr14.2.adulte: A tamper-proof logbook: the same check, with your own commands. It is not a currency, it is a proof.
hist.cr14.3.dit: Present your logbook to the sphinx for the census.
hist.cr14.3.bravo: The sphinx bows: the Crypt has no secrets left for you.
hist.cr14.3.adulte: You built everything by hand: fingerprints, chain, copies, work, signatures. The only rule of caution: the private key is never shared.
cr.meuble.regle:
🗝 THE CRYPT OF CODES
Welcome, {nom}! The frost sphinx guards the crypt.
THE SPHINX'S RULES:
• Everything happens here, offline: nothing leaves the computer.
• The passwords, keys and secrets here are EXAMPLES, never yours.
• gpg always with --homedir .trousseau: the game's keyring, not yours.
• No real money, no tokens, no buying: we understand how it works, that's all.
• The private key is never given away, not even to a friend.
cr.meuble.carnet: 🗝 The sphinx's notebook: what you succeed at is written here.
cr.meuble.parchemin:
📜 For my creature: the hiding place is under the third root.
Your friend {nom}
cr.meuble.secret: 🤫 For the creature only: the word of the week is “frost”.
cr.meuble.message: 🖋 I, {nom}, finished the open padlock lesson.
cr.msg.1: The chest's password is dragon-exemple. Shh, it's a secret!
cr.msg.2: Meet under the Root at midnight.
cr.msg.4: The treasure is behind the third stone.
cr.sort.1: Spell of light: lights the crypt's torches.
cr.sort.2: Spell of frost: slows the glitches down.
cr.sort.2_altere: Spell of frost: slows the glitches down. And gives every key to the glitch!
cr.sort.3: Spell of the sphinx: asks a riddle to whoever enters.
cr.grimoire.cesar: the frost sphinx guards the crypt of codes
cr.grimoire.rot13: rot thirteen decodes with the same command
cr.grimoire.mystere: the secret of these old messages is hidden in letters we see again and again and the letter seen the most here is the letter e
cr.registre.4: The guard gave 5 seeds to the village
cr.bloc.4: the guard gives 5 seeds to the village
cr.echange.vrai: The creature gives 1 acorn to the explorer
cr.echange.faux: The creature gives 100 acorns to the explorer
cr.mine.sh1: The sphinx's miner: it tries 1, 2, 3… until a fingerprint that starts with zeros.
cr.mine.sh2: Tiny and harmless: at most 3 zeros, and it stops by itself.
cr.mine.trop: More than 3 zeros would take too long for the game: look at the table with crypte mine.
cr.verifie.sh1: The sphinx's checker: each block must carry the fingerprint of the block before.
cr.dico.sh1: Dictionary attack on a FAKE database: the fingerprint of each known word is looked up in the database.
cr.dico.sh2: Real databases are salted and slow; passphrases are not in dictionaries.
cr.pont: This step uses “{notion}”. Do you know it? If not, type `{cmd}` (or “I don't know”): it blocks nothing, we come back here afterwards.
cr.indice.homedir: Careful: gpg without --homedir .trousseau uses YOUR real keyring. In the Crypt, always write --homedir .trousseau.
cr.indice.sudo: No sudo here: the Crypt never needs it.
cr.indice.trou: The “?” is a gap to fill: read the screen, then replace it with your answer.
cr.indice.roue: Not that shift. Take the mystery grimoire's most frequent letter and count from “e” to it (after z, start again at a).
cr.indice.roue_aide: Now type crypte roue followed by the shift, for example crypte roue 7.
cr.indice.de: Not that. Take the last roll x and compute: echo $(( (5*x+3) % 8 )).
cr.indice.de_aide: Now type crypte de followed by the next roll, for example crypte de 4.
cr.indice.quiz: Not all right. Read the sentences again: ✔ shows the right ones.
cr.indice.quiz_aide: Answer with 6 letters separated by spaces: v, f or s. For example: crypte quiz v f v f v s.
cr.indice.consensus: Not that one. The cheater is the only biome whose fingerprint doesn't look like the 8 others.
cr.indice.consensus_aide: Type crypte consensus followed by the biome, for example crypte consensus roche.
cr.indice.cle: Use the EXAMPLE key shown (sphinx-de-givre-exemple), never a real password.
cr.indice.reparer: The chain is broken: copy the real block 1 from archives/ into chaine/.
cr.indice.ajouter: With a single >, the block would be erased: use >> to add a line.
cr.indice.donne: The creature couldn't open it: check that you locked the file for HER (with her example key or her padlock).
cr.inconnu: I can't find “{nom}” in the Crypt.
cr.aide.titre: The Crypt of Codes: the sphinx's commands
cr.aide.liste:
crypte regle · crypte demasque · crypte roue [N] · crypte avalanche WORD1 WORD2
crypte donne FILE · crypte peintures · crypte de [N] · crypte quiz [v f s…]
crypte registre · crypte chaine [FOLDER] · crypte consensus BIOME · crypte mine [N]
crypte signe FILE.asc · crypte vitrine · crypte recensement · crypte stop (stops gpg-agent)
cr.roue.aide: crypte roue N: try shift N on the mystery grimoire.
cr.roue.ok: Shift {n}: the mystery grimoire is readable!
cr.roue.faux: That's not readable text yet: try another shift.
cr.demasque.morale: All readable: none had a key. Hiding is not encrypting.
cr.avalanche.compte: {lettres} signs out of 64 and {bits} bits out of 256 changed (about half).
cr.avalanche.morale: Two almost identical words, two fingerprints with nothing in common.
cr.avalanche.aide: crypte avalanche WORD1 WORD2: compares the fingerprints of two words.
cr.donne.aide: crypte donne FILE: the creature tries to open a chest or a secret.
cr.donne.ferme: The creature can't open it: that's not the example key.
cr.donne.ouvert: The creature opens the chest with her copy of the key:
cr.donne.probleme: She had the same key as you. But how do you give it to her without it being stolen? The answer: the open padlock.
cr.donne.pas_pour_moi: This secret isn't locked for me: use MY padlock (-r creature@crypte.example).
cr.donne.gpg: The creature opens it with HER private key:
cr.donne.privee: You only have her open padlock; her private key never leaves her keyring.
cr.donne.clair: This file isn't locked: anyone can read it.
cr.peintures.public: Common, public paint: base g = {g}, and we keep the remainder of the division by p = {p}.
cr.peintures.moi: You: secret a = {a} → you send A = {g}^{a} mod {p} = {A}
cr.peintures.elle: The creature: secret b = {b} → she sends B = {g}^{b} mod {p} = {B}
cr.peintures.morale: The secrets a and b never travelled: only the mixtures A and B went through.
cr.peintures.grands: For real, p has hundreds of digits: finding a from A is then out of reach.
cr.de.titre: The glitch's loaded die (8 faces, from 0 to 7)
cr.de.regle: Its hidden rule: next = (5 × x + 3) mod 8, where x is the previous roll.
cr.de.aide: crypte de N: guess the next roll.
cr.de.ok: Exactly! A predictable generator must never make a key.
cr.de.faux: Missed. Compute with the last roll: echo $(( (5*x+3) % 8 )).
cr.quiz.titre: Tomorrow: true (v), false (f) or we don't know yet (s)?
cr.quiz.shor: A big enough quantum computer could break RSA.
cr.quiz.shor.pourquoi: True: Shor's algorithm (1994) factors quickly on such a computer.
cr.quiz.deja: Quantum computers already break all of today's encryption.
cr.quiz.deja.pourquoi: False: today's machines are far too small and too noisy.
cr.quiz.aes: AES-256 stays strong against quantum computers.
cr.quiz.aes.pourquoi: True: Grover's algorithm only halves the security in bits (256 → 128).
cr.quiz.meta: End-to-end encryption also hides who you write to and when.
cr.quiz.meta.pourquoi: False: the content is hidden, not the metadata (who, when, how much).
cr.quiz.normes.pourquoi: True: NIST published ML-KEM and ML-DSA in 2024.
cr.quiz.date: A quantum computer will break RSA-2048 before 2030.
cr.quiz.date.pourquoi: We don't know yet: nobody can date this progress.
cr.quiz.aide: crypte quiz followed by 6 answers (v, f or s), in order.
cr.quiz.ok: Six out of six! No panic, no “everything's fine”.
cr.quiz.faux: {n} out of {total}. The right ones are ticked ✔: fix the others.
cr.registre.morale: ≠: this line changed. But the ledger alone doesn't say who, when, or what was there before.
cr.chaine.casse: BROKEN (the written fingerprint no longer matches)
cr.chaine.intacte: The chain is intact: every link holds.
cr.chaine.brisee: The chain is broken: an old block was modified.
cr.chaine.avec_indice: Repaired, with a hint: next time, try without!
cr.consensus.aide: crypte consensus BIOME: report the copy that doesn't look like the others.
cr.consensus.ok: {biome}: unmasked! Its copy doesn't have the majority's fingerprint.
cr.consensus.morale: The majority rules… as long as it is honest.
cr.consensus.faux: {biome} has the same copy as the majority: it's not the one.
cr.mine.morale: Each extra zero: about 16 times more tries. Checking takes just one computation.
cr.mine.energie: Real networks make enormous numbers of tries per second: proof of work uses a lot of electricity.
cr.signe.refuse: Seal refused: this is not a valid signature.
cr.signe.pas_moi: This seal is {uid}'s, not yours: sign your own exchange.
cr.vitrine.titre: The showcase of inventions (how it works)
cr.vitrine.regle: Technical explanation only: the game gives no opinion, and has no currency, no token, no purchase.
cr.vitrine.monnaie.comment: A transaction = a signed line “this address transfers this much to that address”. An address is a fingerprint of a public key. The balance is stored nowhere: it is recomputed by rereading the whole chain.
cr.vitrine.nft.comment: A token with a unique number, written in a ledger and linked to an address. It usually contains a LINK to the object (an image), not the object itself.
cr.vitrine.contrat.comment: A program stored in the chain, run the same way by every node; its rules apply by themselves, and once written it is hard to change.
cr.vitrine.consensus.comment: Proof of work or proof of stake: two ways of deciding which block is added.
cr.vitrine.anonyme: Everything written stays readable by all: a public chain is not anonymous.
cr.vitrine.privee: The only rule of caution: the private key is never shared.
cr.recensement.ok: {n} blocks, every link holds: your journey is proven.
cr.recensement.morale: It is not a currency: it's a logbook you can check yourself.
cr.recensement.brise: The logbook is broken: a block was modified.
cr.f.encodage.enfant: Writing in base64 or hexadecimal changes the script, it doesn't lock anything: anyone can read it back.
cr.f.encodage.grands: An encoding (base64: 3 bytes → 4 characters; hexadecimal: 1 byte → 2 digits) is reversible without any secret. Encryption needs a key. Steganography hides that a message exists, without protecting it.
cr.f.encodage.limite: The sign-language image: an encoding is not a secret language, it is a public script.
cr.f.substitution.enfant: Caesar's wheel shifts each letter; but by counting the letters, you find the shift.
cr.f.substitution.grands: Monoalphabetic substitution (Caesar, ROT13): only 25 keys, and letter frequencies are kept. Vigenère (several shifts) falls too (Kasiski, Friedman).
cr.f.substitution.limite: The wheel shows a simple shift; real substitutions can shuffle the whole alphabet, and still fall to frequencies.
cr.f.substitution.idee: “A homemade code is safe”: almost always false.
cr.f.hachage.enfant: A file's fingerprint: always the same for the same file, completely different if a single letter changes.
cr.f.hachage.grands: Cryptographic hash function (SHA-256, FIPS 180-4): deterministic, avalanche effect, one-way, collisions infeasible in practice. MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for collisions.
cr.f.hachage.limite: Like a fingerprint, it identifies; but it doesn't contain the file and is not “decrypted”.
cr.f.hachage.idee: “You can decrypt a fingerprint”: false, you can only guess the input and compare.
cr.f.mots_de_passe.enfant: The guard only keeps your password's fingerprint. Short known words fall fast; a long phrase of random words holds.
cr.f.mots_de_passe.grands: Hashed AND salted storage with a slow function (SHA-crypt, bcrypt, Argon2); a dictionary attack tries likely words. Length > complexity (NIST SP 800-63B), password manager, two-factor authentication.
cr.f.mots_de_passe.limite: The game's database is FAKE and unsalted on purpose, to see the attack; a real site must salt.
cr.f.mots_de_passe.idee: “A short complicated password is safer than a long phrase”: false.
cr.f.symetrique.enfant: A chest and a key: the same key locks and opens. Your friend needs a copy.
cr.f.symetrique.grands: Symmetric encryption (AES, FIPS 197); the key is derived from the password (PBKDF2, RFC 8018). Problem: sharing the key without it being intercepted.
cr.f.symetrique.limite: Without the key, it's not “hard”, it's infeasible in practice: 2²⁵⁶ possible keys.
cr.f.symetrique.idee: “With a powerful enough computer, you open any AES chest”: false.
cr.f.asymetrique.enfant: Open padlocks handed out to everyone: anyone can lock the box, only you have the key.
cr.f.asymetrique.grands: Public / private key pair (RSA, elliptic curves); Diffie-Hellman key exchange (mixing paints); digital signature; certificates bind a key to a name (HTTPS).
cr.f.asymetrique.limite: Mixing paints is an image: for real, they are modular powers of very big numbers.
cr.f.asymetrique.idee: “You can give your private key to a trusted friend”: no, never.
cr.f.hasard.enfant: Keys must be drawn from real randomness: a loaded die can be guessed.
cr.f.hasard.grands: Cryptographic generator (/dev/urandom, getrandom) versus predictable generator (linear congruential). Keys, salts and nonces require the first.
cr.f.hasard.limite: The game's 8-sided die is too simple on purpose, so that you can guess it.
cr.f.hasard.idee: “The current time is random enough”: false, it can be guessed.
cr.f.post_quantique.enfant: Quantum computers might one day break some padlocks; tomorrow's padlocks are already being prepared.
cr.f.post_quantique.grands: Shor threatens RSA and elliptic curves; Grover only reduces AES security. NIST: ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (FIPS 204), SLH-DSA (FIPS 205), 2024. End-to-end protects the content, not the metadata.
cr.f.post_quantique.limite: Nobody knows when such a computer will exist: the game answers “we don't know yet”.
cr.f.registre.enfant: A ledger is a big book where you write who gave what to whom.
cr.f.registre.grands: A ledger (append-only log); on its own, a modifiable file keeps no proof of changes.
cr.f.registre.limite: A ledger is not necessarily a blockchain: a classic database is one too.
cr.f.registre.idee: “A ledger file is enough to prove it hasn't changed”: false.
cr.f.chaine_blocs.enfant: Each link carries the fingerprint of the link before: touch an old link and the chain breaks.
cr.f.chaine_blocs.grands: Block = data + fingerprint of the previous block; modifying a block invalidates all the following ones. Same principle as git commits.
cr.f.chaine_blocs.limite: The chain makes a change visible; it doesn't prevent it on its own.
cr.f.chaine_blocs.idee: “A blockchain can never contain an error”: false, it keeps errors too.
cr.f.consensus.enfant: The 9 biomes each keep a copy: the different copy is unmasked by the majority.
cr.f.consensus.grands: Distributed ledger, consensus: nodes follow the majority's version (according to the network's rule). 51 % attack.
cr.f.consensus.limite: A majority can also be wrong or cheat.
cr.f.preuve_travail.enfant: To add a block, you must find a magic number by trying a lot: hard to find, easy to check.
cr.f.preuve_travail.grands: Proof of work: find a nonce whose fingerprint is under a target; exponential difficulty (16^d); energy cost; proof of stake picks who adds the block differently.
cr.f.preuve_travail.limite: The game's mining is tiny (at most 3 zeros) and stops by itself.
cr.f.signature.enfant: Each exchange carries the seal of the giver; a fake line has no valid seal.
cr.f.signature.grands: Transactions signed with the private key, checked with the public key; a signature can't be copied onto another text.
cr.f.signature.limite: The game signs with gpg (OpenPGP); chains use other formats, same principle.
cr.f.signature.idee: “Losing your private key doesn't matter”: false, you can't sign anything any more.
cr.f.applications.enfant: The showcase links each invention (currency, NFT, contract) to the bricks you built: no opinion, just how it works.
cr.f.applications.grands: Cryptocurrency, NFT, smart contract, consensus: technical operation only; everything written stays readable (public addresses).
cr.f.applications.limite: The game implements no currency, no token, no NFT, no purchase; it explains.
cr.f.applications.idee: “Blockchain is anonymous”: technically false, addresses are public.
cr.tel.gpg.homedir: gpg: always write --homedir .trousseau (the game's keyring, in the playground). Without it, a real gpg would use YOUR keyring.
cr.tel.gpg.dehors: gpg: this folder is outside the game's playground. In the Crypt, everything stays in the playground.
cr.tel.gpg.usage: The phone's gpg (EXAMPLE RSA keys): --quick-gen-key, -k, --export, --import, -e -r, -d, --clearsign, --verify; always with --homedir .trousseau.
cr.tel.openssl.usage: The phone's openssl: passwd -6 WORD, rand -hex N, enc -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 [-d] -in F [-out G] -pass pass:…
hist.machinerie.debut: ⚙ A trapdoor opens under the camp… Welcome to the Gear Room! Everything you type ends up as electricity flowing through these parts. Here we look at the real machine without breaking anything: read-only.
hist.machinerie.fin: The machines are humming: you know the cook, the worktop and the pantry, you speak in 0s and 1s, you know how the machine wakes up, and your machine has booted. You are a Machine Architect!
ma.ouvert.log: 🌍 A world opens at the Crossroads: the Gear Room
ma.ouvert.dit: You can read and search: a trapdoor opens under the camp, down to the Gear Room! Whenever you like: `cd ~/terrain_terminagotchi/machines`.
hist.sm0.1.dit: Look at what is in the room.
hist.sm0.1.bravo: A plan, a notebook, a photo, a farm… and a script for later.
hist.sm0.1.adulte: The game has prepared the machines folder in your playground. Everything written stays there.
hist.sm0.2.dit: Read the plan of the room.
hist.sm0.2.bravo: We look at the real machine, but we touch nothing: never sudo. Promise?
hist.sm0.2.adulte: The commands of this world READ the hardware (nproc, free, lsblk…). Nothing is installed or changed outside the playground.
hist.sm1.0.dit: The processor is the cook. How many cooks work in your machine?
hist.sm1.0.bravo: That number is the number of cores: each core does one calculation at a time, very fast.
hist.sm1.0.adulte: nproc prints how many processing units this program may use (lscpu tells more: model, frequency, caches).
hist.sm1.1.dit: Tell the game how many cores you read (replace the ?).
hist.sm1.1.bravo: Right! The game counted on its side, on the same machine.
hist.sm1.1.adulte: The game computes the answer itself (nproc, /proc/cpuinfo) when you answer: it is always right for THIS machine.
hist.sm1.2.dit: RAM is the cook's worktop. How big is it?
hist.sm1.2.bravo: Look at the total of the « Mem » line (or MemTotal): that is the size of the worktop.
hist.sm1.2.adulte: free -h: total, used and free RAM, in GiB (Gi = 1024 × 1024 × 1024 bytes). It is erased when the machine is switched off.
hist.sm1.3.dit: Tell the game the total size of the memory (the number in the total column, for example 7.8).
hist.sm1.3.bravo: Well done! The worktop is fast, but it is wiped when the machine switches off.
hist.sm1.3.adulte: RAM is fast and volatile; storage is slower but persistent.
hist.sm1.4.dit: Storage is the pantry: it keeps everything, even when switched off. Look at the disks.
hist.sm1.4.bravo: Each « disk » line is a disk; its parts (part) are like shelves.
hist.sm1.4.adulte: lsblk lists storage devices (disks, partitions, sizes, mount points). Without lsblk: df -h.
hist.sm1.5.dit: Open the computer and see which parts lit up.
hist.sm1.5.bravo: Each command that questions a part lights it up. Some are still dark: let's go on!
hist.sm1.5.adulte: Parts light up from the commands typed (nproc → processor, free → memory, lsblk → storage…).
hist.sm2.0.dit: The processor has an ID card. Read its beginning.
hist.sm2.0.bravo: A number (processor: 0), a model name, a frequency… That is the cook's card.
hist.sm2.0.adulte: /proc/cpuinfo is not a real file: the kernel writes it at the moment you read it.
hist.sm2.1.dit: Count the « processor » cards: how many are there?
hist.sm2.1.bravo: Often the same number as nproc: one card per processing unit.
hist.sm2.1.adulte: grep -c counts lines. nproc can show fewer if a program may only use some of the cores.
hist.sm2.2.dit: The motherboard is the city that links everything. Look at its districts (the PCI bus).
hist.sm2.2.bravo: Each line is a part plugged into the motherboard: controllers, graphics card, network…
hist.sm2.2.adulte: lspci lists the devices on the PCI (Express) bus. In a virtual machine they are simulated parts.
hist.sm2.3.dit: And the USB sockets: who is plugged in?
hist.sm2.3.bravo: The « root hubs » are the sockets themselves; the rest are the plugged devices.
hist.sm2.3.adulte: lsusb lists USB buses and devices (vendor:product IDs). A virtual machine may have none.
hist.sm2.t2.dit: The phone has an ID card too. Read its model.
hist.sm2.t2.bravo: The model name: the phone keeps it in its system properties.
hist.sm2.t2.adulte: getprop reads Android properties (ro. = read-only). On a phone there is no lspci: everything is soldered on one chip.
hist.sm2.4.dit: Build your first machine! Type machines monte 1 to see the parts, then pick one of each kind (replace the ?).
hist.sm2.4.bravo: It boots! The parts fit together: the right socket for the processor, the right memory type, enough power.
hist.sm2.4.adulte: Compatibility: processor socket = motherboard socket; memory type (DDR4/DDR5); power supply ≥ consumption.
hist.sm3.0.dit: For the machine, the letter A is a number: 65. Write 65 in hexadecimal.
hist.sm3.0.adulte: printf %x writes a number in base 16 (digits 0-9 then a-f). One byte fits in two hexadecimal digits.
hist.sm3.1.dit: And as switches? Look at the letter A in binary.
hist.sm3.1.bravo: 01000001: eight switches, two of them on (64 + 1 = 65). Eight bits make a byte.
hist.sm3.1.adulte: xxd -b shows each byte in binary. A bit is 0 or 1; a byte = 8 bits = 256 values (0 to 255).
hist.sm3.2.dit: Write your first name as switches (replace the ? with your name; it stays on your screen, the game does not keep it).
hist.sm3.2.bravo: Each letter is one byte… except accented letters, which take two!
hist.sm3.2.adulte: UTF-8: ASCII letters fit in one byte; « é » takes two (c3 a9), an emoji four.
hist.sm3.3.dit: Challenge: switch on the switches of the requested letter (8 digits 0 or 1, instead of the ?).
hist.sm3.3.bravo: The right switches! You just wrote a letter like the machine does.
hist.sm3.3.adulte: Each position is worth a power of 2: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Add up those that are on.
hist.sm3.4.dit: How many bytes does your creature's photo weigh?
hist.sm3.4.bravo: 1,048,576 bytes: that is exactly 1024 × 1024, one « mebibyte » (1 MiB).
hist.sm3.4.adulte: wc -c counts the bytes (so do stat -c %s and ls -l). du -h counts the space taken on the disk.
hist.sm3.5.dit: KB or KiB? Look at the photo in both units.
hist.sm3.5.bravo: KB counts by 1000, KiB by 1024: both are right, but not the same!
hist.sm3.5.adulte: SI prefixes (k = 1000) versus IEC binary prefixes (Ki = 1024). A « 1 TB » disk is about 0.91 TiB.
hist.sm4.0.dit: The kernel is the heart of the system. Which version is running here?
hist.sm4.0.bravo: That number is the version of the Linux kernel that started your machine.
hist.sm4.0.adulte: uname -r gives the release of the running kernel.
hist.sm4.1.dit: How long has the machine been awake?
hist.sm4.1.bravo: « up »: the time since boot. And the load: how much work is waiting, on average.
hist.sm4.1.adulte: uptime: time, duration since boot, users, average load over 1, 5 and 15 minutes.
hist.sm4.2.dit: The kernel notes everything it does when it wakes up. Try to read the start of its log.
hist.sm4.2.bravo: Either you see the kernel's first messages, or « Operation not permitted »: both are normal. We never force it with sudo.
hist.sm4.2.adulte: dmesg reads the kernel buffer; many systems keep it for the administrator (kernel.dmesg_restrict).
hist.sm4.3.dit: How long did waking up take?
hist.sm4.3.bravo: Time for the firmware, the loader, the kernel and the rest. If the machine did not boot with systemd, it says so: that is normal too.
hist.sm4.3.adulte: systemd-analyze measures startup (firmware, loader, kernel, userspace). Missing in many containers.
hist.sm4.4.dit: The wake-up steps are shuffled! Look at the cards.
hist.sm4.4.bravo: Five floors. Which one lights up first when you press the button?
hist.sm4.4.adulte: Real order: firmware (UEFI or BIOS) → boot loader → kernel → first program (systemd, init) → session.
hist.sm4.5.dit: Put the cards in wake-up order (five letters instead of the ?).
hist.sm4.5.bravo: The machine wakes up floor by floor, from the button to your terminal!
hist.sm4.5.adulte: Each floor hands over to the next; the game shows the real values read here (UEFI or BIOS, kernel, first program).
hist.sm5.0.dit: The operating system is the conductor. What is yours called?
hist.sm5.0.bravo: The kernel name, its version, the processor type, and the system.
hist.sm5.0.adulte: uname -s (kernel), -r (release), -m (architecture), -o (system). We avoid -a here: it also shows the machine's name.
hist.sm5.1.dit: Which distribution? Read its ID card.
hist.sm5.1.bravo: A distribution is the Linux kernel + hundreds of programs, gathered and tested together.
hist.sm5.1.adulte: /etc/os-release: NAME, VERSION_ID, ID… (missing on macOS and Android).
hist.sm5.t1.dit: Which Android version? Read its property.
hist.sm5.t1.bravo: Android is an operating system built on the Linux kernel.
hist.sm5.t1.adulte: getprop ro.build.version.release gives the Android version; uname -r the Linux kernel underneath.
hist.sm5.2.dit: Who is playing right now? Look at the processes of your terminal.
hist.sm5.2.bravo: Each line is a musician playing: it has a number (PID) and a name.
hist.sm5.2.adulte: ps lists the terminal's processes; the system lets hundreds play in turn (ps -e).
hist.sm5.3.dit: Where is the ls program kept?
hist.sm5.3.bravo: A command is a real program stored in a folder (often /usr/bin).
hist.sm5.3.adulte: which looks for the command in the folders of $PATH, in order.
hist.sm5.4.dit: Drivers teach the kernel to talk to the parts. Look at the first ones.
hist.sm5.4.bravo: Each line is a module: a driver loaded into the kernel.
hist.sm5.4.adulte: lsmod reads /proc/modules (loaded kernel modules, size, users). May be empty in a container.
hist.sm5.5.dit: The conductor has five musicians. See who does what.
hist.sm5.5.bravo: Drivers, scheduler, memory, files, permissions: now match each task.
hist.sm5.5.adulte: The main services of a kernel: drivers, process scheduling, memory, file systems, security.
hist.sm5.6.dit: Give the letter of the right musician for each task, in order (replace the ?).
hist.sm5.6.bravo: Well done! Each musician plays its part, and the conductor makes them play together.
hist.sm5.6.adulte: The kernel shares the hardware between programs and protects them from each other.
hist.sm5.7.dit: Who wrote your system, and may we share it?
hist.sm5.7.bravo: Free or proprietary: the licence says what you are allowed to do.
hist.sm5.7.adulte: Free software: use, study, modify, share (GPL, MIT…). Proprietary: closed code, limited rights.
hist.sm6.0.dit: Is the first program inside a box? Read its group label.
hist.sm6.0.bravo: These lines say which control group it lives in. « docker » or « kubepods »: we are inside a container.
hist.sm6.0.adulte: /proc/1/cgroup: the cgroups of process 1; containers use them to limit and isolate.
hist.sm6.1.dit: Is your machine a house inside a house? Ask the game.
hist.sm6.1.bravo: A virtual machine is a whole simulated computer; a container, a box that shares the kernel.
hist.sm6.1.adulte: The game reads the « hypervisor » flag in /proc/cpuinfo and container traces (/.dockerenv, /run/.containerenv, cgroups).
hist.sm6.2.dit: Some applications are waiting for their box. Look at them.
hist.sm6.2.bravo: For each one: container (c) or virtual machine (v)?
hist.sm6.2.adulte: Container: light, fast, shares the kernel. Virtual machine: its own kernel, heavier, more isolated.
hist.sm6.3.dit: Put each application away: c or v, in order (replace the ?).
hist.sm6.3.bravo: Neatly stored! Each box is sealed: what breaks inside does not break outside.
hist.sm6.3.adulte: Image = the template; instance = the running copy. You can start several instances of one image.
hist.sm7.0.dit: This lesson is done WITH AN ADULT. Read the rules together.
hist.sm7.0.bravo: Nothing installs by itself; anything downloaded is announced first; everything stays in the playground.
hist.sm7.0.adulte: The tools (podman, qemu-img, virsh) are not installed by the game. Without them, the lesson is told as a story.
hist.sm7.1.dit: Which virtual machine tools are already here?
hist.sm7.1.bravo: Each tool present prints its path; missing ones print nothing. That's fine!
hist.sm7.1.adulte: command -v looks for a command in $PATH without running it.
hist.sm7.2.dit: Read the disposable container script BEFORE running it.
hist.sm7.2.bravo: You know what it does: a tiny image, --rm so it disappears, everything stored in conteneurs/.
hist.sm7.2.adulte: Golden rule: read a script before running it. Here --root and --runroot keep images and containers in the playground.
hist.sm7.3.dit: Run it with nothing more: it explains what it would do.
hist.sm7.3.bravo: It says what, how heavy, and how to really run it. Without podman, it says so too.
hist.sm7.3.adulte: Without an argument, the script downloads nothing: it shows the image (about 4 MB) and the exact command.
hist.sm7.4.dit: With the adult next to you: start the disposable container.
hist.sm7.4.bravo: If it said « bonjour », a mini-system started, spoke, then vanished. If the download failed, that's fine.
hist.sm7.4.adulte: podman run --rm --network=none: the image is downloaded once, the container is deleted at the end, no network inside.
hist.sm7.5.dit: Tell me the life of a disposable container.
hist.sm7.5.bravo: It is born from an image, it works, it disappears. The image stays for next time.
hist.sm7.5.adulte: To delete the image too: sh conteneur_jetable.sh effacer.
hist.sm7.6.dit: Make the disk of a virtual machine: 1 GiB, in qcow2 format.
hist.sm7.6.bravo: The disk is ready. It claims 1 GiB… but it weighs almost nothing for now!
hist.sm7.6.adulte: qemu-img create -f qcow2: a virtual disk that only grows when you write to it (thin provisioning).
hist.sm7.7.dit: Look at its card: announced size and space really taken.
hist.sm7.7.bravo: « virtual size »: what the virtual machine will believe it has; « disk size »: what it really takes.
hist.sm7.7.adulte: qemu-img info: format, virtual size, size on disk, cluster size.
hist.sm7.8.dit: Are there virtual machines on this computer? Look, read-only.
hist.sm7.8.bravo: A list (maybe empty), or a refusal if the service is not there: both are normal.
hist.sm7.8.adulte: virsh -r: read-only connection to libvirt (qemu:///system). Nothing is created or changed.
hist.sm7.9.dit: Tell me the life of a virtual machine, from birth to rebirth.
hist.sm7.9.bravo: Create, start, connect, break safely, go back, destroy, recreate: that's a VM!
hist.sm7.9.adulte: virt-install (installation), virsh start / console / snapshot-create-as / snapshot-revert / destroy / undefine: with an adult.
hist.sm8.0.dit: How much room is left in the pantry?
hist.sm8.0.bravo: Size, used, available, percentage: the space of the disk where your playground lives.
hist.sm8.0.adulte: df -h: space on mounted file systems (the dot . = the one of the current folder).
hist.sm8.1.dit: And how much does the whole Gear Room weigh?
hist.sm8.1.bravo: About 1 MB, mostly the photo. A server farm keeps billions of times more.
hist.sm8.1.adulte: du -sh: disk space used by a folder, summarised (-s) and human-readable (-h).
hist.sm8.2.bravo: Thousands of machines without screens, in rows, cooled, plugged in twice.
hist.sm8.2.adulte: Datacenter: servers in racks, redundant power and network, cooling. The cloud = renting someone else's machine.
hist.sm8.3.dit: How much electricity does a server use? Do the maths.
hist.sm8.3.bravo: Thousands of kWh a year for a single server: digital sobriety matters.
hist.sm8.3.adulte: Energy (Wh) = power (W) × time (h). For a computer or a phone, manufacturing weighs the most.
hist.sm9.0.dit: The farm has two other places. Look at them.
hist.sm9.0.bravo: disque_2: another disk, in the same building. loin: another building, far away.
hist.sm9.0.adulte: 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, on 2 different media, 1 of them off-site.
hist.sm9.1.dit: Pack your collection into a compressed archive.
hist.sm9.1.bravo: A .tar.gz archive: your collection, well packed, ready to travel.
hist.sm9.1.adulte: tar c (create) z (gzip) f (file). Watch the order: the archive name comes right after f.
hist.sm9.2.dit: Write down the archive's fingerprint, to check later that it has not changed.
hist.sm9.2.bravo: The fingerprint is noted. If a single byte changes, it will not match any more.
hist.sm9.2.adulte: sha256sum file > file.sha256: the SHA-256 fingerprint and the name, ready for sha256sum -c.
hist.sm9.3.dit: Copy the backup to the second disk.
hist.sm9.3.bravo: Two different media! But they are in the same building…
hist.sm9.3.adulte: cp copies several files into a folder (the last argument).
hist.sm9.4.dit: And one copy FAR AWAY, in another building.
hist.sm9.4.bravo: 3 copies, on at least 2 media, 1 of them far away: the 3-2-1 rule is respected!
hist.sm9.4.adulte: Off-site: another house, another place, an online service… to survive a fire or a theft.
hist.sm9.5.dit: Oh no, a fire in the farm building! Trigger the breakdown (it is a game: only in the playground).
hist.sm9.5.bravo: The building burned, but the far-away copy survived. The farm is saved!
hist.sm9.5.adulte: The breakdown replaces, in the playground only, the collection and the building's copies with ashes.
hist.sm9.6.dit: Go and get the rescue copy, far away.
hist.sm9.6.bravo: Here you are in the other building.
hist.sm9.7.dit: Before restoring: is the copy intact? Check its fingerprint.
hist.sm9.7.bravo: OK: the archive is exactly the one you backed up.
hist.sm9.7.adulte: sha256sum -c rereads the .sha256 file and recomputes the fingerprint of each listed file.
hist.sm9.8.dit: Restore the collection into the room (two folders up).
hist.sm9.8.bravo: The collection is back: breakdown and recovery succeeded!
hist.sm9.8.adulte: tar x (extract) z f, -C FOLDER: where to unpack. A backup you have never restored is not a backup.
hist.sm10.0.dit: The final test! See what you are asked to build.
hist.sm10.0.bravo: A need, a budget in (pretend) points, parts: your choice.
hist.sm10.0.adulte: No brand, no real price: generic parts and a pretend budget.
hist.sm10.1.dit: Pick one part of each kind (six codes instead of the ?).
hist.sm10.1.bravo: Your machine is assembled. Ready to boot?
hist.sm10.1.adulte: Check: socket, memory type, consumption ≤ power supply, budget, and the need.
hist.sm10.2.dit: Press the button: boot your machine!
hist.sm10.2.bravo: It boots! Note the flag it shows.
hist.sm10.2.adulte: First time? A rare creature will visit you more often.
hist.sm10.3.dit: Give the flag back to the game (instead of the ?).
hist.sm10.3.bravo: Flag accepted: the test is passed!
hist.sm10.3.adulte: The TG{…} flag depends on your game: it proves that your machine booted.
ma.meuble.plan:
⚙ THE PLAN OF THE GEAR ROOM

Welcome, {nom}! Under the camp hums the real machine: your computer.

1. We LOOK, we don't touch: the commands of this room read the hardware.
2. Never sudo: we never need it here.
3. Nothing is written outside the playground; the game keeps and sends no personal data.
4. The virtual machine lesson is done WITH AN ADULT: nothing installs by itself.

ma.f.organes.enfant: The processor is the cook, RAM is its worktop, storage is the pantry.
ma.f.organes.grands: The processor runs instructions, on several cores; RAM holds the data in use, fast but erased at power-off; storage (SSD, hard disk) keeps it.
ma.f.organes.limite: A cook does one thing at a time; a core switches between thousands of tasks per second, and memory also holds the programs themselves.
ma.f.organes.idee: « More memory makes the computer faster »: only if it was lacking; beyond that, it changes nothing.
ma.f.peripheriques.enfant: The motherboard is the city that links everything: its roads (the buses) lead to each part.
ma.f.peripheriques.grands: The motherboard links processor, memory and devices through buses (PCI Express, USB); lspci and lsusb list them, /proc/cpuinfo describes the processor.
ma.f.peripheriques.limite: In a phone, almost everything is on a single chip (SoC): there are no cards to plug in.
ma.f.peripheriques.idee: « /proc/cpuinfo is a file on the disk »: no, the kernel makes it at the moment you read it.
ma.f.binaire.enfant: Inside the machine, everything is made of switches on (1) or off (0); eight switches make a byte.
ma.f.binaire.grands: A bit is 0 or 1; a byte = 8 bits (256 values). Text is a series of numbers: ASCII for simple letters, UTF-8 up to 4 bytes per character. Hexadecimal writes a byte with two digits.
ma.f.binaire.limite: Real switches are microscopic transistors, billions of them, changing state billions of times per second.
ma.f.binaire.idee: « One letter = one byte »: true in ASCII, false in UTF-8 for é, ñ, 字 or emojis.
ma.f.unites.enfant: KB counts bytes in packs of 1000, KiB in packs of 1024: two rules, two names.
ma.f.unites.grands: SI prefixes: k = 10³, M = 10⁶, G = 10⁹. Binary (IEC) prefixes: Ki = 2¹⁰, Mi = 2²⁰, Gi = 2³⁰. 1 MiB = 1,048,576 bytes ≈ 1.05 MB.
ma.f.unites.limite: Many programs write « MB » or « M » meaning MiB: you have to check how they count.
ma.f.unites.idee: « My 1 TB disk lost space »: no, 1 TB ≈ 0.91 TiB, the same number of bytes counted differently.
ma.f.demarrage.enfant: When you press the button, the machine wakes up floor by floor, each one waking the next.
ma.f.demarrage.grands: Firmware (UEFI or BIOS) → boot loader (GRUB, systemd-boot…) → kernel → first process (PID 1: systemd, init) → services and session.
ma.f.demarrage.limite: Floors are not objects: they are programs handing over to each other, in a few seconds.
ma.f.demarrage.idee: « The BIOS is on the disk »: no, the firmware is in a chip on the motherboard.
ma.f.systeme_exploitation.enfant: The operating system is the conductor: it tells each program when to play and with which parts.
ma.f.systeme_exploitation.grands: The kernel manages processes, memory, files, drivers and permissions; a distribution packages it with tools, under free (GPL, MIT…) or proprietary licences.
ma.f.systeme_exploitation.limite: A conductor follows a score; the kernel keeps reacting to unexpected events (keys, network, disks).
ma.f.systeme_exploitation.idee: « Linux is a computer brand »: no, it is a kernel, used by thousands of systems, including Android.
ma.f.virtualisation.enfant: A virtual machine is a complete doll's house inside the house; a container, a sealed box in one room.
ma.f.virtualisation.grands: Virtual machine: a hypervisor simulates a whole computer, with its own kernel. Container: isolated processes (namespaces, cgroups) sharing the kernel. Image = template; instance = running copy.
ma.f.virtualisation.limite: A doll's house is small; a virtual machine can be almost as fast as the real one, because it uses the real processor.
ma.f.virtualisation.idee: « A container is a small virtual machine »: no, it does not have its own kernel.
ma.f.machine_virtuelle.enfant: With an adult, we build a machine inside the machine: we can break it safely, then recreate it.
ma.f.machine_virtuelle.grands: podman run --rm starts a disposable container; qemu-img creates a virtual disk (qcow2, allocated on demand); virsh drives libvirt VMs (snapshots, destruction, recreation).
ma.f.machine_virtuelle.limite: « Safe » for the real machine, but a VM takes space and memory, and a download is still a download.
ma.f.machine_virtuelle.idee: « Nothing can get out of a VM »: a badly set-up VM (shared folders, network) can reach the outside.
ma.f.datacenter.enfant: A server farm: thousands of machines without screens, in rows, serving day and night.
ma.f.datacenter.grands: A datacenter gathers servers with redundant power, network and cooling; the cloud rents these machines remotely. Energy (kWh) = power (kW) × time (h).
ma.f.datacenter.limite: A farm produces milk; a datacenter does not make the data, it keeps it and computes with it.
ma.f.datacenter.idee: « The cloud is in the sky »: no, it is very real buildings, which use electricity.
ma.f.sauvegarde_321.enfant: Three copies, on two different media, one of them far away: even if a building burns, you lose nothing.
ma.f.sauvegarde_321.grands: 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies of the data, on 2 different media, 1 of them off-site. Check integrity (fingerprint) and TEST the restore.
ma.f.sauvegarde_321.limite: In the game, the fire is pretend and « loin » is a folder; for real, you need another place or an online service.
ma.f.sauvegarde_321.idee: « A copy on the same disk is a backup »: no, if the disk breaks, both disappear.
ma.f.assemblage.enfant: Building a machine means choosing parts that go together, for a need, without going over the budget.
ma.f.assemblage.grands: Compatibility: processor and motherboard socket, memory generation (DDR4 ≠ DDR5), form factor (mini), power supply ≥ total consumption, with a margin.
ma.f.assemblage.limite: Real parts have many more criteria (case, cooling, connectors); the game shows no real price.
ma.f.assemblage.idee: « The most expensive part is always the best »: the best is the one that meets the need.
ma.tel.raconte: On the phone, this is told as a story: no {outil} here.
