hist.ondes.debut: 📡 On the cliff above the harbour, a tower hums in every colour… Welcome to the Tower of Waves! Here we listen to radio waves. Listening is free; transmitting is regulated: the game itself never transmits.
hist.ondes.fin: You can tune a wave, sort the spectrum, send a tiny message very far and get a message through a storm. You are a Master of Waves!
recomp.ondes.onde: the message that gets through the storm
on.ouvert.log: 🌍 A world opens at the Crossroads: the Tower of Waves
on.ouvert.dit: You know the harbour's docks and doors, and the units of the Gear Room: the Tower of Waves lights up on the cliff! Whenever you like: `cd ~/terrain_terminagotchi/ondes`.
on.pont: This step is about {notion}. Do you know it? If not, type `{cmd}`: we cross the bridge, then come back here.
hist.on9.titre: The real mesh network (with an adult)
hist.on0.1.dit: Look at what is in the tower.
hist.on0.1.bravo: A plan, a logbook… and a sensor file for later.
hist.on0.1.adulte: The game prepared the ondes folder in your playground. Everything written stays there.
hist.on0.2.dit: Read the plan of the tower.
hist.on0.2.bravo: Listening is free, transmitting is regulated. And we never copy the names of the neighbours' networks. Promise?
hist.on0.2.adulte: This world's commands READ the radio (nmcli, rfkill, iw) without changing anything. The game never transmits; it keeps no network name and no MAC address.
hist.on1.0.dit: A wave is an invisible ripple travelling at the speed of light. Look at the Wi-Fi one.
hist.on1.0.bravo: The frequency is the number of waves per second: 2.4 billion for this Wi-Fi!
hist.on1.0.adulte: Frequency in hertz (Hz = oscillations per second); 2.4 GHz = 2,400,000,000 Hz. The drawing is not to scale.
hist.on1.1.dit: Tune the frequency: look at LoRa's wave, which is lower.
hist.on1.1.bravo: Fewer waves per second… and each wave is longer!
hist.on1.1.adulte: Try also: ondes onde fm, ondes onde 5G, ondes onde 868M, ondes onde 2.4G.
hist.on1.2.dit: The length of a wave = speed divided by frequency. Compute Wi-Fi's with bc.
hist.on1.2.bravo: 0.125 metre: 12.5 centimetres, about the size of your hand.
hist.on1.2.adulte: λ = v / f = 300,000,000 / 2,400,000,000 = 0.125 m. bc -l computes with decimals (20 digits).
hist.on1.3.dit: Your turn: LoRa's wavelength (868 MHz), in centimetres. Compute it, then replace the ?.
hist.on1.3.bravo: Right! The lower the frequency, the longer the wave.
hist.on1.3.adulte: 300,000,000 / 868,000,000 ≈ 0.3456 m ≈ 34.6 cm. The game accepts the answer within 5 %, in cm or in m.
hist.on1.4.dit: A wall stands in front of the waves. See what gets through to the other side.
hist.on1.4.bravo: The wall weakens every wave, but not equally: high frequencies lose more.
hist.on1.4.adulte: Loss is counted in decibels (dB): −3 dB = half the power, −10 dB = a tenth. Try ondes mur beton 2.
hist.on1.5.dit: Which one goes through walls best: lora, wifi24 or wifi5? Replace the ?.
hist.on1.5.bravo: LoRa! That's why it is used to talk far, even through walls.
hist.on1.5.adulte: In general, the lower the frequency, the less materials absorb it. But a low frequency carries less data.
hist.on2.0.dit: Does your machine have a Wi-Fi card? Look at its radio interfaces.
hist.on2.0.bravo: If an interface appears, you see its channel and power. If not (no Wi-Fi here), that's normal too.
hist.on2.0.adulte: iw dev reads the state of Wi-Fi cards (interface, channel, transmit power). It also shows YOUR card's MAC address: it stays on your screen.
hist.on2.1.dit: Look at the networks around you, but only the anonymous columns: channel, frequency, signal.
hist.on2.1.bravo: No names, no addresses: just channels and signal strengths. That's enough to understand waves!
hist.on2.1.adulte: -f picks the columns; --rescan no reads the list already known without starting a new scan. Without -f, nmcli also shows the neighbours' names (SSID) and addresses (BSSID).
hist.on2.2.dit: How many networks did you count? Replace the ? with the number.
hist.on2.2.bravo: Right! The game counted too, without looking at the names.
hist.on2.2.adulte: The game only reads the FREQ column again (nmcli -t -f FREQ … --rescan no) when checking, and writes nothing. The list changes: it accepts a small difference.
hist.on2.3.dit: Are the channels crowded? Look at the histogram.
hist.on2.3.bravo: When many networks talk on the same channel, they get in each other's way, like people shouting in the same room.
hist.on2.3.adulte: At 2.4 GHz, channels are 20 MHz wide but only 5 MHz apart: only 1, 6 and 11 don't overlap.
hist.on2.4.dit: Why do we never copy the names of the neighbours' networks? Read.
hist.on2.4.bravo: Other people's names and addresses belong to them. We look at the waves, not at people.
hist.on2.4.adulte: A network name or a MAC address can identify a household: it is personal data (GDPR). The game neither records nor sends them.
hist.on3.0.dit: Which radios are on in your machine? Ask nmcli.
hist.on3.0.bravo: « enabled »: on; « disabled »: off. We only look, we touch nothing.
hist.on3.0.adulte: nmcli radio shows the state of Wi-Fi and mobile broadband (WWAN), hardware and software. Never type nmcli radio … off here.
hist.on3.1.dit: The kernel has a switch for each radio. Look at the list.
hist.on3.1.bravo: « Soft blocked »: turned off by a program; « Hard blocked »: by a real button. Always read-only!
hist.on3.1.adulte: rfkill list reads the state; rfkill block / unblock would change it: never in the game. In a virtual machine the list can be empty.
hist.on3.2.dit: And Bluetooth? Read only the « Powered » and « Discoverable » lines.
hist.on3.2.bravo: You filtered with grep: you see only what you care about. If there is no Bluetooth, nothing shows, that's normal.
hist.on3.2.adulte: bluetoothctl show describes your own Bluetooth chip; timeout 5 avoids waiting if there is no Bluetooth service. We do NOT run « scan on »: it looks for the neighbours' devices.
hist.on3.3.dit: Make a summary of your machine's radios.
hist.on3.3.bravo: Each radio has its band. Your phone has even more: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, 4G, 5G, GPS…
hist.on3.3.adulte: The game reads /sys/class/rfkill/*/type, soft and hard: the kind of radio and its state, nothing else.
hist.on4.0.dit: All waves live on a big ruler: the spectrum. Look at it.
hist.on4.0.bravo: Each technology has its place on the ruler, like each instrument has its notes.
hist.on4.0.adulte: The ruler is logarithmic: each mark multiplies the frequency by 10 (powers of 10).
hist.on4.1.dit: Six technologies got mixed up! Look at the cards.
hist.on4.1.bravo: Which one is the lowest? And the highest?
hist.on4.1.adulte: FM ≈ 100 MHz, LoRa 868 MHz, GPS 1575 MHz, Bluetooth 2.4 GHz, 5G 3.5 GHz, Wi-Fi 5 GHz.
hist.on4.2.dit: Sort them from the lowest frequency to the highest (six letters instead of the ?).
hist.on4.2.bravo: Well done! The spectrum ruler is sorted.
hist.on4.2.adulte: In Europe, LoRa uses 863-870 MHz; in the United States, 902-928 MHz.
hist.on4.3.dit: Some bands are free, others are reserved. Read the rule.
hist.on4.3.bravo: Free does not mean « no rules »: limited power, limited talking time.
hist.on4.3.adulte: Free bands (ISM, short-range devices): no individual licence, but with limits. Reserved bands: assigned (operators, broadcasting, aviation, GPS…).
hist.on4.4.dit: Free (l) or reserved (r)? One letter for each use, in order.
hist.on4.4.bravo: Right! Listening is free, transmitting is regulated.
hist.on4.4.adulte: In France, ANFR manages the frequency table; Arcep sets the rules for free bands.
hist.on5.0.dit: LoRa talks very far while whispering very softly. Discover its secret.
hist.on5.0.bravo: Its secret: « chirps », sliding whistles. They can be heard even under the noise.
hist.on5.0.adulte: LoRa: chirp spread spectrum modulation (CSS). Long range (km), very low data rate (0.3 to 5 kbit/s), very little energy.
hist.on5.1.dit: How long does a single whistle last at the slowest setting (SF12)? Compute 2 to the power 12 divided by 125,000.
hist.on5.1.bravo: 0.032768 second: about 33 thousandths of a second for a single symbol!
hist.on5.1.adulte: Symbol duration = 2^SF / bandwidth (125 kHz). Each extra SF doubles the duration.
hist.on5.2.dit: Look how long a 10-letter message lasts, depending on the setting.
hist.on5.2.bravo: The bigger the setting (SF), the farther the message goes… but the longer it takes.
hist.on5.2.adulte: Time on air (Semtech AN1200.13) = (preamble + 4.25 + payload symbols) × symbol duration.
hist.on5.3.dit: A valley separates your tower from the one opposite. Look at its width and the ranges.
hist.on5.3.bravo: The range must be longer than the width of the valley.
hist.on5.3.adulte: The game's ranges are indicative (line of sight): in reality they depend on terrain, antennas, weather.
hist.on5.4.dit: Choose the SMALLEST SF setting that crosses the valley (replace the ? with a number from 7 to 12).
hist.on5.4.bravo: The message crosses the valley, and it wastes no airtime!
hist.on5.4.adulte: The smallest sufficient SF: the range is there, and the transmission is shortest (less energy, less disturbance for others).
hist.on5.5.dit: In Europe, on 868 MHz, you may only transmit 1 % of the time. How many seconds per hour?
hist.on5.5.bravo: 36 seconds per hour: that's the 1 % rule.
hist.on5.5.adulte: Duty cycle of 1 % in the 868.0-868.6 MHz sub-band (ETSI EN 300 220): 3600 s × 1 / 100 = 36 s.
hist.on5.6.dit: With your setting, how many messages can you send in one hour? Replace the ?.
hist.on5.6.bravo: Right! We share the waves: everyone talks a little, taking turns.
hist.on5.6.adulte: Messages per hour = 36 s / time on air of one message (keep the whole part).
hist.on6.0.dit: First way: gateways that relay to the Internet. Look.
hist.on6.0.bravo: That's LoRaWAN: sensors talk to a gateway, which sends everything to a server over the Internet.
hist.on6.0.adulte: LoRaWAN: star-of-stars architecture; gateways relay to a network server.
hist.on6.1.dit: Second way: the mesh, with no central antenna. Look.
hist.on6.1.bravo: Each device repeats the others' messages: no Internet needed!
hist.on6.1.adulte: Direct mesh (Meshtastic, MeshCore): each node relays; a message carries a hop limit.
hist.on6.2.dit: Four situations. Which needs what? Look.
hist.on6.2.bravo: Think: is there Internet and a gateway nearby?
hist.on6.2.adulte: Gateway: organised coverage, data to a server. Mesh: autonomy, no infrastructure.
hist.on6.3.dit: Gateway (p) or mesh (m)? One letter for each situation, in order.
hist.on6.3.bravo: Well done! Each way has its strengths.
hist.on6.3.adulte: A mesh uses more airtime (each relay retransmits); a gateway depends on the Internet.
hist.on7.0.dit: The Terminaworld machines become radios! Look at the mesh map.
hist.on7.0.bravo: Each node hears its close neighbours. The number of hops is how many times the message is repeated.
hist.on7.0.adulte: It's the Harbour's simulated network, in mesh mode: nothing goes over a real radio.
hist.on7.1.dit: Send a message to the fire biome.
hist.on7.1.bravo: The message spreads step by step, like a wave: the first one to arrive wins.
hist.on7.1.adulte: Managed flooding (Meshtastic): each node retransmits once; the destination keeps the first copy.
hist.on7.2.dit: Oh no, the rock node goes dark! Cut it.
hist.on7.2.bravo: A node is cut. Will the message still get through?
hist.on7.2.adulte: In a real mesh, a node can go off (empty battery, failure, terrain).
hist.on7.3.dit: Send the same message to the fire again.
hist.on7.3.bravo: It found another path! That's the strength of a mesh: no single point of failure.
hist.on7.3.adulte: Redundancy: several paths exist; the message takes the shortest of those left.
hist.on7.4.dit: Look at the new path to the fire.
hist.on7.4.bravo: One more hop, but it arrives. A detour is better than a lost message.
hist.on7.4.adulte: Each hop adds airtime; the hop limit (3 by default in Meshtastic, 7 at most) prevents endless messages.
hist.on7.5.dit: Switch all the nodes back on.
hist.on7.5.bravo: The whole mesh is on again.
hist.on7.5.adulte: mesh-coupe -r switches everything on; mesh-coupe -r glace switches only one back on.
hist.on9.0.dit: The real mesh is with an adult and a small radio board. Read the rules.
hist.on9.0.bravo: It's optional: without a radio board, we tell the story, and you still move on.
hist.on9.0.adulte: Free 868 MHz band: 25 mW at most, 1 % of the time. The game installs nothing and never transmits.
hist.on9.1.bravo: A path is shown if it is there; otherwise nothing. Both answers are normal.
hist.on9.1.adulte: To install it, an adult types pip install meshtastic themselves (in a virtual environment): the game never does it.
hist.on9.2.dit: With the adult: read your node's card.
hist.on9.2.bravo: The node's name, its radio, its settings… If no board is plugged in, it says so: that's normal.
hist.on9.2.adulte: meshtastic --info reads the configuration of the board plugged in over USB (read-only).
hist.on9.3.dit: Who is in range? Look at the list of nodes.
hist.on9.3.bravo: These are other people's nodes: we look at them, we copy neither their names nor their positions.
hist.on9.3.adulte: meshtastic --nodes lists the nodes heard (names, distance, sometimes a GPS position): other people's data.
hist.on9.4.dit: With the adult, and only if you both agree: send « bonjour » on the mesh.
hist.on9.4.bravo: You transmitted, not the game: a short message, in the free band, respecting the 1 %.
hist.on9.4.adulte: --sendtext really transmits on 868 MHz (public channel by default, readable by everyone): nothing personal in the message.
hist.on9.5.dit: Listen to the story of a node (or read it again if you did it for real).
hist.on9.5.bravo: A node is a little radio that relays other people's messages, without the Internet.
hist.on9.5.adulte: Open projects: Meshtastic (GPL-3.0) and MeshCore; classes can build their own mesh.
hist.on10.0.dit: With a software radio, we listen to the sky. Only listening! Read the rules.
hist.on10.0.bravo: Receive only, and we keep nothing that could recognise someone.
hist.on10.0.adulte: A software-defined radio (SDR) dongle only receives. Listening to public signals is free; disclosing private communications is not.
hist.on10.1.dit: Are the software radio tools there?
hist.on10.1.bravo: If they're missing, we tell the rest: nothing blocks.
hist.on10.1.adulte: rtl_test (rtl-sdr), rtl_433 (433/868 MHz sensors), dump1090 (aircraft, 1090 MHz): to install with an adult.
hist.on10.2.dit: With the adult: test the radio dongle.
hist.on10.2.bravo: « Found 1 device »: the dongle is there. « No supported devices »: no dongle, that's normal too.
hist.on10.2.adulte: rtl_test -t checks the dongle and its tuner; timeout 10 stops it anyway.
hist.on10.3.dit: Planes are flying over the Terminaworld! Look.
hist.on10.3.bravo: Altitude, speed, direction: that's all we keep. No registration.
hist.on10.3.adulte: Planes announce their position on 1090 MHz (ADS-B). The game's planes are fictional.
hist.on10.4.dit: Here is what a weather-sensor receiver writes. Read the file.
hist.on10.4.bravo: Each line has an « id »: it could recognise the neighbour's house. We don't keep it!
hist.on10.4.adulte: rtl_433 -F json format (one JSON line per message). The values in this file are fictional.
hist.on10.5.dit: Keep only the temperatures, with grep -o.
hist.on10.5.bravo: Only the temperatures: the identifiers were left aside. That's anonymising.
hist.on10.5.adulte: grep -o shows only the part matching the pattern. To go further: jq '.temperature_C'.
hist.on10.6.bravo: You listen to the world without spying on people. Well done!
hist.on10.6.adulte: Data minimisation (GDPR, art. 5): collect only what is useful, and nothing that identifies someone.
hist.on1.t2.dit: The length of a wave = speed divided by frequency. Compute Wi-Fi's, in millimetres.
hist.on1.t2.bravo: 125 millimetres: 12.5 centimetres, about the size of your hand.
hist.on1.t2.adulte: The phone's shell has no bc: we compute with whole numbers, in millimetres (300,000,000 / 2,400,000 = 125).
hist.on5.t1.dit: How long does a single whistle last at the slowest setting (SF12)? Compute it in microseconds.
hist.on5.t1.bravo: 32,768 microseconds: about 33 thousandths of a second for a single symbol!
hist.on5.t1.adulte: 2^12 = 4096; 4096 / 125,000 s = 32,768 µs. Each extra SF doubles the duration.
hist.on5.t5.dit: In Europe, on 868 MHz, you may only transmit 1 % of the time. How many seconds per hour?
hist.on5.t5.bravo: 36 seconds per hour: that's the 1 % rule.
on.meuble.plan:
📡 THE TOWER OF WAVES — the plan

Hello {nom}! Welcome to the tower.

THE TOWER'S RULES
  1. Listening is free; transmitting is regulated. The game NEVER transmits by itself.
  2. We READ the radio, we don't change it: never sudo, never rfkill block, no connecting, no pairing.
  3. The names and addresses of the neighbours' networks belong to them: we don't copy them, the game doesn't keep them.
  4. The radio board, the radio dongle: only with an adult, and only if you want. Without them, we tell the story.

THE FLOORS
  the wave room        (ondes onde, ondes mur)
  the spectrum ruler   (ondes spectre)
  the LoRa valley      (ondes vallee)
  the mesh             (mesh-route, mesh-envoie, mesh-coupe)
  the sky balcony      (ondes ecoute, ondes avions)
on.meuble.carnet: # The tower's logbook: the game notes what you succeeded at (never a network name, never a message).
on.usage.fm: the radio music in the car
on.usage.lora: a little sensor that talks very far
on.usage.quatreg: the phone that calls and goes on the Internet
on.usage.gps: the satellites that tell you where you are
on.usage.cinqg: the phone at very high speed
on.usage.wifi5: the router, faster but shorter range
on.sens.cherche: an active scan (the card sends calls)
on.sens.change: it would change the radio (never in the game)
on.sens.simule: the game's mesh (nothing on a real radio)
on.onde.morale: The higher the frequency, the shorter the wave.
on.onde.aide: ondes onde [fm | lora | gps | wifi24 | 5g | wifi5 | 868M | 2.4G]: tunes the frequency.
on.longueur.aide: ondes longueur L: LoRa's wavelength ({f}), in centimetres (or in metres with m).
on.longueur.morale: An antenna is often a quarter of the wavelength: about 8.6 cm for LoRa.
on.longueur.faux: Not quite. Divide 300,000,000 by the frequency in hertz ({f}), then multiply by 100 to get centimetres.
on.mur.perte: −{db} dB: {amp} % of the wave's height is left, {pui} % of its power
on.mur.morale: The wall weakens high frequencies more: Wi-Fi 5 GHz loses more than LoRa.
on.mur.grands: Indicative values (ITU-R P.2040): every real wall is different. −3 dB = power divided by 2, −10 dB = by 10.
on.traverse.aide: ondes traverse lora | wifi24 | wifi5: which one goes through walls best?
on.traverse.ok: Yes: LoRa, the lowest frequency, goes through best.
on.traverse.morale: But careful: a low frequency carries less data per second.
on.traverse.faux: Look at ondes mur again: which one keeps the biggest wave behind the wall?
on.reseaux.aide: ondes reseaux N: the number of networks you counted (the lines, without the title line).
on.reseaux.sans: No nmcli here: we tell the story. In a home you often see between 3 and 30 networks.
on.reseaux.ok: Right: the game counts {n} on its side (it only read the frequencies).
on.reseaux.morale: All these networks share the same bands: they must spread out over the channels.
on.reseaux.faux: Not quite. Count the lines under the title (or add | wc -l, then take away 1).
on.canaux.exemple: (no Wi-Fi list here: here is an EXAMPLE neighbourhood, made up)
on.canaux.bandes: {n} networks: {b24} at 2.4 GHz, {b5} at 5 GHz, {b6} at 6 GHz.
on.canaux.axe: channel →  (each █ = one network; no name, no address)
on.canaux.morale: Channels 1, 6 and 11 don't step on each other: that's where routers fit best.
on.canaux.grands: A 2.4 GHz channel is 20 MHz wide; the numbers are only 5 MHz apart.
on.voisins.titre: Why we don't copy other people's names
on.voisins.texte:
Waves go through walls: your machine hears the neighbours' routers.
Their network name, or their router's MAC address, can tell WHO lives where.
It is their data, like their name on the letterbox.
So we look at the waves (channel, signal strength, number), not at people.
The game keeps no name, sends it nowhere, and never writes it.
on.radios.aucune: No radio visible here (a virtual machine or a container often has none).
on.radios.telephone: A phone often has six: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, 4G/5G, GPS, NFC, and sometimes FM radio.
on.radios.grands: Read from /sys/class/rfkill (type, soft, hard): no address, no name.
on.spectre.titre: The spectrum ruler (from 10 MHz to 10 GHz)
on.spectre.morale: Each mark multiplies the frequency by 10.
on.spectre.grands: Logarithmic scale; Wi-Fi and Bluetooth share the 2.4 GHz band.
on.regle.aide: ondes regle L L L L L L: the six letters, from the lowest frequency to the highest.
on.regle.faux: {n} well placed out of {total}. Look at the ruler (ondes spectre) and try again.
on.regle.morale: Higher on the ruler: more data rate, but less range.
on.libre.regle:
Free: anyone may transmit without a licence, but with low power and little time.
Reserved: only those who received an authorisation may transmit.
Listening, on the other hand, is free everywhere.
on.libre.aide: ondes libre l r …: one letter per use (l = free, r = reserved), in order.
on.libre.wifi24.pourquoi: Wi-Fi uses a free band: everyone installs their router without a licence.
on.libre.bluetooth.pourquoi: Bluetooth shares the same free band as Wi-Fi, at very low power.
on.libre.lora.pourquoi: LoRa uses a free band (868 MHz): 25 mW and 1 % of the time at most.
on.libre.fm.pourquoi: To broadcast on FM, a radio station must receive an authorisation.
on.libre.gps.pourquoi: The GPS band is protected: nobody may transmit there (we can only listen to the satellites).
on.libre.quatreg.pourquoi: Operators pay to use the 4G bands.
on.lora.chirp: The chirp: a whistle that rises, again and again; each way of starting it carries a few bits.
on.lora.portee: Range: several kilometres, sometimes more than ten in line of sight.
on.lora.debit: Data rate: tiny, a few words per message, no video or photos.
on.lora.energie: Energy: a battery can last months, even years.
on.lora.bande: The band: 868 MHz in Europe, a free band, shared by everyone.
on.lora.grands: CSS modulation (Chirp Spread Spectrum); SF7 to SF12; 125 kHz; data rate about 0.3 to 5.5 kbit/s.
on.temps.morale: SF +1: each symbol lasts twice as long, and it goes a little farther.
on.temps.grands: Semtech calculation (AN1200.13): 125 kHz, coding 4/5, preamble 8, header, CRC; low data rate optimisation from SF11. Indicative ranges.
on.vallee.aide: ondes vallee SF: the smallest setting (7 to 12) whose range is longer than the valley.
on.vallee.court: The message falls in the middle of the valley: the range is too short. Take a bigger SF.
on.vallee.lent: It crosses, but it takes {ms} ms while a smaller SF is enough ({ms2} ms). Wasting the airwaves bothers others!
on.vallee.ok: The message crosses the valley at SF{sf}, in {ms} ms: just the right setting!
on.messages.aide: ondes messages N: how many SF{sf} messages (each lasts {ms} ms) fit into 36 seconds?
on.messages.ok: Right: {n} messages per hour at SF{sf}.
on.messages.morale: A sensor sending the temperature every quarter of an hour is far from the limit.
on.messages.grands: Messages = 36,000 ms / time of one message, whole part (Python: 36000 // ms; bc: scale=0).
on.messages.faux: Not quite. Divide 36 seconds (36,000 ms) by the duration of one message ({ms} ms), and keep the whole part.
on.passerelle.texte:
📟 Sensors talk to a nearby gateway 🗼.
The gateway sends everything, over the Internet 🌐, to a server 🖥.
If the gateway or the Internet fails, messages no longer get through.
on.passerelle.grands: Star of stars; nodes don't talk to each other; a network server sorts and removes duplicates.
on.maillage.titre: The mesh: everyone repeats for the others
on.maillage.texte:
📟 Each device repeats the messages it hears.
No central antenna, no Internet needed.
If a device goes off, the message takes a detour.
on.maillage.grands: Meshtastic and MeshCore: a hop limit; each relay retransmits, so more airtime in total.
on.choix.ville: The city's sensors send air quality to the town hall, which has the Internet.
on.choix.randonnee: Hikers in the mountains want to write to each other, without any phone network.
on.choix.tempete: After a storm, the Internet is cut in the whole village.
on.choix.compteur: Water meters send their readings to the water company.
on.choix.aide: ondes choix p m …: one letter per situation (p = gateway, m = mesh), in order.
on.choix.ville.pourquoi: The city has the Internet and gateways: LoRaWAN brings the data to the server.
on.choix.randonnee.pourquoi: No network in the mountains: the mesh links the hikers to each other.
on.choix.tempete.pourquoi: Without the Internet, only the mesh keeps working.
on.choix.compteur.pourquoi: The readings go to a server: a LoRaWAN gateway takes them there.
on.mesh.isole: No path left to {dest}: it is isolated.
on.mesh.aide: mesh-route [node] · mesh-envoie node "message" · mesh-coupe node · mesh-coupe -r [node]
on.mesh.inconnu: « {nom} » is not a node of the mesh.
on.mesh.camp: The camp is you: send the message to another node.
on.mesh.camp_coupe: The camp is your radio: we don't cut it.
on.mesh.envoie.aide: mesh-envoie node "message": for example mesh-envoie feu "bonjour".
on.mesh.rate.isole: The message doesn't arrive: {dest} is isolated, no path left.
on.mesh.rate.loin: Too far: it would need {n} hops, the limit is {max}.
on.mesh.rate.coupe: {dest} is cut: it can't receive anything.
on.mesh.arrive: Arrived at {dest} in {n} hop(s) ({reste} hops were still allowed).
on.mesh.detour: With {n} node(s) cut, the message took a detour: the mesh repaired itself.
on.mesh.coupe.aide: mesh-coupe node: switches a node off; mesh-coupe -r: switches them all back on.
on.mesh.rallume_tout: All the nodes are back on.
on.mesh.autre_chemin: The mesh still has a path to the fire: send to see.
on.mesh.plus_de_chemin: There is no path to the fire any more: switch a node back on (mesh-coupe -r).
on.defi.regles:
The storm is going to switch nodes off. Your target: {dest}.
Cut {n} nodes, one by one, each on the CURRENT path to {dest} (mesh-coupe node).
Then send « SOS » to {dest}. The message must get through!
Watch out for nodes everything depends on…
on.defi.pas_cible: We don't cut the target ({cible}): it's the one we're writing to!
on.defi.coupe_ok: Node of the path cut: {n} of {total}.
on.defi.isole: No path left to {dest}: it is isolated! Switch everything back on (mesh-coupe -r) and start again (ondes defi).
on.defi.hors_chemin: {nom} was not on the path to {dest}: it doesn't count. Here is the path:
on.defi.reussi: The message got through despite {n} nodes cut! The storm could do nothing.
on.defi.pas_assez: Arrived, but with only {n} node(s) of the path cut out of {total}.
on.adulte.titre: The real mesh (with an adult, optional)
on.adulte.regles:
You need a small LoRa radio board (868 MHz in Europe) with its antenna: never without the antenna.
It's optional: without a board, the tower tells the story, and you still move on.
The adult installs the tool themselves (pip install meshtastic): the game installs nothing.
Free band: {mw} mW at most, and no more than {pc} % of the time.
The game never transmits. It's you, with the adult, who decide to send a message.
The names and positions of other nodes belong to their owners: we don't copy them.
on.adulte.absent: not installed: the rest is told (ondes noeud)
on.noeud.etape1: We plug in the radio board and its antenna; the adult checks the region (EU_868).
on.noeud.etape2: meshtastic --info: the board tells its name, its radio, its channel.
on.noeud.etape3: meshtastic --nodes: the nodes heard, with their distance in hops.
on.noeud.etape4: meshtastic --sendtext: a short message leaves; every node that hears it repeats it.
on.noeud.etape5: The message reaches a friend a few kilometres away, without the Internet or a phone.
on.noeud.classe: In a class, each group can have its node: the map of the class's nodes is your very own mesh.
on.noeud.grands: The default public channel is readable by everyone: never any personal data in a message.
on.ecoute.regles:
A software radio (a small USB dongle) only RECEIVES: it never transmits.
Listening to public signals is free.
But we keep nothing that could recognise someone: no registration, no identifier.
on.ecoute.fm: FM radio (88 to 108 MHz): rtl_fm turns it into sound.
on.ecoute.meteo: Garden weather sensors (433 or 868 MHz): rtl_433 decodes them.
on.ecoute.avions: Planes (1090 MHz) announce their position: dump1090 draws them on a map.
on.avions.prive: We keep altitude, speed and direction. Never the registration or the call sign.
on.avions.grands: ADS-B (1090 MHz): each plane broadcasts its ICAO address, position and altitude. The game keeps none of them.
on.anonyme.texte:
You kept the temperatures and left the identifiers: that's ANONYMISING.
We collect only what is useful, and nothing that could recognise someone.
That's true for waves, sensors, planes… and the Internet.
You listen to the world without spying on people. 📡
on.indice.sudo: No sudo in the tower: we read the radio, we never change it.
on.indice.change: This command would change the radio (switch off, connect, pair): never in the game. Here, we only read.
on.indice.cherche: This command starts an active scan (your card calls every device around): rather read the list already known, with --rescan no.
on.indice.longueur: Compute 300,000,000 divided by 868,000,000 (with bc -l), then multiply by 100 to get centimetres.
on.indice.traverse: Look at ondes mur: which wave keeps the biggest ripple behind the wall?
on.indice.reseaux: Count the lines under the list's title, or add | wc -l and take away 1.
on.indice.regle: Look at ondes spectre: FM radio is far left, Wi-Fi 5 GHz far right.
on.indice.libre: Read ondes libre again: who must ask for an authorisation to transmit?
on.indice.vallee: Look at ondes vallee: the range must be longer than the valley, and we take the smallest SF that makes it.
on.indice.messages: Divide 36,000 (milliseconds) by the duration of one message, and keep the whole part.
on.indice.choix: Is there Internet and a gateway? Yes: p. No: m.
on.indice.isole: The target is isolated. Type mesh-coupe -r to switch everything back on, then ondes defi to start again.
on.indice.hors_chemin: This node was not on the path. Look at the path (mesh-route) and cut one of its nodes.
on.indice.recoupe: First cut 3 nodes of the path (mesh-coupe node), then send « SOS ».
on.garde.noms: These network names are the neighbours': we read them, we don't copy them. Tip: nmcli -f CHAN,FREQ,SIGNAL … shows only anonymous columns.
on.garde.emet: You are really transmitting: with an adult, a short message, nothing personal, and 1 % of the time at most.

on.f.ondes.enfant: A wave is an invisible ripple: its frequency counts the waves per second, its wavelength measures one wave.
on.f.ondes.grands: Electromagnetic wave: frequency f (Hz), wavelength λ = c / f (c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s), amplitude. The higher f: more possible data rate, less range, more absorption by obstacles.
on.f.ondes.limite: A water wave needs water; a radio wave travels even in a vacuum, and the game's drawing is not to scale.
on.f.ondes.idee: « Wi-Fi waves are more powerful than FM radio waves »: no, they are higher in frequency, not stronger.
on.f.wifi_machine.enfant: Your machine hears the routers around: we look at the channels and the signal strength, not the neighbours' names.
on.f.wifi_machine.grands: nmcli and iw read the Wi-Fi card's state; -f picks the columns, --rescan no avoids a new scan. 2.4 GHz channel = (f − 2407) / 5; 5 GHz = (f − 5000) / 5.
on.f.wifi_machine.limite: The list keeps changing: networks appear and disappear depending on distance and walls.
on.f.wifi_machine.idee: « A network name is not personal data »: it is, it can identify a household (with the MAC address).
on.f.radios.enfant: Each radio in your machine has a switch: we can see whether it's on, without touching it.
on.f.radios.grands: rfkill (Linux kernel): a software (soft) or hardware (hard) block per radio; nmcli radio sums up Wi-Fi and WWAN; bluetoothctl show describes the Bluetooth adapter.
on.f.radios.limite: In a virtual machine there is often no radio at all: the list is empty, that's normal.
on.f.radios.idee: « Airplane mode = no waves at all »: the phone can keep GPS (reception) and let you switch Wi-Fi back on.
on.f.spectre.enfant: The spectrum is a big ruler where each technology has its place, from low to high frequencies.
on.f.spectre.grands: The radio spectrum is shared out by the ITU and, in France, by ANFR: reserved bands (licences) and free bands (ISM, short-range devices) subject to power and time limits.
on.f.spectre.limite: The same technology can use several bands (4G has several, Wi-Fi three).
on.f.spectre.idee: « Free band = do whatever you want »: no, power and transmission time are limited.
on.f.lora.enfant: LoRa talks very far while whispering: sliding whistles, heard even under the noise.
on.f.lora.grands: Chirp spread spectrum modulation (CSS); spreading factor SF7-SF12: each step doubles the symbol duration (2^SF / BW); time on air limited by the 1 % duty cycle at 868 MHz.
on.f.lora.limite: The game's ranges are indicative: a hill, a forest or a building changes everything.
on.f.lora.idee: « LoRa is for sending photos »: no, a few dozen bytes per message.
on.f.lorawan.enfant: Two ways to talk: through a gateway connected to the Internet, or by repeating messages between neighbours.
on.f.lorawan.grands: LoRaWAN: star of stars, gateways to a network server. Mesh (Meshtastic, MeshCore): each node relays, with no infrastructure, with a hop limit.
on.f.lorawan.limite: In real life the two are often mixed (a gateway can link a mesh to the Internet).
on.f.lorawan.idee: « LoRa and LoRaWAN are the same »: LoRa is the way of transmitting; LoRaWAN, a way of organising the network.
on.f.maillage.enfant: In a mesh, everyone repeats the message: if a node goes off, the message takes a detour.
on.f.maillage.grands: Mesh network: a graph of radio nodes; managed flooding (each node retransmits once); limited number of hops; redundancy (several disjoint paths) protects against failures.
on.f.maillage.limite: The game takes the shortest path in hops; a real radio also depends on the quality of each link.
on.f.maillage.idee: « More nodes = always better »: each relay retransmits and occupies the airwaves; too many relays clog the channel.
on.f.meshtastic.enfant: With an adult, a small radio board becomes a node that relays messages, without the Internet.
on.f.meshtastic.grands: Meshtastic: free firmware for LoRa boards (ESP32, nRF52), driven by the meshtastic command (Python): --info, --nodes, --sendtext; EU_868 region, free-band limits.
on.f.meshtastic.limite: The default public channel is readable by everyone: it is not a private messenger.
on.f.meshtastic.idee: « Without the Internet, nobody can read »: on the public channel, every node in range reads the message.
on.f.sdr.enfant: A software radio listens to the sky: the radio, garden weather, planes. It never talks.
on.f.sdr.grands: SDR (rtl-sdr): receive only; rtl_fm (FM), rtl_433 (sensors), dump1090 (ADS-B). Minimisation: keep only the useful quantities, never an identifier (ICAO address, sensor id).
on.f.sdr.limite: The game's planes and sensors are fictional; real signals depend on the antenna and the place.
on.f.sdr.idee: « What goes through the air belongs to everyone »: listening is allowed, but keeping or spreading what identifies someone is not.
maths.frequence.question: Do you know frequency (how many times per second)?
maths.frequence.enfant: Frequency is how many times something repeats in one second: 3 waves per second = 3 hertz.
maths.frequence.grands: f = number of oscillations / duration (in seconds); unit: the hertz (Hz = s⁻¹). 1 kHz = 10³ Hz, 1 MHz = 10⁶ Hz, 1 GHz = 10⁹ Hz.
maths.frequence.limite: A radio wave doesn't « count » its waves: we measure how many oscillations pass a point each second.
maths.frequence.idee: « A high frequency goes faster »: no, all radio waves travel at the same speed; only their waves are tighter.
maths.frequence.ex1: 12 waves in 4 seconds: 12 / 4 = 3 waves per second = 3 Hz.
maths.frequence.ex2: Your heart beats 60 times in 60 seconds: 1 beat per second = 1 Hz.
maths.frequence.exo: A wave makes {n} waves in {s} seconds. How many waves per second (in hertz)?
maths.frequence.erreur: Divide the number of waves ({n}) by the number of seconds ({s}).
maths.frequence.kw: frequency hertz hz wave waves oscillation per second radio period
maths.puissances_10.question: Do you know powers of 10 (10, 100, 1000…)?
maths.puissances_10.enfant: 10 to the power 3 is 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000: a 1 followed by 3 zeros.
maths.puissances_10.grands: 10ⁿ = 1 followed by n zeros; 10⁻ⁿ = 0.00…1 (n digits after the decimal point). Prefixes: kilo 10³, mega 10⁶, giga 10⁹, milli 10⁻³, micro 10⁻⁶.
maths.puissances_10.limite: The shell only computes with whole numbers: for 10⁻³ you need bc.
maths.puissances_10.kw: power powers of 10 ten zero zeros kilo mega giga milli micro exponent scientific notation
maths.longueur_onde.question: Can you compute a wavelength (speed divided by frequency)?
maths.longueur_onde.enfant: The length of a wave = the distance travelled in one second, shared between all the waves of that second.
maths.longueur_onde.grands: λ = v / f. For radio waves, v = c ≈ 300,000,000 m/s. Example: 100 MHz → 3 m; 2.4 GHz → 0.125 m.
maths.longueur_onde.limite: The exact speed is 299,792,458 m/s in a vacuum; a little less in air or in a cable.
maths.longueur_onde.idee: « The higher the frequency, the longer the wave »: it's the other way round.
maths.longueur_onde.exo: A wave at {f} MHz: what is its wavelength, in metres (speed: 300,000,000 m/s)?
maths.longueur_onde.erreur: Divide 300 by {f}: the millions in the speed and in the MHz cancel out.
maths.longueur_onde.kw: wavelength wave length lambda speed frequency divide metre metres antenna
maths.temps_emission.question: Can you compute how long a message lasts (number × duration)?
maths.temps_emission.enfant: A message is made of small pieces; if there are 10 and each lasts 4 milliseconds, the message lasts 40 milliseconds.
maths.temps_emission.grands: Duration = number of symbols × symbol duration (2^SF / BW for LoRa); then messages per hour = allowed time (36 s at 1 %) / duration of one message.
maths.temps_emission.limite: The real calculation adds the preamble and the header: the game does it for you in ondes temps.
maths.temps_emission.idee: « A slower message goes farther because it is louder »: no, it goes farther because each symbol lasts longer and stands out better from the noise.
maths.temps_emission.ex2: A 577 ms message: 36,000 / 577 ≈ 62 messages per hour.
maths.temps_emission.exo: A message has {n} symbols, and each symbol lasts {t} milliseconds. How many milliseconds in all?
maths.temps_emission.erreur: Multiply the number of symbols ({n}) by the duration of one symbol ({t}).
maths.temps_emission.kw: transmission duration message symbol symbols milliseconds lora duty cycle percent
on.tel.raconte: On the phone, it's told: the app has no access to {outil}.
on.tel.radios: Your phone has several radios: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, 4G/5G, GPS, often NFC. Each on its own band.
hist.on8.0.dit: A storm is coming! Read the challenge.
hist.on8.0.bravo: Your mission: cut three nodes of the path, one by one, and still get the message through.
hist.on8.0.adulte: Each cut must hit a node of the CURRENT path (mesh-route shows it): the path changes every time.
hist.on8.1.dit: Cut three nodes of the path, one by one (replace the ? with a name). After each cut, the new path is shown.
hist.on8.1.bravo: Three nodes of the path cut, and there is still a path! Quick, send your message.
hist.on8.1.adulte: Avoid a node everything depends on (the only neighbour of the camp or of the target). Menger's theorem: the number of nodes to cut to separate everything = the number of paths that don't touch.
hist.on8.2.dit: Send « SOS » to the storm's target (replace the ? with its name).
hist.on8.2.bravo: The message got through the storm! The sky creatures saw it…
hist.on8.2.adulte: « Wave » feat: more frequent encounters with the sky's rare variants (to be trained, never given).
on.indice.encore: Node of the path cut: {n} of {total}. Read the new path, then cut another of its nodes.
hist.guilde.debut: 🛠 Next to the Forge stands a big house of craftspeople: on its wall, hundreds of shared plans. Welcome to the Free Builders' Guild! Here we read other people's code, compile it, improve it and share it.
hist.guilde.fin: You know the 4 freedoms, you read the game's real code, compiled your first program, prepared a contribution, made a part and saved an old PC. You are a Free Builder!
gu.ouvert.log: 🌍 A world opens at the Crossroads: the Free Builders' Guild
gu.ouvert.dit: You can read, search and connect commands: the Free Builders' Guild opens its door, next to the Forge! Whenever you like: `cd ~/terrain_terminagotchi/guilde`.
gu.pont: This step uses a maths idea: {notion}. Do you know it? If not, type `{cmd}`: we cross the bridge, then come back here.
hist.gu6.titre: Bringing an old PC back to life
hist.gu0.1.dit: Look at what's in the Guild.
hist.gu0.1.bravo: A wall of plans, a notebook, a small project, a workshop… Everyone shares here.
hist.gu0.1.adulte: The game prepared the guilde folder in your playground. Everything written in this world stays there.
hist.gu0.2.dit: Read the big wall of plans.
hist.gu0.2.bravo: Here we install nothing, push nothing to the Internet, and we never touch real disks. Promise?
hist.gu0.2.adulte: The game never uses sudo, creates no account, sends nothing. Real installs, contributions and prints are only explained, to be done with an adult.
hist.gu1.0.dit: Free software gives you 4 freedoms. Discover them.
hist.gu1.0.bravo: Use, study, share, improve: those are the 4 freedoms.
hist.gu1.0.adulte: Free Software Foundation definition (freedoms 0 to 3). "Open source" (OSI definition) covers almost the same software.
hist.gu1.1.dit: Each situation has its freedom (0, 1, 2 or 3). Replace the ? in the order of the situations.
hist.gu1.1.bravo: Well done! You can recognise the 4 freedoms.
hist.gu1.1.adulte: Freedom 1 (study) and freedom 3 (improve) only work if the source code is available.
hist.gu1.2.dit: Every free project has a file that states its rules: its licence. Read the small project's one.
hist.gu1.2.bravo: The MIT licence: you can do anything with this code, as long as you keep the authors' names and this text.
hist.gu1.2.adulte: Licences are almost always in English; the text is what counts in court. MIT is a "permissive" licence.
hist.gu1.3.dit: Your computer is full of free software too. Look at the licence shelf.
hist.gu1.3.bravo: One folder per program, and inside, its licence!
hist.gu1.3.adulte: On Fedora, /usr/share/licenses; on Debian and Ubuntu, the licence is in /usr/share/doc/<program>/copyright.
hist.gu1.4.dit: Ask the package manager for bash's licence.
hist.gu1.4.bravo: GPL: the free licence of the GNU project.
hist.gu1.4.adulte: rpm -q reads the database of installed packages, without downloading anything. The game doesn't use dnf info bash: it may fetch lists from the Internet.
hist.gu1.5.dit: Find the licence of 5 programs: replace the ? with a name (bash, git, python3, gcc, firefox…).
hist.gu1.5.bravo: 5 licences found! You know where to look for a program's rules.
hist.gu1.5.adulte: The game reads /usr/share/licenses and /usr/share/doc/…/copyright; otherwise it answers from its small catalogue.
hist.gu1.6.dit: Does free mean costless? Look at these 4 programs.
hist.gu1.6.bravo: For each one, ask yourself: can I read and change its code?
hist.gu1.6.adulte: In English "free" means both libre AND costless; hence the famous phrase: "free as in freedom, not as in free beer".
hist.gu1.7.dit: For each one: l (libre, free) or p (not free, even if it costs nothing). Replace the ?.
hist.gu1.7.bravo: Free ≠ costless: a costless game can be closed, and free software can be sold!
hist.gu1.7.adulte: Costless but closed software is called freeware. The opposite of free software is proprietary software.
hist.gu2.0.dit: Terminagotchi's code is public: anyone can read it. Let's look at it!
hist.gu2.0.bravo: A repository is a project's folder with its whole history.
hist.gu2.0.adulte: The repository is on GitHub. You can read it without an account. The game never pushes anything to it.
hist.gu2.1.dit: Copy the game's repository into the Guild with git clone.
hist.gu2.1.bravo: If the Internet answers, all the game's code comes to you. If not, no problem: the Guild has a copy.
hist.gu2.1.adulte: --depth 1 only takes the latest version (lighter). The clone stays in your playground.
hist.gu2.2.dit: Check that the code is here (without a network, the Guild puts down its copy).
hist.gu2.2.bravo: The code is here, in code_du_jeu.
hist.gu2.2.adulte: The copy is made of the real Python files of the game installed on your computer.
hist.gu2.3.dit: Look at the project's tree, two levels only.
hist.gu2.3.bravo: pc/tg: that's where the computer version of the game lives.
hist.gu2.3.adulte: -L 2 limits the depth. Without tree, find … -maxdepth 2 does the same job.
hist.gu2.4.dit: Which files talk about « faim » (French for hunger)? Search the whole code.
hist.gu2.4.bravo: Lots of files talk about hunger! But only one decides.
hist.gu2.4.adulte: grep -r searches every subfolder; -l only shows file names.
hist.gu2.5.dit: The function that says whether your creature is hungry is called etat_de. Find where it is written (def).
hist.gu2.5.bravo: The file name is at the start of the line, before the colon.
hist.gu2.5.adulte: -n shows the line number. In Python, def creates a function.
hist.gu2.6.dit: So, in which file does your creature decide it is hungry? Replace the ?.
hist.gu2.6.bravo: Found it! You just read your creature's real code.
hist.gu2.6.adulte: Reading other people's code is freedom 1 (study). It's also how bugs are found.
hist.gu2.7.dit: Open this file and read the beginning (q to quit).
hist.gu2.7.bravo: Numbers, conditions, comments: the recipe for hunger!
hist.gu2.7.adulte: In less: / searches for a word, space moves one page down, q quits.
hist.gu3.0.dit: Go to the workshop: we're going to turn text into a program.
hist.gu3.0.bravo: The compiler translates your text into machine language.
hist.gu3.0.adulte: gcc compiles the C language. Python, on the other hand, is interpreted: it reads the text when you run it.
hist.gu3.1.bravo: printf prints a sentence. Every C program starts with main.
hist.gu3.1.adulte: #include <stdio.h> brings in the input-output library; return 0 means "all good".
hist.gu3.2.dit: Is there a compiler on this computer?
hist.gu3.2.bravo: Now you know whether you can compile here.
hist.gu3.2.adulte: The game installs nothing. If it's missing, an adult can install it (on Fedora: sudo dnf install gcc make).
hist.gu3.3.dit: Compile bonjour.c, then run the program.
hist.gu3.3.adulte: -o bonjour names the output file; && only runs the program if compiling succeeded.
hist.gu3.4.dit: What is this bonjour file? Ask file.
hist.gu3.4.bravo: ELF: it's a Linux program, not text any more.
hist.gu3.4.adulte: ELF (Executable and Linkable Format) is the format of programs on Linux.
hist.gu3.5.dit: Look at the program's first 4 bytes, in hexadecimal.
hist.gu3.5.bravo: 7f 45 4c 46: a secret code, then E, L, F. Every Linux program starts like this.
hist.gu3.5.adulte: It's ELF's "magic number". 45 4c 46 are the ASCII codes of E, L and F.
hist.gu3.6.dit: Your program needs help to print: from which libraries?
hist.gu3.6.bravo: libc: the big library shared by almost every program.
hist.gu3.6.adulte: ldd lists the dynamic libraries loaded at start-up. Only use it on programs you trust.
hist.gu3.7.dit: make knows the recipe by itself: build etoiles, then run it.
hist.gu3.7.bravo: make found the rule "from etoiles.c to etoiles" without being told!
hist.gu3.7.adulte: make has implicit rules; in a real project, a Makefile describes the steps, and make only redoes what changed.
hist.gu4.0.dit: Contributing means helping a project. Prepare the Guild's exercise.
hist.gu4.0.bravo: A copy of a few sentences from the game is waiting for you in contribution. A mistake is hiding in it!
hist.gu4.0.adulte: A small local git repository, prepared by the game, with no link to the Internet. The game's real files are not touched.
hist.gu4.1.dit: Go into contribution and ask git where things stand.
hist.gu4.1.bravo: On the main branch, nothing to report: everything is clean.
hist.gu4.1.adulte: git status: the branch, changed files, and those ready for the next commit.
hist.gu4.2.dit: We don't work on the main branch: create your own branch.
hist.gu4.2.bravo: Your branch: a path of your own, next to the main path.
hist.gu4.2.adulte: git switch -c creates the branch and moves onto it (like the older git checkout -b).
hist.gu4.3.dit: Read the language file. Find the misspelled word.
hist.gu4.3.bravo: Did you see it? One misspelled word, just one.
hist.gu4.3.adulte: Each line: a key (its name in the code) = the text shown.
hist.gu4.4.dit: Fix the mistake: replace the first ? with the wrong word and the second with the right word.
hist.gu4.4.bravo: Fixed! Only one thing changed: that's a good correction.
hist.gu4.4.adulte: sed -i 's/old/new/' replaces inside the file. You can also use an editor like nano.
hist.gu4.5.bravo: In red (-) the old line, in green (+) the new one. That's exactly what the project's keepers will read.
hist.gu4.5.adulte: git diff compares the file with the last saved version.
hist.gu4.6.dit: Save your correction with a clear message.
hist.gu4.6.bravo: Your correction is saved on your branch, with your message.
hist.gu4.6.adulte: -a adds files already tracked, -m gives the message. The identity "Apprenti de la Guilde" only applies in this small repository.
hist.gu4.7.bravo: Two versions: the Guild's, and yours on top.
hist.gu4.7.adulte: --oneline: one line per commit (its short identifier and its message).
hist.gu4.8.dit: And then? Discover the merge request.
hist.gu4.8.bravo: Your contribution is ready! For a real one, ask an adult.
hist.gu4.8.adulte: A real merge request (pull request) goes through the project's platform, with an account: to be done with an adult, never by the game.
hist.gu5.0.dit: Go to the fabrique (the factory): we're going to draw an object… with code!
hist.gu5.0.bravo: Your creature's key ring: a plate with a hole.
hist.gu5.0.adulte: OpenSCAD is free 3D modelling software: you describe the part with code instead of drawing it with the mouse.
hist.gu5.1.bravo: A cube, minus a cylinder: difference() digs the hole.
hist.gu5.1.adulte: Measurements are in millimetres; translate([x, y, z]) moves the cylinder.
hist.gu5.2.dit: At which coordinates is the hole (x then y)? Replace both ?.
hist.gu5.2.bravo: Right! The hole is in the middle of the width.
hist.gu5.2.adulte: z = -1 and a height of epaisseur + 2: the cylinder sticks out below and above, to drill cleanly.
hist.gu5.3.dit: How many cubic millimetres of material (not counting the hole)? Replace the ?.
hist.gu5.3.bravo: Length × width × thickness: you know how much plastic it will take!
hist.gu5.3.adulte: 1 cm³ = 1,000 mm³. The hole removes just a tiny bit of material.
hist.gu5.4.dit: Ask OpenSCAD to make the 3D file (STL).
hist.gu5.4.bravo: OpenSCAD turned your code into a part!
hist.gu5.4.adulte: The computation can take a few seconds. -o chooses the output file.
hist.gu5.5.dit: Look at the part you made.
hist.gu5.5.bravo: Triangles, millimetres: that's what a 3D printer receives.
hist.gu5.5.adulte: Without OpenSCAD, the game makes the plate itself (without the hole) so you can carry on.
hist.gu5.6.dit: Open the beginning of the STL file.
hist.gu5.6.bravo: solid, facet, vertex: the part is described by thousands of little triangles.
hist.gu5.6.adulte: STL: each triangle has its normal (its direction) and its 3 corners (vertex).
hist.gu6.0.dit: Go and see the old PC: we're going to bring it back to life.
hist.gu6.0.bravo: A saved old PC is a new PC that doesn't need to be made.
hist.gu6.0.adulte: Most of a computer's footprint comes from making it. Keeping it a long time is the best saving.
hist.gu6.1.dit: Look at the disks of YOUR computer. We look, we touch nothing.
hist.gu6.1.bravo: Each disk, its size, its pieces (partitions) and where they are mounted.
hist.gu6.1.adulte: lsblk only reads. RM = 1: removable (a USB stick, a USB disk).
hist.gu6.2.dit: Prepare the exercise: a fake Linux image and a fake USB stick, as files.
hist.gu6.2.bravo: The image, its fingerprint, the stick: they are all files in your playground.
hist.gu6.2.adulte: A real installation image is downloaded from the distribution's official website, with an adult. The game downloads nothing.
hist.gu6.3.adulte: If a single byte changes, the SHA-256 fingerprint changes completely.
hist.gu6.4.dit: Compare it with the published fingerprint.
hist.gu6.4.bravo: OK: the image was not damaged or changed.
hist.gu6.4.adulte: Distributions publish (signed) fingerprints next to their images. Always check before installing.
hist.gu6.5.dit: Here are the disks of the computer to save (pretend). Which one is the stick?
hist.gu6.5.bravo: Look carefully at the sizes and the RM column.
hist.gu6.5.adulte: A "16 GB" stick shows as 14.6G: lsblk counts in GiB (1 GiB = 1.07 GB).
hist.gu6.6.bravo: That's the one! Picking the wrong disk means erasing the wrong one.
hist.gu6.6.adulte: dd erases EVERYTHING on its destination, without asking. Hence checking with lsblk.
hist.gu6.7.dit: Copy the image onto the fake stick with dd (they are FILES).
hist.gu6.7.bravo: Copied! dd copied the image byte by byte.
hist.gu6.7.adulte: if = the input file, of = the output, bs = the block size. On a real stick: only with an adult.

gu.meuble.mur:
🛠 THE FREE BUILDERS' GUILD — the wall of plans

Hello {nom}! Here we share our plans so that everyone can read them, remake them and improve them.

THE GUILD'S RULES
  1. Everything stays in your playground: the game installs nothing, sends nothing, creates no account.
  2. Never sudo. Installing a tool, contributing for real, printing: with an adult.
  3. Real disks and real USB sticks: we NEVER write to them here, we practise on files.
  4. When a tool is missing, we tell the story: nothing is blocked.

THE WORKSHOPS
  free software        (guilde libertes, guilde licence)
  real code            (git clone, guilde copie, guilde faim)
  the workshop         (gcc, make)
  contribution         (git switch, git diff, git commit)
  the factory          (openscad, guilde piece)
  the old PC           (lsblk, sha256sum, dd to a file)

Terminagotchi's code is public: anyone can read it, without an account.
A repository is the project's folder with its whole history (git).
git clone makes a copy on your computer. If the Internet doesn't answer, the Guild has a copy: `guilde copie`.

gu.compiler.texte:
The processor doesn't understand text: it only knows numbers (machine language).
The COMPILER (gcc) translates your text (the source code) into a program (a binary).
The program uses LIBRARIES: code already written, shared by everyone (to print, read a file…).

With an adult, it can be installed (Fedora: sudo dnf install gcc make; Debian, Ubuntu: sudo apt install build-essential).
Meanwhile, the compiling steps are told as a story.

gu.contrib.texte:
You can help a project in lots of ways: report a bug, translate, fix a text, improve the code.
The method: a BRANCH of your own, the change, git diff to reread it, a COMMIT with a clear message,
then a MERGE REQUEST: you propose your change, the project's keepers review it and decide.

gu.fusion.texte:
For real: you send your branch to the project's platform, then open a merge request (pull request).
The keepers review, ask questions, and merge… or explain why not. That's normal!
It needs an account: do it WITH AN ADULT. The game itself pushes nothing and creates no account.

gu.vieux.titre: Bringing an old PC back to life
gu.vieux.texte:
A computer that is too slow often isn't broken: its system has become too heavy for it.
You can install a light Linux on it. The steps: 1. prepare an installation USB stick, 2. boot from it,
3. install, 4. do the updates. Most of a computer's footprint comes from making it:
keeping it longer is digital sobriety.

gu.indice.dev: STOP: /dev/… are the REAL disks. Here we only write to files in the playground (cle_usb.img). On a real disk, dd erases everything.
gu.indice.sudo: No sudo in the Guild: the game installs nothing and doesn't touch the system.
gu.indice.local: Everything stays in your playground: no push, no merge request from the game. A real contribution is done with an adult.
gu.indice.trou: Replace the ? with your answers (don't copy them).
gu.indice.rep.libertes: Read the 4 freedoms again: use (0), study (1), share (2), improve (3).
gu.indice.rep.gratuit: Ask yourself just one question: can I read and change its code?
gu.indice.licence: Try a common program: bash, git, python3, gcc, firefox, vlc, gimp…
gu.indice.rep.faim: Look for the line that starts with def etat_de: the file name is just before the colon.
gu.indice.rep.trou: x is the first number in translate; y is the width divided by 2.
gu.indice.rep.volume: Multiply the plan's three numbers: length × width × thickness.
gu.indice.disque.systeme: Careful: that's the system disk (the one with /)! If we wrote to it, the computer wouldn't start any more.
gu.indice.disque.sauvegarde: That one is removable, but far too big for the stick: it's the backup disk.
gu.indice.disque.partition: That's a partition (a piece of a disk): give the name of the whole disk.
gu.indice.disque.inconnu: That name isn't in the list: read `guilde disques` again.
gu.indice.clone: No network? No problem: `guilde copie` gives you the game's code.
gu.indice.faute: The file isn't right yet: just one word to change, the misspelled one, and nothing else.
gu.indice.commit: The commit must contain your correction (git commit -am: the a adds the changed file), and be on YOUR branch, not main (git switch -c).
gu.indice.copie: The stick isn't an exact copy yet: if=the image, of=cle_usb.img.
gu.garde.dev: ⛔ A command to /dev/… targets a REAL disk. Never do it without an adult: dd erases everything on it. In the Guild, we practise on files.
gu.garde.local: Guild reminder: everything stays local. Sending a real contribution is done with an adult.
gu.garde.installe: Installing software changes the computer: always ask an adult. The game itself installs nothing.
gu.f.libre.enfant: Free software gives you 4 freedoms: use it, study it, share it, improve it. Its licence says so.
gu.f.libre.grands: Free software (FSF, freedoms 0 to 3) and open source (OSI definition). Copyleft licences (GPL: modified versions stay free) or permissive ones (MIT, BSD, Apache); Creative Commons for works (images, texts). Free ≠ costless.
gu.f.libre.limite: A licence doesn't say whether software is good or safe: it only says what you are allowed to do with it.
gu.f.libre.idee: "Free means costless": no. Free software can be sold, and costless software can be closed.
gu.f.lire_code.enfant: A free project's code can be read like a book: you copy it to your computer, look at its tree, search for a word.
gu.f.lire_code.grands: git clone copies a repository (the project and its history); tree shows the folder tree; grep -rn searches a pattern in every file; less reads page by page.
gu.f.lire_code.limite: Reading a big project takes time: start with one precise question ("where is hunger decided?").
gu.f.lire_code.idee: "To read code you have to understand everything": no, you follow a thread (a word, a function) and learn along the way.
gu.f.compiler.enfant: The compiler translates a program's text into machine language. The result is a new file: the program.
gu.f.compiler.grands: gcc compiles C into an ELF binary (magic number 7f 45 4c 46); it is linked to shared libraries (libc, listed by ldd); make applies rules (implicit or from a Makefile) and only redoes what changed.
gu.f.compiler.limite: Not every language is compiled in advance: Python and bash are interpreted when you run them.
gu.f.compiler.idee: "The compiled program still contains my text": no, it only contains instructions for the processor (and not the comments).
gu.f.contribuer.enfant: Contributing means helping a project: on a branch of your own, you fix, check, save, then propose.
gu.f.contribuer.grands: git switch -c (a branch), git diff (reread), git commit (save), then a merge request (pull request) reviewed by the maintainers. Bugs, translations and texts are contributions just like code.
gu.f.contribuer.limite: In the game, everything stays local: a real merge request needs an account on the project's platform, with an adult.
gu.f.contribuer.idee: "A contribution is always code": no, fixing a typo or translating helps just as much.
gu.f.fabriquer.enfant: With OpenSCAD, you describe an object with code (a cube minus a cylinder), and you get a file for the 3D printer.
gu.f.fabriquer.grands: Parametric modelling (OpenSCAD: cube, cylinder, translate, difference); STL export (a mesh of triangles: normal + 3 vertices); a slicer cuts it into layers (G-code) for the printer.
gu.f.fabriquer.limite: The STL file only keeps the shape: not the colour, the material, or the code's "smart" measurements.
gu.f.fabriquer.idee: "The 3D printer reads the STL file directly": no, it must be sliced into layers first.
gu.f.redonner_vie.enfant: An old PC can live again with a light Linux: a well-checked installation USB stick, on the right disk, with an adult.
gu.f.redonner_vie.grands: lsblk identifies disks (size, RM, mount points); sha256sum -c checks the downloaded image; dd if=image of=<disk> copies byte by byte and erases the destination; then install and update. Sobriety: manufacturing weighs most in the footprint.
gu.f.redonner_vie.limite: In the game, the stick is a file: on a real stick, a wrong disk name erases the wrong disk.
gu.f.redonner_vie.idee: "dd asks for confirmation before erasing": no, it writes straight away, without asking anything.
maths.coordonnees.question: Can you locate a point with two numbers (x and y)?
maths.coordonnees.enfant: A point is located with two numbers: x (how many steps to the right) and y (how many steps up).
maths.coordonnees.grands: Orthonormal frame: a point M(x; y); in 3D, add z. The distance between two points on the same horizontal line is |x₂ − x₁|.
maths.coordonnees.limite: In the game, the steps are millimetres; on a screen they are pixels, and y sometimes goes downwards!
maths.coordonnees.idee: "(2; 5) and (5; 2) are the same": no, order matters, x first, then y.
maths.coordonnees.ex1: The hole at (6; 12): 6 mm to the right, 12 mm up.
maths.coordonnees.ex2: A at (3; 4), B at (10; 4): they are on the same line, 10 − 3 = 7 steps apart.
maths.coordonnees.ex3: `echo $((10 - 3))` prints 7: the distance between x = 3 and x = 10.
maths.coordonnees.exo: A is at ({a}; {y}) and B at ({b}; {y}). How many steps between A and B?
maths.coordonnees.erreur: Both points are on the same line: compute {b} − {a}.
maths.coordonnees.kw: coordinates coordinate grid point x y z axis position distance translate
maths.volume.question: Can you compute the volume of a box (length × width × height)?
maths.volume.enfant: Volume is the space an object takes: a box 3 cubes long, 2 wide and 2 high holds 12 little cubes.
maths.volume.grands: Volume of a cuboid: V = L × l × h; in mm³ if the lengths are in mm; 1 cm³ = 10³ mm³, 1 L = 1 dm³ = 1,000 cm³.
maths.volume.limite: A real printed part isn't solid: the printer often fills it with a honeycomb to save material.
maths.volume.idee: "A part 2 times bigger in every direction takes 2 times more material": no, 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 times more!
maths.volume.ex2: The 40 mm × 24 mm × 4 mm key ring: 40 × 24 × 4 = 3,840 mm³, about 3.8 cm³.
maths.volume.exo: A box measures {a} × {b} × {c} little cubes. How many little cubes in all?
maths.volume.kw: volume cube cubes cuboid box length width height thickness mm3 cm3 litre material
hist.gu2.t3.dit: Look at all the folders and files of the copy.
hist.gu2.t3.bravo: pc/tg: that's where the computer version of the game lives.
hist.gu2.t3.adulte: ls -R goes into every subfolder (the phone has no tree).
hist.gu2.t7.dit: Read the beginning of this file.
hist.gu2.t7.bravo: Numbers, conditions, comments: the recipe for hunger!
hist.gu2.t7.adulte: head -40 shows the first 40 lines (the phone has no less).
hist.gu4.t5.dit: Show what you changed: compare the original and your version.
hist.gu4.t5.bravo: After < the old line, after > the new one: that's what the project's keepers will read.
hist.gu4.t5.adulte: On a computer, git diff does the same in a git repository; the phone has no git.
gu.tel.raconte: On the phone, it's told as a story: the app doesn't have {outil}.
gu.tel.licences: On the phone, the Guild answers from its catalogue (bash, git, python3, gcc, firefox, gimp…).
gu.tel.copie: On the phone, the copy contains EXTRACTS of the game's real code (pc/tg).
gu.tel.gcc: The phone has no compiler: on a computer, gcc turns bonjour.c into a program.
gu.indice.sed_i: Without -i, sed SHOWS the corrected text but doesn't change the file. Add -i: sed -i 's/wrong/right/' langues/fr.txt.
gu.indice.inverse: Mind the direction! if = what we READ (the image), of = what we OVERWRITE (the stick). The image has just been overwritten: type `guilde cle` to put everything back.
