hist.observatoire.debut: 🔭 At the very top of the hill, a dome opens onto the stars… Welcome to the AI Observatory! Here we give missions to little robot helpers, we check their work, and we discover how a machine "learns". All the robots here are small programs of the game: no real AI, nothing is sent anywhere.
hist.observatoire.fin: You can give a clear instruction, check a piece of work, hide a key, refuse a dangerous action and stop an agent that runs wild. You know how a guesser learns, why it makes mistakes and why it can make things up. You are Chief of the Robots!
ob.ouvert.log: 🌍 A world opens at the Crossroads: the AI Observatory
ob.ouvert.dit: You can read, connect commands and set padlocks: the AI Observatory opens its dome to you! There we learn to command robots… and to check what they do. Whenever you like: `cd ~/terrain_terminagotchi/observatoire`.
ob.pont: This step uses a maths idea: {notion}. Do you know it? If not, type `{cmd}`: we cross the bridge, then come back here.
ob.pas_vraie_ia: The Observatory's robots are small programs of the game, not real AIs. Real AIs are much bigger, but the principle is right. Nothing is sent over the Internet.
ob.pas_vraie_ia_court: a small program of the game, not a real AI
hist.ob0.1.dit: Look at what is under the dome.
hist.ob0.1.bravo: The dome, the notebook, the missions… Everything is ready.
hist.ob0.1.adulte: The game prepared the observatoire folder in your playground. Everything written in this world stays there.
hist.ob0.2.dit: Read the rules of the dome.
hist.ob0.2.bravo: Here, the robots are small programs of the game. And you are always the one who decides.
hist.ob0.2.adulte: No network call, no account, no API key: the assistant, the guessers and the agents are game code, deterministic, readable in pc/tg/observatoire.py.
hist.ob1.0.dit: A mission is a text. Find out what a good instruction must say.
hist.ob1.0.bravo: WHAT to do, ON WHICH file, and what to look for: a clear instruction answers all of that.
hist.ob1.0.adulte: AI assistants read instructions in natural language ("prompts"); the more precise they are, the more useful the result.
hist.ob1.1.dit: Go into missions and read the first instruction.
hist.ob1.1.bravo: "Do something": not very clear, is it?
hist.ob1.1.adulte: A vague instruction lets the tool guess; it may then do anything at all.
hist.ob1.2.dit: Give this vague instruction to the assistant.
hist.ob1.2.bravo: It doesn't know what to do. At least it says so!
hist.ob1.2.adulte: Our assistant only recognises a few words (count, sort, list) and a file name. A real AI would often invent an answer rather than say it didn't understand.
hist.ob1.3.dit: Write a clear instruction in mission.txt (replace the ?), for example: Count the Fire creatures in creatures.txt
hist.ob1.3.bravo: A clear instruction: what, on which file, and what to look for.
hist.ob1.3.adulte: echo writes the text, > puts it in a file (replacing what was there).
hist.ob1.4.dit: Give mission.txt to the assistant and put its report in rapport.txt.
hist.ob1.4.bravo: A tool reads a file and writes a file: that's the whole principle!
hist.ob1.4.adulte: What the assistant SAYS is shown (standard error); what it PRODUCES goes into rapport.txt (standard output, redirected by >).
hist.ob1.5.bravo: The report is there. But… is it right? That's the next lesson.
hist.ob1.5.adulte: We keep the instruction and the report in files: we can reread them, compare them and redo them.
hist.ob2.0.dit: A good chief always checks. Find out how.
hist.ob2.0.bravo: Count, compare, test: three ways to check.
hist.ob2.0.adulte: An AI assistant can be wrong with great confidence: we check with simple, safe tools.
hist.ob2.1.dit: Ask the assistant to sort creatures.txt, and put the result in tri.txt.
hist.ob2.1.bravo: It says it sorted everything. Really everything?
hist.ob2.1.adulte: This little assistant has a flaw on purpose: when it sorts, it forgets one line. Real tools make mistakes too.
hist.ob2.2.dit: Count the lines of both files.
hist.ob2.2.bravo: 20 on one side, 19 on the other: one is missing!
hist.ob2.2.adulte: wc -l counts lines; with two files, it also gives the total.
hist.ob2.3.dit: Compare the right sort with the assistant's.
hist.ob2.3.bravo: The < shows the line that is in the right sort but not in tri.txt.
hist.ob2.3.adulte: diff - tri.txt compares the input (the -, here the output of sort) with the file. "7d6": line 7 was deleted.
hist.ob2.4.dit: Run the test prepared by the Observatory.
hist.ob2.4.bravo: The test says it at once: FAILED.
hist.ob2.4.adulte: A test is a small program that checks a result. It never gets tired: you can run it again after every change.
hist.ob2.5.dit: Which creature did the assistant forget? Replace the ? with its name.
hist.ob2.5.bravo: Unmasked! Without checking, nobody would have seen it.
hist.ob2.5.adulte: Reread, count, compare, test: that is the real job of someone who uses assistants.
hist.ob2.6.dit: Do the sort yourself with sort, then run the test again.
hist.ob2.6.bravo: PASSED! The right tool, and the proof that it is right.
hist.ob2.6.adulte: && only runs the test if the sort worked. sort does the same job every time: we can trust it, and we still check.
hist.ob3.0.dit: Real online assistants often ask for a secret key. Find out how to protect it.
hist.ob3.0.bravo: An API key is a password for a machine.
hist.ob3.0.adulte: With an API key, a program uses an online service on someone's behalf (often on their paid account). Here, the key is an EXAMPLE that works nowhere.
hist.ob3.1.dit: Go into secrets. Check whether there is a key in the file shared with the whole class.
hist.ob3.1.bravo: The key is in plain text, and everybody can read it. Oops!
hist.ob3.1.adulte: grep -n shows the number of the line found. People often search for forgotten keys like this before sharing code.
hist.ob3.2.dit: Remove the key's line from the shared file.
hist.ob3.2.bravo: No more key in the shared file.
hist.ob3.2.adulte: sed -i '/pattern/d' deletes the lines containing the pattern. A real key that was shared must also be changed: we treat it as lost.
hist.ob3.3.dit: Put the example key in a separate file, .env.
hist.ob3.3.bravo: .env: a hidden file, just for secrets.
hist.ob3.3.adulte: The dot at the start hides the file (ls -a to see it). The name .env is a common habit.
hist.ob3.4.dit: Put a padlock on it: only you can read .env.
hist.ob3.4.bravo: 600: read and write for you, nothing for the others.
hist.ob3.4.adulte: chmod 600 = rw-------: just like at the Citadel.
hist.ob3.5.dit: Tell git never to take .env along.
hist.ob3.5.bravo: In .gitignore, .env will never leave with the code.
hist.ob3.5.adulte: git ignores the files listed in .gitignore: they are neither added nor sent.
hist.ob3.6.dit: Another way: put the key in a variable of your terminal.
hist.ob3.6.bravo: The key lives in your terminal's memory, not in a file.
hist.ob3.6.adulte: export makes the variable visible to programs started from this terminal; it disappears when you close it.
hist.ob3.7.dit: Ask the Observatory whether it can see the key.
hist.ob3.7.bravo: It sees it, but never shows it in full.
hist.ob3.7.adulte: A program reads environment variables (os.environ). A good habit: never write a key in a log or on the screen.
hist.ob4.0.dit: An agent is a robot that ACTS on its own. Find out how we watch over it.
hist.ob4.0.bravo: An agent acts, so we read its log and keep control.
hist.ob4.0.adulte: An AI agent chains actions (reading, writing, running commands). The rules: limits, a log, a review, and a stop button.
hist.ob4.1.dit: Go into chantier and start Robot-Tidier.
hist.ob4.1.bravo: It worked, and it is still proposing things…
hist.ob4.1.adulte: Robot-Tidier is fictional: it only acts in chantier/ and only through the game's code.
hist.ob4.2.bravo: What it did, and what it wants to do. One of the proposals is dangerous!
hist.ob4.2.adulte: The log lets you find out afterwards what the agent did, and why.
hist.ob4.3.dit: Look at exactly what it changed in the list.
hist.ob4.3.bravo: Red for before, green for after: nothing hidden.
hist.ob4.3.adulte: git diff compares the file with the recorded version. ALWAYS review an agent's work before accepting it.
hist.ob4.4.dit: Refuse the dangerous proposal: replace the ? with its number.
hist.ob4.4.bravo: Refused! And the game would never have run it.
hist.ob4.4.adulte: rm -rf deletes everything, with no recycle bin. An agent must not be allowed to run that: we limit what it can do.
hist.ob4.5.dit: The rest is fine: approve the agent's work.
hist.ob4.5.bravo: Work reviewed, danger refused, work approved.
hist.ob4.5.adulte: The human approves: the agent proposes, the chief decides.
hist.ob4.6.dit: This agent goes round in circles! Start it, then stop it with Ctrl+C.
hist.ob4.6.bravo: Ctrl+C: the terminal's stop button. You keep control!
hist.ob4.6.adulte: Ctrl+C sends the SIGINT signal to the foreground program. Here, the agent also stops by itself after 20 seconds: a time limit is a safeguard.
hist.ob5.0.dit: How does a machine "learn"? With examples. Discover the type guesser.
hist.ob5.0.bravo: We show it creatures, saying "Fire" or "not Fire". It counts.
hist.ob5.0.adulte: That's machine learning: labelled examples → a rule. Our guesser only counts, transparently.
hist.ob5.1.dit: Go into devineur and look at the first 5 examples.
hist.ob5.1.bravo: A name, a family, a place, and the answer: Fire or not Fire.
hist.ob5.1.adulte: Each line is an example; the last column is the label (the expected answer).
hist.ob5.2.dit: How many "Fire" and "not Fire" examples? Count the 4th column.
hist.ob5.2.adulte: awk '{print $4}' keeps the 4th column; sort | uniq -c counts each value (the frequencies).
hist.ob5.3.dit: Train the guesser on the examples.
hist.ob5.3.adulte: "Training" fills a table of counts. Real AIs adjust billions of numbers, but the idea is the same: the examples become numbers.
hist.ob5.4.bravo: No magic: just numbers you can read.
hist.ob5.4.adulte: For each family and each place: how many examples were Fire, how many were not.
hist.ob5.5.dit: Show it a creature it has never seen.
hist.ob5.5.bravo: It got it wrong, and was sure of itself!
hist.ob5.5.adulte: Testing on never-seen examples is the only way to know whether the learned rule really works.
hist.ob5.6.dit: What fooled it: the family or the place? Replace the ?.
hist.ob5.6.bravo: It had never seen a Demon that wasn't Fire. It doesn't "understand": it counts.
hist.ob5.6.adulte: A model generalises from what it has seen; a case it has never seen can fool it completely.
hist.ob6.0.dit: And what if we only showed it one corner of the world? Discover bias.
hist.ob6.0.bravo: Examples coming only from volcanoes… Let's see what happens.
hist.ob6.0.adulte: A bias is an error that always goes the same way, often because of the training data.
hist.ob6.1.dit: Where do the examples in volcan.txt come from? Count the 3rd column (the place).
hist.ob6.1.bravo: Volcano, lava, ashes… only hot places!
hist.ob6.1.adulte: cut -d ' ' -f 3 keeps the 3rd column (columns are separated by spaces).
hist.ob6.2.dit: And the answers? Count the 4th column.
hist.ob6.2.bravo: 12 Fire, and not a single "not Fire".
hist.ob6.2.adulte: Only one answer in the data: the guesser can only learn that one.
hist.ob6.3.bravo: It learned… that everything is Fire.
hist.ob6.3.adulte: Data makes the AI: even a good program learns badly from badly chosen examples.
hist.ob6.4.dit: Test it on 5 creatures from elsewhere.
hist.ob6.4.bravo: 1 out of 5: it sees Fire everywhere!
hist.ob6.4.adulte: 1 success out of 5 is 20%. The guesser answers "Fire" because that's all it has seen.
hist.ob6.5.dit: Why was it wrong? Choose the right explanation.
hist.ob6.5.bravo: The examples only showed one corner of the world.
hist.ob6.5.adulte: Quality, quantity, representativeness: the three questions to ask about training data.
hist.ob6.6.dit: Train it again on the varied examples.
hist.ob6.6.bravo: Examples from everywhere, Fire and not Fire.
hist.ob6.6.adulte: Fixing a bias often starts with fixing the data.
hist.ob6.7.dit: Test it again on the 5 creatures from elsewhere.
hist.ob6.7.bravo: 5 out of 5! The same calculations, better data.
hist.ob6.7.adulte: 5 out of 5 here does not mean "perfect" everywhere: we saw in O5 that a never-seen case can still fool it.
hist.ob7.0.dit: A word guesser guesses how a sentence goes on. Discover it.
hist.ob7.0.bravo: It read the game's story. Let's see how it guesses.
hist.ob7.0.adulte: Language models predict the next word (actually a "token") from statistics learned on huge texts.
hist.ob7.1.dit: Go into mots. Which words come up most often in the story?
hist.ob7.1.bravo: The little words come up all the time!
hist.ob7.1.adulte: tr ' ' '\n' puts one word per line; sort | uniq -c counts; sort -rn sorts from largest to smallest.
hist.ob7.2.dit: Put one word per line in mots.txt.
hist.ob7.2.bravo: A long ribbon of words, one per line.
hist.ob7.2.adulte: < histoire.txt gives the file to tr, > mots.txt stores the result.
hist.ob7.3.dit: Now count the PAIRS of words that follow each other.
hist.ob7.3.bravo: Here is the guesser's table: which word follows which word, and how many times.
hist.ob7.3.adulte: tail -n +2 shifts the ribbon by one word; paste glues each word to the next one. These are "bigrams".
hist.ob7.4.dit: Ask the guesser what follows a word of the story (replace the ?, for example the).
hist.ob7.4.bravo: The most frequent word has the best chance of being chosen.
hist.ob7.4.adulte: Count ÷ total = the estimated probability of the next word.
hist.ob7.5.dit: Make it write a sentence that starts with a word (replace the ?).
hist.ob7.5.bravo: It sounds like the story… but is it true?
hist.ob7.5.adulte: Each word is drawn according to the pairs. The sentence can sound right and still be false or absurd: that's the idea of "hallucinations".
hist.ob7.6.dit: True or false? Replace the ? with v (vrai, true) or f (faux, false).
hist.ob7.6.bravo: It guesses what comes next; it never checks whether it is true.
hist.ob7.6.adulte: Real models are immensely bigger and finer (they look at the whole beginning of the text, not just the previous word), but the principle "guess what comes next" is right.
hist.ob8.0.dit: The detective believes nothing without proof. Discover the method.
hist.ob8.0.bravo: An answer can be checked: with a command, a source, or by cross-checking.
hist.ob8.0.adulte: Cross-checking: comparing several independent sources. An AI's answer is not a source.
hist.ob8.1.dit: The assistant answered 5 questions. Read its answers.
hist.ob8.1.bravo: It looks very sure of itself. Yet two answers are wrong!
hist.ob8.1.adulte: The answers are made by the game, on purpose, to practise checking.
hist.ob8.2.dit: Check question 1: count the lines of the examples.
hist.ob8.2.adulte: A safe command, a result you can redo.
hist.ob8.3.bravo: The terminal never gets tired and never bluffs.
hist.ob8.3.adulte: % is the remainder of the division (the modulo).
hist.ob8.4.dit: Check question 5 with the game's glossary: what does rm do?
hist.ob8.4.bravo: The game's glossary is a checked source.
hist.ob8.4.adulte: For question 4 (ls), same method: explique ls. For question 3, you know how to count words (O7).
hist.ob8.5.dit: Which answers are wrong? Replace the ? with their two numbers.
hist.ob8.5.bravo: Unmasked! You checked instead of believing.
hist.ob8.5.adulte: Even an assistant that is often right can be wrong: we check what matters.
hist.ob8.6.dit: What we can ask, and what we keep to ourselves: look at these 6 messages.
hist.ob8.6.bravo: Some messages contain things you must never give away.
hist.ob8.6.adulte: What you write to an online service may be stored, read again or used to train models.
hist.ob8.7.dit: For each message: c (I can ask) or g (I keep it to myself). Replace the ?.
hist.ob8.7.bravo: Address, passwords, photos of other people: we keep them to ourselves.
hist.ob8.7.adulte: Personal data (full name, address, school, photos, passwords) is not given to an AI service; a photo of someone else needs their permission.
hist.ob8.8.dit: Some ideas worth knowing about AI: look at these 5 sentences.
hist.ob8.8.bravo: Some are true, others are misconceptions.
hist.ob8.8.adulte: Deepfakes, copyright, energy: serious topics, to discuss without fear.
hist.ob8.9.dit: True or false? Replace the ? with v (vrai, true) or f (faux, false).
hist.ob8.9.bravo: You have the critical mind of a real detective.
hist.ob8.9.adulte: An AI can be very useful; knowing its limits lets you use it well.
hist.ob9.0.dit: One big task, three agents. Meet the team.
hist.ob9.0.bravo: Sorter, Counter, Quill… and Copier. The chief is you.
hist.ob9.0.adulte: Leading agents: split the task, give clear instructions, review, test, refuse, keep control.
hist.ob9.1.dit: In which order should the 3 subtasks be done? Replace the ? with the numbers in the right order.
hist.ob9.1.bravo: First the list, then the count, finally the invitations.
hist.ob9.1.adulte: Splitting a task into small checkable steps is the basis of working with agents.
hist.ob9.2.dit: Which instruction should you give the team? Replace the ? with its letter.
hist.ob9.2.bravo: Clear, precise, and within safe limits.
hist.ob9.2.adulte: A good instruction says what to do, where, and what is forbidden.
hist.ob9.3.dit: Go into equipe and start the agents.
hist.ob9.3.bravo: Oh no: the Copier agent is running wild!
hist.ob9.3.adulte: The agents are fictional: the game writes their files in equipe/ only. Copier adds copies with every command you type.
hist.ob9.4.bravo: Stopped! The STOP file tells all the agents to stop.
hist.ob9.4.adulte: An emergency stop ("kill switch") must be simple, fast and always within reach.
hist.ob9.5.dit: How many copies did it make?
hist.ob9.5.bravo: That's why you stop an agent that runs wild quickly.
hist.ob9.5.adulte: ls copies | wc -l counts the files in the folder.
hist.ob9.6.bravo: One proposal is dangerous. Did you see it?
hist.ob9.6.adulte: sudo gives full powers; chmod -R 777 would open everything to everyone.
hist.ob9.7.dit: Refuse the dangerous proposal: replace the ? with its number.
hist.ob9.7.adulte: The chief keeps control: nothing dangerous without their agreement, and the game never runs these texts.
hist.ob9.8.dit: Review the Sorter's work: compare the guests and its list.
hist.ob9.8.bravo: It sorted and removed the duplicates. Good work!
hist.ob9.8.adulte: diff shows the lines missing (<) and added (>).
hist.ob9.9.bravo: A test fails: the Counter made a mistake!
hist.ob9.9.adulte: It counted the guests WITH the duplicates. A test spotted it for you.
hist.ob9.10.dit: Fix the count yourself with wc.
hist.ob9.10.bravo: The right number, calculated by you.
hist.ob9.10.adulte: wc -l < liste.txt gives only the number (without the file name).
hist.ob9.11.adulte: We run the tests again after every fix.
hist.ob9.12.adulte: The report keeps a record: what was done, refused, stopped and fixed.
ob.mot.lister: list listing show display find search
ob.meuble.coupole:
🔭 THE AI OBSERVATORY — the rules of the dome

Hello {nom}! Here we give missions to robots, check their work and discover how a machine learns.

THE RULES OF THE DOME
  1. No real AI: our robots are small programs of the game. Nothing is sent over the Internet.
  2. We ALWAYS check: a robot can be wrong while looking sure of itself.
  3. The agents only act in the Observatory. A dangerous proposed action (rm -rf, sudo) is REFUSED: the game never runs it.
  4. We never give our secrets (address, passwords, photos) to a robot.
  5. You are the chief: you can always stop an agent.

THE ROOMS
  the missions       (assistant, wc, diff, test.sh)
  the secrets        (.env, chmod 600, .gitignore)
  the work site      (agent, git diff, Ctrl+C)
  the guesser        (devine-type, uniq -c)
  the words          (tr, paste, devine-mot)
  the team           (agent stop, tests.sh)
ob.meuble.carnet: # The observatory notebook: the game writes down what you managed to do.
ob.meuble.secrets: The secrets room. Here, the only key is an EXAMPLE key: it works nowhere.
ob.meuble.chantier: Robot-Tidier's work site (a fictional agent of the game). Type `agent lance` to put it to work.
ob.meuble.mots: histoire.txt: the real sentences of the game's story, in lower case, without punctuation. The word guesser only trains on this text.
ob.meuble.tache:
THE BIG TASK: prepare the creatures' party.
- We need a guest list without duplicates.
- We need to know how many guests there are.
- We need one invitation per guest.
Your team: Sorter, Counter, Quill and Copier (fictional agents of the game).
ob.mission.exemple: Count the Fire creatures in creatures.txt
ob.mission.texte:
An instruction is a text. A good instruction says:
  • WHAT to do (count, sort, list…)
  • ON WHICH file (creatures.txt)
  • WHAT to look for (for example the Fire type)
Example: {exemple}
Our assistant is a small program of the game: it understands nothing, it recognises a few words.
ob.config.titre: observatory settings (file SHARED with the whole class)
ob.chantier.commit: The list to tidy (before the agent)
ob.copie.texte: copy no.{n} made by the Copier agent (it ran wild)
ob.invitation: Dear {nom} creature, you are invited to the Observatory's big party!
ob.aide.liste:
observatoire plan · mission · verifier · oubli NAME · secrets · cle · agent · apprendre · piege X
observatoire biais [N] · mots · perroquet … · esprit · confier … · nuances … · equipe · decoupe … · consigne X
assistant FILE · assistant questions · assistant fausses N N
agent lance · refuse N · accepte N · valide · boucle · stop · equipe · bilan
devine-type apprends F · teste F · NAME     devine-mot suite WORD · phrase WORD
ob.quiz.faux: {n} out of {total}: reread the explanations and try again.
ob.assistant.aide: Give me an instruction file: assistant mission.txt
ob.assistant.introuvable: I can't find the file {fichier} here.
ob.assistant.pas_compris: I didn't understand. I am missing:
ob.assistant.manque.quoi: WHAT to do (count, sort or list)
ob.assistant.manque.filtre: WHAT to look for in the file (for example Fire)
ob.assistant.conseil: Write a clearer instruction, then give it to me again.
ob.assistant.compris.compter: Understood: COUNT the lines of {fichier} that contain "{filtre}".
ob.assistant.compris.lister: Understood: LIST the lines of {fichier} that contain "{filtre}".
ob.assistant.tri_fini: I sorted the {n} lines, everything is perfect!
ob.verifier.texte:
A robot can be wrong while looking very sure of itself. Three ways to check:
  • COUNT     wc -l
  • COMPARE   diff (lines missing <, added >)
  • TEST      sh test.sh (a small program that says PASSED or FAILED)
The new mission is in mission_tri.txt.
ob.test.titre: The Observatory's test: tri.txt must have all the lines of creatures.txt, in order.
ob.test.reussi: PASSED: tri.txt has all the lines, in order.
ob.test.echec: FAILED: tri.txt has {obtenu} lines instead of {attendu} (or it is not in order).
ob.oubli.aide: Give the name of the forgotten creature: observatoire oubli NAME
ob.oubli.morale: It said "everything is perfect". Without checking, you would have believed it.
ob.cle.absente: I don't see any key in the environment. First type: export CLE_API=exemple-pas-une-vraie-cle
ob.cle.ok: I see a key in the environment: {debut}… ({n} characters). I don't write it anywhere.
ob.cle.morale: It will disappear when you close this terminal.
ob.agent.aide:
agent lance · agent refuse N · agent accepte N · agent valide · agent boucle
agent equipe · agent stop · agent bilan
ob.journal.titre: Log of Robot-Tidier (a FICTIONAL agent of the game: it only acts in chantier/)
ob.journal.trie: I sorted the lines in alphabetical order
ob.journal.comment: your agreement: agent accepte N, or agent refuse N
ob.prop.copie: keep a copy of the list
ob.prop.resume: write a summary of the party
ob.prop.sudo: "open everything to everyone, to go faster"
ob.prop.sauvegarde: keep a copy of the list
ob.refuse.aide: Give the number of the proposal: agent refuse N
ob.refuse.sure: Proposal {n} is not dangerous: you can keep it. Look for the one that deletes or gives all powers.
ob.refuse.ok: Proposal {n} refused. It will never be run.
ob.refuse.morale: An agent proposes; the chief decides. Danger, we refuse it.
ob.accepte.aide: Give the number of the proposal: agent accepte N
ob.accepte.jamais: No! Proposal {n} is dangerous: the game will NEVER run it, even if you accept.
ob.accepte.jamais2: With a real agent, it could have deleted or opened everything. Refuse it: agent refuse N.
ob.accepte.ok: Proposal {n} accepted: the agent did it, in the Observatory only.
ob.valide.pas_encore: Not so fast! A dangerous proposal is still waiting for your answer. Refuse it first.
ob.valide.ok: Work approved: list tidied, duplicates removed, danger refused.
ob.valide.morale: Review, refuse, approve: you supervised your first agent.
ob.boucle.debut: Robot-Spinner tidies… and tidies again… Stop it with Ctrl+C!
ob.boucle.limite: It stopped by itself at the end of its time limit. Next time, stop it with Ctrl+C!
ob.apprendre.texte:
The trainer shows 20 creatures and says for each one: "Fire" or "not Fire".
The type guesser COUNTS: for each family and each place, how many were Fire.
Then, facing a new creature, it makes its family and its place vote.
The files are in devineur/: exemples.txt (to learn), nouvelle.txt (to test).
ob.cerveau.titre: The guesser's brain: what it counted in {fichier} ({n} examples)
ob.cerveau.vraies: A real AI has billions of numbers; this one has a few dozen, but the idea is the same.
ob.devine.aide:
devine-type apprends exemples.txt   (it counts the examples)
devine-type teste nouvelle.txt      (it guesses, then we compare)
devine-type NAME                     (it guesses one creature)
ob.devine.aide_apprends: Tell it which file to learn from: devine-type apprends exemples.txt
ob.devine.aide_teste: Tell it which file to test: devine-type teste nouvelle.txt
ob.devine.vide: I found no example in {fichier} (4 columns are needed: name family place answer).
ob.devine.appris: Learned: {n} examples from {fichier} → {k} numbers in cerveau.txt.
ob.devine.cerveau: See what it remembered: cat cerveau.txt
ob.devine.pas_appris: I haven't learned anything yet: devine-type apprends exemples.txt
ob.devine.trompe: It got it wrong, and it looked sure of itself!
ob.devine.piege_question: What fooled it? observatoire piege family   or   observatoire piege place
ob.devine.autres_ok: With varied examples, it guesses the creatures from elsewhere well.
ob.devine.autres_biais: It sees what it learned everywhere… And what if the problem came from the examples?
ob.piege.aide: Answer: observatoire piege family   or   observatoire piege place
ob.piege.ok: Yes: the family. All the Demons it had seen were Fire; the mist, it had never seen.
ob.piege.morale: It doesn't "understand" what a Demon is: it counts. A never-seen case can fool it.
ob.biais.texte:
If we only show the guesser the creatures from volcanoes, what will it learn?
New files in devineur/: volcan.txt (to learn) and autres.txt (5 creatures from elsewhere, to test).
ob.biais.question: Why does the guesser see Fire everywhere?
ob.biais.exemples: The examples only showed one corner of the world (the volcanoes).
ob.biais.mechant: The guesser loves Fire and doesn't want to answer anything else.
ob.biais.puissance: The guesser isn't powerful enough: it would need a bigger computer.
ob.biais.aide: Answer with the number: observatoire biais N
ob.biais.morale:
A program has no wishes: it reproduces what it has seen.
Quality, quantity, representativeness: good examples, enough of them, coming from everywhere.
With real AIs too: if examples leave out people or places, the AI is wrong more often for them.
ob.mots.texte:
The word guesser read the game's story (mots/histoire.txt).
To guess what comes next, it looks at which word most often comes AFTER the previous word.
It's like a parrot that has read the whole library: it repeats what comes up often.
ob.devinemot.aide:
devine-mot suite WORD    (what comes after WORD, and how many times)
devine-mot phrase WORD   (it writes a sentence starting with WORD)
ob.devinemot.aide_suite: Give a word from the story: devine-mot suite the
ob.devinemot.aide_phrase: Give the first word: devine-mot phrase the
ob.devinemot.inconnu: The word "{mot}" is never followed by another word in the story. Try a word from the pair table.
ob.devinemot.proba: It will choose "{suivant}" {n} times out of {total}, about {pc} chances out of 100.
ob.devinemot.sonne: It sounds like the story… but it never checked whether it is true.
ob.devinemot.encore: Run devine-mot phrase {mot} again: chance changes what comes next.
ob.perroquet.titre: The word guesser: true (v) or false (f)?
ob.perroquet.frequent: It chooses a word that often comes after the previous word.
ob.perroquet.frequent.pourquoi: True: it follows its pair table.
ob.perroquet.verifie: It checks that its sentence is true before writing it.
ob.perroquet.verifie.pourquoi: False: it doesn't know what is true, it knows what is frequent.
ob.perroquet.invente: It can write a false sentence that sounds right.
ob.perroquet.invente.pourquoi: True: that's what we call a "hallucination".
ob.perroquet.aide: Answer in order: observatoire perroquet v f v
ob.perroquet.morale: Real text AIs guess what comes next too, on a much bigger scale: they can be wrong with confidence.
ob.esprit.texte:
The detective believes nothing without proof.
  • Check with a command, when possible.
  • Look for a reliable source (the game's glossary, documentation, a book).
  • Cross-check: several independent sources that say the same thing.
The assistant answered 5 questions: assistant questions
ob.questions.aide: Check each answer, then give the two wrong ones: assistant fausses N N
ob.q.lignes: How many lines are in devineur/exemples.txt?
ob.q.modulo: What is 17 % 5 (the remainder of 17 divided by 5)?
ob.q.mot: Which word comes up most often in mots/histoire.txt?
ob.q.mot.pourquoi: tr ' ' '\n' < mots/histoire.txt | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -1 gives the real one.
ob.q.ls: What does the ls command do?
ob.q.ls.vrai: It shows what is in a folder.
ob.q.ls.faux: It deletes all the files in a folder.
ob.q.ls.pourquoi: ls shows the contents of a folder; it deletes nothing (explique ls).
ob.q.rm: What does rm -r do to a folder?
ob.q.rm.vrai: It deletes the folder and everything in it, without going through the recycle bin.
ob.q.rm.faux: It puts the folder in the recycle bin: you can always get it back.
ob.q.rm.pourquoi: rm doesn't use the recycle bin: what is deleted is lost (explique rm).
ob.fausses.aide: Give the numbers of the two wrong answers: assistant fausses N N
ob.fausses.ok: Well done, detective! The wrong answers were:
ob.fausses.morale: It looked sure of itself every time. Confidence is not proof.
ob.fausses.faux: {j} out of {total} found ({trop} too many). Check again with the commands.
ob.confier.titre: What we ask, what we keep: c (I can ask) or g (I keep it to myself)?
ob.confier.expliquer: "Explain to me what the ls command does."
ob.confier.expliquer.pourquoi: A question about a command: no information about you.
ob.confier.adresse: "I live at 12 Lilac Street and I go to Jules Verne school."
ob.confier.adresse.pourquoi: Your address and your school say where to find you: we keep them to ourselves.
ob.confier.mot_de_passe: "Here is the password of my parents' tablet."
ob.confier.mot_de_passe.pourquoi: A password is never given, neither to a robot nor to anyone.
ob.confier.photo: "Here is a photo of my friend, he doesn't know."
ob.confier.photo.pourquoi: Someone's photo belongs to them: you always need their permission.
ob.confier.idees: "Give me ideas of names for my creature."
ob.confier.naissance: "My name is Lea Martin, I was born on 3 May 2017."
ob.confier.naissance.pourquoi: Your full name and your date of birth are personal data.
ob.confier.aide: Answer in the order of the messages: observatoire confier c g g g c g
ob.confier.ok: Perfect! You know what not to give away.
ob.confier.morale: What you write to an online service may be stored and read. If in doubt, ask an adult.
ob.nuances.assuree: An AI can be wrong while looking very sure of itself.
ob.nuances.assuree.pourquoi: True: a confident tone proves nothing, we check.
ob.nuances.deepfake: An image, a voice or a video made by an AI can look real (it's called a "deepfake").
ob.nuances.deepfake.pourquoi: True: before sharing, we ask where the image comes from; and we never make a fake image of someone.
ob.nuances.droits: Everything an AI makes is free to use: I can copy everything without checking anything.
ob.nuances.droits.pourquoi: False: it's more complicated. A creation can look like an author's work protected by copyright, and the rules differ between countries: we credit and we check.
ob.nuances.energie: An AI uses no energy, since everything happens "in the cloud".
ob.nuances.energie.pourquoi: False: the "cloud" is real computers in data centres, which use electricity (and often water to cool down).
ob.nuances.forcement: If an AI says it, it must be true.
ob.nuances.forcement.pourquoi: False: it guesses the most likely continuation; it can be wrong or make things up.
ob.nuances.aide: Answer in order: observatoire nuances v f v f f
ob.nuances.ok: Well done! You know the strengths and the limits of AIs.
ob.nuances.morale: An AI can help a lot; knowing its limits is how you use it well.
ob.decoupe.liste: make the guest list, without duplicates
ob.decoupe.aide: Give the numbers in the right order: observatoire decoupe N N N
ob.decoupe.ok: The right order: the list first, then the count, then the invitations.
ob.decoupe.morale: Without the right list, the count and the invitations would be wrong.
ob.consigne.titre: Which instruction should you give the team?
ob.consigne.claire: "In equipe/ only: make the guest list without duplicates, count them, write one invitation per guest. Delete nothing and ask me before any other action."
ob.consigne.dangereuse: "Do whatever it takes, even with sudo, I don't want to be disturbed."
ob.consigne.aide: Answer with the letter: observatoire consigne a
ob.consigne.ok: Clear, precise, with limits: a real chief's instruction.
ob.consigne.morale: Say where to act, what to do, and what is forbidden.
ob.consigne.non.floue: Too vague: the agents would have to guess what to do.
ob.consigne.non.dangereuse: Dangerous: we never give all powers to an agent.
ob.equipe.lancee: Your team is at work in equipe/!
ob.equipe.emballe: The Copier agent is running wild: already {n} copies, and it goes on with every command!
ob.jequipe.titre: Team log (FICTIONAL agents of the game: they only act in equipe/)
ob.jequipe.trieur: I tidied the {n} lines of invites.txt into liste.txt: {k} guests without duplicates
ob.jequipe.compteur: I counted {n} guests in invites.txt and wrote it in compte.txt
ob.jequipe.copieur: I copy, I copy, I copy… into copies/
ob.stop.fichier: EMERGENCY STOP: all the agents stop.
ob.stop.ok: Emergency stop! The STOP file is in place: the Copier agent stops after {n} copies.
ob.stop.morale: A good chief always knows where the stop button is.
ob.tests.titre: The team's tests: the count, the invitations, the emergency stop.
ob.tests.invitations_ko: FAILED: some invitations are missing (or there are too many).
ob.tests.stop_ok: the emergency stop is in place.
ob.tests.stop_ko: FAILED: no emergency stop (STOP) is in place.
ob.bilan.pas_encore: Not yet: you must split the task, choose the instruction, refuse the danger, fix the count, and all the tests must pass.
ob.bilan.texte:
Chief: {nom}
Task: the creatures' party, {n} guests.
✔ task split, clear instruction given
✔ Copier agent stopped after {copies} copies (emergency stop)
✔ dangerous proposal refused (never run)
✔ Sorter's work reviewed (diff)
✔ Counter's mistake found by the tests and fixed
The agents were small programs of the game: everything stayed in the Observatory.
ob.bilan.morale: Split, instruct, watch, refuse, test, stop: you are Chief of the Robots.
ob.indice.danger: Stop! sudo and rm -rf can break everything. In the Observatory, we never run them without an adult.
ob.indice.trou: Replace the ? with your answer (without the question mark).
ob.indice.rep.oubli: It's not that one. Compare: sort creatures.txt | diff - tri.txt (the line with <).
ob.indice.rep.piege: Look at cerveau.txt: which line, for the new creature's family or place, voted?
ob.indice.rep.biais: Reread the output of uniq -c: where did ALL the examples come from?
ob.indice.rep.perroquet: The guesser follows its pair table… but does it know what is true?
ob.indice.rep.fausses: Check each answer with a command: wc -l, echo $((17 % 5)), explique ls, explique rm, and the word count.
ob.indice.rep.confier: Address, school, password, other people's photos, full name: those we keep (g).
ob.indice.rep.nuances: Reread the explanations in green: an AI is sometimes wrong, uses energy, and what it makes is not necessarily free to use.
ob.indice.rep.decoupe: Can we count the guests before having a list without duplicates?
ob.indice.rep.consigne: Choose the instruction that says WHERE to act, WHAT to do and what is FORBIDDEN.
ob.indice.rep.refus: Read the log: which proposal deletes everything or gives all powers?
ob.indice.rep.suite: Choose a word that appears in the pair table (for example the).
ob.indice.rep.phrase: Choose a first word that appears in the pair table.
ob.indice.mission.quoi: Your instruction doesn't say WHAT to do: use count, sort or list.
ob.indice.mission.fichier: Your instruction doesn't say ON WHICH file: write creatures.txt in it.
ob.indice.mission.filtre: Your instruction doesn't say WHAT to look for: a type, for example Fire.
ob.indice.redirection: Put what the assistant produces in a file with > (for example > rapport.txt).
ob.indice.tri: The test wants all the lines, sorted: sort creatures.txt > tri.txt
ob.indice.chmod: The 600 padlock: chmod 600 .env (in the secrets folder).
ob.indice.ctrl_c: While it runs, press Ctrl (Control) and C at the same time.
ob.indice.reapprendre: It remembers volcan.txt: first train it again on exemples.txt.
ob.indice.compte: wc -l < liste.txt gives just the number; > compte.txt puts it in the file.
ob.indice.tests: A test still fails: reread its message (the count? the emergency stop?).
ob.garde.danger: ⛔ sudo, rm -rf ~ or chmod -R 777 can break everything. In the Observatory, these commands are REFUSED: never without an adult.
ob.f.mission.enfant: A mission is a text: WHAT to do, ON WHICH file, WHAT to look for. The tool reads the instruction and writes its report.
ob.f.mission.grands: A command-line assistant reads an instruction (a "prompt") and produces output that we redirect into a file (>). The more precise the instruction (task, data, expected format, limits), the more usable the result.
ob.f.mission.limite: Our assistant recognises a few words; a real AI assistant understands much more varied sentences, but it may also guess wrongly instead of saying it didn't understand.
ob.f.mission.idee: "An AI understands what I mean, even if it's vague": no, a vague instruction often gives an off-target result.
ob.f.verifier.enfant: We always check a robot's work: we count, we compare, we test.
ob.f.verifier.grands: Checking an output: simple checks (wc -l), comparison with a reference (diff), automated tests (exit code 0 = passed). We don't confuse confidence with accuracy.
ob.f.verifier.limite: A test only checks what we ask it to: a passing test doesn't prove everything is right.
ob.f.verifier.idee: "If it says it's finished and perfect, then it's true": no, confidence is not proof.
ob.f.secrets.enfant: An API key is a password for a machine: never in a shared file.
ob.f.secrets.grands: Secrets (API keys, tokens) are kept out of the code: environment variable (export) or a .env file with permissions 600, listed in .gitignore. An exposed key must be revoked and replaced.
ob.f.secrets.limite: A .gitignore doesn't erase a key already recorded in git's history: you then have to change the key.
ob.f.secrets.idee: "If I delete the line, the key is no longer at risk": a key that was shared must be changed.
ob.f.superviser.enfant: An agent acts on its own: we read its log, review its changes, refuse danger and can stop it.
ob.f.superviser.grands: Human supervision of an agent: least privilege (it only acts where needed), action log, review of changes (git diff) before approval, refusal of destructive actions, interruption (Ctrl+C, SIGINT) and time limits.
ob.f.superviser.limite: Our agents are game scripts whose behaviour is fixed in advance; a real agent can make unexpected choices, hence the importance of limits.
ob.f.superviser.idee: "An agent knows what is dangerous and won't do it": no, it's up to the chief to limit and review.
ob.f.apprendre.enfant: A machine learns from examples: we show it creatures with the answer, it counts and draws a rule from them.
ob.f.apprendre.grands: Supervised machine learning: labelled examples (training) produce a model, evaluated on never-seen examples (test). Our guesser is a counting classifier (close to a simplified naive Bayes).
ob.f.apprendre.limite: The guesser doesn't "understand" like we do: it counts similarities. An AI doesn't understand like a human either.
ob.f.apprendre.idee: "An AI that has learned well is never wrong": no, a never-seen case can fool it.
ob.f.biais.enfant: If we only show the volcanoes, the guesser believes everything is Fire: data makes the AI.
ob.f.biais.grands: Data bias: an unrepresentative training set produces systematic errors. Quality, quantity and representativeness of data; measuring errors per group.
ob.f.biais.limite: Fixing the data is not always enough: errors must also be measured for each group.
ob.f.biais.idee: "A machine is neutral, it can't be biased": it reproduces the biases of its data.
ob.f.modele_langage.enfant: The word guesser guesses the next word from what often comes after: like a parrot that has read the whole library.
ob.f.modele_langage.grands: Language model: it estimates the probability of the next token. Here, bigrams counted with tr, paste, sort and uniq -c; large models use neural networks trained on huge texts and take the whole context into account.
ob.f.modele_langage.limite: Real models are much bigger and finer, but the principle "guess what comes next" is right. They have no "database of truth": they can make things up (hallucination).
ob.f.modele_langage.idee: "A well-written text is a true text": no, a sentence can sound right and be false.
ob.f.esprit_critique.enfant: The detective believes nothing without proof: they check with a command or a source, and keep their secrets to themselves.
ob.f.esprit_critique.grands: Critical thinking: checking (command, documentation), cross-checking sources, protecting personal data, respecting copyright and image rights, caution with deepfakes, awareness of the energy cost of data centres.
ob.f.esprit_critique.limite: We can't check everything ourselves: we choose reliable sources and check what matters.
ob.f.esprit_critique.idee: "It comes from an AI, so it's neutral and true": no, an AI's answer is not a source.
ob.f.equipe_agents.enfant: The captain of a robot crew splits the task, gives clear instructions, reviews, tests, refuses danger and can stop everything.
ob.f.equipe_agents.grands: Orchestrating agents: breaking down into subtasks, instructions with a scope and prohibitions, emergency stop (STOP file, signal), logs, review (diff), automated tests, human approval.
ob.f.equipe_agents.limite: The more agents there are, the more tests and reviews are needed: you can't watch everything by eye.
ob.f.equipe_agents.idee: "The more agents, the less work for me": you also have to lead them and check their work.
maths.effectifs.question: Do you know how to count how many times each thing comes up (the frequency)?
maths.effectifs.enfant: The frequency is how many times a thing comes up: in 🔥 💧 🔥, the frequency of 🔥 is 2.
maths.effectifs.grands: In statistics, the frequency (count) of a value is the number of times it appears; the sum of the counts is the total. sort | uniq -c gives the count of each line.
maths.effectifs.limite: uniq -c only counts identical lines that follow each other: you must sort with sort first.
maths.effectifs.idee: "uniq counts the whole file": no, without sort, two identical lines far apart are counted separately.
maths.effectifs.ex1: 🔥 💧 🔥 🔥: the count of 🔥 is 3, that of 💧 is 1, the total is 4.
maths.effectifs.ex2:
`printf 'Feu
Eau
Feu
' | sort | uniq -c` shows 1 Eau and 2 Feu.
maths.effectifs.ex3: In exemples.txt: 10 Fire and 10 not_Fire, total 20.
maths.effectifs.erreur: Count only the 🔥, one by one.
maths.effectifs.kw: frequency count counts how many times statistics uniq table data
maths.frequences.question: Do you know how to calculate a relative frequency (how many out of 100)?
maths.frequences.enfant: The relative frequency is the share of a thing in the whole: 10 Fire out of 20 creatures is half, 50 out of 100.
maths.frequences.grands: Relative frequency = count ÷ total count; as a percentage, × 100. A relative frequency is between 0 and 1 (0% and 100%).
maths.frequences.limite: The shell's `$(( ))` calculation rounds down (whole numbers): 1 × 100 / 3 gives 33.
maths.frequences.idee: "2 successes is better than 1 success": not necessarily, 2 out of 10 (20%) is worse than 1 out of 2 (50%).
maths.frequences.exo: {n} successes out of {total} tries: how many out of 100?
maths.frequences.kw: relative frequency percentage percent share proportion out of 100 statistics score
maths.probabilites.question: Do you know what a probability is (a chance out of how many)?
maths.probabilites.enfant: A probability is the chance that something happens: in a bag of 3 red marbles and 1 blue one, you draw a red one 3 times out of 4.
maths.probabilites.grands: Probability of an event = favourable cases ÷ possible cases (if all cases are equally likely), between 0 and 1. A word guesser estimates the probability of the next word by its frequency in texts.
maths.probabilites.limite: A probability says what happens OFTEN, not what will happen next time.
maths.probabilites.idee: "The most likely always happens": no, 75 chances out of 100 leave 25 chances out of 100 for something else.
maths.probabilites.ex1: 3 red marbles and 1 blue: 3 chances out of 4 of drawing a red one, 75 out of 100.
maths.probabilites.ex2: After "the", the guesser saw "world" 3 times and "nest" 1 time: it chooses "world" 3 times out of 4.
maths.probabilites.exo: After a word, the guesser saw "creature" {a} times and another word {b} times. How many chances out of 100 for "creature"?
maths.probabilites.kw: probability probabilities chance chances random draw out of 100 percentage prediction next word
ob.tel.raconte: On the phone, it is told as a story: the app doesn't have {outil}.
ob.tel.boucle: Robot-Spinner goes round in circles… On the phone, you stop it with: agent stop
ob.tel.export: On the phone, each line has its own terminal: export and echo go on the same line.
hist.ob3.t6.dit: Put the example key in a variable, and count its characters, on the same line.
hist.ob3.t6.bravo: The key lives in a variable, not in a file.
hist.ob3.t6.adulte: On the phone, each line has its own terminal: the variable disappears at the end of the line. ${#CLE_API} gives its length.
hist.ob4.t3.dit: Compare the list from before (.avant) with the agent's.
hist.ob4.t3.bravo: The lines missing (<) and added (>): nothing hidden.
hist.ob4.t3.adulte: The phone doesn't have git: diff compares two files.
hist.ob4.t7.bravo: Stopped! On a computer, it's Ctrl+C.
hist.ob4.t7.adulte: Ctrl+C sends the SIGINT signal to the foreground program; on the phone, agent stop plays that role.
hist.ob5.t2.dit: How many "Fire" and "not Fire" examples? Count the 4th column.
hist.ob5.t2.adulte: cut -d ' ' -f 4 keeps the 4th column; sort | uniq -c counts each value (the frequencies).
ob.indice.accepte: You wanted to ACCEPT the dangerous action! The game never runs it, but a real agent would. Refuse it: agent refuse N.
hist.donnees.debut: 📊 Behind a glass door, a sorting laboratory hums: a sieve, scissors, a mill, a scholar's calculator, a magic copyist… Welcome to the Data Room! Here we count, sort and calculate on YOUR collection of critters. Everything stays in your play area.
hist.donnees.fin: You can export your collection as a table, count, sort, cut out columns, fix a text, calculate a mean, a median and a range, chain tools together and query a real database. You are a Data Scholar!
dn.ouvert.log: 🌍 A world opens at the Crossroads: the Data Room
dn.ouvert.dit: You can read, search and connect commands: the Data Room opens its laboratory to you! There we do statistics on YOUR collection. Whenever you like: `cd ~/terrain_terminagotchi/donnees`.
dn.pont: This step uses a maths idea: {notion}. Do you know it? If not, type `{cmd}`: we cross the bridge, then come back here.
hist.dn0.1.dit: Look at what is in the laboratory.
hist.dn0.1.bravo: The laboratory and its notebook. The instruments are waiting for your data!
hist.dn0.1.adulte: The game prepared the donnees folder in your play area. Everything you make in this world stays there.
hist.dn0.2.bravo: Each tool has its instrument. And the data are YOUR critters.
hist.dn0.2.adulte: Data analysts often start with these small tools to look at a big file, before opening a spreadsheet or a program.
hist.dn1.0.dit: The game can write your collection as a table. Put that table in collection.csv.
hist.dn1.0.bravo: Your collection has become a table: one line per critter, columns separated by commas.
hist.dn1.0.adulte: CSV = "comma-separated values". No personal data: the species, the type, the stats, the rarity, the day of capture. Some exercises need a minimum number of creatures: the game says so and the step waits, without blocking anything.
hist.dn1.1.dit: Look at the top of the table.
hist.dn1.1.bravo: The first line gives the names of the columns; then one critter per line.
hist.dn1.1.adulte: The header line names each column: nom, type, famille, attaque…
hist.dn1.2.dit: Count the lines of the table.
hist.dn1.2.bravo: One line per critter, plus the line of titles!
hist.dn1.2.adulte: wc -l counts lines. The number of critters = lines − 1 (the header).
hist.dn1.3.dit: How many critters are in the table? Replace the ? with your answer.
hist.dn1.3.bravo: Right! You remembered to remove the line of titles.
hist.dn1.3.adulte: A classic analyst's mistake: counting the header as data.
hist.dn1.4.dit: Ask the mill to prepare two simple lists.
hist.dn1.4.bravo: especes.txt (one name per line) and forces.txt (attack, then name).
hist.dn1.4.adulte: Two columns taken out of the CSV by the game, to start without a separator. In the next level you will cut them yourself with cut.
hist.dn1.5.dit: Which species do you have most of? Sort, count the twins, then sort the numbers.
hist.dn1.5.bravo: uniq -c counts identical lines that follow each other: that's why we sort first!
hist.dn1.5.adulte: sort | uniq -c | sort -rn is the great classic for counting frequencies.
hist.dn1.6.dit: Your 3 strongest critters! Sort the numbers from biggest to smallest and keep the first 3 in top3.txt.
hist.dn1.6.bravo: Your podium is in top3.txt! Like the "Retro" trial of training, but with YOUR critters.
hist.dn1.6.adulte: sort -n sorts as numbers (9 before 10), -r in reverse; head -3 keeps the first 3 lines.
hist.dn2.0.dit: Discover the table's columns and their numbers.
hist.dn2.0.bravo: 13 columns, numbered from 1 to 13. Number 2 is the type; number 4, the attack.
hist.dn2.0.adulte: The column names and values stay the same in every language: they are data words.
hist.dn2.1.dit: Replace the commas of the first line with line breaks.
hist.dn2.1.bravo: tr changed each comma into a line break: one column per line.
hist.dn2.1.adulte: tr replaces characters one by one; '\n' means "line break".
hist.dn2.2.dit: Cut column 2 (the type), remove the line of titles, then count each type.
hist.dn2.2.bravo: Here is how many critters of each type you have!
hist.dn2.2.adulte: cut -d, -f2: the separator is the comma (-d,), we keep field 2 (-f2). tail -n +2 starts at line 2.
hist.dn2.3.dit: How many shiny ones? Cut column 10 and count the 1s.
hist.dn2.3.bravo: grep -c counts the lines that contain 1: those are your shiny ones.
hist.dn2.3.adulte: If there are none, grep -c shows 0 and answers "not found" (code 1): it is not an error.
hist.dn2.4.dit: Give your answer: how many shiny ones?
hist.dn2.4.bravo: Right! Shiny ones are rare: 1 chance in many.
hist.dn2.4.adulte: The game counted on the same file, at the same moment.
hist.dn2.5.dit: Put the names column in noms.txt and the types column in types.txt.
hist.dn2.5.adulte: && runs the second command only if the first one succeeded.
hist.dn2.6.dit: Glue the two columns back side by side with paste.
hist.dn2.6.bravo: paste glues line by line: name:type. The opposite of cut!
hist.dn2.6.adulte: paste -d: chooses the colon as separator.
hist.dn3.0.dit: The keeper wrote a notebook… with a mistake. Go and get it.
hist.dn3.0.bravo: A name is misspelled everywhere. The magic copyist will fix it.
hist.dn3.0.adulte: sed (stream editor) changes a text line by line, without an editor.
hist.dn3.1.bravo: Can you see the misspelled name?
hist.dn3.1.adulte: The misspelled name is the species you have most of, with two letters swapped.
hist.dn3.2.dit: Try the copyist: s/WRONG/RIGHT/ replaces the first ? with the second (the wrong name, then the right one).
hist.dn3.2.bravo: Look closely at the line where the name appears TWICE: without g, only the first one is fixed!
hist.dn3.2.adulte: s/a/b/ replaces the FIRST time on each line. sed shows the result; the file has not changed.
hist.dn3.3.dit: Add g ("everywhere") and put the corrected notebook in carnet_corrige.txt.
hist.dn3.3.bravo: Fixed everywhere, even twice on the same line!
hist.dn3.3.adulte: s/a/b/g: g = global, every time on each line.
hist.dn3.4.dit: Compare the old and the new notebook.
hist.dn3.4.bravo: < the old line, > the new one: only the wrong lines changed.
hist.dn3.5.dit: The copyist can also copy a piece: show lines 2 to 4.
hist.dn3.5.adulte: -n: nothing is shown except what p (print) asks for.
hist.dn3.6.dit: Fix the original directly with -i (in place).
hist.dn3.6.bravo: The keeper's notebook is fixed for good!
hist.dn3.6.adulte: sed -i changes the file itself: handy, but there is no going back. Keep a copy first (here carnet_corrige.txt).
hist.dn4.0.bravo: awk cuts each line into columns: $1, $2, $3… and it can calculate.
hist.dn4.0.adulte: awk reads line by line; -F, says that the columns are separated by commas.
hist.dn4.1.dit: Show the name ($1) and the attack ($4) of the first 5 lines.
hist.dn4.1.bravo: awk picked two columns. NR is the line number.
hist.dn4.1.adulte: NR<=5: only lines 1 to 5 (Number of Records).
hist.dn4.2.dit: Add up all the attacks (without the line of titles).
hist.dn4.2.bravo: The sum of all the attacks of your troop!
hist.dn4.2.adulte: s+=$4 adds column 4 to s; END {…} runs at the end of the file.
hist.dn4.3.dit: Now the mean: the sum divided by the number of critters.
hist.dn4.3.bravo: The average attack of your troop!
hist.dn4.3.adulte: n++ counts the lines; s/n is the mean. awk writes at most 6 digits.
hist.dn4.4.dit: Give the mean you found (a rounded value is enough).
hist.dn4.4.bravo: A correct statistic on your own collection!
hist.dn4.4.adulte: The game accepts the value within 0.5: rounding to a whole number is fine.
hist.dn4.5.dit: Put all the attacks, sorted as numbers, in attaques.txt.
hist.dn4.5.bravo: The attacks are in order, from the smallest to the biggest.
hist.dn4.5.adulte: cut keeps column 4, tail removes the header, sort -n sorts as numbers.
hist.dn4.6.dit: The median is the value in the middle of the sorted list. Look at attaques.txt (nl numbers the lines) and give it.
hist.dn4.6.bravo: The median cuts your troop into two equal halves!
hist.dn4.6.adulte: With an even number of values, the median is between the two middle ones (the game accepts both and their mean).
hist.dn4.7.dit: Show the first and the last line of attaques.txt.
hist.dn4.7.bravo: The smallest and the biggest attack.
hist.dn4.7.adulte: sed -n '1p;$p': line 1 and the last one ($).
hist.dn4.8.dit: The range is the biggest minus the smallest. Give it.
hist.dn4.8.bravo: The range tells whether your troop is very different or all alike.
hist.dn4.8.adulte: Range = maximum − minimum: a simple measure of spread.
hist.dn5.0.dit: Discover the machines in a chain: the pattern sieve, the dispenser and the switch.
hist.dn5.0.bravo: We are going to build your collection report!
hist.dn5.0.adulte: grep -E (patterns), xargs (lines become arguments) and tee (write AND show).
hist.dn5.1.dit: Keep the water OR ice critters: the | inside the pattern means "or".
hist.dn5.1.bravo: The pattern sieve keeps the lines that contain eau or glace.
hist.dn5.1.adulte: grep -E: extended regular expressions; a|b means a or b. Careful: the | BETWEEN quotes is an "or", not a pipe.
hist.dn5.2.dit: Make a single line with the names of your species (no duplicates).
hist.dn5.2.bravo: xargs puts the lines one after another, like words for a command.
hist.dn5.2.adulte: sort -u sorts and removes duplicates; xargs echo gives all the lines to echo at once.
hist.dn5.3.dit: Build an enclosure: one file per species, thanks to xargs.
hist.dn5.3.bravo: One file per species in enclos/, in a single line!
hist.dn5.3.adulte: sed builds each file name (enclos/NAME.txt), then xargs gives them all to touch at once.
hist.dn5.4.dit: The podium (the 3 strongest attacks) goes to the screen AND into rapport.txt thanks to tee.
hist.dn5.4.bravo: tee is a railway switch: it shows and writes at the same time.
hist.dn5.4.adulte: sort -t, -k4 -nr: comma separator, sort on column 4, as numbers, in reverse.
hist.dn5.5.dit: Add the mean at the end of the report (>> appends without erasing).
hist.dn5.5.bravo: Your report has the podium and the mean.
hist.dn5.5.adulte: > replaces, >> appends at the end. tee -a appends too.
hist.dn5.6.dit: Have your report checked by the laboratory.
hist.dn5.6.bravo: Report checked: the scholar's certificate is in your laboratory!
hist.dn5.6.adulte: The game reads rapport.txt again and recalculates everything on collection.csv.
hist.dn6.0.dit: Put your collection in a real database.
hist.dn6.0.bravo: collection.db is a SQLite database: tables, rows, columns.
hist.dn6.0.adulte: SQLite is a database in a single file, used everywhere (phones, browsers). Here the game builds the tables from collection.csv.
hist.dn6.1.dit: Ask the database for the list of its tables.
hist.dn6.1.bravo: Two tables: creatures (your collection) and especes (the species you have).
hist.dn6.1.adulte: Commands starting with a dot (.tables, .schema) belong to the sqlite3 tool, not to the SQL language.
hist.dn6.2.dit: Look at how the creatures table is built.
hist.dn6.2.bravo: Each column has a name and a kind: TEXT or INTEGER (whole number).
hist.dn6.2.adulte: .schema shows the CREATE TABLE statement that built the table.
hist.dn6.3.dit: Your first query: the 3 strongest, with ORDER BY … DESC and LIMIT 3.
hist.dn6.3.bravo: The same podium as sort | head, in one sentence!
hist.dn6.3.adulte: SELECT columns FROM table ORDER BY column DESC LIMIT n: choose, sort, keep.
hist.dn6.4.dit: Filter with WHERE: only the critters of type eau.
hist.dn6.4.bravo: WHERE keeps the rows that meet the condition. Nothing? Try a type you have!
hist.dn6.4.adulte: In SQL, texts are written between single quotes: 'eau'.
hist.dn6.5.dit: Count by type with COUNT(*) and GROUP BY.
hist.dn6.5.bravo: GROUP BY makes bundles, COUNT(*) counts them: like sort | uniq -c!
hist.dn6.5.adulte: Aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) summarise each group.
hist.dn6.6.dit: Which type do you have most of? Give your answer.
hist.dn6.6.bravo: Right! Your collection has a favourite type.
hist.dn6.6.adulte: With a tie, each of the top types is accepted.
hist.dn6.7.dit: Link two tables with JOIN: the name of each critter and the habitat of its species.
hist.dn6.7.bravo: JOIN links the rows that have the same name in both tables.
hist.dn6.7.adulte: c and e are nicknames for the tables; ON says which column links them.
hist.dn6.8.dit: Last query: the average attack with AVG.
hist.dn6.8.bravo: The same mean as with awk! Two paths, one result: you can check.
hist.dn6.8.adulte: sqlite3 writes more digits (15) than awk (6): the value is the same.
dn.f.collection_csv.enfant: Your collection becomes a table: one line per critter, columns separated by commas. wc counts, sort sorts, uniq -c counts twins, head keeps the beginning.
dn.f.collection_csv.grands: CSV (RFC 4180): one record per line, fields separated by commas, often a header line. sort -n sorts numerically, uniq -c counts consecutive identical lines.
dn.f.collection_csv.limite: A real CSV may have commas BETWEEN quotes inside a field; the game's never does, so cut and awk are enough.
dn.f.collection_csv.idee: "uniq removes all duplicates": no, only those that follow each other. You must sort first.
dn.f.colonnes.enfant: cut is a pair of scissors that cuts out a column, tr a translator that changes letters, paste a glue pot that sticks columns back together.
dn.f.colonnes.grands: cut -d SEP -f N extracts fields; tr translates or deletes characters; paste merges files line by line.
dn.f.colonnes.limite: cut cannot skip commas between quotes: for complicated CSV files, use a real tool (awk with care, Python, a spreadsheet).
dn.f.colonnes.idee: "cut -f2 cuts the 2nd character": no, it is the 2nd field; the 2nd character is cut -c2.
dn.f.copiste.enfant: sed is a magic copyist: it copies a text while replacing one word with another, once per line, or everywhere with g.
dn.f.copiste.grands: sed 's/pattern/replacement/g' substitutes; -n and p choose the lines to print; -i changes the file in place.
dn.f.copiste.limite: The pattern is a regular expression: a dot means "any character". For simple names it changes nothing.
dn.f.copiste.idee: "sed fixes the file": only with -i; otherwise it shows a corrected copy.
dn.f.calculatrice.enfant: awk is the scholars' calculator: it cuts each line into columns ($1, $2…) and can add, count and divide.
dn.f.calculatrice.grands: awk -F, 'pattern {…} END {…}': NR is the line number, $N field N; print writes numbers with the %.6g format.
dn.f.calculatrice.limite: awk calculates with decimal numbers: the mean may have many digits, it shows 6.
dn.f.calculatrice.idee: "The mean is the value in the middle": no, that is the median; the mean is the sum divided by the count.
dn.f.chaine.enfant: Machines in a chain: the pattern sieve (grep -E), the dispenser (xargs) that turns a list into words for a command, and the switch (tee) that shows AND writes.
dn.f.chaine.grands: grep -E accepts extended regular expressions (a|b, ^, $, +); xargs builds command lines from its input; tee copies the output into a file.
dn.f.chaine.limite: xargs splits at spaces: a name with a space would become two words. Critter names have none.
dn.f.chaine.idee: "tee is like >": > writes without showing, tee shows AND writes.
dn.f.sql.enfant: A database stores tables. We ask it questions in SQL: SELECT (show), WHERE (filter), ORDER BY (sort), GROUP BY (make bundles), JOIN (link two tables).
dn.f.sql.grands: SQL is a declarative language: you say what you want, the database finds how. SQLite fits in one file; the sqlite3 tool adds dot commands (.tables, .schema).
dn.f.sql.limite: Here the database is small and built by the game; real databases have millions of rows, access rights and backups.
dn.f.sql.idee: "WHERE type = eau": the quotes are missing; without them, SQL thinks eau is a column.
maths.moyenne.question: Do you know how to calculate a mean (an average)?
maths.moyenne.enfant: The mean is sharing fairly: add everything, then divide by the number of values.
maths.moyenne.grands: Arithmetic mean = sum of the values ÷ count. It is sensitive to extreme values.
maths.moyenne.limite: The shell's `$(( ))` keeps only whole numbers; awk keeps the digits after the decimal point.
maths.moyenne.idee: "The mean is always one of the values": no, the mean of 1 and 2 is 1.5.
maths.moyenne.exo: What is the mean of {a}, {b} and {c}?
maths.moyenne.kw: mean average share sum divide statistics attack troop
maths.mediane.question: Do you know how to find a median (the middle value)?
maths.mediane.enfant: Put the numbers in order from smallest to biggest; the median is the one in the middle: as many numbers before as after.
maths.mediane.grands: Median: the value that splits the ordered series into two halves of the same size; for an even count, we often take the mean of the two central values.
maths.mediane.limite: With an even number of values there are two values in the middle: the game accepts one, the other or their mean.
maths.mediane.idee: "The median is the middle number of the UNSORTED list": no, sort first.
maths.mediane.ex2: 5 values: the 3rd is in the middle (2 before, 2 after).
maths.mediane.erreur: First sort the 5 numbers, then take the 3rd.
maths.mediane.kw: median middle central value sort order half statistics
maths.etendue.question: Do you know how to calculate a range (biggest minus smallest)?
maths.etendue.enfant: The range is the gap between the biggest and the smallest number: the bigger it is, the more different the values.
maths.etendue.grands: Range = maximum − minimum: the simplest measure of spread.
maths.etendue.limite: A single very big value is enough to make the range huge.
maths.etendue.idee: "The range is the biggest number": no, it is the biggest MINUS the smallest.
maths.etendue.ex2: Attacks from 20 to 25: range 5, a very even troop.
maths.etendue.erreur: Find the biggest and the smallest, then subtract.
maths.etendue.kw: range spread gap dispersion maximum minimum biggest smallest statistics
maths.pourcentages.question: Do you know how to calculate a percentage?
maths.pourcentages.enfant: A percentage says "how many out of 100": 3 shiny out of 12 is like 25 out of 100, 25%.
maths.pourcentages.grands: p% of N = N × p ÷ 100; the share of a in N is a × 100 ÷ N %.
maths.pourcentages.idee: "50% + 50% = 100% more": no, they are two halves of the same whole.
maths.pourcentages.exo: {n} critters out of {total} are of type eau: what percentage?
maths.pourcentages.kw: percentage percent per cent share proportion out of 100 rate
dn.meuble.laboratoire:
📊 THE SORTING LABORATORY

The instruments:
  🔍 the sieve ........... grep (keeps the lines that contain a word)
  ✂  the scissors ........ cut (cuts out a column)
  🔤 the translator ...... tr (changes letters)
  ⚙  the mill ............ sort | uniq -c (sorts and counts)
  🧮 the calculator ...... awk (adds up, makes means)
  ✎  the magic copyist ... sed (replaces one word with another)
  🗄  the librarian ....... sqlite3 (the database)

The rules:
  - The data are YOUR critters (tg collection --csv). No personal data, nothing is sent.
  - Some exercises need a minimum number of creatures: the game tells you how many, and where to meet them.
  - Everything stays here, in your play area.

These names and values (feu, eau, commune, 0, 1…) are the same in every language.
The number is used by cut (-f2) and awk ($4).

awk -F, reads each line and cuts it at the commas: $1 is the name, $4 the attack.
NR is the line number (NR>1: without the line of titles).
END {…} happens at the very end.

📦 xargs: the dispenser, which gives lines as words to a command
🔀 tee: the switch, which shows AND writes into a file
Your goal: a collection report in rapport.txt.

dn.tel.awk: The app's little awk (a single command, no pipe): -F, patterns NR>1, {print}, sums, END.
