hist.forge.debut: 🔨 Clang! Clang! Behind a big door, the fire roars and the scrolls glow. Welcome to the Forge! Here you make your own tools: recipes the computer follows all by itself, programs, a game, a website and even moving pictures. Everything stays in your play area.
hist.forge.fin: You can write recipes, put things in boxes, choose and repeat, run a Python program, build your own game, serve your website and animate your creature. You are a Master of the Forge!
fo.ouvert.log: 🌍 A world opens at the Crossroads: the Forge
fo.ouvert.dit: You can write into files and connect commands: the Forge lights its fire for you! There you write recipes the computer follows all by itself. Whenever you like: `cd ~/terrain_terminagotchi/forge`.
fo.pont: This step uses a maths idea: {notion}. Do you know it? If not, type `{cmd}`: we cross the bridge, then come back here.
fo.premier_coup: Your recipe worked on the first try!
fo.sans_indice: Level “{palier}” finished without a single hint!
hist.fo0.1.dit: Look at what is in the Forge.
hist.fo0.1.bravo: An anvil and a notebook. The fire is ready!
hist.fo0.1.adulte: The game prepared the forge folder in your play area. Everything you make in this world stays there.
hist.fo0.2.dit: Read what is engraved on the anvil.
hist.fo0.2.bravo: The rules of the Forge and its workshops. Let's get to work!
hist.fo0.2.adulte: The rules: everything stays in the play area, the website stays on your computer, the example photo has fake information.
hist.fo1.0.dit: Ask the forge what a recipe is.
hist.fo1.0.bravo: A recipe is a list of commands in a file. The computer does them all, in order!
hist.fo1.0.adulte: A shell script is a text file of commands. We'll write one line by line with echo, > and >>.
hist.fo1.1.dit: Write the magic first line of the hut recipe. Keep the single quotes ' '.
hist.fo1.1.bravo: #!/bin/sh says: “this recipe is read with sh”. It is always the first line.
hist.fo1.1.adulte: The “shebang” (#!) names the interpreter. Single quotes stop bash from transforming the ! .
hist.fo1.2.dit: Add the line that builds the hut. Careful: two arrows >> to ADD.
hist.fo1.2.bravo: With >>, the line is added at the end. With a single >, the whole file would have been erased!
hist.fo1.2.adulte: > replaces the file, >> adds at the end. mkdir -p does not complain if the folder already exists.
hist.fo1.3.dit: Add the line that puts in the door and the roof.
hist.fo1.3.bravo: The recipe is complete: three lines.
hist.fo1.3.adulte: touch creates empty files. Each line of the script is a command, as if you typed it.
hist.fo1.4.bravo: The magic line, then the two commands, in order.
hist.fo1.4.adulte: Reading before running: programmers do it all the time.
hist.fo1.5.dit: Run the recipe with sh. Watch the scroll catch fire!
hist.fo1.5.bravo: Whoosh! The hut is built, with its door and its roof. You just ran your first program!
hist.fo1.5.adulte: sh reads the file and runs each line. You can check with ls cabane.
hist.fo1.6.dit: 🌉 A little detour to the padlocks: give your recipe the right to be run on its own.
hist.fo1.6.bravo: The x (execute) is set: the recipe has become a real little program.
hist.fo1.6.adulte: chmod +x adds the execute permission (seen in level 6, the padlocks). Without it, ./cabane.sh answers “Permission denied”.
hist.fo1.7.dit: Now run it like a program, with ./ in front.
hist.fo1.7.bravo: ./ means “the program that is here”. And the magic first line chose sh for you!
hist.fo1.7.adulte: The shell does not look for programs in the current folder: ./ gives the exact path.
hist.fo2.0.dit: Ask the forge what boxes are.
hist.fo2.0.bravo: A variable is a box with a label: you put a word in it and take it out with $.
hist.fo2.0.adulte: Shell variables: name=value (no space around the =), then $name to read it.
hist.fo2.1.dit: Put the word Pixel in a box called nom. No space around the = !
hist.fo2.1.bravo: The box nom holds Pixel. Nothing is shown: that's normal, we just put it away.
hist.fo2.1.adulte: With spaces (nom = Pixel), the shell would think nom is a command.
hist.fo2.2.dit: Open the box with $nom in a sentence.
hist.fo2.2.bravo: $nom was replaced by what is in the box.
hist.fo2.2.adulte: Double quotes let the shell replace $nom; single quotes stop it.
hist.fo2.3.dit: Write a recipe that greets someone. $1 will be the name given when it runs.
hist.fo2.3.bravo: salut.sh is waiting for a name: $1 is the first word after the recipe's name.
hist.fo2.3.adulte: $1, $2… are the positional parameters; single quotes write $1 as it is into the file.
hist.fo2.4.bravo: The recipe said hello to Léa. Try with your name or your creature's!
hist.fo2.4.adulte: Same recipe, different result depending on what you give it: that's the idea of a parameter.
hist.fo2.5.dit: Add a line that counts the names it received, with $#.
hist.fo2.5.bravo: $# counts how many words were given to the recipe.
hist.fo2.5.adulte: $# is the number of parameters; $@ would be the list of all of them.
hist.fo2.6.bravo: Hello to the first one, and 3 names counted!
hist.fo2.6.adulte: $1 is always the first word; $# counts 3.
hist.fo2.7.dit: Write a recipe that ASKS a question: read puts the answer in the box prenom.
hist.fo2.7.bravo: question.sh will wait for an answer.
hist.fo2.7.adulte: read reads a line from the keyboard (standard input) and stores it in a variable.
hist.fo2.8.dit: Run question.sh. It waits: type a name, then press Enter.
hist.fo2.8.bravo: The recipe listened to you, then answered. A recipe can talk with you!
hist.fo2.8.adulte: You can also answer through a pipe: echo Léa | sh question.sh.
hist.fo2.9.dit: On the phone, you answer the question through a pipe: echo gives the name to question.sh.
hist.fo2.9.bravo: read got Léa through the pipe and the recipe answered.
hist.fo2.9.adulte: The app's terminal has no keyboard for a waiting script: the pipe | fills read's input.
hist.fo2.10.dit: Put the word Pixel in the box nom, then open it, on the same line (the ; separates the two commands).
hist.fo2.10.bravo: $nom was replaced by what is in the box. No space around the = !
hist.fo2.10.adulte: On the phone, each line is a new shell: a box filled on one line is empty on the next.
hist.fo3.0.dit: Ask the forge how a recipe chooses and repeats.
hist.fo3.0.bravo: A railway switch (if) chooses a path, a merry-go-round (for, while) goes round and round.
hist.fo3.0.adulte: Conditions and loops: with them, a script becomes a real program.
hist.fo3.1.dit: Look for a ghost that doesn't exist, then ask $? how it went.
hist.fo3.1.bravo: ls did not find the ghost: $? is not 0. 0 means “all good”, another number means “problem”.
hist.fo3.1.adulte: $? is the exit code of the last command. GNU ls answers 2 for a missing file, toybox (phone) answers 1.
hist.fo3.2.dit: Which number did echo $? show? Replace the ? with that number.
hist.fo3.2.bravo: Right! Anything that isn't 0 means “it didn't work”.
hist.fo3.2.adulte: Scripts test this code to decide what comes next (if, &&, ||).
hist.fo3.3.dit: A railway switch: if the hut's door exists, say so.
hist.fo3.3.bravo: The condition [ -f … ] is true, so the then path was taken.
hist.fo3.3.adulte: [ -f file ] tests that a file exists. The spaces after [ and before ] are required.
hist.fo3.4.dit: A merry-go-round: go round three times with for.
hist.fo3.4.bravo: One turn per number in the list: 1, 2, 3. $i changes at each turn.
hist.fo3.4.adulte: for VARIABLE in LIST; do …; done repeats the block for each item.
hist.fo3.5.dit: Build a whole village: 10 huts in ONE line!
hist.fo3.5.bravo: Ten numbered huts, without typing mkdir ten times. That's the power of a loop!
hist.fo3.5.adulte: seq 1 10 writes the numbers from 1 to 10; $(…) puts that result into the line.
hist.fo3.6.dit: Count the huts in the village.
hist.fo3.6.adulte: ls writes one name per line when it writes into a pipe; wc -l counts the lines.
hist.fo3.7.dit: A countdown with while: as long as n is bigger than 0, keep going.
hist.fo3.7.bravo: 3, 2, 1… The merry-go-round stops when the condition becomes false.
hist.fo3.7.adulte: while repeats as long as the condition is true; $((n - 1)) calculates. Without the n - 1, the loop would never stop (Ctrl+C stops it).
hist.fo3.8.dit: A merry-go-round riddle: how many turns will the loop make? Type forge tours to see it, then answer.
hist.fo3.8.bravo: Well counted: you count the first AND the last number.
hist.fo3.8.adulte: seq A Z gives Z − A + 1 numbers: the classic mistake is forgetting the + 1.
hist.fo4.0.dit: Wake up the forge's mechanical snake.
hist.fo4.0.bravo: Python is another language for writing programs. It also runs from the terminal!
hist.fo4.0.adulte: Python is a widely used interpreted language (science, games, websites). On PC, the Terminagotchi game itself is written in Python.
hist.fo4.1.dit: Ask the snake for its version.
hist.fo4.1.bravo: Python 3 is here, ready to work.
hist.fo4.1.adulte: python3 --version shows the installed version; always check before using a tool.
hist.fo4.2.dit: Make the snake calculate. What will it answer?
hist.fo4.2.bravo: 14 and not 20: multiplication comes before addition, just like in maths!
hist.fo4.2.adulte: python3 -c runs a single line of Python. The order of operations is the same as in maths.
hist.fo4.3.dit: Show a name 3 times, with a Python loop.
hist.fo4.3.bravo: range(3) goes round three times: 0, 1, 2. Put your name instead of Pixel!
hist.fo4.3.adulte: for i in range(3) is Python's loop; the : and the indentation mark what is repeated.
hist.fo4.4.dit: Read the program serpent.py that the forge prepared.
hist.fo4.4.bravo: sys.argv are the words given when it starts, like $1 in a recipe.
hist.fo4.4.adulte: Lines starting with # are comments: Python ignores them, humans read them.
hist.fo4.5.dit: Run serpent.py WITHOUT giving it anything. It's going to complain, on purpose!
hist.fo4.5.bravo: A Traceback! It's Python's error report. Don't panic: read the LAST line.
hist.fo4.5.adulte: The Traceback shows where the error happened (file, line), then its name and explanation.
hist.fo4.6.dit: What is the name of the error, at the start of the last line? Replace the ? with that word.
hist.fo4.6.bravo: IndexError: the snake was looking for the 1st word, but you hadn't given it any.
hist.fo4.6.adulte: IndexError: list index out of range = we asked for a slot in the list that doesn't exist.
hist.fo4.7.dit: Run serpent.py with a name and a number.
hist.fo4.7.bravo: Hisss! The snake repeated the name the right number of times.
hist.fo4.7.adulte: Arguments arrive as text: int() turns “3” into the number 3.
hist.fo4.8.dit: The phone doesn't have Python. But the app has its own game, written in Kotlin: start it!
hist.fo4.8.bravo: That game is a program too: code files turned into an app. You can change it with edite.
hist.fo4.8.adulte: On the phone, the snake is told as a story; the Doom to build (doom, edite) is the programming workshop.
hist.fo5.0.dit: Ask the forge to prepare your guessing game.
hist.fo5.0.bravo: The folder mon_jeu is here, with a ready-made guessing game.
hist.fo5.0.adulte: The guessing game puts together everything we saw: variables, read, while, if.
hist.fo5.1.dit: Read the game's recipe. Do you recognise while, read and if?
hist.fo5.1.bravo: The game picks a number, then repeats: read your answer, say bigger or smaller.
hist.fo5.1.adulte: The secret number comes from the clock (date +%s): a bit of chance without a special tool.
hist.fo5.2.dit: Play! Type a number between 1 and 10, then Enter, until you find it.
hist.fo5.2.bravo: Your first game works! Your friends can play it on your computer.
hist.fo5.2.adulte: Ctrl+D (end of input) or Ctrl+C stops the game if you want to leave early.
hist.fo5.3.dit: Let a robot play: seq whispers 1, 2, 3… up to 10.
hist.fo5.3.bravo: The robot tried everything in order and found it in the end. A pipe can replace the keyboard!
hist.fo5.3.adulte: Testing a program with ready-made answers is what automatic tests do.
hist.fo5.4.dit: Write a recipe that digs a dungeon with three rooms.
hist.fo5.4.bravo: donjon.sh is ready: one loop, three rooms.
hist.fo5.4.adulte: A script can make other files and folders: we say it “generates” the level.
hist.fo5.5.adulte: mkdir -p also creates the parent folders (mon_jeu/donjon) if they are missing.
hist.fo5.6.dit: Hide a treasure in the last room.
hist.fo5.6.bravo: The treasure waits for adventurers in room 3.
hist.fo5.6.adulte: Players will explore with cd, ls and cat: your dungeon is a real level made of folders.
hist.fo5.7.dit: Give your game a name: it will appear on the map as a new place!
hist.fo5.7.bravo: Your game is a place in the Terminaworld! Look at the map (key m).
hist.fo5.7.adulte: forge carte puts a small hidden file mon_jeu/.lieu: the map recognises it and draws your game.
hist.fo5.8.dit: Look at your game as a tree.
hist.fo5.8.bravo: The guessing game, the dungeon and its treasure: your whole game, made by you.
hist.fo5.8.adulte: To keep the versions of your game, the Library of Time (git) is waiting for you.
hist.fo6.0.dit: Ask the forge how to make a website.
hist.fo6.0.bravo: A web page is a text file in HTML. The site folder is ready.
hist.fo6.0.adulte: HTML describes the content (headings, paragraphs), CSS the look (colours, sizes).
hist.fo6.1.dit:
Write the big title of your page, between

and

.
hist.fo6.1.bravo:
opens the title,

closes it. Your page has a title!
hist.fo6.1.adulte: Tags almost always come in pairs: the opening one and the closing one, with /.
hist.fo6.2.dit:
Add a paragraph about your creature, between

and

.
hist.fo6.2.bravo: A title and a paragraph: that's already a real page.
hist.fo6.2.adulte: >> again, to add at the end of the file without erasing it.
hist.fo6.3.dit: Write the style sheet: h1 titles will be orange.
hist.fo6.3.bravo: A CSS rule: who (h1), then what between curly brackets (color: orange).
hist.fo6.3.adulte: The CSS is in a separate file: you can change the look without touching the content.
hist.fo6.4.dit: Link the page to its style sheet with <link>.
hist.fo6.4.bravo: The page now knows where to find its colours.
hist.fo6.4.adulte: rel="stylesheet" tells the browser to load style.css and apply it.
hist.fo6.5.bravo: Three lines of HTML: a title, a paragraph, a link to the style.
hist.fo6.5.adulte: A real website often starts like this; browsers are very forgiving.
hist.fo6.6.dit: Light the lantern that serves your page. --bind 127.0.0.1: only for your computer! The & lets it work in the background.
hist.fo6.6.bravo: Your page is served on port 8642… and nobody but your computer can see it.
hist.fo6.6.adulte: http.server serves the site folder. Without --bind 127.0.0.1, it would listen to the whole local network: the Port's rule.
hist.fo6.7.dit: Ask the server for your page with curl, like a browser would.
hist.fo6.7.bravo: curl received your page, exactly! You can also open http://localhost:8642 in the browser.
hist.fo6.7.adulte: localhost = 127.0.0.1, the computer itself. The browser will also apply the CSS colour.
hist.fo6.8.dit: Put out the lantern: fg brings it back in front of you, then press Ctrl+C.
hist.fo6.8.bravo: Lantern out. Ctrl+C stops the program that is working in front of you.
hist.fo6.8.adulte: fg brings back to the foreground the job started with &; Ctrl+C tells it to stop (kill %1 works too).
hist.fo6.9.dit: And so that everyone can see your website? Ask the forge.
hist.fo6.9.bravo: Publishing means copying your site to a computer that is on day and night. It's done with an adult.
hist.fo6.9.adulte: A host keeps the site on a public server; it needs an account, often an e-mail address, and rules. The game publishes nothing.
hist.fo6.10.dit: Light the app's lantern: it serves your site folder, only on 127.0.0.1.
hist.fo6.10.bravo: Your page is served on port 8642, inside the phone.
hist.fo6.10.adulte: The phone doesn't have Python: the app serves the folder, bound to 127.0.0.1 like the Port's lighthouse.
hist.fo6.11.bravo: Lantern out: nobody answers on port 8642 any more.
hist.fo6.11.adulte: On a computer, you would stop the server with Ctrl+C.
hist.fo7.0.bravo: The forge put down pictures of your creature, a fanfare and an example photo.
hist.fo7.0.adulte: Pictures, sounds and videos can also be made from the command line. Here, only with the game's files.
hist.fo7.1.dit: Look at what is in the workshop.
hist.fo7.1.bravo: Four pictures of your creature jumping, a fanfare and a photo.
hist.fo7.1.adulte: creature_1.png to creature_4.png are the pictures of a little animation.
hist.fo7.2.dit: Put the 4 pictures together into an animated GIF!
hist.fo7.2.bravo: creature.gif: your creature jumps in a loop! Open it in the browser or an image viewer.
hist.fo7.2.adulte: -delay 20 = 20 hundredths of a second per picture; -loop 0 = start again forever. (convert on older versions.)
hist.fo7.3.dit: Make a sound: the note A, 440 vibrations per second, for half a second.
hist.fo7.3.bravo: la.wav is ready: it's the note used to tune instruments!
hist.fo7.3.adulte: sox -n (nothing as input) synth makes a sound; 440 Hz is the reference A.
hist.fo7.4.dit: Cut the end of the fanfare: starting at 0.5 seconds, for 0.5 seconds.
hist.fo7.4.bravo: fin.wav only keeps the last two notes.
hist.fo7.4.adulte: ffmpeg -ss = where to start, -t = how long to keep. It works for videos too.
hist.fo7.5.dit: Unmask the example photo: its hidden metadata.
hist.fo7.5.bravo: The photo was hiding the camera brand, the date… and the place (GPS)! Here, everything is made up.
hist.fo7.5.adulte: Phone photos often contain this Exif metadata, including the GPS position. We practise on the game's picture, never on someone's photos.
hist.fo7.6.dit: What is the brand of the camera that took the photo? Replace the ? with that word.
hist.fo7.6.bravo: Right! A simple photo says a lot.
hist.fo7.6.adulte: Before sharing a photo, you can remove its metadata.
hist.fo7.7.dit: Remove all the metadata from the example photo.
hist.fo7.7.bravo: The photo is clean: the picture is the same, but it no longer tells anything hidden.
hist.fo7.7.adulte: -all= erases all metadata; -overwrite_original avoids keeping a copy with it. Many apps offer this when sharing too.
hist.fo7.8.dit: Take stock of everything you forged.
hist.fo7.8.bravo: Your Master of the Forge certificate is in the forge folder!
hist.fo7.8.adulte: Hut, village, snake, game, website, cleaned photo: everything stays in the play area.
fo.meuble.enclume:
🔨 THE FORGE — engraved on the anvil

Here you make your own tools: recipes the computer follows all by itself.

THE RULES OF THE FORGE
  1. Everything stays in your play area: your recipes, your game, your website, your pictures.
  2. Your website stays on your computer (127.0.0.1). Publishing it is done with an adult.
  3. The example photo has made-up information. Never someone's photos.
  4. When a tool is missing, the forge tells the story: nothing is blocked.

THE WORKSHOPS
  recipes               (forge recette)
  boxes                 (forge boites)
  the railway switch    (forge aiguillage)
  the snake (Python)    (forge serpent)
  your game             (forge jeu)
  your website          (forge site)
  multimedia            (forge multimedia)
fo.meuble.carnet: 📒 The forge's notebook: the game writes down what you forged.
fo.aide.liste:
forge plan              the anvil and the rules
forge recette           a recipe = commands in a file
forge boites            variables, $1, $#, read
forge aiguillage        $?, if, for, while
forge code N / tours N  the railway switch riddles
forge serpent           Python from the terminal
forge erreur WORD       the name of the Traceback's error
forge jeu / carte NAME  your game, and its place on the map
forge site / publier    your website
forge multimedia        pictures, sounds, metadata
forge exif FILE         read the metadata of a photo in the play area
forge nettoie FILE      remove them
forge bilan             your certificate
fo.recette.texte:
A recipe (a script) is a text file with commands, one per line.
The computer does them all, in order, without getting tired.

  1st line : #!/bin/sh       → “this recipe is read with sh”
  then     : the commands    → as if you typed them

Run it with: sh cabane.sh
Or, with the x permission: ./cabane.sh
fo.boites.texte:
A variable is a box with a label.

  nom=Pixel        → puts Pixel in the box nom (no space!)
  echo "$nom"      → opens the box

In a recipe:
  $1, $2…   → the words given when it starts (sh salut.sh Léa: $1 = Léa)
  $#        → how many words were given
  read x    → asks a question and puts the answer in x
fo.aiguillage.titre: The railway switch and the merry-go-round
fo.aiguillage.texte:
$?      → the code of the last command: 0 = all good, anything else = problem
if      → the railway switch: if it's true, take this path
          if [ -f file ]; then …; fi
for     → the merry-go-round: one turn for each item of a list
          for i in 1 2 3; do …; done
while   → the merry-go-round that turns AS LONG AS it's true
seq 1 10 → writes the numbers from 1 to 10
fo.code.aide: Type forge code followed by the number echo $? showed after ls fantome.
fo.code.ok: Yes: {n} isn't 0, so ls said “problem” (the ghost doesn't exist).
fo.tours.aide:
The loop: for i in $(seq {a} {z}); do echo $i; done
How many turns does it make? Type forge tours followed by your answer.
fo.tours.ok: Yes: from {a} to {z}, that makes {n} turns (count the first and the last).
fo.serpent.texte:
Python is a language for writing programs, more powerful than sh recipes.
  python3 --version          → the version
  python3 -c "print(2 + 3)"  → a single line of Python
  python3 serpent.py Pixel 3 → a program, with its arguments
When something goes wrong, Python writes a Traceback: read the LAST line.
Python is interpreted (read as it goes); gcc, at the Guild, compiles.
fo.serpent.absent: 🐍 Python isn't installed on this computer (it's not your fault). Here is what the snake would have answered without arguments:
fo.serpent.com1: serpent.py: the Forge's mechanical snake repeats a name.
fo.serpent.com3: the 1st word after serpent.py (like $1 in a recipe)
fo.serpent.com4: the 2nd word, turned into a number
fo.erreur.aide: Type forge erreur followed by the first word of the Traceback's last line.
fo.erreur.ok: Yes: IndexError. The snake looked for the 1st word given… but the list was empty.
fo.jeu.texte:
The folder mon_jeu is ready, with devinette.sh: a complete guessing game.
  cat mon_jeu/devinette.sh   → read it
  sh mon_jeu/devinette.sh    → play
Then you'll add a dungeon made by YOUR recipe, and put your game on the map.
fo.devinette.com: The Forge's guessing game: find the number between 1 and 10.
fo.devinette.debut: I picked a number between 1 and 10. Guess!
fo.carte.aide: Type forge carte followed by your game's name, in quotes: forge carte "La grotte de Pixel".
fo.carte.pas_de_jeu: You need the folder mon_jeu first: type forge jeu.
fo.carte.ok: “{nom}” is now a place in the Terminaworld!
fo.carte.texte:
Look at the map (key m, or tg carte): 🎮 {nom} is in the Forge.
Your friends can play it: cd mon_jeu, sh devinette.sh, and explore the dungeon.
fo.site.texte:
A web page is a text file in HTML, kept in the site folder.

…

a big title

…

a paragraph style.css the colours (CSS) Then we serve it with a lantern bound to 127.0.0.1 (only your computer): python3 -m http.server {port} --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory site & curl localhost:{port} → the page, as a browser sees it fg, then Ctrl+C → put out the lantern
fo.site.port_pris: Port {port} is already taken on this computer: use {autre} instead of {port} in the commands.
fo.site.sans_python: Python isn't installed here: the lantern is told as a story. Your page still opens in the browser (the file site/index.html).
fo.publier.texte:
Your lantern only serves your computer. For everyone to see a website, it has to be copied
to a computer that is on day and night and connected to the Internet: a host.
  · It's done WITH AN ADULT: you need an account and to accept rules.
  · Anything published can be read, copied and kept by anyone.
  · Never your full name, address, school or a photo of you on a public website.
The game publishes nothing and creates no account.
fo.multimedia.texte:
In multimedia/:
  creature_1.png … creature_4.png   your creature jumping (4 pictures)
  fanfare.wav                       C E G C, made by the game
  photo_exemple.jpg                 an EXAMPLE photo with MADE-UP information
The tools: magick (pictures), sox (sounds), ffmpeg (sounds and videos), exiftool (metadata).
fo.multimedia.outils: Installed here: {presents}. Missing (told as a story): {absents}.
fo.exif.aide: Type forge exif followed by a file in the play area: forge exif multimedia/photo_exemple.jpg
fo.exif.aucune: No Exif metadata: this photo tells nothing hidden.
fo.exif.morale: 0° N 0° E is “Null Island”: an imaginary place in the middle of the ocean. A real phone photo can give the exact address where it was taken!
fo.exif.hors_terrain: The forge only reads files in the play area (never your photos or other people's).
fo.appareil.aide: Type forge appareil followed by the brand read in the metadata.
fo.appareil.ok: Yes: {marque}. The photo said it all by itself!
fo.nettoie.aide: Type forge nettoie followed by a photo in the play area: forge nettoie multimedia/photo_exemple.jpg
fo.nettoie.ok: {fichier} is clean: no Exif metadata left.
fo.bilan.m.serpent: the name of the snake's error (forge serpent)
fo.bilan.m.jeu: your game on the map (forge carte)
fo.bilan.m.site: the title of your website (forge site)

🏅 {nom}, Master of the Forge

fo.indice.rep.code: Look at the number echo $? showed right after ls fantome: it isn't 0.
fo.indice.rep.tours: Count the first AND the last number: from A to Z there are Z − A + 1 numbers.
fo.indice.rep.erreur: Read the very last line of the Traceback: its first word ends with Error.
fo.indice.rep.appareil: Look for the line “Make” (or “Camera brand”) in the metadata.
fo.indice.guillemets_simples: With double quotes, bash tries to transform the !: use single quotes ' '.
fo.indice.efface: Oops: a single > erased the recipe. Start again with the line #!/bin/sh and >, then add the others with >>.
fo.indice.recette: Something is missing in cabane.sh: {ligne}. Read it with cat cabane.sh.
fo.indice.chmod: “Permission denied”: the recipe doesn't have the x permission yet. Type chmod +x cabane.sh.
fo.indice.prenom: Give a name after salut.sh: sh salut.sh Léa.
fo.indice.partout: ⚠ Your lantern listens to the WHOLE network (port {port})! Put it out (fg then Ctrl+C) and light it again with --bind 127.0.0.1.
fo.indice.pas_de_page: First you need a page with an <h1> title in site/index.html.
fo.indice.allume_d_abord: First, light the lantern that serves your page (the command with http.server); curl comes right after.
core.inconnue.egal: No space around the = ! Write {cmd}=… all stuck together. With spaces, the terminal thinks “{cmd}” is a command.
fo.indice.serveur_eteint: The lantern is out: light it again with python3 -m http.server … & before curl.
fo.indice.ctrl_c: The lantern is still shining: type fg, then press Ctrl+C (the Ctrl and C keys at the same time).
fo.f.recette.enfant: A recipe (a script) is a list of commands in a file: the computer does them all, in order.
fo.f.recette.grands: A shell script starts with #!/bin/sh (the interpreter); sh script.sh runs it, or chmod +x then ./script.sh.
fo.f.recette.limite: “The recipe” is an image: a script can also decide, repeat and talk with you (if, for, read).
fo.f.recette.idee: “./cabane.sh always works”: no, it first needs the x permission (chmod +x), otherwise “Permission denied”.
fo.f.parametres.enfant: A variable is a box with a label; $1 is the first word given to the recipe, $# the number of words.
fo.f.parametres.grands: name=value (no spaces), $name to read it; $1… the positional parameters, $# how many; read reads standard input.
fo.f.parametres.limite: A box holds text: to calculate, use $(( … )).
fo.f.parametres.idee: “nom = Pixel”: with spaces, the shell thinks nom is a command.
fo.f.aiguillage.enfant: if is a railway switch that chooses a path, for and while are merry-go-rounds that go round, $? tells whether the last command worked.
fo.f.aiguillage.grands: Exit code 0 = success; if [ test ]; then …; fi ; for x in list; do …; done ; while condition; do …; done.
fo.f.aiguillage.limite: The exact code of a failure depends on the tool: GNU ls answers 2, toybox (Android) 1. We only test “0 or not 0”.
fo.f.aiguillage.idee: “[-f file]”: you need spaces after [ and before ], otherwise the shell doesn't recognise the test.
fo.f.python.enfant: Python is a language for writing programs; you run it from the terminal with python3.
fo.f.python.grands: python3 -c runs one line; python3 file.py ARGS runs a program (sys.argv); an error shows a Traceback, read from the end.
fo.f.python.limite: Python is interpreted: it reads the program while running it; a compiled language (C, at the Guild) is translated first.
fo.f.python.idee: “A Traceback means the computer is broken”: no, it's an error report, and the last line says what.
fo.f.mini_jeu.enfant: A game is everything together: boxes, a loop, questions, choices. And a script can build a dungeon!
fo.f.mini_jeu.grands: The guessing game combines read, while, if and variables; a script can generate files and folders (a level).
fo.f.mini_jeu.limite: The secret number comes from the clock: it's not real randomness, just enough to play.
fo.f.mini_jeu.idee: “A pipe can't play for me”: it can, seq 1 10 | sh devinette.sh answers each read.
fo.f.site_web.enfant: A web page is a text file in HTML; CSS gives the colours; a server hands it to the browser.
fo.f.site_web.grands: HTML (tags), CSS (style rules), HTTP (the server answers GET); http.server --bind 127.0.0.1 stays on the machine.
fo.f.site_web.limite: http.server is for learning and testing, not for hosting a real website (“not recommended for production”).
fo.f.site_web.idee: “My site on localhost, everyone sees it”: no, localhost is only your computer.
fo.f.multimedia.enfant: Pictures, sounds and videos can also be made with commands; and a photo hides information: its metadata.
fo.f.multimedia.grands: magick/convert (pictures, GIF), sox (audio synthesis), ffmpeg (cut, convert), exiftool (read and erase Exif metadata, including GPS).
fo.f.multimedia.limite: Removing the metadata doesn't erase what the picture itself shows (a sign, a face, a school).
fo.f.multimedia.idee: “A photo is just a picture”: no, it can contain the camera, the date and the exact place.
maths.boucles.question: Do you know how to count how many turns a loop makes?
maths.boucles.enfant: A loop from 3 to 7 goes through 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7: 5 turns. Count the first AND the last.
maths.boucles.grands: From a to z (integers, z ≥ a) there are z − a + 1 values: the “off by one” error is a famous programming trap.
maths.boucles.limite: range(3) in Python starts at 0 and stops BEFORE 3: 0, 1, 2 (still 3 turns).
maths.boucles.idee: “From 3 to 7 makes 7 − 3 = 4 turns”: no, 5, you have to add 1.
maths.boucles.ex2: A 10-metre fence with one post per metre: 11 posts!
maths.boucles.exo: How many turns does for i in $(seq {a} {z}) make?

maths.priorites.question: Do you know which operation is calculated first in 2 + 3 × 4?
maths.priorites.enfant: Multiplication comes before addition: 2 + 3 × 4 = 2 + 12 = 14. Brackets come before everything.
maths.priorites.grands: Order: brackets, powers, multiplications and divisions (left to right), additions and subtractions.
maths.priorites.limite: In $(( )), the shell only keeps whole numbers: 7 / 2 gives 3.
maths.priorites.idee: “We calculate left to right: 2 + 3 = 5, then × 4 = 20”: no, the × first.

hist.robots.debut: 🤖 On a big workbench, little robots are waiting, an LED blinks, wires dangle… Welcome to the Workshop! Here your robot is SIMULATED: a grid, obstacles, and files that you read and write with the terminal. No hardware needed.
hist.robots.fin: You can light an LED by writing to a file, read a sensor, make a robot decide with AND, OR, NOT, write its brain and run it in a loop without ever bumping into anything. You also know what a real Raspberry Pi or an Arduino board does. You are a Roboticist!
at.ouvert.log: 🌍 A world opens at the Crossroads: the Robot Workshop
at.ouvert.dit: You can find your way, read, search and connect commands: the Workshop opens its workbench to you! There we build a (simulated) robot that you drive with the terminal. Whenever you like: `cd ~/terrain_terminagotchi/robots`.
at.pont: This step uses a maths idea: {notion}. Do you know it? If not, type `{cmd}`: we cross the bridge, then come back here.
at.pas_ouvert: The Workshop is not open yet: first finish the early levels (find your way, build, read, connect commands).
hist.at2.titre: The sensor, the motor and the grid
hist.at3.titre: AND, OR, NOT: the robot decides
hist.at6.titre: The real Raspberry Pi (with an adult)
hist.at0.1.dit: Look at what is on the workbench.
hist.at0.1.bravo: The plan, the notebook, the robot folder and an example brain. Everything is ready!
hist.at0.1.adulte: The game prepared the robots folder in your play area. The robot is simulated: no hardware is used.
hist.at0.2.bravo: The robot lives in files, and you drive it with the terminal.
hist.at0.2.adulte: On a real Raspberry Pi, the Linux kernel also shows the hardware as files (in /sys). Here it is the same idea, with no risk.
hist.at1.0.dit: Look at what is in the robot folder.
hist.at1.0.bravo: Three files, three parts of the robot: the LED, the motor and the distance sensor.
hist.at1.0.adulte: “Everything is a file”: on Linux, many devices are read and written like files.
hist.at1.1.bravo: 0: the LED is off. 1 would mean on.
hist.at1.1.adulte: 0 and 1 are the language of circuits: current cut or current flowing.
hist.at1.2.dit: Turn the LED on: write 1 into its file.
hist.at1.2.bravo: You wrote 1 into robot/led… the LED lights up!
hist.at1.2.adulte: The > sign sends the text into a file (it replaces what was there). On a real robot, that 1 would send current through the LED.
hist.at1.3.bravo: 💡 Your LED is shining! The game read the file and drew the robot.
hist.at1.3.adulte: The game command reads the robot's files, just like the program of a real robot would.
hist.at1.4.bravo: 0: off. On, off: you just drove “hardware” with text.
hist.at1.4.adulte: An LED left on for nothing wastes energy: a battery robot switches off what it does not use.
hist.at1.5.bravo: The sensor gives a distance in centimetres: how much room is left in front of the robot before an obstacle.
hist.at1.5.adulte: An ultrasonic sensor does the same: it sends a sound too high for us to hear and measures the time of the echo.
hist.at2.0.dit: Look at the grid where your robot lives.
hist.at2.0.bravo: The arrow is your robot, facing the way the arrow points. ▓ is an obstacle.
hist.at2.0.adulte: x counts the columns to the right, y the rows going down, like the pixels of a screen. One square = 10 cm.
hist.at2.1.dit: Tell the motor to go forward: write avance into its file.
hist.at2.1.bravo: The motor got the order. But the world has not moved yet…
hist.at2.1.adulte: The motor understands four words: avance (forward), gauche (left), droite (right), stop. They are data words, the same in every language.
hist.at2.2.dit: Move time forward by one step: the game reads the motor and moves the robot.
hist.at2.2.bravo: Your robot moved one square, and the sensor was updated!
hist.at2.2.adulte: atelier pas is the “physics” of the world: a moment passing. The robot does what its motor says.
hist.at2.3.dit: Where is your robot? Give its coordinates, x then y (replace the ?).
hist.at2.3.bravo: Right! x first (the column), y next (the row).
hist.at2.3.adulte: Coordinates are used everywhere: screens, maps, 3D printers, robot arms.
hist.at2.4.dit: Tell the motor to turn right.
hist.at2.4.bravo: Order received. At the next step, the robot will turn on the spot.
hist.at2.4.adulte: Turning on the spot means spinning one wheel one way and the other wheel the other way.
hist.at2.5.bravo: Your robot turned a quarter turn: its arrow changed, and its sensor looks somewhere else.
hist.at2.5.adulte: The sensor is fixed at the front: when the robot turns, it measures another direction.
hist.at2.6.dit: The sensor says how many centimetres. How many free squares in front of the robot? (one square = 10 cm)
hist.at2.6.bravo: Well done: you converted centimetres into squares.
hist.at2.6.adulte: Squares × 10 = centimetres. Robots keep converting between the units of their sensors and those of their map.
hist.at3.0.dit: Find out how a robot decides.
hist.at3.0.bravo: True or false, and three ways to combine them: AND, OR, NOT.
hist.at3.0.adulte: This is Boolean algebra: all of computing is built from these three gates.
hist.at3.1.dit: Ask the shell: is 5 smaller than 10?
hist.at3.1.bravo: vrai (true)! [ … ] tests, && runs the next part if it is true, || if it is false.
hist.at3.1.adulte: -lt means “less than”. && is an AND between commands, || an OR.
hist.at3.2.dit: Now the robot's real test: read the sensor, and say obstacle if it is closer than 10 cm.
hist.at3.2.bravo: Your robot can decide! if… then… else… fi: if, then, otherwise, end.
hist.at3.2.adulte: $(cat …) puts the output of a command into a variable. That is exactly what the robot's brain will do.
hist.at3.3.dit: Look at the truth table of a gate.
hist.at3.3.bravo: Four rows: every way to combine two true-or-false answers.
hist.at3.3.adulte: A truth table lists every possible input: with 2 inputs, 2 × 2 = 4 rows.
hist.at3.4.dit: Fill in the table: the 4 outputs, from top to bottom (replace the ?).
hist.at3.4.bravo: Correct table! You reason like a circuit.
hist.at3.4.adulte: AND is true only if both are; OR is true as soon as one of them is.
hist.at3.5.bravo: For each one: AND, OR or NOT?
hist.at3.5.adulte: Turning a real-life rule into AND / OR / NOT is the heart of programming.
hist.at3.6.dit: Answer for the three situations, in order (replace the ?).
hist.at3.6.bravo: Perfect: you know how to pick the right gate.
hist.at3.6.adulte: “Both are needed” → AND; “one is enough” → OR; “the opposite” → NOT.
hist.at4.0.dit: Read the sensor three times, once per second.
hist.at4.0.bravo: Three turns of the loop: for repeats, sleep 1 waits one second.
hist.at4.0.adulte: for i in 1 2 3: the variable i takes 1, then 2, then 3. do … done surrounds what is repeated.
hist.at4.1.dit: A loop that never stops! Start it, then stop it with Ctrl+C.
hist.at4.1.bravo: Ctrl+C: the terminal's emergency stop button. A real robot always has one.
hist.at4.1.adulte: while true repeats as long as it is true… so forever. Ctrl+C sends the interrupt signal (SIGINT).
hist.at4.2.bravo: It reads the sensor… but always goes forward, whatever it sees. Hmm.
hist.at4.2.adulte: A robot “brain” is a small list of instructions read at every turn: read the sensors, decide, act.
hist.at4.3.dit: Copy it: cerveau.sh will be YOUR brain.
hist.at4.3.bravo: cerveau.sh is yours. You can change it.
hist.at4.3.adulte: We keep the example untouched and work on a copy: a good habit.
hist.at4.4.dit: Put the robot back at the start of the test grid.
hist.at4.4.bravo: The robot is waiting at the start, motor stopped.
hist.at4.4.adulte: Resetting before a test: engineers do the same to compare their tests.
hist.at4.5.dit: The big loop: 10 times, the brain decides, then the world takes a step.
hist.at4.5.bravo: 💥 Ouch! The example brain rushes straight ahead… and bumps. It needs to be made smart.
hist.at4.5.adulte: This is the loop of every robot: read, decide, act, start again. On an Arduino board, this loop is called loop().
hist.at4.6.dit: Change cerveau.sh: if the sensor says less than 10 cm, turn right; otherwise, go forward. (Need help? `atelier aide-cerveau`)
hist.at4.6.bravo: Your brain has a condition: it turns in front of the obstacle. Ready for the challenge!
hist.at4.6.adulte: Any editor will do (nano, or another one). The game checks that there is an if, the sensor, avance and a direction.
hist.at5.0.dit: Start the challenge: a new grid, with obstacles.
hist.at5.0.bravo: The robot is waiting at the start of the arena. Read the rules carefully.
hist.at5.0.adulte: Each game has its own arena. The challenge: 20 steps, no bump, and explore at least 12 squares.
hist.at5.1.dit: 20 turns of the loop with YOUR brain. Avoid every obstacle!
hist.at5.1.bravo: 🏆 Your robot explored the arena without ever bumping! You wrote a real autonomous robot program.
hist.at5.1.adulte: If the robot bumps or gets stuck, fix cerveau.sh and start the challenge again (atelier defi): that is how roboticists work.
hist.at6.0.bravo: A real little Linux computer: everything you learned works on it.
hist.at6.0.adulte: Optional, and always with an adult. The game never touches real hardware.
hist.at6.1.dit: Your computer also has LEDs… as files! Look.
hist.at6.1.bravo: These names are real LEDs of your computer (keyboard, board…). We look, we do not touch.
hist.at6.1.adulte: We only read. Changing a real LED would need administrator rights: that is not a game.
hist.at6.2.dit: Are the Raspberry Pi pin tools installed here?
hist.at6.2.bravo: On an ordinary computer, often nothing: these tools live on the Raspberry Pi.
hist.at6.2.adulte: command -v tells where a command is, without running it. No answer: it is not installed.
hist.at6.3.dit: Look at the GPIO pins of a Raspberry Pi.
hist.at6.3.bravo: 40 little pins: the “sockets” where you plug LEDs, motors and sensors.
hist.at6.3.adulte: An LED is always wired with a resistor, and never straight onto the 5 V. Always with an adult.
hist.at6.4.dit: How does a robot start on its own, without you?
hist.at6.4.bravo: At start-up, the system launches the robot's program, and it writes everything into a log.
hist.at6.4.adulte: cron (@reboot) or a systemd service starts the program; the log helps to understand what happened.
hist.at6.5.dit: Read the end of YOUR robot's log.
hist.at6.5.bravo: Every step is written down: the motor, the position, the sensor. A roboticist always reads the log!
hist.at6.5.adulte: tail -5 shows the last 5 lines: the most recent ones, the ones you want to see after a breakdown.
hist.at6.6.dit: Do you have scheduled tasks? Look (without changing anything).
hist.at6.6.bravo: crontab -l shows the list. “no crontab” means: none. We change nothing here.
hist.at6.6.adulte: Reading is enough. Scheduling a task is done on the robot's Raspberry Pi, with an adult.
hist.at7.0.dit: Microcontroller or computer? Find out the difference.
hist.at7.0.bravo: The Raspberry Pi is a computer; an Arduino or ESP32 board is a microcontroller: a single program, which starts right away.
hist.at7.0.adulte: A microcontroller has no system like Linux: it does one single thing, very fast and with very little energy.
hist.at7.1.dit: How long does your brain take to decide? Measure it.
hist.at7.1.bravo: time measures the duration. “real” is the time that really went by.
hist.at7.1.adulte: Starting a script takes a few milliseconds: for a fast robot, every millisecond counts.
hist.at7.2.dit: The robot's reflex: read the problem.
hist.at7.2.bravo: Speed × time = distance. Work it out!
hist.at7.2.adulte: In real time, what counts is answering in time, not only answering right.
hist.at7.3.dit: How many centimetres before it reacts? (replace the ?)
hist.at7.3.bravo: Right! That is why a fast robot needs a fast brain.
hist.at7.3.adulte: cm/s × ms ÷ 1000 = cm. Car brakes, a drone, a robot arm: they all have this calculation.
hist.at7.4.dit: How do you program an Arduino or ESP32 board from the terminal?
hist.at7.4.bravo: Compile, upload, listen to the serial port: it is told here, to be done one day with an adult.
hist.at7.4.adulte: arduino-cli, screen and esptool.py really exist; the game only explains them and never touches the ports.
hist.at7.5.bravo: Often not: you only install them when you have a board, with an adult.
hist.at7.5.adulte: command -v runs nothing: it only looks.
hist.at7.6.bravo: A phone is a pocket robot: sensors, a little motor that vibrates, a lamp!
hist.at7.6.adulte: Accelerometer, gyroscope, light sensor, proximity sensor: the phone is full of them.
hist.at7.7.dit: Your phone has a real LED: turn on the lamp.
hist.at7.7.bravo: 💡 The phone's real LED lights up, just like robot/led earlier!
hist.at7.7.adulte: It is the same idea: an order from the program sends current through the LED.
hist.at7.8.dit: And a real little motor: make the phone vibrate.
hist.at7.8.bravo: The vibrator is a tiny motor with an off-centre weight that makes it shake.
hist.at7.9.dit: And a real sensor: read the battery.
hist.at7.9.bravo: A sensor measures the battery: the phone, like a robot, watches its energy.
hist.at7.9.adulte: An autonomous robot must go back to recharge before it runs flat: one more condition in its brain.
at.f.robot_fichiers.enfant: The robot lives in files: writing 1 into robot/led turns the LED on, reading robot/capteur_distance gives the distance.
at.f.robot_fichiers.grands: On Linux, the kernel exposes hardware in /sys: /sys/class/leds/*/brightness, and formerly /sys/class/gpio (replaced by the libgpiod interface: gpioset, gpioget).
at.f.robot_fichiers.limite: Here nothing is connected to a real circuit: the game reads and writes plain files, then draws the robot.
at.f.robot_fichiers.idee: “Writing into a file cannot make anything move”: on a real system it can, when the file is a kernel interface. That is why you touch it with an adult.
at.f.conditions_robot.enfant: A robot decides with tests: if it is true, it does one thing; otherwise, another. AND, OR, NOT combine the tests.
at.f.conditions_robot.grands: [ a -lt b ] (test) returns code 0 if it is true; if, &&, || use that code. Inside $(( )), && || ! compute 1 or 0.
at.f.conditions_robot.limite: The game's tests compare whole numbers; a real sensor sometimes gives noisy values that must be smoothed.
at.f.conditions_robot.idee: “AND means you have one and the other, so one is enough”: no, AND needs BOTH; one being enough is OR.
at.f.boucle_robot.enfant: A robot repeats non-stop: read its sensors, decide, act. That is a loop.
at.f.boucle_robot.grands: for and while repeat a do … done block; sleep sets the pace; Ctrl+C (SIGINT) stops an endless loop. On Arduino: setup() once, loop() forever.
at.f.boucle_robot.limite: In the game, each turn waits for the script to finish; a real robot sometimes has to react while it is computing (interrupts).
at.f.boucle_robot.idee: “An endless loop is always a bug”: no, a robot loops as long as it is switched on; it just needs a safe way to stop it.
at.f.vrai_pi.enfant: A Raspberry Pi is a real little Linux computer: you connect to it with ssh, update it with an adult, and it can start the robot on its own at boot.
at.f.vrai_pi.grands: ssh pi@address, sudo apt update (with an adult), gpioset / pinctrl for the pins, crontab @reboot or a systemd --user service, logs (journalctl, or a file).
at.f.vrai_pi.limite: The game connects to no Raspberry Pi and changes no pin: it tells the story, and only offers commands that read.
at.f.vrai_pi.idee: “sudo is for going faster”: no, sudo gives every right over the machine; you only use it with an adult, knowing what the command does.
at.f.embarque.enfant: An Arduino or ESP32 board is a microcontroller: a very small computer that runs just one program, right away, with very little energy.
at.f.embarque.grands: Real time: answering within a guaranteed delay. arduino-cli compile / upload, screen /dev/ttyUSB0 115200 (the serial port), esptool.py (flashing an ESP32): with an adult.
at.f.embarque.limite: The game never touches /dev/tty* or a board: these commands are only explained.
at.f.embarque.idee: “A Raspberry Pi and an Arduino board are the same”: no, one is a computer with a system (Linux), the other a microcontroller with a single program.
maths.logique.question: Do you know what AND, OR and NOT mean when we talk about true and false?
maths.logique.enfant: True = 1, false = 0. AND: true only if both are true. OR: true if at least one is true. NOT: the opposite.
maths.logique.grands: Boolean algebra: a ∧ b, a ∨ b, ¬a. Truth tables; De Morgan's laws: NOT (a AND b) = (NOT a) OR (NOT b).
maths.logique.limite: In the game an answer is 0 or 1; in life we sometimes have “maybe”: computers always decide.
maths.logique.idee: “OR means one or the other, but not both”: in logic, OR is also true when both are true (the “exclusive or” is another gate).
maths.logique.ex1: The way is clear (1) AND the battery is charged (1) → the robot moves (1).
maths.logique.ex2: It is raining (0) OR it is windy (1) → we take a jacket (1).
maths.logique.exo: The robot moves if the way is clear ({a}) AND its battery is charged ({b}). (1 = true, 0 = false.) Does it move? Answer 1 or 0.
maths.logique.erreur: AND is true (1) only if BOTH are 1: here, {a} and {b}.
maths.logique.kw: logic and or not true false boolean boole truth table gate condition if test robot
at.meuble.plan:
🤖 THE ROBOT WORKSHOP

Welcome, {nom}! Here your robot is SIMULATED: no hardware needed.
• robot/led: write 1 to turn it on, 0 to turn it off.
• robot/moteur: write avance (forward), gauche (left), droite (right) or stop.
• robot/capteur_distance: the distance in front of the robot, in centimetres (one square = 10 cm).
• `atelier pas`: time moves forward one step, the robot does what its motor says.
• cerveau_exemple.sh: a robot brain to copy and improve.

GOLDEN RULE: the game never touches real hardware. A real Raspberry Pi, Arduino or ESP32 board is optional, and always with an adult.

at.cerveau.c2: It reads the sensor… then ALWAYS goes forward. Your turn to make it smart!

The arrow shows where the robot looks; ▓ = obstacle; · = square already visited; one square = 10 cm.

at.ou.aide: Give the robot's coordinates: `atelier ou X Y` (x first, y next).

at.logique.titre: AND, OR, NOT: how a robot decides
at.logique.texte:
A test answers TRUE (1) or FALSE (0). “The sensor says less than 10 cm” is a test.
• AND: true only if both tests are true.
• OR: true if at least one of the tests is true.
• NOT: the opposite of the test.
In the shell: [ 5 -lt 10 ] tests “5 smaller than 10”; && runs the next part if it is true, || if it is false.
at.verite.titre: The truth table of the {porte} gate
at.verite.texte:
A = “obstacle ahead”, B = “button pressed” (1 = true, 0 = false).
What is A {porte} B for each row?
at.verite.repondre: Answer with the 4 outputs, from top to bottom: `atelier verite 0 1 1 0` (for example).
at.verite.ok: Correct table: you know the {porte} gate!
at.verite.faux: Not yet. Read `atelier logique` again, then try row by row.
at.choix.titre: Three robots, three rules: AND, OR or NOT?
at.choix.arret: The robot must stop if it sees an obstacle, or if its battery is empty: just one of the two reasons is enough.
at.choix.porte: The garage door opens when you have the card and the right code: both are needed.
at.choix.veilleuse: The night light turns on when it is not daytime: it is the opposite of “it is daytime”.
at.choix.avance: The robot moves only if the way is clear and it still has battery: both are needed.
at.choix.alarme: The alarm rings if the door opens, or if the window opens: just one is enough.
at.choix.arrosage: The sprinkler runs when the soil is not damp: it is the opposite of “the soil is damp”.
at.choix.repondre: Answer in order with {et}, {ou} or {non}: for example `atelier choix et ou non`.
at.choix.ok: All three are right: you can turn a rule into logic!
at.choix.faux: Check again: situation(s) {liste}. “Both are needed” or “one is enough”?
at.essai.titre: The test grid: the robot is at the start
at.essai.texte:
Now start the loop: at each turn, your brain decides, then the world takes a step.
`for i in $(seq 10); do sh cerveau.sh; atelier pas; done`
at.defi.regles:
In {pas} steps, your robot must explore at least {min} different squares, WITHOUT EVER BUMPING.
Your cerveau.sh runs at every turn: `for i in $(seq 20); do sh cerveau.sh; atelier pas; done`
at.defi.ok: CHALLENGE COMPLETE: {cases} squares explored without a single bump!
at.defi.choc: Your robot bumped into something: the challenge stops here.
at.defi.peu: No bump, well done… but only {cases} squares out of {min}: your robot goes round in circles or stays put.
at.defi.recommence: Fix cerveau.sh, then start the challenge again: `atelier defi`.
at.aidec.texte: Open your brain with `nano cerveau.sh` and write these lines (Ctrl+O to save, Ctrl+X to quit):
at.aidec.fin: if … then … else … fi: IF the sensor says less than 10 cm, THEN turn, OTHERWISE go forward.
at.pi.titre: The real Raspberry Pi (optional, with an adult)
at.pi.texte:
A Raspberry Pi is a real little Linux computer, the size of a playing card: ls, cat, nano, loops… everything works on it.
• You connect to it from another computer with `ssh pi@address` (the Port taught you ssh).
• You update it with an adult: `sudo apt update` then `sudo apt upgrade`.
• Its GPIO pins are driven with `gpioset` or `pinctrl`, always with an adult.
The game itself connects to nothing and touches no pin.
at.gpio.titre: The GPIO pins (the start of the row of 40)
at.gpio.texte:
Each pin has a number. An LED is wired to a GPIO pin (with a resistor!) and a GND pin.
On a real Pi, `gpioset gpiochip0 17=1` would set pin 17 to 1: the LED would light up. Just like your echo 1 > robot/led.
Rules: never without an adult, never straight onto the 5 V, always unplug before wiring.
at.autonome.titre: The autonomous robot: starting on its own, writing everything down
at.autonome.texte:
A robot has no screen and no keyboard: at start-up, it must launch its program on its own.
• cron: a line `@reboot sh /home/pi/robot/cerveau.sh` in the crontab.
• or a service: `systemctl --user` (the Control Post will tell you about it).
• and a LOG: every action written into a file, to understand afterwards.
Your simulated robot already keeps its log: robot/journal.txt.
at.embarque.texte:
🍓 Raspberry Pi: a computer. Linux starts in a few seconds, several programs run together.
🔌 Arduino or ESP32 board: a microcontroller. ONE program, which starts in an instant, with very little energy (days on a battery).
REAL TIME: answering IN TIME, always. A robot brake that reacts too late is useless, even if it reacts right.
An Arduino board's program has two parts: setup() once, then loop() forever… just like your loop!
at.reflexe.texte:
Your robot rolls at {v} cm per second. Its brain takes {ms} milliseconds to decide (1 second = 1000 ms).
While it thinks, it keeps rolling: how many centimetres before it reacts?
Answer: `atelier reflexe N`
at.reflexe.ok: Yes: {v} cm/s × {ms} ms ÷ 1000 = {cm} cm. The obstacle must be seen at least {cm} cm ahead!
at.reflexe.faux: Not quite: {v} × {ms}, then divide by 1000 (ms into seconds).
at.arduino.titre: Programming a board from the terminal (told, with an adult)
at.arduino.texte:
With a board plugged in by USB, and an adult:
1. `arduino-cli compile`: translates the program for the board.
2. `arduino-cli upload`: sends it into the board through the cable.
3. `screen /dev/ttyUSB0 115200`: listens to what the board says (the serial port); Ctrl+A then K to quit.
4. For an ESP32, `esptool.py` can erase and rewrite its memory.
The game does NONE of this: it never touches the ports or the boards.
One day, your Terminagotchi egg could live in a little board like that… but that is for later!
at.telephone.texte:
A phone is full of sensors: accelerometer (it feels being shaken), gyroscope (it feels being turned), light, proximity (the screen goes off against your ear), GPS…
It also has “actuators”: an LED (the lamp), a little motor (the vibrator), a loudspeaker.
On the phone, the Terminagotchi app can turn on the lamp (`lampe on`), vibrate (`vibre 300`) and read the battery (`batterie`).
at.indice.trou: Replace each ? with your answer (without the ?).
at.indice.ou: x = the column (the number at the top), y = the row (the number on the left). Look at `atelier grille`.
at.indice.cases: Divide the sensor's centimetres by 10: a square is 10 cm.
at.indice.verite: Row by row: AND is 1 only if A and B are 1; OR is 1 as soon as one of them is 1.
at.indice.choix: “Both are needed” → et; “one is enough” → ou; “the opposite” → non.
at.indice.reflexe: Multiply the speed by the time in milliseconds, then divide by 1000.
at.indice.led: The LED only understands 0 or 1: `echo 1 > robot/led`.
at.indice.moteur: The motor understands avance, gauche, droite or stop: `echo avance > robot/moteur`.
at.indice.redirection: Don't forget the > sign to write INTO the file: `echo 1 > robot/led`.
at.indice.boucle: In the loop, you need both: the brain (`sh cerveau.sh`) THEN the world's step (`atelier pas`).
at.indice.malin: Your cerveau.sh must read the sensor, have an if, turn (droite or gauche) and go forward (avance). Need the lines? `{cmd}`
at.indice.choc: 💥 Your robot bumped. Does your brain turn when the sensor says less than 10 cm? Fix it, then `atelier defi`.
at.indice.peu: No bump, but not enough squares: your robot must TURN in front of the obstacle (not stop), then set off again. Then `atelier defi`.
at.indice.materiel: 🔌 The game never touches real hardware (serial port, pins, flashing) and never uses sudo. Here everything is simulated: use the files in robot/.
at.garde.materiel: Careful: this command talks to real hardware (or asks for sudo). Real hardware is always with an adult, never for the game: your Workshop robot is simulated.

at.sens.ecrit: an order is written to it

hist.sommet.debut: ⛰ Above the clouds, a hut clinging to the rock: the Summit. Here you no longer learn one command at a time: you write solid scripts, tame regular expressions, chain tools in one line, debug, and learn an unknown tool on your own. The fragile and broken scripts are provided by the game, in your play area.
hist.sommet.fin: Robust scripts, regex, one-liners, debugging, documentation, a combined CTF: you reached the Summit. You are a Summit Master!
som.ouvert.log: 🌍 The Summit opens above the Crossroads
som.ouvert.dit: Three worlds at level 3 ({mondes}): the path to the Summit is open! This is Expert++. Whenever you like: `cd ~/terrain_terminagotchi/sommet`.
som.ferme: The Summit is not open yet: you need 3 Crossroads worlds at level 3.
som.pont: This step uses a maths idea: {notion}. Do you know it? If not, type `{cmd}`: we cross the bridge, then come back here.
hist.som2.titre: The clean bivouac: trap, mktemp, getopts
hist.som6.titre: Map and compass: reading the docs
hist.som0.1.dit: Look at what is in the hut.
hist.som0.1.bravo: The hut rules and your rope-team notebook.
hist.som0.2.bravo: The rules are clear: everything stays here, and the broken scripts are provided by the game.
hist.som1.0.dit: The hut keeper wrote a backup script. Ask the game for it.
hist.som1.0.bravo: fragile.sh is here, with “carnet de bord.txt” and a coffre/ folder.
hist.som1.1.dit: Read the script before running it: that is the first rule.
hist.som1.1.bravo: Three lines: it takes a name ($1), copies it into coffre/ and says all went well.
hist.som1.2.dit: Run it on the logbook (the name contains spaces, hence the quotes).
hist.som1.2.bravo: cp looked for THREE files (carnet, de, bord.txt): the unquoted variable was split at the spaces. And yet the script says “backup succeeded”…
hist.som1.3.dit: Every command returns an exit code: 0 if all is well, something else otherwise. Show the script's code.
hist.som1.3.bravo: 0: the script LIES. cp failed, but the last command (echo) succeeded, so the whole script says “success”.
hist.som1.4.dit: Add the safety belt on line 2: set -euo pipefail (stop at the first error, refuse empty variables, watch the pipes).
hist.som1.4.bravo: -e: stop at the first error. -u: an unset variable is an error. -o pipefail: a pipe fails if any of its commands fails.
hist.som1.5.dit: Run it again and show its exit code straight away.
hist.som1.5.bravo: This time it stops at the error and returns 1: it no longer lies. Now fix the real cause.
hist.som1.6.dit: The real cause: $carnet without quotes. Put it in quotes.
hist.som1.6.bravo: "$carnet" keeps the whole name, spaces included. Golden rule: quotes around every variable.
hist.som1.7.dit: And if we forget the name? Run the script with nothing.
hist.som1.7.bravo: “unbound variable”: thanks to -u, the script refuses to work with an empty variable instead of doing anything at all.
hist.som1.8.dit: Now, the real backup of the logbook.
hist.som1.8.bravo: Backup succeeded, for real this time: the logbook is in coffre/. Your script is robust.
hist.som2.0.dit: Two bivouac scripts are waiting: a messy one and a clean one. Ask the game for them.
hist.som2.0.bravo: sale.sh and bivouac.sh are in place.
hist.som2.1.dit: Run the messy script: it prepares a ration in a draft file… then breaks down.
hist.som2.1.bravo: It stopped with an error. But what happened to its draft?
hist.som2.2.bravo: A forgotten draft! A script that crashes leaves its temporary files behind.
hist.som2.3.dit: Read the clean script: getopts for the options, mktemp for the draft, trap to tidy up.
hist.som2.3.bravo: trap '…' EXIT: “whatever happens, when leaving, do this”. mktemp makes up a unique file name.
hist.som2.4.bravo: getopts read -n 3; the bag holds 3 rations.
hist.som2.5.dit: Count the drafts lying around now.
hist.som2.5.bravo: Still 1: only the messy script's. The clean script tidied its own thanks to trap.
hist.som2.6.dit: Give it an option it does not know, -x.
hist.som2.6.bravo: getopts refuses -x, the script shows its usage and returns code 2: a clear error is better than a wrong result.
hist.som2.7.dit: Do the cleaning the messy script did not do: delete the drafts.
hist.som2.7.bravo: Clean bivouac. Remember: set -euo pipefail, trap, mktemp, getopts — a script's survival kit.
hist.som3.0.dit: The expedition log is carved in the rock. Ask the game for it.
hist.som3.0.bravo: journal.log is here. Dates, tags [INFO], [ALERTE], [ERREUR]… and a few traps.
hist.som3.1.dit: Read the start of the log.
hist.som3.1.bravo: Some lines start with a YYYY-MM-DD date; others are indented continuation lines.
hist.som3.2.dit: Count the lines that START with a date: ^ anchors to the start, [0-9] is a class, {4} repeats 4 times.
hist.som3.2.bravo: Without ^, a date in the middle of a line would count too. The anchor changes everything.
hist.som3.3.dit: Now ALL the dates, even in the middle of lines: -o shows only the matched part. Then count the different ones.
hist.som3.3.bravo: grep -o cuts out, sort -u keeps each date once, wc -l counts.
hist.som3.4.dit: How many different dates are in the log? Answer the game.
hist.som3.4.bravo: Right. The dates hidden in continuation lines count too.
hist.som3.5.dit: Count the lines where ALERTE or ERREUR appears (the | means “or”).
hist.som3.5.bravo: Careful: this number also counts a “fausse ALERTE” (false alert) written in the middle of a note.
hist.som3.6.dit: Keep only the REAL alerts: a date at the start, then [ALERTE] or [ERREUR]. Store them in alertes.txt.
hist.som3.6.bravo: The brackets are protected by \: otherwise [ … ] would be a character class.
hist.som3.7.dit: How many real alerts? Answer the game.
hist.som3.7.bravo: Right: the anchored pattern is more precise than plain “ALERTE|ERREUR”.
hist.som3.8.dit: Rewrite the dates day-first with sed -E: ( ) capture, \1 \2 \3 put them back in the order you want.
hist.som3.8.bravo: YYYY-MM-DD becomes DD/MM/YYYY. Captures mean cutting up, then gluing back.
hist.som4.0.dit: A rockfall of stones (files) blocks the path. Ask the game for it.
hist.som4.0.bravo: eboulis/: folders nord, sud, grotte… and stones whose names contain spaces.
hist.som4.1.dit: List all the stones, in all the subfolders.
hist.som4.1.bravo: find goes down everywhere. Notice the names with spaces.
hist.som4.2.dit: Try to measure each stone by passing the names to xargs.
hist.som4.2.bravo: “No such file”: xargs splits at spaces, “pierre ronde.txt” becomes two names. Spaces are the enemy.
hist.som4.3.dit: The right way: -print0 separates names with a null character, -0 reads them the same way. Then sort and keep the top.
hist.som4.3.bravo: The first line is the total; the next 5 are the 5 heaviest stones in the play area.
hist.som4.4.dit: Which stone is the heaviest? Answer the game with its name.
hist.som4.4.bravo: Right. One command line did the work of a whole program.
hist.som4.5.dit: Put a command's result INSIDE a sentence with $( ).
hist.som4.5.bravo: The shell first runs the command inside $( ), then puts its output in its place.
hist.som4.6.dit: Compare the north and south stones without an intermediate file: <( ) passes a command off as a file.
hist.som4.6.bravo: <: only in the north; >: only in the south. <( ) is a bash speciality.
hist.som4.7.dit: awk reads several files at once: FNR restarts at 1 in each file, FILENAME gives its name.
hist.som4.7.bravo: The first line of each northern stone, with the file name: awk over several files.
hist.som5.0.dit: Two of the guide's scripts are damaged. Ask the game for them.
hist.som5.0.bravo: casse.sh does not even start; boucle.sh starts… but gets it wrong.
hist.som5.1.dit: -n reads the script WITHOUT running it and looks for syntax errors.
hist.som5.1.bravo: Error at the “fi” on line 8. The shell reports where it noticed the problem, often a little after the real mistake.
hist.som5.2.dit: Which line does the shell report? Answer the game.
hist.som5.2.bravo: Right. The “if” on line 6 has no “then”: that is where to fix it.
hist.som5.3.dit: Add “; then” at the end of line 6 with sed.
hist.som5.3.bravo: 6s/$/; then/: on line 6, replace the end of the line ($) with “; then”.
hist.som5.4.dit: Check the syntax, and if it is fine (&&), run the script.
hist.som5.4.bravo: No more error: 100 steps in total. && runs the next part only if the first command succeeded.
hist.som5.5.dit: The second script adds up the altitudes of the huts. Run it.
hist.som5.5.bravo: 0? No error, but a wrong result: the worst kind of bug.
hist.som5.6.dit: -x shows each command before running it, with the real values: a head torch inside the script.
hist.som5.6.bravo: Look at the “+ totl=…” lines: the sum goes into ANOTHER variable than total.
hist.som5.7.dit: What is the name of the misspelled variable? Answer the game.
hist.som5.7.bravo: Right: totl instead of total. A typo the shell cannot guess.
hist.som5.8.dit: Fix the typo and run it again.
hist.som5.8.bravo: 5450 metres: the right total. Read the trace, find, fix, check again.
hist.som5.9.dit: shellcheck is an automatic script reviewer. Have it read the fragile script.
hist.som5.9.bravo: It points out known traps (SC2086: an unquoted variable…) before they bite.
hist.som5.10.dit: One last tool, as an idea: strace, which shows the calls a program makes to the system.
hist.som5.10.bravo: You know it exists and what it shows: it is often the experts' last-resort tool.
hist.som6.0.dit: Someone left you a tool you have never seen, a compass. Ask the game for it.
hist.som6.0.bravo: boussole.sh is here. Your mission is written above: where do you end up?
hist.som6.1.dit: The manual has sections: 1 commands, 5 file formats, 8 administration… Look for the “passwd” pages.
hist.som6.1.bravo: passwd (1) is the command, passwd (5) the format of the /etc/passwd file: same name, two pages.
hist.som6.2.dit: You do not know the tool's name? apropos searches the manual's descriptions.
hist.som6.2.bravo: apropos (or man -k) starts from a keyword and finds the tools that talk about it.
hist.som6.3.dit: An unknown tool? Always start with --help.
hist.som6.3.bravo: The usage: the -c and -p options, and what they expect.
hist.som6.4.dit: Run the compass with your mission's heading and number of steps (replace the ?).
hist.som6.4.bravo: The compass answered and wrote your arrival into arrivee.txt.
hist.som6.5.dit: Where did you arrive? Answer the game.
hist.som6.5.bravo: Right. You learned a tool you had never seen just by reading its help.
hist.som6.6.dit: A real tool's help is long: filter it. Which grep option shows only the matched part?
hist.som6.6.bravo: -o, --only-matching: the answer was in the help. -- tells grep that what follows is not an option.
hist.som7.0.dit: The combined CTF: three hidden fragments, three skills. Ask the game for it.
hist.som7.0.bravo: The clock is running. ctf/ holds a register, a rockfall and a door.
hist.som7.1.dit: Fragment 1: in the register, the only “fragment1=” followed by lowercase letters.
hist.som7.1.bravo: The decoys (spaces around =, capitals) do not match the pattern.
hist.som7.2.dit: Fragment 2: a .frag file hidden in a folder whose name contains spaces.
hist.som7.2.bravo: -print0 and -0: the space did not stop you.
hist.som7.3.dit: Fragment 3: a door. Read its help.
hist.som7.3.bravo: The door opens with a key: fragment 1.
hist.som7.4.dit: Open the door with -k and the key (replace the ?).
hist.som7.5.dit: The flag is TG{fragment1-fragment2-fragment3}. Give it to the game.
hist.som7.5.bravo: Flag captured! Three skills combined in a single challenge.
hist.som7.6.dit: Every day, a challenge: 3 training-room exercises to do with gold. Look at today's.
hist.som7.6.bravo: The challenge changes every day. Its exercises are checked by the website like the others.
hist.som7.7.dit: Beyond Giga: Tera, Peta, Exa. See what they require.
hist.som7.7.bravo: Peta = 10^15, Exa = 10^18: ranks for the most determined, earned with exercises and diamonds.
hist.som7.8.dit: Finally, your records: the CTF time and those of the training room.
hist.som7.8.bravo: You are at the Summit. Come back to beat your records and do the daily challenge!
som.meuble.refuge:
⛰ THE SUMMIT HUT
- Here we write and repair SCRIPTS. They are provided by the game, in this folder.
- Always read a script before running it.
- No Summit script leaves this folder, asks for sudo or uses the network.
- What your computer lacks (shellcheck, man, strace…) is told as a story, never required.
- The daily challenge: training-room exercises, checked by the website like the others.

som.fragile.texte:
fragile.sh copies a file into coffre/ and announces “Backup succeeded”.
Read it, run it on “carnet de bord.txt”… and check whether it tells the truth.
som.bivouac.texte:
sale.sh: a draft, a breakdown, and nothing tidied.
bivouac.sh: set -euo pipefail, getopts (the -n and -h options), mktemp (a draft with a unique name) and trap (tidy up when leaving, whatever happens).
som.journal.texte:
journal.log: one line per event, “YYYY-MM-DD [TAG] message”.
Watch out for continuation lines: they start with spaces, and some hide a date or the word ALERTE in the middle.
som.dates.aide: How many DIFFERENT dates are in journal.log? `sommet dates 7` (for example)
som.dates.ok: {n} different dates (and {lignes} lines that start with a date).
som.alertes.aide: How many REAL alerts (a date at the start, then [ALERTE] or [ERREUR])? `sommet alertes 4`
som.eboulis.texte:
eboulis/: stones (files) in nord/, sud/, grotte/… Their weight = their size in bytes.
Some names contain spaces: that is where naive one-liners break.
som.lourd.aide: Which stone is the heaviest? `sommet lourd quartz` (for example)
som.lourd.ok: “{nom}”, {taille} bytes: the heaviest in the rockfall.
som.casse.texte:
casse.sh: a SYNTAX error (it does not start).
boucle.sh: a LOGIC error (it starts, but gets it wrong).
The tools: -n (read without running), -x (follow step by step), shellcheck (a reviewer).
som.ligne.aide: Which line does the shell report in casse.sh? `sommet ligne 3` (for example)
som.ligne.ok: That's it. The mistake is on line {ligne}: an “if” without “then”.
som.bug.aide: What is the name of the misspelled variable in boucle.sh? `sommet bug name`
som.bug.ok: Well spotted. Once fixed, the script will find {juste}.
som.strace.texte:
strace runs a program and shows every SYSTEM CALL it makes: open a file (openat), read (read), write (write), start another program (execve)…
Example: strace -f -e trace=openat cat refuge.txt shows the file cat opens; -f also follows the programs it starts.
Useful when nothing else explains a problem (“which file is it looking for?”). It may be missing or forbidden on some machines: here, it is told as a story.
som.boussole.texte:
Mission: leave the hut heading {cap}, {pas} steps. Where do you arrive?
You do not know this tool: read its help (--help), then run it.
som.sections.texte:
The manual sections: 1 commands, 2 system calls, 3 library functions, 5 file formats, 7 concepts, 8 administration.
man 5 passwd: the page in section 5. man -f NAME (whatis): the pages with that name. apropos WORD (man -k): search by keyword.
som.arrivee.aide: Where did you arrive? `sommet arrivee lac-gele` (for example)

som.indice.sudo: Never sudo at the Summit: everything happens in your play area, without special rights.
som.indice.trou: Replace the ? with your answer (read the screen, or the result of the previous command).
som.indice.rep.dates: Not quite. grep -oE finds dates everywhere; sort -u removes duplicates; wc -l counts.
som.indice.rep.alertes: Not quite. Count only the lines that START with a date followed by [ALERTE] or [ERREUR] (wc -l alertes.txt).
som.indice.rep.lourd: Not quite. Look at the 2nd line of the sorted list (the 1st is the total): the file name, without the folder.
som.indice.rep.ligne: Not quite. Read the -n message again: “line …”.
som.indice.rep.bug: Not quite. In the -x trace, look for the variable that receives the sum: it is not called total.
som.indice.rep.arrivee: Not quite. Run the compass again with YOUR mission's heading and number of steps (`sommet boussole` repeats them).
som.indice.rep.drapeau: Not quite. The flag: TG{fragment1-fragment2-fragment3}, only the words after the =.
som.indice.bash: Run the script with the shell in front: `bash name.sh` (without execute permission, ./name.sh is refused).
som.indice.zero: -print0 and xargs -0 go together: one writes the names separated by a null character, the other reads them that way.
som.indice.bash_seul: <( ) only exists in bash (not in sh): type the command in bash.
som.indice.sed_i: Without -i, sed shows the result but does not change the file: add -i.
som.cordee.noms_zero: names separated by a null character
som.tel.sh: On the phone, the shell is called sh (not bash): the same options -n, -x, set -euo pipefail, trap and getopts work there.
som.tel.raconte: {outil} does not exist on the phone: the game tells you about it, nothing is required.
som.f.script_robuste.enfant: A robust script does not lie: it stops at the first error (set -e), refuses an empty variable (set -u), watches its pipes (pipefail) and puts quotes around every variable.
som.f.script_robuste.grands: set -euo pipefail; "$var" everywhere (otherwise word splitting and globbing); $? = exit code of the last command (0 = success); a script's code = that of its last command.
som.f.script_robuste.limite: set -e has exceptions (inside an if, before && or ||): it is not an absolute guarantee, you must also test.
som.f.script_robuste.idee: “The script printed ‘success’, so it worked”: wrong, only the exit code and the result prove it.
som.f.bivouac_propre.enfant: trap says what to do when leaving (tidy up), mktemp makes up a unique name for a draft, getopts reads options like -n 3.
som.f.bivouac_propre.grands: trap 'cmd' EXIT (also INT, TERM); mktemp [-d] ./template.XXXXXX; while getopts "n:h" opt; case $opt …; $OPTARG; code 2 for a bad option.
som.f.bivouac_propre.limite: trap can do nothing if the script is killed brutally (kill -9): nothing runs then.
som.f.bivouac_propre.idee: “A temporary file disappears by itself”: no, it stays until someone deletes it.
som.f.regex_avancees.enfant: A regular expression is a pattern: ^ the start, $ the end, [0-9] a digit, {4} four times, (a|b) a or b, and ( ) capture a piece.
som.f.regex_avancees.grands: ERE: grep -E, grep -o (only the match), grep -c (count); sed -E 's/(…)-(…)/\2\1/' (captures \1…\9); escape metacharacters ([ ] . * \) with \.
som.f.regex_avancees.limite: A regex does not “understand” a date: 2026-99-99 passes the pattern [0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}.
som.f.regex_avancees.idee: “grep ALERTE finds the alerts”: it also finds the word ALERTE written anywhere, even in “fausse ALERTE”.
som.f.one_liners.enfant: One line, several tools: find finds, xargs passes the names, $( ) puts a result in a sentence, <( ) passes a command off as a file.
som.f.one_liners.grands: find … -print0 | xargs -0 (names with spaces or newlines); $(cmd) command substitution; <(cmd) process substitution (bash, zsh); awk: FNR (line in the file), NR (line overall), FILENAME.
som.f.one_liners.limite: A one-liner that is too long becomes unreadable: beyond a few pipes, a small commented script is better.
som.f.one_liners.idee: “File names never have spaces”: they do, and xargs without -0 splits them.
som.f.debogage.enfant: Debugging is investigating: -n reads without running, -x shows each command with its values, shellcheck points out traps, strace shows what the program asks the system.
som.f.debogage.grands: bash -n (syntax), bash -x / set -x (trace on standard error, + prefix), shellcheck (SC2086…), strace -f -e trace=openat,execve (system calls).
som.f.debogage.limite: -n only finds syntax: a typo in a variable name passes without error.
som.f.debogage.idee: “The error is on the line shown”: often a little before (a forgotten then or parenthesis).
som.f.documentation.enfant: An unknown tool? --help first, then the manual (man), arranged in sections; apropos searches by keyword when you do not know the name.
som.f.documentation.grands: man N page (1 commands, 2 system calls, 3 libraries, 5 formats, 7 concepts, 8 admin); man -f = whatis; man -k = apropos; help for bash built-ins; filter: cmd --help | grep -- -o.
som.f.documentation.limite: Manual pages are not always installed (phone, small containers): --help is almost always there.
som.f.documentation.idee: “You must know everything by heart”: no, experts read the help every day.
som.f.defis_sommet.enfant: A combined CTF asks for several skills in a row to find a flag; the daily challenge and the records bring you back to practise.
som.f.defis_sommet.grands: Offline CTF (capture the flag); daily challenge drawn from the training room's daily seed (exercises checked by the website: seed, counter, fingerprint, time); Peta (10^15) and Exa (10^18) ranks.
som.f.defis_sommet.limite: The CTF time is a local record: only the website verifies, and only the training-room exercises.
som.f.defis_sommet.idee: “A flag can be guessed”: it is built, fragment by fragment.
hist.som0.1.adulte: ls lists the current directory: the scripts and files the game left in the hut.
hist.som0.2.adulte: cat prints a text file. The rules remind you that everything happens in the play area, with no sudo and no network.
hist.som1.0.adulte: The game writes fragile.sh in the current directory: a deliberately fragile script to study and then fix.
hist.som1.1.adulte: Always read a script before running it: here, cp $carnet without quotes and no error checking.
hist.som1.2.adulte: Without quotes, $carnet is split on spaces (word splitting): cp gets three names instead of one.
hist.som1.3.adulte: $? holds the exit status of the last command. A script returns the status of its last command: here echo, so 0.
hist.som1.4.adulte: set -e stops at the first failure, -u rejects unset variables, -o pipefail makes a pipeline fail as soon as one of its commands fails.
hist.som1.5.adulte: With set -e, the script stops when cp fails and returns a non-zero status: the error is no longer hidden.
hist.som1.6.adulte: "$var" in double quotes keeps the value as one argument, spaces included. Rule: quotes everywhere.
hist.som1.7.adulte: With set -u, an unset $1 causes an « unbound variable » error instead of a silent wrong cp.
