hist.som1.8.adulte: The fixed script really copies the file into coffre/ and returns 0: this time the success is real.
hist.som2.0.adulte: The game drops sale.sh (which forgets its temporary files) and bivouac.sh (which cleans them up with trap).
hist.som2.1.adulte: sale.sh creates a temporary file, then exits with an error (exit 1) without deleting it.
hist.som2.2.adulte: The pattern brouillon.* shows the temporary files left behind: a classic script leak.
hist.som2.3.adulte: getopts reads short options, mktemp creates a unique name, trap '…' EXIT runs the cleanup whatever happens.
hist.som2.4.adulte: -n 3 is read by getopts (n: expects a value, stored in $OPTARG). The trap deletes the draft on exit.
hist.som2.5.adulte: The number does not change: bivouac.sh left no draft behind, thanks to trap EXIT.
hist.som2.6.adulte: An unknown option sends getopts to the * case: the script prints its usage on standard error and returns 2.
hist.som2.7.adulte: rm with a pattern: first check with ls what the pattern matches, then delete.
hist.som3.0.adulte: The game writes journal.log, unique to your game: dates, INFO, ALERTE, ERREUR levels, and a few false positives.
hist.som3.1.adulte: head -5 prints the first 5 lines: always look at the format before writing a regular expression.
hist.som3.2.adulte: grep -E enables extended regular expressions. ^ anchors at the start of the line, [0-9]{4} means exactly four digits.
hist.som3.3.adulte: grep -o prints each match on its own line; sort -u sorts and removes duplicates; wc -l counts.
hist.som3.4.adulte: The number printed by wc -l in the previous step is the number of distinct dates.
hist.som3.5.adulte: -c counts matching lines; | is the alternation of extended regex. Some lines are not real alerts.
hist.som3.6.adulte: Anchoring the pattern (^, escaped brackets \[ \]) removes false positives; > stores the result in a file.
hist.som3.7.adulte: wc -l alertes.txt gives the number of real alerts.
hist.som3.8.adulte: Groups ( ) capture; \1, \2, \3 put them back in the replacement. The / in the result is escaped as \/.
hist.som4.0.adulte: The game creates eboulis/: files of various sizes, some with spaces in their names.
hist.som4.1.adulte: find walks directories recursively; -type f keeps only regular files.
hist.som4.2.adulte: xargs splits its input on spaces and newlines: names with spaces are broken into pieces.
hist.som4.3.adulte: -print0 and xargs -0 separate names with the NUL character, the only one forbidden in a file name. sort -nr sorts from largest to smallest.
hist.som4.4.adulte: Below the total line, the first line of the sorted list is the heaviest stone.
hist.som4.5.adulte: $( ) is command substitution: the shell runs the command and puts its output in its place.
hist.som4.6.adulte: <( ) is process substitution (bash, zsh): a command's output becomes a file that diff can read.
hist.som4.7.adulte: NR counts lines across all files, FNR those of the current file; FNR==1 targets the first line of each file.
hist.som5.0.adulte: The game drops casse.sh (a syntax error) and boucle.sh (a typo in a variable name).
hist.som5.1.adulte: bash -n checks the syntax without running. The error is reported where the shell notices it, not always where it is.
hist.som5.2.adulte: The number after « line » in the bash -n message is the line where the shell noticed the error.
hist.som5.3.adulte: The if on line 6 has no then: bash only notices at the fi. '6s/$/; then/' appends the text at the end of line 6.
hist.som5.4.adulte: && runs the second command only if the first succeeds (status 0): you do not run a badly written script.
hist.som5.5.adulte: The script runs without error but prints a wrong total: a logic bug that bash -n cannot see.
hist.som5.6.adulte: bash -x prints each command after expansion (lines with +): you see the real values of the variables at each turn.
hist.som5.7.adulte: In the trace, the loop writes to a variable whose name differs from the one printed at the end.
hist.som5.8.adulte: With set -u, this typo would have been caught at once (unset variable).
hist.som5.9.adulte: shellcheck is a static analyser: it flags unquoted variables (SC2086) and many other pitfalls.
hist.som5.10.adulte: strace -f follows the system calls of a program and its children (open, read, write…). Useful to understand a failure; not run here.
hist.som6.0.adulte: The game writes boussole.sh, a tool you do not know: the method matters more than the tool.
hist.som6.1.adulte: man -f (like whatis) gives the pages for a name and their section: passwd(1) the command, passwd(5) the file format.
hist.som6.2.adulte: apropos searches a word in the manual page descriptions; -s 1 limits it to commands.
hist.som6.3.adulte: --help (or -h) summarises the options, often faster than man; tldr gives short examples if installed.
hist.som6.4.adulte: The -c and -p options are read by getopts in the script. The values are the ones given by sommet boussole.
hist.som6.5.adulte: The arrival place is the last line printed by the compass.
hist.som6.6.adulte: The first grep reads the help on standard input; -- marks the end of options, so '-o,' is taken as the pattern.
hist.som7.0.adulte: Combined CTF: each fragment needs a different skill (precise regex, find on names with spaces, an unknown tool).
hist.som7.1.adulte: The decoys: spaces around =, capital letters. [a-z]+ only accepts lowercase letters right after =.
hist.som7.2.adulte: The folder name contains spaces: without -print0 and -0, xargs would break the path.
hist.som7.3.adulte: Same method as with the compass: read the help first, run afterwards.
hist.som7.4.adulte: The key is fragment 1. The script also writes porte_ouverte.txt (with tee), which lets the game check.
hist.som7.5.adulte: The timer stops at the right flag: that is your record, kept only in your save.
hist.som7.6.adulte: The challenge exercises are training-room ones; the website checks them like the others (seed, fingerprint).
hist.som7.7.adulte: Kilo, Mega, Giga, Tera, Peta, Exa: each grade is 1000 times the previous one (10^3, 10^6 … 10^18).
hist.som7.8.adulte: Records stay in your save, on your device; nothing is sent.
hist.at3.1.ps.bravo: vrai (true)! if ( … ) tests; PowerShell runs the {{ … }} block if it is true, and the block after else if it is false.
hist.at3.1.ps.adulte: -lt means “less than”; -gt, “greater than”. PowerShell compares with the same words as bash.
hist.at3.2.ps.bravo: Your robot can decide! if (…) {{ … }} else {{ … }}: if, then, otherwise.
hist.at3.2.ps.adulte: $d = … stores a value in a variable; [int] turns it into a whole number so the comparison is right. That is exactly what the robot's brain will do.
hist.at4.0.ps.bravo: Three turns of the loop: ForEach-Object repeats, Start-Sleep 1 waits one second.
hist.at4.0.ps.adulte: 1..3 makes the numbers 1, 2, 3; the pipe | hands them one by one to ForEach-Object, which repeats the {{ … }} block.
hist.at4.1.ps.adulte: while ($true) repeats as long as it is true… so forever. Ctrl+C stops the running command.
hist.at4.6.ps.adulte: Any editor will do (Notepad, or another one). Set-Content robot\moteur droite writes into the file, like echo droite > robot\moteur. The game checks that there is an if, the sensor, avance and a direction.
hist.at6.5.ps.adulte: Get-Content … -Tail 5 shows the last 5 lines: the most recent ones, the ones you want to see after a breakdown.
hist.at7.1.ps.bravo: Measure-Command measures the duration. TotalMilliseconds is the time that really went by, in milliseconds.
at.ps.aidec.texte: Open your brain with `notepad cerveau.ps1` and write these lines, then save (Ctrl+S) and close Notepad:
at.ps.aidec.fin: if (…) {{ … }} else {{ … }}: IF the sensor says less than 10 cm, THEN turn, OTHERWISE go forward.
at.ps.politique:
If PowerShell says “running scripts is disabled on this system”, it is not your fault: Windows blocks scripts to be careful. In the game's terminal, your brain already works. Elsewhere, run it like this, without changing any of the computer's settings:
`1..20 | ForEach-Object {{ powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\cerveau.ps1; atelier pas }}`
If Windows still refuses: `1..20 | ForEach-Object {{ & ([scriptblock]::Create((Get-Content .\cerveau.ps1 -Raw))); atelier pas }}`
at.ps.indice.politique: Your robot did not move: its motor stayed on stop, so cerveau.ps1 wrote nothing. If PowerShell showed “running scripts is disabled on this system”, Windows blocked your script (not your fault). Type `atelier aide-cerveau`: it shows how to run it without changing anything on the computer (for the challenge, first run `atelier defi` again).
at.ps.meuble.plan:
🤖 THE ROBOT WORKSHOP

Welcome, {nom}! Here your robot is SIMULATED: no hardware needed.
• robot/led: write 1 to turn it on, 0 to turn it off.
• robot/moteur: write avance (forward), gauche (left), droite (right) or stop.
• robot/capteur_distance: the distance in front of the robot, in centimetres (one square = 10 cm).
• `atelier pas`: time moves forward one step, the robot does what its motor says.
• cerveau_exemple.ps1: a robot brain to copy and improve.

GOLDEN RULE: the game never touches real hardware. A real Raspberry Pi, Arduino or ESP32 board is optional, and always with an adult.
at.ps.aide.liste:
`atelier robot`: see your robot (LED, sensor, motor)
`atelier grille`: the grid and its coordinates
`atelier pas`: time moves forward one step
`atelier ou X Y`: where is the robot?
`atelier logique`, `atelier verite`, `atelier choix`: AND, OR, NOT
`atelier essai`: the robot goes back to the start of the test grid
`atelier defi`: the obstacle challenge
`atelier aide-cerveau`: help to write cerveau.ps1
`atelier pi`, `atelier gpio`, `atelier autonome`: the real Raspberry Pi (told)
`atelier embarque`, `atelier reflexe`, `atelier arduino`, `atelier telephone`: embedded systems and real time
at.ps.essai.texte:
Now start the loop: at each turn, your brain decides, then the world takes a step.
`1..10 | ForEach-Object {{ .\cerveau.ps1; atelier pas }}`
at.ps.defi.regles:
In {pas} steps, your robot must explore at least {min} different squares, WITHOUT EVER BUMPING.
Your cerveau.ps1 runs at every turn: `1..20 | ForEach-Object {{ .\cerveau.ps1; atelier pas }}`
at.ps.defi.recommence: Fix cerveau.ps1, then start the challenge again: `atelier defi`.
at.ps.indice.boucle: In the loop, you need both: the brain (`.\cerveau.ps1`) THEN the world's step (`atelier pas`).
at.ps.indice.malin: Your cerveau.ps1 must read the sensor, have an if, turn (droite or gauche) and go forward (avance). Need the lines? `{cmd}`
hist.at4.3.ps.dit: Copy it: cerveau.ps1 will be YOUR brain.
hist.at4.3.ps.bravo: cerveau.ps1 is yours. You can change it.
hist.at4.6.ps.dit: Change cerveau.ps1: if the sensor says less than 10 cm, turn right; otherwise, go forward. (Need help? `atelier aide-cerveau`)
hist.at5.1.ps.adulte: If the robot bumps or gets stuck, fix cerveau.ps1 and start the challenge again (atelier defi): that is how roboticists work.
hist.at3.1.ps.dit: Ask the shell: is 5 smaller than 10?
hist.at3.2.ps.dit: Now the robot's real test: read the sensor, and say obstacle if it is closer than 10 cm.
hist.at4.0.ps.dit: Read the sensor three times, once per second.
hist.at4.1.ps.dit: A loop that never stops! Start it, then stop it with Ctrl+C.
hist.at4.1.ps.bravo: Ctrl+C: the terminal's emergency stop button. A real robot always has one.
hist.at4.3.ps.adulte: We keep the example untouched and work on a copy: a good habit.
hist.at4.6.ps.bravo: Your brain has a condition: it turns in front of the obstacle. Ready for the challenge!
hist.at5.1.ps.dit: 20 turns of the loop with YOUR brain. Avoid every obstacle!
hist.at5.1.ps.bravo: 🏆 Your robot explored the arena without ever bumping! You wrote a real autonomous robot program.
hist.at6.5.ps.dit: Read the end of YOUR robot's log.
hist.at6.5.ps.bravo: Every step is written down: the motor, the position, the sensor. A roboticist always reads the log!
hist.at7.1.ps.dit: How long does your brain take to decide? Measure it.
hist.at7.1.ps.adulte: Starting a script takes a few milliseconds: for a fast robot, every millisecond counts.
app.pan.monde.dit: Look at the World tab: your creatures live in your real biome/ folders!
monde.aide: drag to move · wheel to zoom · click a region to enter it · Esc to go back
monde.ouvert_grand: The world is open full size (Esc to go back).
monde.ouvert: The biome world, full size! Esc or ✕ to go back.
monde.tk: This backup window keeps the Map: the 3D world needs GTK 4.
monde.vide: Your world has no region yet.
monde.toucher: Tap a creature (in the world or here) to see its card. One creature per plot: those waiting for a spot play at the shelter, nobody is lost!
monde.attend: At the shelter: the {region} region is full ({n}/{n}). To make it bigger:
monde.compagnon: Your companion, hatched from the egg: it has been with you from the start.
efx.dit.parcelle: A new plot! One more folder = one more spot for a creature.
efx.dit.dossier_plus: mkdir made a folder: a new place in the world.
efx.dit.dossier_moins: The folder is gone, with everything inside. No recycle bin in the terminal!
efx.dit.objet_plus: A new object appeared: every file is an object in the world.
efx.dit.objet_moins: The object turned into confetti: rm deletes for good, there is no recycle bin.
efx.dit.objet.touch: touch placed a brand-new object (an empty file).
efx.dit.objet.ecrire: The words flew to a new sign: > creates the file if it doesn't exist.
efx.dit.objet.messager: The messenger pigeon brought back an object from another machine.
efx.dit.objet.caisse: A crate! An archive holds copies of objects (the originals stay).
efx.dit.touche: The object already existed: touch only changes its time.
efx.dit.deplace: mv moved the object: there is still only one.
efx.dit.renomme: mv changed the name on the label: same object, new name.
efx.dit.copie: cp photocopied the object: the original stays, the copy flies off.
efx.dit.jokers: The star * aimed at all these objects at once.
efx.dit.cd: cd walked you here: the yellow dot is you.
efx.dit.pwd: pwd shows your path, step by step, separated by /.
efx.dit.ls: ls lights up each thing that is here, one after another.
efx.dit.ls_a: ls -a opens the curtain: names starting with a dot are hidden.
efx.dit.find: find sends a wave through every folder and plants a beacon on each find.
efx.dit.lire: cat unrolls the scroll: you read what's inside without changing anything.
efx.dit.ecrit.efface: A single > erases the whole sign before writing: careful!
efx.dit.ecrit.ajoute: >> adds a line at the end, without erasing anything.
efx.dit.droits: chmod sets a glass bell: three padlocks, for me, my club and the others.
efx.dit.refus.droits: Permission denied: the guardian said no. Look at the padlocks with ls -l.
efx.dit.refus.introuvable: "?": that path doesn't exist here. Check with ls or the Tab key.
efx.dit.refus.pas_vide: The plot shakes but holds: rmdir only removes empty folders.
efx.dit.refus.existe: It already exists! Pick another name.
efx.dit.refus.dossier: That's a folder, not an object: try ls or cd.
efx.dit.refus.commande: I don't know that word. Check how the command is spelled.
efx.dit.refus.autre: Nothing changed: read the command's message again, it says why.
efx.dit.lucioles.voir: Each firefly is a running program, with its number (PID).
efx.dit.lucioles.part: & sends a firefly to work in the background: you can keep typing.
efx.dit.lucioles.eteint: kill turns off a firefly: that program stops.
efx.dit.messager: The messenger pigeon flew to the other machine and came back.
efx.dit.messager.rate: The pigeon couldn't find that address: check the machine's name.
efx.dit.photo: Click! git commit took a photo of the garden and put it in the album.
efx.dit.empreinte: The object's fingerprint: a tiny change changes it completely.
efx.dit.tuyau: Pipes | pass one command's result to the next, like a chain.
efx.dit.caisse: A crate! An archive holds copies of objects.
efx.caisse.ouvre: {n} object(s) come out of the crate
efx.dit.caisse.ferme: tar puts COPIES of the objects in a crate: the originals stay where they are.
efx.dit.caisse.ouvre: The crate opens: the objects come out, where you asked.
efx.dit.caisse.serre: gzip squeezes the object so it takes less room (gunzip unsqueezes it).
efx.dit.caisse.voir: tar -t looks inside the crate without taking anything out.
efx.dit.lien: ln set up a shortcut: a glowing thread links it to the real object.
efx.dit.lien.mort: The thread is broken: this shortcut points to an object that does not exist (a dead link).
efx.dit.taille: du weighs what is here: the taller the column, the heavier it is.
efx.dit.disque: df shows the tank of the whole disk: what is used and what is left.
efx.dit.arbre: tree lifts the mist level by level: every folder and what it holds.
efx.dit.memoire: free shows the memory shelf: each box is taken by a running program.
efx.dit.lanternes: Each service is a lantern: the glowing ones are running. We look, we touch nothing.
efx.dit.reveil: crontab -l shows the alarms: the machine will run these commands by itself, at the set time.
efx.dit.journal: journalctl opens the machine's logbook: each line tells what happened.
efx.dit.etoile: git add puts a star: this object will be in the next photo (the next commit).
efx.dit.album.voir: git log flips through the album: each photo has its number and its message.
efx.dit.album.neuf: git init opens a brand-new album: it is waiting for its first photo.
efx.dit.branche.nouvelle: A branch is a parallel world: try anything you like, the main world does not move.
efx.dit.branche.change: You move to another branch: the objects become as they are in that world.
efx.dit.fusion: git merge brings the two branches together: what you did comes back into the main world.
efx.dit.fusion.conflit: Conflict! Both branches changed the same line: open the file and choose.
efx.dit.rembobine: git restore turns the clock backwards: the object becomes as it was in the last photo.
efx.dit.robot.led: Everything is a file: writing 1 into led turns the robot's light on, 0 turns it off.
efx.dit.robot.moteur: The robot will read its motor file at the next step: forward, left, right or stop.
efx.dit.robot.capteur: The sensor measures the distance to the obstacle, in centimetres.
efx.dit.robot.pas: One step: the robot reads its motor, moves one square and measures the distance ahead.
efx.dit.grimoire: The command's spellbook: everything is explained in it (q to close it).
efx.dit.loupe: shellcheck brings out the magnifying glass: each fragile line of the script is highlighted.
efx.dit.loupe.ok: The magnifying glass found nothing: this script is solid.
efx.dit.filet: trap stretches a net: whatever happens, the tidy-up command will run on the way out.
efx.dit.sablier: mktemp puts an object with a unique name, made not to last: remember to tidy it up.
efx.dit.espion: strace spies on a program: each request it makes to the system goes under the magnifying glass.
hist.temps.debut: ⏳ Shelves up to the ceiling, a great clock, and albums that remember everything. Welcome to the Library of Time! Here, git takes photos of your files: you can travel back in time, open parallel worlds and bring them together.
hist.temps.fin: You can create a git album, take photos, travel back in time, find a lost version, open a branch, solve a conflict, share a copy and read fingerprints. You are an Archivist of Time!
tp.ouvert.log: 🌍 A world opens at the Crossroads: the Library of Time
tp.ouvert.dit: You can read, search and connect commands: the Library of Time opens its albums to you! Here you learn git, the camera for files. Whenever you like: `cd ~/terrain_terminagotchi/temps`.
tp.pont: This step uses a maths idea: {notion}. Do you know it? If not, type `{cmd}`: we cross the bridge, then come back here.
hist.tp0.1.dit: Look at what's in the Library.
hist.tp0.1.bravo: A register and a notebook. The albums are yours to make!
hist.tp0.1.adulte: The game prepared the temps folder in your playground. All the git repositories of this world will be created there.
hist.tp0.2.bravo: Here everything stays in your playground: we push nothing to the Internet and create no account.
hist.tp0.2.adulte: No real remote, no push, no account. git's name and e-mail are examples, set in each repository (never git config --global).
hist.tp1.0.dit: A git album keeps photos of your files. Find out how.
hist.tp1.0.bravo: A folder becomes an album; each photo (a commit) has a caption and a date.
hist.tp1.0.adulte: git is a version control system: it keeps the history of every file of a project, in the hidden .git folder.
hist.tp1.1.dit: Make the album: a folder called album with git inside.
hist.tp1.1.bravo: The album is ready! Its photos will be kept in the secret passage .git.
hist.tp1.1.adulte: `git init -b main album` creates the album folder and an empty repository whose main branch is called main.
hist.tp1.2.bravo: Here we are. git commands act on the album of the folder you are in.
hist.tp1.2.adulte: git looks for the repository in the current folder (then in its parents).
hist.tp1.3.dit: Every photo is signed. Give THIS album an example name (no --global!).
hist.tp1.3.bravo: Signed! This name is stored in album/.git/config, for this album only.
hist.tp1.3.adulte: Without --global, git config writes into the current repository. With --global it would change the settings of the whole computer: we don't do that here.
hist.tp1.4.dit: Add an example address (it ends in .invalid: it doesn't exist).
hist.tp1.4.bravo: Perfect. You never need a real address to learn.
hist.tp1.4.adulte: The .invalid domain is reserved (RFC 2606): no address exists there. On a real public project, choose with an adult what you show.
hist.tp1.5.dit: Write the first page of your chronicle.
hist.tp1.5.bravo: A page! But the album hasn't photographed it yet.
hist.tp1.5.adulte: The file is in the folder, but git doesn't track it yet.
hist.tp1.6.dit: Ask the album what it sees.
hist.tp1.6.bravo: chronique.txt is « Untracked »: the album sees it but doesn't keep it yet.
hist.tp1.6.adulte: git status: the branch, and the files that are modified, staged or untracked. Pros type it all the time.
hist.tp1.7.dit: Put the page in front of the lens.
hist.tp1.7.bravo: The page is in front of the lens: it will be in the next photo.
hist.tp1.7.adulte: git add puts the file in the index (staging area): the list of what goes into the next commit.
hist.tp1.8.dit: Click! Take the photo, with its caption.
hist.tp1.8.bravo: Your very first photo (root-commit)! It has a unique number, its fingerprint.
hist.tp1.8.adulte: git commit -m records a snapshot of the index with a message, an author and a date. The 7 characters shown are the start of its SHA-1 fingerprint.
hist.tp2.0.dit: The Librarian lends you her old spellbook, with all its photos.
hist.tp2.0.bravo: The spellbook is on the table. Someone lost a spell in it… let's find it.
hist.tp2.0.adulte: The game creates a grimoire repository with 6 commits at fixed dates: their fingerprints are the same on every computer.
hist.tp2.1.adulte: A git repository is a folder like any other, with its .git.
hist.tp2.2.dit: Unroll the film: all the photos, one per line.
hist.tp2.2.bravo: Six photos, the newest at the top. The start of each line is its fingerprint.
hist.tp2.2.adulte: git log --oneline: one line per commit (short fingerprint and message), newest first. q to quit if it's long.
hist.tp2.3.dit: Oops! Make a stain in the spellbook.
hist.tp2.3.bravo: The spellbook has changed since its last photo…
hist.tp2.3.adulte: >> adds a line at the end of the file.
hist.tp2.4.dit: Compare the spellbook with its last photo.
hist.tp2.4.bravo: + gribouillis: the added line. A removed line would have a -.
hist.tp2.4.adulte: git diff shows what changed since the last commit, in « unified diff » format (+ added, - removed).
hist.tp2.5.dit: Undo the stain: put the file back as in the last photo.
hist.tp2.5.bravo: Gone! The file is back as in the photo.
hist.tp2.5.adulte: git restore puts a file back as in the last commit. Careful: the unsaved change is lost for good.
hist.tp2.6.dit: A secret spell has vanished! Find the photos where the word secret appears or disappears.
hist.tp2.6.bravo: Two photos: the one where the secret appeared (bottom) and the one where it disappeared (top).
hist.tp2.6.adulte: git log -S looks for commits that change how many times a text appears: git's « pickaxe ».
hist.tp2.7.dit: Look at the photo where the secret disappeared: replace ? with its fingerprint (the 7 characters).
hist.tp2.7.bravo: The line with - is the erased spell! Someone tidied up a bit too hard.
hist.tp2.7.adulte: git show shows a commit: its author, date, message and its differences with the photo before.
hist.tp2.8.dit: Tell the Librarian which photo lost the spell: replace ? with its fingerprint.
hist.tp2.8.bravo: That's the one. The photo JUST BEFORE still had the spell: we call it FINGERPRINT~1.
hist.tp2.8.adulte: HASH~1 means a commit's parent (the photo before); HEAD~1 the parent of the last one.
hist.tp2.9.dit: Bring the spellbook back from the photo before: replace ? with the fingerprint you found.
hist.tp2.9.bravo: The spell is back in the spellbook!
hist.tp2.9.adulte: git checkout HASH~1 -- grimoire.txt (or git restore --source=HASH~1 grimoire.txt) brings this file back from an old commit, without changing the others.
hist.tp2.10.dit: Take a new photo (-a: with the changed file), so you never lose it again.
hist.tp2.10.bravo: Saved! You found a lost version: rare creatures come prowling near the shelves…
hist.tp2.10.adulte: Nothing is erased in the history: the commit that lost the spell stays, and a new commit puts it back.
hist.tp3.0.dit: A branch is a parallel world. Find out how it works.
hist.tp3.0.bravo: Two paths leave from the same photo; later, they can be joined.
hist.tp3.0.adulte: A branch is a name pointing to a commit; it moves forward with each new commit.
hist.tp3.1.dit: In the album, open a parallel world: the branch reve.
hist.tp3.1.bravo: You are in the « reve » world. The « main » world is waiting for you.
hist.tp3.1.adulte: git switch -c reve creates the branch reve and moves onto it (older form: git checkout -b reve).
hist.tp3.2.dit: In that world, day 2 is a dream.
hist.tp3.2.adulte: For now the file changes only in the working folder.
hist.tp3.3.dit: Photograph the dream (-a takes all files already tracked).
hist.tp3.3.bravo: The photo of the dream is stored in the branch reve.
hist.tp3.3.adulte: git commit -a first stages modified tracked files (not new ones), then commits.
hist.tp3.4.dit: Go back to the main world.
hist.tp3.4.bravo: Look at the chronicle: here, the dream never happened!
hist.tp3.4.adulte: Switching branches puts the files back as in that branch's last commit.
hist.tp3.5.dit: In this world, day 2 is a walk.
hist.tp3.5.adulte: Both branches have now changed the same line of the file, each in its own way.
hist.tp3.6.adulte: The history has two tips: main and reve, with a common ancestor.
hist.tp3.7.dit: Bring the two stories together: merge the reve world into main.
hist.tp3.7.bravo: CONFLICT! Both worlds wrote in the same place: git doesn't choose for you.
hist.tp3.7.adulte: git merge combines changes; when two branches change the same lines, it stops and asks for a resolution (the exit code is not 0).
hist.tp3.8.bravo: Between <<<<<<< and =======: your world (HEAD). Between ======= and >>>>>>>: the reve world.
hist.tp3.8.adulte: These are conflict markers; `temps conflit` explains them.
hist.tp3.9.dit: Keep both memories: remove only the 3 marker lines.
hist.tp3.9.bravo: No more markers, and both days are kept.
hist.tp3.9.adulte: Resolving a conflict = writing the version you want. Here sed deletes lines starting with 7 times <, = or >; you can also edit the file (nano, notepad).
hist.tp3.10.dit: Take the photo that joins the two stories.
hist.tp3.10.bravo: The two worlds are joined: this photo has TWO parent photos.
hist.tp3.10.adulte: A merge commit has two parents. At the Guild, that's what you ask for with a « merge request ».
hist.tp3.11.dit: Look at the drawing of the paths.
hist.tp3.11.bravo: Two paths that split and then meet again!
hist.tp3.11.adulte: git log --graph draws the history with characters: | / \ and * for each commit.
hist.tp4.0.dit: How do you share an album? Find out.
hist.tp4.0.bravo: A copy, a page added by a friend, and you get it back.
hist.tp4.0.adulte: Here everything stays in the playground: the copy is a folder next door, not a server.
hist.tp4.1.dit: Make a copy of this album (the dot .) for your friend, right next to it.
hist.tp4.1.bravo: A complete copy, with all the photos!
hist.tp4.1.adulte: git clone . ../copie_de_mon_ami copies the current repository (.) into a neighbouring folder, with the whole history, and remembers where it came from (origin).
hist.tp4.2.dit: Your friend adds a page in their copy.
hist.tp4.2.bravo: Your friend took a photo in their copy. Your album doesn't have it yet.
hist.tp4.2.adulte: The game makes a commit in the copy, signed with the friend's example identity, set in the copy only.
hist.tp4.3.dit: Does your album have your friend's page? Look at its film.
hist.tp4.3.bravo: Not yet: your friend's photo is only in their copy.
hist.tp4.3.adulte: Each repository has its own history; nothing syncs by itself.
hist.tp4.4.bravo: Fast-forward: your friend's photo arrives in your album.
hist.tp4.4.adulte: git pull = fetch then merge. Here from a neighbouring folder; on a real project, from a server.
hist.tp4.5.dit: Some files must never be photographed. Write the list of the forgotten ones.
hist.tp4.5.adulte: .gitignore lists file patterns that git won't offer to add (drafts, secret files…).
hist.tp4.7.dit: Ask the album what it sees.
hist.tp4.7.bravo: It sees .gitignore, but not brouillon.tmp: it's ignored!
hist.tp4.7.adulte: An ignored file doesn't show up in git status; .gitignore itself is photographed like the others.
hist.tp4.8.dit: Go and see your friend's copy.
hist.tp4.8.adulte: A clone is a complete, independent repository.
hist.tp4.9.dit: Where does this copy come from? Ask it.
hist.tp4.9.bravo: origin: it's your album, the folder the copy came from.
hist.tp4.9.adulte: A « remote » is another repository we remember. Here it's a folder of the playground; on a real project it's often a server like GitHub.
hist.tp4.10.dit: And to send your photos to a shared shelf? Ask the boat.
hist.tp4.10.bravo: git push sends the photos to the shared shelf. Here, we only tell the story.
hist.tp4.10.adulte: A real push needs an account on a server: to be done with an adult. The game never pushes anything.
hist.tp5.0.dit: Every photo has a fingerprint. Where does it come from? Open the fingerprint corner.
hist.tp5.0.bravo: A little word and three dated files are waiting for you in empreintes.
hist.tp5.0.adulte: git's fingerprints are SHA-1s: 40 hexadecimal digits computed from the content.
hist.tp5.1.adulte: This folder isn't a repository: git hash-object works anyway.
hist.tp5.2.dit: Ask git for the word's fingerprint.
hist.tp5.2.bravo: 40 characters from 0 to 9 and a to f: that's hexadecimal.
hist.tp5.2.adulte: git hash-object computes the fingerprint the file would have in a repository (a « blob »), without writing anything.
hist.tp5.3.dit: Do the same calculation by hand: « blob », the size (6), a hidden zero, then the word.
hist.tp5.3.bravo: The same fingerprint! git has no magic: it's a calculation anyone can redo.
hist.tp5.3.adulte: A blob's fingerprint = SHA-1(« blob <size>\0<content> »). That's what the Crypt calls a hash function (K3).
hist.tp5.4.dit: Change just one letter: make it a capital.
hist.tp5.4.adulte: The content is now « Temps » instead of « temps ».
hist.tp5.5.bravo: Completely different! One letter changes everything: you can't cheat without it showing.
hist.tp5.5.adulte: That's the avalanche effect of a hash function.
hist.tp5.6.adulte: We're going to read the inside of a photo.
hist.tp5.7.dit: Open the last photo and read what it really contains.
hist.tp5.7.bravo: tree: the content; parent: the fingerprint of the photo before. Each photo is tied to the previous one: a chain!
hist.tp5.7.adulte: A commit contains the fingerprint of its tree and of its parents: changing an old photo would change all the later ones. Like the Crypt's blockchain.
hist.tp5.8.dit: Go back to the fingerprint corner.
hist.tp5.8.adulte: A little detour through the Citadel: without git, how do you know what changed?
hist.tp5.9.dit: A little detour through the Citadel: find the files changed AFTER the marker.
hist.tp5.9.bravo: nouveau.txt, and mot.txt that you just changed! find compares dates; git compares contents.
hist.tp5.9.adulte: find -newer F lists what was modified after F (the modification time), an investigation tool from the Citadel.
hist.tp5.10.bravo: You are an Archivist of Time! Your certificate is stored in temps.
hist.tp5.10.adulte: The certificate is a plain text file in your playground.
tp.meuble.registre:
⏳ THE LIBRARY OF TIME — the register

Hello {nom}! Here git is a camera for your files: each photo (a commit) has a caption, a date and a fingerprint.

THE LIBRARY'S RULES
  1. All the albums (git repositories) are in your playground, here.
  2. We push nothing to the Internet and create no account: git push is only explained.
  3. The name and address on the photos are examples, set in the album (never --global).
  4. When git is missing, we tell the story: nothing is blocked.

THE SHELVES
  the album             (git init, git add, git commit)
  back in time          (git log, git diff, git restore, git show)
  parallel worlds       (git switch, git merge)
  sharing               (git clone, git pull, .gitignore)
  fingerprints          (git hash-object, git cat-file)
tp.meuble.carnet: # The notebook of time: the game writes down what you achieved.
tp.aide.liste:
temps plan         the register
temps album        how a git album works
temps grimoire     the Librarian's spellbook (temps grimoire neuf: a new one)
temps perdu HASH   the photo that lost the spell
temps branches     parallel worlds
temps conflit      reading conflict markers
temps partage      copying, fetching
temps ami          your friend's page
temps bateau       git push, explained
temps empreintes   the fingerprint corner
temps bilan        your certificate
tp.sans_git: git isn't installed on this computer: the Library TELLS you what it would do. To install it, ask an adult (Fedora: sudo dnf install git; Ubuntu: sudo apt install git; Windows: Git for Windows).
tp.album.texte:
git init: a folder becomes an album (the secret passage .git keeps the photos).
git status: what the album sees (new, modified, ready).
git add: put a file in front of the lens.
git commit -m "caption": click! a photo, forever.
tp.album.identite: Each photo is signed with a name and an address. Here they are EXAMPLES, set in the album only: git config user.name (without --global).
tp.grimoire.texte:
An old spellbook, six photos taken day after day.
A secret spell was in it… then it vanished.
git log, git show and git checkout will find it.
tp.grimoire.git: ✔ The spellbook is ready in temps/grimoire (6 photos).
tp.grimoire.deja: ✔ The spellbook is already on the table (temps/grimoire). For a new one: temps grimoire neuf.
tp.grimoire.fichiers: Without git, here is only today's spellbook (temps/grimoire), without its photos.
tp.grimoire.rate: ✖ Couldn't set up the spellbook (is there already a grimoire folder?). Try: temps grimoire neuf.
tp.grim.titre: 📖 The spellbook of the Library of Time
tp.grim.f1: waking spell: tick, tock, up you get!
tp.grim.f2: sleeping spell: hush, the moon counts to three
tp.grim.f3: snack spell: a crumb for every creature
tp.secret.0: three turns of the hourglass grow a star
tp.secret.1: a warm pebble talks to fossils
tp.secret.2: the midnight shadow keeps the keys
tp.secret.3: a feather from yesterday writes tomorrow
tp.secret.4: the clock goes backwards when you laugh
tp.perdu.sans_grimoire: You need the spellbook first: temps grimoire
tp.perdu.aide: Replace HASH with the fingerprint (at least 4 characters) of the photo that lost the spell. git log --oneline -S secret helps.
tp.perdu.suite: The photo before, {h}~1, still had it: git checkout {h}~1 -- grimoire.txt
tp.branches.texte:
git switch -c reve: a new world starting from here.
Each world has its photos. git switch main: come back.
git merge reve: join the two stories (a merge).
If both wrote in the same place: a conflict, and you choose.
tp.conflit.ici: ← the start: what's in YOUR world (HEAD)
tp.conflit.la: ← the end: what's in the reve world
tp.conflit.texte:
To resolve: write the version you want to keep, remove the 3 marker lines, then git commit -am "…".
Here we keep both days: sed -i '/^[<=>]\{7\}/d' chronique.txt (or nano chronique.txt).
tp.partage.texte:
git clone . ../copie_de_mon_ami: a complete copy of the album, with all the photos.
Your friend takes a photo there; git pull brings it into your album.
.gitignore: the list of files never to photograph.
Everything stays here, in your playground.
tp.ami.ligne: Day 3: your friend draws your creature
tp.ami.ok: Your friend added a page and took a photo in copie_de_mon_ami.
tp.ami.deja: Your friend already added their page in copie_de_mon_ami.
tp.ami.suite: Your album doesn't have it yet: cd album, then git pull ../copie_de_mon_ami
tp.ami.pas_de_copie: You need the copy first: in the album, git clone . ../copie_de_mon_ami
tp.ami.rate: Your friend's page couldn't be photographed.
tp.ami.sans_git: Without git, your friend can't take a photo: the Library only tells you the story.
tp.bateau.texte:
On a real project, the album also lives on a shared shelf (a server, like GitHub or GitLab).
git push sends your new photos there; git pull brings back the others'.
You need an account: do it with an adult. Here, the game NEVER pushes anything.
tp.empreintes.texte:
Every photo, every file has a fingerprint: 40 characters computed from the content (SHA-1).
Same content = same fingerprint, everywhere. One letter changes = everything changes.
Each photo keeps the fingerprint of the previous one: a chain.
tp.empreintes.pose: ✔ The corner is ready: temps/empreintes (mot.txt, ancien.txt, repere.txt, nouveau.txt).
tp.empreintes.rate: ✖ The fingerprint corner couldn't be prepared.
tp.bilan.pas_encore: Not yet: you need your first photo, the spell found and photographed, the two worlds joined and your friend's page in your album.
tp.bilan.texte:
⏳ ARCHIVIST OF TIME CERTIFICATE

{nom} can create a git album, take photos, travel back in time,
find a lost version, join two worlds and read fingerprints.
Photos in your album: {n}
On {date}, at the Library of Time.
tp.bilan.morale: Almost all the software in the world is kept like this, with git.
tp.indice.global: No --global here: it would change the settings of the whole computer. Type the command WITHOUT --global, in the album.
tp.indice.sudo: No need for sudo: everything happens in your playground.
tp.indice.push: Here we push nothing and add no server: everything stays in your playground (temps bateau explains git push).
tp.indice.trou: Replace the ? with a fingerprint: the 7 characters at the start of a line of git log --oneline.
tp.indice.apparue: That's the photo where the spell APPEARED. Look for the one where it DISAPPEARED (the newer of the two).
tp.indice.perdu: Not that photo. git log --oneline -S secret shows the two photos about the secret; the newer one erased it.
tp.indice.detache: You sent the whole album into the past (« detached HEAD »). Come back with git switch main, then bring back only the file: git checkout HASH~1 -- grimoire.txt
tp.indice.init_nom: Give the album a name: git init -b main album. (Your plain git init made an album of the folder you're in: that's fine.)
tp.indice.config: Type it in the album (cd album first), and without --global.
tp.indice.identite: git wants to know who signs the photo: set the example name AND address in the album (both git config).
tp.indice.pas_retrouvee: The spell isn't back in grimoire.txt yet: git checkout HASH~1 -- grimoire.txt first.
tp.indice.commit: Nothing to photograph? Change the file first; then git commit -am "caption" (-a takes files already tracked; a new file needs git add).
tp.indice.master: Your album is called master (git init without -b main): type git switch master instead of main.
tp.indice.sed_i: -i is missing: without it, sed shows the result but doesn't change the file.
tp.indice.bornes: Some markers are left, or one of the two days is gone: read the chronicle again (cat chronique.txt).
tp.indice.retrouve: Add ~1 after the fingerprint (the photo BEFORE), then -- grimoire.txt: git checkout HASH~1 -- grimoire.txt
tp.indice.pull: Tell git where to fetch from: git pull ../copie_de_mon_ami
tp.indice.clone_existe: A copie_de_mon_ami folder already exists and isn't an album: choose another name, or ask an adult to tidy it.
tp.garde.global: Careful: --global changes git's settings for the WHOLE computer (~/.gitconfig). Here we only set the album, without --global. If it's already done, an adult can check: git config --global --list
tp.garde.local: Here we push nothing and add no server: everything stays in your playground. (temps bateau explains git push.)
tp.f.git_album.enfant: git is a camera for your files: git init makes the album, git add puts a file in front of the lens, git commit takes the photo with a caption.
tp.f.git_album.grands: git init creates a repository (.git); git config without --global sets the current repository; git status shows the state; git add fills the index; git commit records a snapshot (author, date, message).
tp.f.git_album.limite: A « photo » doesn't copy everything each time: git stores each content once and reuses what hasn't changed.
tp.f.git_album.idee: No: git add doesn't save yet. Only git commit records the photo in the history.
tp.f.git_histoire.enfant: git log unrolls the film, git diff shows what changed, git restore erases a mistake, and git checkout PHOTO -- file brings a file back from the past.
tp.f.git_histoire.grands: git log (--oneline, -S text), git show COMMIT, git diff, git restore FILE, git checkout COMMIT~1 -- FILE (or git restore --source=): read and reuse the history.
tp.f.git_histoire.limite: We don't really « go back » in time: we copy an old content into the present, and the history keeps everything.
tp.f.git_histoire.idee: No: git restore can't find what was never photographed. Without a commit, an erased change is lost.
tp.f.git_branches.enfant: A branch is a parallel world: you try ideas there, then git merge joins the two stories. If both wrote in the same place, you choose.
tp.f.git_branches.grands: git switch -c creates a branch; git merge merges (fast-forward or a merge commit with two parents); on conflict, you edit the <<<<<<< ======= >>>>>>> zones then commit.
tp.f.git_branches.limite: Worlds aren't copies of the folder: a branch is just a label on a photo, which moves forward with new photos.
tp.f.git_branches.idee: No: a conflict isn't a serious error. git simply asks a human to choose.
tp.f.git_partage.enfant: git clone copies a whole album, git pull brings back the photos of a copy, and .gitignore says which files never to photograph.
tp.f.git_partage.grands: git clone (with origin), git pull = fetch + merge, git remote -v, .gitignore; git push to a server needs an account (done with an adult, never by the game).
tp.f.git_partage.limite: Here the « friend's copy » is a neighbouring folder; in real life it's often a shared server.
tp.f.git_partage.idee: No: .gitignore doesn't hide a file already photographed; it only avoids adding new ones.
tp.f.git_empreintes.enfant: Every file and every photo has a fingerprint computed from its content: one letter changes, everything changes. And each photo keeps the fingerprint of the previous one.
tp.f.git_empreintes.grands: Blob: SHA-1(« blob <size>\0<content> ») = git hash-object; git cat-file -p shows a commit (tree, parent, author). find -newer compares modification times.
tp.f.git_empreintes.limite: A fingerprint isn't a summary you can read back: you can't get the content back from it.
tp.f.git_empreintes.idee: No: two different files (in practice) never have the same fingerprint, even if they look very much alike.
tp.tel.git: The app's little git: init, config, status, add, commit, log, diff, show, restore, checkout, switch, branch, merge, clone, pull, remote, hash-object, cat-file. In the playground only, no push, no server.
tp.tel.inconnu: The app's little git doesn't know « git {cmd} ». What it can do: git help
tp.tel.tuyau: The app's little git doesn't plug into a pipe or a redirection: type the git command on its own.
tp.tel.hors_terrain: The app's little git only works in your playground (terrain_terminagotchi).
tp.tel.global: The app's little git has no --global: each album keeps its own name (without --global).
tp.tel.push: The app's little git never pushes anything: temps bateau explains git push.
tp.tel.version: the little git of the Terminagotchi app
tp.tel.editeur: The app's little git doesn't open an editor: give the caption with -m "…".
hist.controle.debut: 📟 A round room full of gauges, lights and screens: this is the ship's Control Room. Here we watch the inhabitants at work (the processes), the pantry (memory), the warehouse (the disk), the logbook and the alarm clocks. We look at everything, we break nothing.
hist.controle.fin: You can see your machine's inhabitants, read its gauges, pack your backpack, read the logbook, set an alarm, recognise your distribution, its store, its services and its crew, and stop a wave of suspects without touching the watchman. You are a Control Room Admin!
ct.ouvert.log: 🌍 A world opens at the Crossroads: the Control Room
ct.ouvert.dit: You know the common trunk up to the padlocks: the Control Room lights up for you! Whenever you like: `cd ~/terrain_terminagotchi/controle`.
ct.pont: This step uses a maths idea: {notion}. Do you know it? If not, type `{cmd}`: we cross the bridge, then come back here.
hist.ct0.1.dit: Look at what's in the Control Room.
hist.ct0.1.bravo: Instructions, a warehouse, a backpack, alarm clocks, the crew list… Everything is ready.
hist.ct0.1.adulte: The game prepared the controle folder in your playground. Everything written in this world stays there.
hist.ct0.2.bravo: Here we LOOK at the real machine, we change nothing. Promise?
hist.ct0.2.adulte: The game reads /proc, free, df, /etc/os-release, the list of packages and services; it stops no real program, installs nothing and creates no user. Whatever changes the machine is only explained, to be done with an adult.
hist.ct1.0.dit: Inhabitants live and work in your machine: the processes. Show the ones of your terminal.
hist.ct1.0.bravo: Each line is an inhabitant, with its number: the PID.
hist.ct1.0.adulte: `ps` shows the terminal's processes; `ps aux` those of the whole machine. PID = Process IDentifier.
hist.ct1.1.dit: Your terminal is an inhabitant too! Show its number with $$.
hist.ct1.1.bravo: That's the PID of your terminal (its shell).
hist.ct1.1.adulte: $$ is a special shell variable: the PID of the shell itself. In PowerShell, it's $PID.
hist.ct1.2.dit: Here is a magic place: /proc, the inhabitants' mirror. Look at your terminal's folder.
hist.ct1.2.bravo: This folder isn't on the disk: the kernel invents it when you look at it!
hist.ct1.2.adulte: /proc is a virtual file system: each process has a folder named after its number (status, cmdline, environ…).
hist.ct1.3.dit: Read the first 3 lines of its record (status).
hist.ct1.3.bravo: Name: its name; State: what it is doing (S = it sleeps while waiting for you to type).
hist.ct1.3.adulte: State can be R (working), S (sleeping, waiting), D (waiting for the disk), T (stopped), Z (zombie: finished, not yet collected).
hist.ct1.4.dit: How many inhabitants are working, how many are sleeping? Ask the Control Room.
hist.ct1.4.bravo: Almost all of them sleep: they wait until they are needed. That's normal!
hist.ct1.4.adulte: The game counts the states in /proc/*/stat (read-only); it keeps no list.
hist.ct1.5.dit: Start an inhabitant in the foreground: it sleeps 5 seconds, and you wait.
hist.ct1.5.bravo: For 5 seconds the terminal was busy: that's the foreground.
hist.ct1.5.adulte: In the foreground, the shell waits for the command to finish before giving the prompt back.
hist.ct1.6.dit: Now start it in the background with &: it sleeps 60 seconds, and you carry on.
hist.ct1.6.bravo: [1] and a number: the terminal stayed free!
hist.ct1.6.adulte: & runs the command in the background: [1] is the job number, the other number its PID. (You already did it in the dormitory.)
hist.ct1.7.bravo: Running: it is still sleeping, in the background.
hist.ct1.7.adulte: `jobs` lists the terminal's jobs. `fg` brings a job back to the foreground, Ctrl+Z pauses it, `bg` restarts it in the background.
hist.ct1.8.dit: Stop job number 1 with kill (only that one!).
hist.ct1.8.bravo: Stopped. %1 means "my job number 1", not PID 1!
hist.ct1.8.adulte: `kill %1` sends the TERM signal to the terminal's job 1. `kill 1` would target the very first process of the machine: we never do that.
hist.ct1.9.dit: Watch the inhabitants live, the busiest at the top (q to quit).
hist.ct1.9.bravo: At the top: the load and the memory; below, the inhabitants working the most.
hist.ct1.9.adulte: `top` refreshes every 3 seconds; q quits. In PowerShell: Get-Process sorted by CPU.
hist.ct2.0.dit: The ship's pantry is the memory. How much is left?
hist.ct2.0.bravo: total, used, free… and available: what can still be used.
hist.ct2.0.adulte: `free -h`: the RAM. "available" also counts what the system can free quickly (the cache).
hist.ct2.1.dit: The warehouse is the disk. Look at the space on the disk where your playground lives.
hist.ct2.1.bravo: Size, Used, Avail and Use%: the disk gauge.
hist.ct2.1.adulte: `df -h .` shows the file system that contains the current folder (the dot).
hist.ct2.2.dit: In the Control Room's warehouse, 4 crates. Weigh them all.
hist.ct2.2.bravo: One crate is much heavier than the others!
hist.ct2.2.adulte: `du -sh entrepot/*`: the size of each file in the warehouse (* = everything it contains), in readable units (K, M, G).
hist.ct2.3.dit: Which crate is the heaviest? Replace the ? with its name.
hist.ct2.3.bravo: Found it! When a disk is full, that's how we look for the culprit.
hist.ct2.3.adulte: On a real disk: `du -sh * | sort -h` sorts from lightest to heaviest (we only look in our own folders).
hist.ct2.4.dit: How long has the ship been on, and are its engines blowing hard?
hist.ct2.4.bravo: up = for how long; load average = the load over 1, 5 and 15 minutes.
hist.ct2.4.adulte: The load counts the inhabitants that want to work (or wait for the disk). We compare it with the number of cores.
hist.ct2.5.dit: How many cooks (cores) does the ship have?
hist.ct2.5.bravo: A load smaller than this number: the engines aren't straining.
hist.ct2.5.adulte: `nproc` gives the usable cores (seen in the Gear Room). Load 2 on 8 cores = 25 %.
hist.ct2.6.dit: Switch on the Control Room's gauge panel.
hist.ct2.6.bravo: Memory, disk, load: system administrators watch exactly this all day long.
hist.ct2.6.adulte: The game computes: used × 100 ÷ total (a percentage); for the load, load ÷ cores.
hist.ct3.0.dit: Each inhabitant carries a backpack: the environment variables. Look at HOME, your home.
hist.ct3.0.bravo: HOME: the folder you land in when you type cd on its own.
hist.ct3.0.adulte: Environment variables are handed by each process to the ones it starts. `env` shows them all.
hist.ct3.1.dit: PATH is the tools' address book. Show it, one folder per line.
hist.ct3.1.bravo: When you type ls, the shell looks for ls in these folders, in order.
hist.ct3.1.adulte: In PATH, folders are separated by ":" (";" on Windows); `tr ':' '\n'` puts them one per line.
hist.ct3.2.dit: How many folders in your address book? Replace the ? with the number.
hist.ct3.2.bravo: Right! A tool that is in none of these folders "doesn't exist" for the shell.
hist.ct3.2.adulte: Duplicates count or not: the game accepts both.
hist.ct3.3.dit: Where does the shell find ls? Ask it.
hist.ct3.3.bravo: The tool's full path, found thanks to the address book.
hist.ct3.3.adulte: `which` goes through PATH like the shell. `type ls` also says whether it's an alias.
hist.ct3.4.dit: Put a variable in the backpack: your favourite colour.
hist.ct3.4.bravo: export: the variable will travel with the inhabitants this terminal starts.
hist.ct3.4.adulte: Without export, the variable stays in the shell. With export, it is copied into the environment of child processes.
hist.ct3.5.dit: Start a new inhabitant (a little bash) and ask it your colour.
hist.ct3.5.bravo: It knows it: it took the backpack along!
hist.ct3.5.adulte: The single quotes stop your terminal from replacing $COULEUR: the new bash does it.
hist.ct3.6.dit: An alias is a nickname for a command. Invent salut.
hist.ct3.6.bravo: Type salut whenever you like… until you close this terminal.
hist.ct3.6.adulte: An alias lives in the current shell. To keep it, we write it in a file read at each start (~/.bashrc: the lesson "Forever").
hist.ct3.7.dit: The Control Room prepared a ready-made backpack. Read it.
hist.ct3.7.bravo: Some exports and an alias: like a small ~/.bashrc.
hist.ct3.7.adulte: ~/.bashrc is read by each new terminal. Here we practise with a playground file: your real settings don't change.
hist.ct3.8.dit: Load this backpack into your terminal with source.
hist.ct3.8.bravo: source reads the file INSIDE your terminal: its variables and aliases stay.
hist.ct3.8.adulte: `source f` (or `. f`) runs f in the current shell; `bash f` would run it in another inhabitant, which forgets everything when it leaves.
hist.ct3.9.adulte: Close the terminal and open it again: POSTE will be gone. That's why we keep our settings in ~/.bashrc.
hist.ct4.0.dit: The ship writes everything down in a logbook: a log. Ask the Control Room to open its own.
hist.ct4.0.bravo: carnet_de_bord.log is there: one line per event, with the time.
hist.ct4.0.adulte: Real logs live in /var/log or in the systemd journal. This one is a game file.
hist.ct4.1.dit: Read only the last 5 lines: the most recent ones.
hist.ct4.1.bravo: In a log, the most recent is at the bottom.
hist.ct4.1.adulte: `tail -n 5` shows the end of a file. Handy: logs often have thousands of lines.
hist.ct4.2.dit: How many ALERTE lines? Let grep count.
hist.ct4.2.bravo: grep -c counts the lines that contain the word.
hist.ct4.2.adulte: -c = count. With just `grep ALERTE`, you would see the lines themselves.
hist.ct4.3.dit: Tell the Control Room how many alerts you counted.
hist.ct4.3.bravo: That's it! An administrator reads the alerts first.
hist.ct4.3.adulte: Real logs have levels: debug, info, warning, err, crit…
hist.ct4.4.dit: Watch the logbook live: new lines will arrive by themselves. Ctrl+C to stop.
hist.ct4.4.bravo: tail -f waits for new pages. Ctrl+C stops it (not the Control Room!).
hist.ct4.4.adulte: -f = follow. Administrators keep it open in a corner of the screen.
hist.ct4.5.dit: Your real computer has a logbook too. Read the last 20 pages of your session.
hist.ct4.5.bravo: These are the real events of YOUR session. We read, we copy nothing.
hist.ct4.5.adulte: `journalctl --user` shows your session's journal (systemd). Without systemd, or in a container, it may refuse: that's normal, the step still counts.
hist.ct4.6.dit: And the kernel's logbook? The last 3 lines of dmesg.
hist.ct4.6.bravo: If it refuses, it's reserved for the administrator: that's normal, the step still counts.
hist.ct4.6.adulte: On many systems, dmesg needs root rights (kernel.dmesg_restrict). We don't use sudo for that.
hist.ct5.0.dit: cron is the ship's programmed alarm clock. See how it is set.
hist.ct5.0.bravo: 5 fields (minute, hour, day, month, day of the week), then the command to run.
hist.ct5.0.adulte: Each user has a crontab; the cron service reads it and runs the commands at the given time.
hist.ct5.1.dit: Do you already have alarms on your real machine? List them (without changing anything).
hist.ct5.1.bravo: "no crontab" means: no alarm. We read, we don't touch.
hist.ct5.1.adulte: `crontab -l` lists; `crontab -e` would change the real crontab: only with an adult. `crontab -r` would erase it all!
hist.ct5.2.bravo: The first rings Monday to Friday at 7 a.m.; the second every 30 minutes.
hist.ct5.2.adulte: 1-5 = Monday to Friday; */30 = every 30 minutes (the minutes that are multiples of 30).
hist.ct5.3.dit: Write the alarm the Control Room asks for: the 5 fields in quotes, instead of the ?.
hist.ct5.3.bravo: Well set! The quotes protected the *: without them, bash replaces them with file names.
hist.ct5.3.adulte: */15 rings at minutes 0, 15, 30 and 45: those whose remainder when divided by 15 is 0.
hist.ct5.4.dit: Add an alarm to the Control Room's file (>> adds at the end, without erasing).
hist.ct5.4.bravo: Your alarm is in the Control Room's file.
hist.ct5.4.adulte: Careful: > would overwrite the file, >> adds a line. The game NEVER runs these commands: it only says when they would ring.
hist.ct5.5.dit: Ask the Control Room when each alarm will ring.
hist.ct5.5.bravo: The Control Room computes the next ring of each line.
hist.ct5.5.adulte: For a real alarm: `crontab -e`, with an adult. Recent systems also have systemd "timers".
hist.ct6.0.dit: Which system runs your machine? Read its identity card.
hist.ct6.0.bravo: NAME, VERSION, ID: the name of your distribution.
hist.ct6.0.adulte: /etc/os-release is the same file on almost every Linux distribution. (The kernel is Linux; the distribution is everything put around it: seen in the Gear Room.)
hist.ct6.1.dit: Which distribution? Replace the ? with its short name (the ID= line).
hist.ct6.1.bravo: That's the one! Each distribution is a "Linux" prepared by a different team.
hist.ct6.1.adulte: The game also accepts ID_LIKE (the family) and the first word of NAME.
hist.ct6.2.dit: Distributions form families, each with its own tool store. Have a look.
hist.ct6.2.bravo: d for dnf, a for apt, p for pacman: those are the quiz letters.
hist.ct6.2.adulte: Fedora, RHEL, AlmaLinux: .rpm packages (dnf). Debian, Ubuntu, Mint: .deb packages (apt). Arch: pacman.
hist.ct6.3.dit: To each distribution its store: d, a or p, in the order of the list.
hist.ct6.3.bravo: Well done! You recognise the big Linux families.
hist.ct6.3.adulte: The commands change, the idea stays: an official store, signed packages, a tool to install them.
hist.ct6.4.dit: How do you install Linux? The Control Room explains (without installing anything).
hist.ct6.4.bravo: First in a virtual machine, with an adult, and after a backup!
hist.ct6.4.adulte: Installing often wipes a disk. We try in a VM (Gear Room, M5 bis), we check the image's fingerprint (Guild) and we back up first.
hist.ct6.5.dit: How many packages in your store? Count them (read-only).
hist.ct6.5.bravo: Hundreds of packages: that's what a distribution is.
hist.ct6.5.adulte: `rpm -qa` reads the database of installed packages, without downloading anything.
hist.ct6.6.dit: How many packages in your store? Count them (read-only).
hist.ct6.6.bravo: Hundreds of packages: that's what a distribution is.
hist.ct6.6.adulte: `dpkg -l` lists the packages; the "ii" lines are the installed ones.
hist.ct6.7.bravo: Installing and updating need sudo: that's for adults, not for the game.
hist.ct6.7.adulte: Updates fix security holes: we do them often, with the person who looks after the machine.
hist.ct6.8.dit: Some inhabitants never sleep: the services. List the running ones.
hist.ct6.8.bravo: Network, sound, printing… guards always ready.
hist.ct6.8.adulte: systemctl lists them without changing anything. start, stop, restart need sudo: with an adult.
hist.ct6.9.dit: Ask the Control Room what services are for.
hist.ct6.9.bravo: Started when the machine wakes up, they wait until they are needed.
hist.ct6.9.adulte: The first program started (systemd, PID 1, seen in the Gear Room) starts the services.
hist.ct6.10.dit: Who belongs to your machine's crew? The first 3 names.
hist.ct6.10.bravo: root, the captain, always comes first. The others are often accounts for services.
hist.ct6.10.adulte: /etc/passwd lists the accounts (name:x:UID:GID:…). The passwords aren't there (they are in /etc/shadow, unreadable).
hist.ct6.11.dit: Hire a new member for the CONTROL ROOM's crew: replace the ? with a name (lowercase).
hist.ct6.11.bravo: Welcome aboard! They got the next number (their UID).
hist.ct6.11.adulte: On a real machine, `sudo useradd -m name` creates an account: try it only in a virtual machine, with an adult.
hist.ct6.12.dit: Look at the end of the crew register.
hist.ct6.12.bravo: Same format as /etc/passwd: name, x, UID, GID, home, shell.
hist.ct6.12.adulte: UID 0 = root; below 1000, system accounts; from 1000 on, people.
hist.ct7.0.dit: 🚨 Alert in the Control Room! Suspicious inhabitants have appeared. Trigger the alert to see them arrive.
hist.ct7.0.bravo: Three suspects and a watchman. Read carefully who is who!
hist.ct7.0.adulte: They are processes created by the game (renamed sleeps): they only sleep, then switch off by themselves.
hist.ct7.1.dit: Find them in the list of all inhabitants: their name ends with "fictif".
hist.ct7.1.bravo: Their PID is in the 2nd column. The watchman is there too: we don't stop him!
hist.ct7.1.adulte: `ps aux | grep fictif`: the pipe keeps the lines containing "fictif". (grep's own line shows up too.)
hist.ct7.2.dit: Stop the 3 suspects with kill and their numbers (not the watchman!).
hist.ct7.2.adulte: `kill 1234 5678` sends TERM to these PIDs. We always check with ps whom we stop: on your real machine, we never stop a stranger.
hist.ct7.3.dit: Look at the dashboard: is the wave pushed back?
hist.ct7.3.bravo: Wave pushed back, watchman spared. The Control Room is calm!
hist.ct7.3.adulte: The game checks the number AND the name of its processes before saying they are stopped.
ct.meuble.consignes:
📟 CONTROL ROOM INSTRUCTIONS

Welcome to the Control Room, {nom}!

1. We LOOK at the real machine: processes, memory, disk, logs, packages, services.
2. We change NOTHING on the real machine: no sudo, nothing installed, no service stopped, no account created.
3. We only stop the game's inhabitants (their name ends with "fictif").
4. The Control Room's alarms and crew are practice files, here.
5. Whatever really changes the machine is done WITH AN ADULT.
ct.meuble.registre: # Control Room register: the game notes here what you found.
ct.sac.entete: The Control Room's backpack: read into your terminal by "source sac_a_dos.sh"
ct.reveils.entete:
The Control Room's alarms (crontab format): minute hour day month day-of-week command
The game READS them and says when they would ring; it never runs them.
ct.aide.liste:
controle consignes · habitants · jauges · entrepot NAME · path N
controle journal · alertes N · reveils · cron "M H D M W"
controle distribution NAME · familles · installer · magasin · services · useradd NAME
controle alerte · ps · arrete PID · tableau · stop
ct.habitants.dorment: sleeping: they are waiting (S, I, D)
ct.habitants.total: {n} inhabitants in all. The game counted them, it didn't copy them.
ct.habitants.raconte: Here the game can't read /proc: on Linux, it would count the inhabitants working and those sleeping.
ct.habitants.texte:
In the foreground, you wait for an inhabitant to finish. With &, it works in the background and the terminal stays free.
Ctrl+Z pauses a job, bg restarts it behind, fg brings it to the front.
ct.entrepot.aide: Weigh the crates with `du -sh entrepot/*`, then: controle entrepot NAME (without .bin).
ct.entrepot.morale: Disk full? First look for what weighs the most, and ask before throwing anything away.
ct.jauges.raconte: Here the game can't read the gauges: on Linux, it would show memory, disk and load.
ct.jauges.texte: A percentage = used × 100 ÷ total. Above 90 % of disk, or a load bigger than the number of cores, the administrator takes a closer look.
ct.path.aide: Show your PATH one folder per line, count, then: controle path N
ct.path.morale: The shell visits them in order: the first ls found wins.
ct.journal.texte:
carnet_de_bord.log: {n} lines, from the oldest (top) to the most recent (bottom).
INFO: all is well. ALERTE: something to look at.
ct.alertes.sans_journal: There's no logbook yet: first type controle journal.
ct.alertes.aide: Count the ALERTE lines with grep -c, then: controle alertes N
ct.alertes.morale: grep -c counts, tail shows the end, tail -f watches: the logs trio.
ct.reveils.texte:
* = all. 1-5 = from 1 to 5. 0,30 = 0 and 30. */15 = every 15 (0, 15, 30, 45).
This example rings Monday to Friday at 7:30.
ct.reveils.fausse: wrong line (5 fields are needed, then a command)
ct.reveils.jamais_lance: The game never runs these commands: it only says when they would ring.
ct.cron.question: The Control Room needs an alarm {situation}.
ct.cron.aide: Write the 5 fields in quotes: controle cron "M H D M W" (e.g. controle cron "0 7 * * *").
ct.cron.morale: Always read a cron line from left to right: minute, hour, day, month, day of the week.
ct.cron.cinq: Exactly 5 fields are needed: minute (0-59), hour (0-23), day (1-31), month (1-12), day of week (0-7).
ct.cron.s.premier_du_mois: on the 1st of each month at 9 a.m.
ct.distribution.aide: Read /etc/os-release (the ID= line), then: controle distribution NAME
ct.distribution.morale: Same Linux kernel, different distributions: like different recipes with the same flour.
ct.familles.lettres:
d · dnf (.rpm packages): the Fedora / Red Hat family
a · apt (.deb packages): the Debian family
p · pacman: the Arch family
ct.familles.aide: One letter per distribution, in order: controle familles d a p …
ct.familles.morale: To help someone on Linux, the first question is: "which distribution?"
ct.quiz.faux: {n} out of {total} right. Read the list again and try again!
ct.installer.texte:
1. With an adult, choose a distribution and download its image from the official website.
2. Check its fingerprint (sha256sum, as in the Guild).
3. Try it first in a VIRTUAL MACHINE (Gear Room, M5 bis): nothing gets erased.
4. On a real computer: back everything up first, because installing can erase the disk.
5. Afterwards: updates, one account per person, and root only when needed.
ct.magasin.adulte: Installing or updating (with an adult, never in the game):
ct.magasin.raconte: Here the game doesn't recognise the store: on Fedora it's dnf, on Debian and Ubuntu apt, on Arch pacman.
ct.magasin.texte: A package = a tool ready to install, signed by the distribution. The store checks the signature, installs what's needed with it, and knows how to uninstall everything.
ct.services.titre: Services: the guards who never sleep
ct.services.actifs: services running (read with systemctl, without changing anything)
ct.services.raconte: Here the game can't list the services: on Linux, systemctl would do it; on Windows, Get-Service.
ct.services.texte:
Started when the machine wakes up, they wait: network, sound, printing, time…
Starting, stopping or restarting a service needs sudo: with an adult.
ct.useradd.aide: Choose a lowercase name (letters, digits, - or _), then: controle useradd NAME
ct.useradd.texte:
This is the CONTROL ROOM's register (equipage.txt), not your machine's.
On a real machine: sudo useradd -m NAME, then sudo passwd NAME… only in a virtual machine, with an adult.
ct.ps.simule: Here the wave is simulated: stop a suspect with controle arrete PID.
ct.alerte.texte:
Find them: ps aux | grep fictif
Stop the suspects: kill PID PID PID (not the watchman!)
Then: controle tableau
ct.alerte.simulee:
Find them: controle ps
Stop the suspects: controle arrete PID (not the watchman!)
Then: controle tableau
ct.suspect.bavard_fictif: it fills the logbook with nonsense
ct.suspect.fouineur_fictif: it rummages in other people's crates
ct.suspect.bruyant_fictif: it makes the engines blow for nothing
ct.veilleur.texte: the Control Room's watchman: he does his rounds, DON'T STOP HIM
ct.arrete.aide: controle arrete PID (the number read in controle ps)
ct.arrete.inconnu: {pid} is not an inhabitant of the wave.
ct.arrete.tous: All the suspects are stopped. Look at the dashboard: controle tableau
ct.tableau.pas_de_vague: No alert going on. To trigger one: controle alerte
ct.tableau.veilleur.oui: the watchman is doing his rounds
ct.tableau.gagne: Wave pushed back, watchman spared: the Control Room is calm.
ct.stop: The game's inhabitants are stopped (only them).
ct.indice.sudo: No sudo in the Control Room: we look, we change nothing. sudo is for doing with an adult.
ct.indice.adulte: This command would change the real machine (install, stop a service, create an account, set an alarm, shut down): only with an adult. Here we practise in the playground.
ct.indice.trou: The ? are gaps to fill with your answer (read the screen)!
ct.indice.guillemets: Put the 5 fields in quotes: without them, bash replaces the * with file names.
ct.indice.veilleur: Oops, the watchman has been stopped! Start a new alert (controle alerte) and only touch the suspects.
ct.indice.pas_a_nous: This number isn't a Control Room inhabitant. Read the 2nd column of ps again: we only stop the suspects.
ct.indice.encore: {n} suspect(s) left: ps aux | grep fictif to read their numbers.
ct.indice.ajoute: Add the line TO THE FILE: put >> reveils.crontab at the end of your command.
ct.indice.export_espaces: No spaces around the =: export COULEUR=bleu (otherwise the shell thinks it's three words).
ct.indice.source: bash sac_a_dos.sh starts ANOTHER inhabitant: it loads the backpack, then leaves with it. source loads it into YOUR terminal.
ct.indice.rep.entrepot: That's not the heaviest. Read the sizes from du -sh entrepot/* again (K < M < G).
ct.indice.rep.path: That's not the right number. Count the lines: echo $PATH | tr ':' '\n' | wc -l
ct.indice.rep.cron: This alarm doesn't ring at the right time. Read again: minute, hour, day, month, day of the week.
ct.indice.rep.distribution: That's not what your machine says. Read the ID= line of /etc/os-release again.
ct.indice.rep.familles: Read the letters again: d (dnf), a (apt), p (pacman).
ct.indice.rep.useradd: A lowercase name, without spaces or accents, starting with a letter (16 characters at most).
ct.garde.adulte: This command changes the real machine: only with an adult. In the Control Room, we look.
ct.garde.kill: This number isn't one of the game's inhabitants! On your real machine, always check with ps before stopping someone.
ct.garde.kill_large: Careful: this command can stop many inhabitants at once (kill 1, kill -1, killall, pkill…). We stop one inhabitant at a time, by its number.
ct.tableau.sens.change: it changes the machine: with an adult
ct.f.processus.enfant: A process is a program that is awake and working: an inhabitant of the machine, with its number (PID).
ct.f.processus.grands: Each process has a PID, a parent, a state (R, S, D, T, Z) and its environment. /proc/PID is its mirror, made by the kernel. In the foreground the shell waits; with & it gives the prompt back (jobs, fg, bg, Ctrl+Z).
ct.f.processus.limite: The "inhabitants" aren't characters: they are lists of instructions that the processor runs in turn, very fast.
ct.f.processus.idee: "Closing the window always stops the program": not necessarily, a process can go on in the background.
ct.f.jauges.enfant: The pantry (memory), the warehouse (disk) and the engines' breath (load): the gauges the administrator watches.
ct.f.jauges.grands: free reads /proc/meminfo (MemAvailable counts the freeable cache); df gives a file system's space, du the size of files; the load average counts tasks ready or waiting for the disk, to compare with the number of cores.
ct.f.jauges.limite: A memory gauge at 100 % isn't necessarily serious: Linux fills free memory with cache, which it gives back when needed.
ct.f.jauges.idee: "The load is a percentage": no, it's a number of tasks; 2.0 on an 8-core machine is calm.
ct.f.environnement.enfant: Each inhabitant carries a backpack of variables (HOME, PATH…); PATH is the tools' address book.
ct.f.environnement.grands: Exported variables are copied into the environment of child processes, never into the parent. PATH is searched in order; source runs a file in the current shell (~/.bashrc at each new terminal).
ct.f.environnement.limite: The backpack is COPIED: if the child changes a variable, the parent doesn't see it.
ct.f.environnement.idee: "export saves the variable forever": no, it disappears with the terminal; to keep it, we write it in ~/.bashrc.
ct.f.journaux_systeme.enfant: The machine's logbook: one line per event, with the time, the most recent at the bottom.
ct.f.journaux_systeme.grands: journalctl reads the systemd journal (--user: your session), dmesg the kernel's (often root only), /var/log the classic files; tail -n, tail -f and grep -c are the basic tools.
ct.f.journaux_systeme.limite: A log only says what a program chose to write: a silent failure leaves nothing there.
ct.f.journaux_systeme.idee: "Logs are secret": often not, and they can contain personal information; we read them, we don't share them just anywhere.
ct.f.cron.enfant: cron is the programmed alarm clock: 5 fields say when (minute, hour, day, month, day of the week), then the command.
ct.f.cron.grands: Each line of a crontab: "m h dom mon dow command"; */n = the multiples of n; if day of month and day of week are both restricted, either one is enough. crontab -l lists, crontab -e edits (with an adult), systemd also offers timers.
ct.f.cron.limite: The alarm only rings if the machine is on at that moment (except anacron and some timers).
ct.f.cron.idee: "*/15 in the hours column means every 15 minutes": no, the field's position matters.
ct.f.distributions.enfant: Linux is a kernel; a distribution is everything a team puts around it to make a complete system.
ct.f.distributions.grands: /etc/os-release (ID, ID_LIKE, VERSION_ID) identifies the distribution. Families are recognised by their package format (.rpm / .deb) and their manager (dnf, apt, pacman). We install first in a virtual machine, after a backup.
ct.f.distributions.limite: Families aren't walls: a distribution can borrow from several.
ct.f.distributions.idee: "Linux is a single system": there are hundreds, with the same kernel.
ct.f.paquets.enfant: A package is a tool, wrapped and signed, stored in the distribution's store.
ct.f.paquets.grands: rpm -qa and dpkg -l read the local database of installed packages; dnf / apt / pacman download, check signatures, handle dependencies. Installing and updating need root rights.
ct.f.paquets.limite: The store doesn't have everything: some tools come from elsewhere (Flatpak, sources), with other rules.
ct.f.paquets.idee: "Updating is just for new features": above all, it fixes security holes.
ct.f.services.enfant: A service is an inhabitant that never really sleeps: a guard started at wake-up, waiting until it's needed.
ct.f.services.grands: systemd (PID 1) starts the services described by units; systemctl list-units / status show them without changing anything; start, stop, restart, enable need root rights. On Windows: Get-Service.
ct.f.services.limite: A service can stop by itself if it crashes; "active" doesn't mean "healthy".
ct.f.services.idee: "Stopping a service you don't know saves memory": you risk breaking the network, the sound or the screen.
ct.f.utilisateurs_systeme.enfant: The machine's crew: each account has a name and a number (UID); root is the captain.
ct.f.utilisateurs_systeme.grands: /etc/passwd lists name:x:UID:GID:comment:home:shell; hashed passwords are in /etc/shadow; UID 0 = root, < 1000 = system accounts. useradd creates an account (root, in a VM to practise).
ct.f.utilisateurs_systeme.limite: An account isn't necessarily a person: many are used by services.
ct.f.utilisateurs_systeme.idee: "/etc/passwd contains the passwords": not for a long time (the x points to /etc/shadow).
ct.f.poste_alerte.enfant: A wave of suspicious inhabitants: we find them with ps, read their numbers, stop them one by one with kill, without touching the watchman.
ct.f.poste_alerte.grands: kill PID sends SIGTERM (the process can finish cleanly); we always check the PID AND the name first (a number can be reused). The game's "suspects" are renamed sleeps (exec -a) that switch off by themselves.
ct.f.poste_alerte.limite: A real malicious program can hide or change its name: defence doesn't stop at ps (see the Citadel).
ct.f.poste_alerte.idee: "kill -9 right away is safer": no, -9 prevents the program from tidying up; we try TERM first.
core.win.apostrophe: In PowerShell, the apostrophe opens a text (hence the >> waiting for the rest). Put your sentence in double quotes: echo "I'm happy"
hist.ct1.t9.dit: Look at the busiest inhabitants, just once (the phone has no q key).
hist.ct1.t9.bravo: At the top: the load and the memory; below, the inhabitants working the most.
hist.ct1.t9.adulte: `top -n 1` shows a single table then stops. On the phone, an app only sees its own inhabitants.
hist.ct3.t4.dit: Put your colour in the backpack, and ask a new inhabitant for it, on the SAME line.
hist.ct3.t4.bravo: It knows it: it took the backpack along!
hist.ct3.t4.adulte: On the phone, each line goes to a new shell: export only lasts for the line. On a computer, it lasts until the terminal is closed.
hist.ct3.t8.dit: Load the Control Room's backpack and check the POSTE variable, on the same line.
hist.ct3.t8.adulte: "." means source: the file is read INSIDE the shell. On the phone, ~/.tgrc is read before each command, like a computer's ~/.bashrc.
hist.ct4.t5.dit: The phone has a logbook too: logcat. Read the last 5 lines of the app's one.
hist.ct4.t5.bravo: These are the app's own messages. We read, we copy nothing.
hist.ct4.t5.adulte: An app can only read its own log (logcat). If it refuses, the step still counts.
hist.ct6.t0.dit: Which system runs the phone? Ask for its Android version.
hist.ct6.t0.bravo: Android is a system based on the Linux kernel, with its own store and its own rules.
hist.ct6.t0.adulte: getprop reads the phone's properties (read-only). On a Linux computer, we would read /etc/os-release.
hist.ct7.t1.dit: Find them in the list of the wave's inhabitants.
hist.ct7.t1.bravo: Their PID is in the 2nd column. The watchman is there too: we don't stop him!
hist.ct7.t1.adulte: On a computer: ps aux | grep fictif. On the phone, the wave is simulated by the app.
ct.tel.simule: On the phone, the wave is simulated: controle ps, then controle arrete PID.
ct.tel.raconte: On the phone, it's told as a story: the app doesn't have {outil}.
ct.tel.sac: On the phone, each command goes to a new inhabitant: the backpack gets lost. The app's ~/.tgrc plays the role of ~/.bashrc.

ad.parent.c1: Typing by themselves is how they learn (copy-paste doesn't feed the creature).
ad.parent.c2.t: A mistake is never a problem.
ad.parent.c2: "not found" just means "I didn't understand". Nothing breaks: the game only touches its terrain_terminagotchi folder.

ad.parent.c3: They give the real technical name of each command, in case the child asks you.
ad.parent.c4.t: They can close the game any time.

ad.fermer.tel: Try it: tap ✕ at the top, then open Terminagotchi again.
